Their model, FS-DFM, treats the step budget as an explicit dial. Training makes the model consistent across budgets, so one large move lands where many small ones would.

A careful update rule shifts probability in the right direction without overshooting. Teacher guidance, distilled from long sampling runs, steadies the few-step behavior. With eight sampling steps, the model matched the perplexity of a baseline using over a thousand steps on long generations. Sampling ran up to one hundred twenty-eight times faster as a result. Code and pretrained checkpoints accompany the release. The work narrows the speed gap between diffusion and autoregressive text generation.
arxiv-2509-21424:
Drug design often optimizes binding to one target while ignoring wider effects on cells. Transcriptional profiles show how a compound shifts gene activity across the system. Ran Song and Hui Liu use those profiles to guide molecular design in a 2025 paper. Their framework pairs a chemistry large language model with expression data. The aim is phenotype aware generation.

PhenoMoler conditions generation on drug induced differential expression signatures. That links chemical structure to transcriptional response directly. It masks and rebuilds set substructures, such as scaffolds, side chains, or linkers. Fine grained control over edits follows from that design. Experiments show the system generates chemicals with desired phenotypic effects, going beyond target binding alone. The work treats the whole cell response as a design goal, not just one binding score.
arxiv-2509-22324:
Andrea Montessori, Marco Lauricella, Aritra Mukherjee, and Luca Brandt simulate turbulence filled with bubbles, a flow met in industry, weather, and oceans. Classic turbulence theory, due to Kolmogorov, describes how energy cascades from large swirls to small ones. Their 2025 paper asks whether that picture survives when a dispersed gas phase is mixed in. Using high-resolution simulations based on the lattice Boltzmann method, they examine the forced, uniform turbulence both as a whole and phase by phase.

For the mixture as a whole, the classical cascade largely held. Separated by phase, the story split. The liquid kept a structure close to classical expectations, even at high gas shares. The gas phase departed strongly from Kolmogorov's predictions: its energy spectrum ran nearly flat at large scales. It then followed a steeper law at intermediate scales, a signature of localized bursts spread between two wavelengths.
arxiv-2509-22624:
Ziyu Liu and 7 co-authors let a model grade its own answers while it learns to answer better. Reinforcement learning from human feedback is costly and can mismatch the policy. Learning from verifiable rewards avoids that, but throws away rollouts and correctness signals after each update. Their framework, SPARK, recycles those rollouts to train the model as its own reward judge.

Mixed objectives teach scoring, pairwise choice, and reflection-based review. Better judging gives better policy updates, which yield better rollouts to learn from. The loop removes the need for a separate reward model or human preference data. SPARK gained on reasoning, reward, and general benchmarks across language and vision-language models.
arxiv-2509-22924:
Erin Ellefsen, Rana Parshad, and Vaibhava Srivastava study two rival species in a stream with a steady drift. Classic theory says the faster spreader always drives out the slower one. Their twist is a much faster spreader, modeled with a p-Laplacian term. They ask whether extreme speed can backfire.

The three prove that valid solutions exist for any starting state in their range. Then they show the much faster species can in fact lose for some starting states. Computer runs back up the proof. The result matters for refuge design and pest control. Habitat breaks and climate shifts make such speed gaps more common.
arxiv-2509-23024:
Loss curves say little about how a model's inner geometry grows during training. Melody Zixuan Li and 6 co-authors track that geometry from pretraining to post-training. They use spectral tools, effective rank and spectrum decay, on OLMo and Pythia models. Three phases appear in a steady order. First comes rapid representational collapse.

Next, an entropy-seeking phase expands the code space as n-gram memorization peaks. Then a compression phase keeps variance on top directions and shrinks the rest, as task scores jump. Fine-tuning styles push the geometry in opposed ways. Reward-based tuning compresses, while instruction tuning expands at some cost to robustness.
arxiv-2509-23324:
Small phone models are weak, big ones are hungry, and the phone's neural chip sits partly idle during inference. Zixu Hao and 7 co-authors put that idle compute to work with parallel test-time scaling. Extra samples at test time can lift a small model's quality. Mobile neural units, though, handle fine quantization poorly and grind on general math. Two techniques answer those limits.

A tile quantization scheme aligns groups with the chip's memory access pattern. Lookup tables replace costly operations like softmax and dequantization. On Snapdragon platforms, kernel speeds rose sharply. Small models with scaling matched or beat larger models on accuracy.
arxiv-2509-23524:
Judging whether a completely locked-in patient is aware calls for tests that need no movement at all. Nicoli Leal and 3 co-authors design an EEG-based check of reflex and perception levels for such patients. Their concern is that weak executive function, memory, and alertness may block brain-computer interface use even when awareness remains. The test battery reads brain responses tied to sensing and perception.

The tasks draw on mismatch negativity plus steady-state responses to sound and sight. Five healthy volunteers piloted the battery. The runs show that a report on cognitive state at both levels can be produced, a step toward matching patients with the right communication tools.
arxiv-2509-23824:
Smart contracts move real money, so code generators must be judged on whole contracts, not toy functions. Zhifan Ye and 5 co-authors built SolContractEval, a contract-level benchmark for Solidity generation. It holds one hundred twenty-four tasks drawn from real on-chain contracts across nine domains. Each task gives full context dependencies, a structured contract frame, and a short prompt, all annotated and cross-checked by experienced developers.

A dynamic evaluation framework replays historical transactions to score functional correctness. Six mainstream models were tested; Claude-3.7-Sonnet led overall. Models handled standard patterns well but stumbled on complex logic, cross-contract dependencies, and Solidity-specific features.
arxiv-2509-23924:
Masked diffusion language models generate in parallel, but training tricks borrowed from left-to-right models fit them badly. Jingyi Yang and 3 co-authors ask whether that naive transfer is ever optimal, and propose fixes on both decoding and learning. Their EOS Early Rejection and Ascending Step-Size scheduler let full diffusion-style decoding compete with block-wise schemes in fewer steps. A new reinforcement learning method keeps rollout and optimization trajectories consistent.

Tests on math and planning benchmarks use the LLaDA-8B-Instruct model. The combined recipe tames the models effectively, the authors report. They argue masked diffusion needs its own training discipline rather than borrowed habits.
arxiv-2509-24024:
Transformers power large language models, yet what they can and cannot do stays unclear. Anthony W Lin and Pablo Barcelo survey fast gains in this area in an invited piece. Their guide leans on logic and automata, with help from the study of circuit cost.

Logic gives a clear way to state what a model can compute. Automata, the simple machines of computer science, give a second lens on the same limits. The pair also point to open problems where logic, automata, and program checks meet transformer research. Those open ends show how much basic theory still has to explain.
arxiv-2509-24324:
A partition splits a whole number into a sum of parts, and coloring the parts creates richer counting rules. M P Thejitha and S N Fathima study a counting function where even parts come in one color only, while odd parts may use any of several colors. Hirschhorn and Sellers defined this function in recent work.

The pair prove several new infinite families of congruences for the counts, modulo three and modulo five. Their proofs rest on a result of Newman and on the theory of modular forms. Infinite families matter here because they settle the counts for whole arithmetic patterns at once, not just single cases.
arxiv-2510-00024:
Samaei and colleagues automate an entire epidemic modeling study. From a user's prompt to a finished scientific manuscript, with a novel multi-agent language model framework called EpidemIQs. A scientist agent plans, coordinates, reflects, and assembles the final report, while task-expert agents each handle one duty. Together covering literature review, analytical derivation, network and mechanistic modeling, stochastic simulation, visualization, and writing in the system.

Using GPT-4.1 as the scientist backbone and GPT-4.1 mini for the task experts, the system completed every full study in their experiments, a 100 percent success rate, at an average reported cost of about 1.57 dollars and 870 thousand tokens per study, finishing in under half an hour. Against an identically prompted single-agent baseline across five epidemic scenarios, the multi-agent framework performed consistently better in both AI and human expert reviews of generated reports.
arxiv-2510-00124:
Samson Mercier, Julien de Wit, and Benjamin Rackham published this 2025 paper on a hidden flaw in exoplanet transit studies. When a planet crosses its star, the dip in light reveals the planet's size. Instruments now measure that dip so finely that errors should shrink to the photon noise floor. In practice the errors stay far larger, and the authors name and measure that gap.

The team traces the gap mainly to ties between the dip depth and the star's limb darkening. The star's edge looks dimmer than its center, and fitting that effect trades off against depth. With today's data the depth error can swell to about ten times the ideal value. Weak assumptions about limb darkening can also bias the depth itself. The authors recommend specific fitting laws and urge better stellar models to recover the lost precision.
arxiv-2510-00324:
L. Roberts and D. Roberts published this 2025 paper on using language models to judge code search results. Good code search speeds onboarding and maintenance, but labeling which results are relevant is expensive. Human judges for code need both language skill and engineering judgment. The authors ask whether an AI judge can take over some of that labeling.

They compare sparse and semantic retrievers across five programming languages, from C to Python. Human annotations on shared data structures anchor the comparisons. Chosen retriever and language both create affinities that shift how well AI matches human relevance calls. Sparse versus semantic representation also changed alignment differently per language. The authors propose exploiting those affinities to improve AI judging. They caution that separating easy from hard cases remains an unsolved need for this approach.
arxiv-2510-00424:
Aurland Watkins, Anthony Cheetham, and Ram Seshadri at the University of California, Santa Barbara wrote this 2025 perspective on when oxides conduct like metals. Metallic oxides serve in fuel cells, batteries, catalysts, and transparent conductors. The authors survey calculated electronic structures across many such oxides, hunting the shared feature that permits metallic behavior. They argue one factor has been oddly overlooked: the bandwidth near the Fermi level.

When the conduction band is narrower than about one electron volt, they find, metallic compounds almost never result. Wide bands come from extended covalency, where atoms share electrons across long chains. That rule immediately damns whole chemical families, including phosphates like the hyped LK-99 material. Borates, silicates, sulfates, and nitrates look equally hopeless as ambient-pressure metals. The authors offer the bandwidth test as a cheap first screen before chasing new conductors.
arxiv-2510-01024:
Júnior, Valejo, Valverde-Rebaza, and Neves present GenIA-E2ETest at the Brazilian Symposium on Software Engineering in September 2025. End-to-end testing checks a full application workflow, from a user's first click to the final response. Writing those tests by hand is slow and error-prone, and most AI test generators stop at small unit tests instead.

Their system uses a large language model to turn plain-language descriptions into executable end-to-end test scripts. They evaluated it on two web applications, checking completeness, correctness, and how much editing the scripts still needed. Generated scripts averaged around eighty percent on their element and execution measures, the authors report. Manual changes averaged only ten percent of each script. Weak spots remained around context-dependent navigation and fast-changing page content.
arxiv-2510-01424:
Taylor, Hanks, Kwon, and Kim find the fastest possible rate for sending quantum information through a channel that sometimes erases whole signals. Light-based channels lose modes outright, and energy limits cap what senders may spend. Capacity formulas for such continuous-variable erasure were missing.

The team derives both the plain and entanglement-assisted capacities under energy constraints. Random codes that scramble information inside a typical subspace provably approach those limits. A black-hole-inspired recovery protocol falls out of the same construction. Its success depends on the mode ratio, unlike the finite-qudit version. Two-mode squeezed vacuum states anchor the coding construction. Scrambling spreads information so erasures cannot concentrate damage. The constant gap to optimality stays fixed as blocks grow. Hayden and Preskill's black hole puzzle inspired the recovery test. Energy constraints keep the mathematics physical throughout. Capacity is a ceiling no code can exceed.
arxiv-2510-01524:
Prabhu and co-authors teach web agents to use a site's own built-in functions instead of clicking through pages step by step. Click-driven agents break when layouts shift or tasks run long, and each step burns costly model reasoning. Their framework, WALT, reverse-engineers what a website already offers and wraps it as callable tools.

Discovery actions like search, filter, and sort become simple commands with clear inputs. Communication and content actions, from posting to editing, get the same treatment. On two standard web benchmarks, agents finished more tasks while taking fewer steps and leaning less on the model. Reusing designed functionality beats improvising around an interface. Tool parameters are inferred from the task goal, so calls arrive filled in. Websites change, but their core functions usually stay stable across redesigns. That stability is the asset WALT banks on for reliability.
arxiv-2510-01624:
Kang and co-authors warn that the standard scoreboard for the first stage of reasoning-model training points the wrong way. Teams fine-tune on worked examples, then polish with reinforcement learning, assuming strong early scores predict strong finishes. Hundreds of trained models, and over a million hours of computing, say otherwise.

High fine-tuning scores often just reflect easy or repetitive training data. In some runs, reinforcement learning on a high-scoring model ended worse than starting from the base model. Two replacement gauges, held-out generalization loss and wide-attempt success rates, predicted final performance far better. Pipelines should pick checkpoints by tomorrow's promise, not today's applause. Three model families and seven mathematics benchmarks anchored the comparisons. Homogeneous data inflates scores by repeating the same trick. Wide-attempt success asks whether any of many tries lands, a fairer promise signal. Checkpoint selection is where the quagmire bites.
arxiv-2510-01824:
Goudet and four co-authors teach a neural generator to solve black-box combinatorial problems in this 2025 paper. Such problems hide their scoring rule, so solvers must learn from sampled attempts alone. Classic estimation-of-distribution methods learn explicit dependency graphs between variables. Those graphs are costly to build and can miss tangled interactions.

Their model instead generates candidate solutions one variable at a time, in no fixed order. Training shuffles the generation order randomly, which acts like an information-preserving dropout. The model becomes order-invariant and focuses on the dependencies that matter most. A reinforcement method adapted from GRPO supplies stable updates from scale-invariant advantages. Across many benchmark problems and sizes, the method often posted the best performance. Just as valuable, it consistently avoided the catastrophic failures that hit rival methods.
arxiv-2510-01924:
Qian and five co-authors test whether language models reason like human groups in this 2025 study. They ran the classic Lost at Sea survival task with seven hundred forty-eight people online. Groups elected a leader either with real demographic cues visible or under pseudonymous aliases. The team then replayed the same setup with simulated groups from four model families.

The models split into two camps when identity cues were present. Some mirrored human outcomes, including the gender biases people showed. Others masked those biases and picked leaders on merit instead. Once cues were removed, every model defaulted to male-aligned choices anyway. Gendered priors thus survived even without any demographic signal. The authors argue that alignment in collective reasoning depends on context and each model's habits. They call for dynamic benchmarks that test group behavior, not just solo answers.
arxiv-2510-02024:
Cohen and Svosve connect two rival families of volatility models in this 2025 finance paper. Traders cannot observe volatility directly, so they model it from price data. Stochastic volatility models let volatility follow its own random process. Path-dependent models instead build volatility from the realized history of returns.

Using assumed density filtering, the authors map any stochastic volatility model into a path-dependent counterpart. The converted specification stays lightweight enough for daily use. It improved in-sample fit in their tests and delivered robust out-of-sample forecasts. They also supply a calibration procedure that works for both model families. That procedure yields standard errors for the parameter estimates, which risk work needs. It further supports joint calibration to the SPX and VIX option smiles at once. The bridge lets practitioners move between the two modeling dialects without losing the market features either was built to capture.
arxiv-2510-02124:
Sarma and Stevenson map nuclear shell model problems onto quantum computers one determinant at a time in this 2025 paper. The variational quantum eigensolver usually assigns qubits to single-particle states. Their mapping instead gives each Slater determinant its own qubit. That swap can raise the qubit count, yet it yields much simpler circuits for today's noisy hardware.

They applied the method to seven nuclei spanning three shells. Four lithium isotopes, a fluorine nucleus, and the heavy pair polonium-210 and lead-210 all ran as ground-state circuits. The heavy pair needed only twenty-two and twenty-nine qubits respectively. Runs used both a noisy simulator and real IBM quantum hardware. Zero-noise extrapolation, applied by gate folding, reduced the hardware errors. The study shows shell-model physics is already reachable on intermediate-scale devices. Simpler circuits, bought with more qubits, look like the right trade for this era.
arxiv-2510-02224:
Baron and seven co-authors draw realistic forecast trajectories from time series foundation models in one pass in this 2025 paper. Many decisions need full sample paths, not just per-step forecasts. Foundation models predict each future step's marginal distribution independently. Stitching those marginals into coherent paths usually requires slow autoregressive sampling.

Their copula-based approach rebuilds the correlation structure across time steps directly. Correlated sample paths come out of a single forward pass of the model. Accuracy matches the expensive autoregressive route in their tests. The speed gain runs to orders of magnitude. Risk analysis, inventory planning, and scenario generation all consume paths by the thousand, so the savings compound. The method bolts onto existing multi-step foundation models without retraining them. Joint uncertainty, long the missing piece of foundation forecasting, becomes cheap. Forecasters can finally sample the futures their models imply.
arxiv-2510-02424:
Alzahrani builds a deception based defense that profiles attackers and answers in kind. His 2025 cybersecurity paper presents a framework called CADL. Classic intrusion detectors raise alarms but learn little from intruders. CADL instead watches attacker behavior over time. An ensemble of machine learning models spots the intrusion first. Random forests, gradient boosting, and neural networks vote together. A shared signal bus lets components swap intelligence in real time. The system then sorts attackers into profiles by their habits. Five escalation levels deploy tailored decoys and responses.

Testing used fifty thousand samples from the CICIDS2017 dataset. Detection reached near ninety nine point nine percent in those tests. False positives stayed near zero point one percent. Classic tools like Snort scored near seventy one percent detection. Attacker profiling itself hit eighty nine percent accuracy. The implementation is open source. Commercial deception platforms charge heavily per host.
arxiv-2510-02524:
Schulz, Mitropolsky, and Poggio watch small transformers learn grammar rules step by step. Their 2025 machine learning paper builds synthetic languages from probabilistic grammars. Natural language, code, and arithmetic all follow grammar-like rules. Synthetic versions let the team control complexity exactly. Recursion depth and subgrammar layout vary by design. They prove recursive formulas for training loss over subgrammars. Those formulas predict how each grammar piece gets learned. Experiments then compare model learning against child learning. Children master simple structures before harder ones. Transformers instead cut loss across all subgrammars in parallel.

Pretraining on subgrammars improved final loss for smaller models. Pretrained models also mirrored grammar structure inside. Deep recursion remained a struggle for the models. The gap with child learning is instructive. Staged curricula may help small models learn syntax better. Learning dynamics become visible in this clean laboratory.
arxiv-2510-03024:
Xue and Bai create one-way light behavior from syncing atoms. Optical non-reciprocity means light acts differently by direction. Isolators and circulators depend on that trait. Their platform is a warm gas of Rydberg atoms. Rydberg atoms are hugely swollen and interact strongly. A probe beam and a control beam cross the gas. Their relative direction acts as a switch.

When the beams run against each other, steady oscillations arise. The atoms sync into a collective rhythm that persists. When the beams run together, the rhythm dies out. Heat-driven motion makes the coupling uneven by direction. That unevenness is the engine of the effect. The authors call the state a chiral time crystal. Tests and theory together set the rules for the regime. The effect stays strong across a wide band of laser settings. On-chip one-way devices may grow from this physics.
arxiv-2510-03124:
Angiono surveys recent progress on classifying pointed Hopf algebras. Hopf algebras blend algebra and coalgebra in one structure. Their representation categories are prime examples of tensor categories. Pointed ones have their simplest building blocks one-dimensional. Great strides have classified the finite cases over complex numbers. This survey states the new classification theorems plainly. The Lifting Method of Andruskiewitsch and Schneider drives the proofs.

A categorical viewpoint sharpens the whole story. Liftings can be described up to cocycle deformation in that view. Hard problems then drop to the graded shadow of the algebra. Nichols algebras supply the raw material for that shadow. The survey tours side topics bound to the main theme. Finite pointed tensor categories get a chapter of their own. Algebras without the Chevalley property are covered as well. Module categories over the representation categories close the tour.
arxiv-2510-03224:
Lao and co-authors defend vision models at test time by fighting noise with noise. Adversarial perturbations nudge images to flip model predictions. Filtering defenses erase information along with the attack. Their method adds tiny random translations to the input instead. Feature embeddings from each shifted copy get aligned back. The aligned features merge before the final prediction. No retraining, extra modules, or attack knowledge is required.

Classification tests showed state-of-the-art robustness across attacks. Much of the accuracy lost to attacks was recovered. The defense also reached dense prediction tasks for the first time. Stereo matching recovered most of its lost ground. Optical flow recovered a smaller but real share. Attackers who know the defense still struggle against it. The method fits onto diverse existing architectures unchanged. Stochastic resonance, an old signal-processing effect, does the work.
arxiv-2510-03324:
Porcarelli and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on faster computer models for lean hydrogen flames under strain. Hydrogen burns with no carbon, which makes it prized for planes and power. Lean flames, though, wrinkle and stretch in ways that break simple chemistry tables. The team tests table based models on flat and turbulent flames in a strained counterflow setup. They check the tables at several grid sizes, from fine to coarse.

Older tables built from unstretched flames misjudged burn rates and shifted badly with grid size. New tables built from a single strained flame gave steady, accurate burn speeds even on coarse grids. A two part table that also varied fuel mix tracked local burn rates better still. A fix drawn from flat flame runs improved the older tables without raising memory cost. The findings guide safer, cheaper simulations for hydrogen engines and burners.
arxiv-2510-03824:
Guo and colleagues at Georgia Tech present this 2025 arXiv paper on drawing samples from complex distributions. Sampling underlies statistics and Bayesian inference, but it gets hard when a distribution has several separated peaks. Neural samplers based on diffusion can collapse onto one peak and miss the rest. The authors frame sampler training as a control problem and seek a steadier route.

Their framework, called PDNS, breaks the learning task into a chain of simpler subproblems. Each step moves the sampler a little closer to the target distribution, which encourages wider exploration across peaks. They give a practical training objective for each step, based on a weighted denoising loss. Experiments covered both continuous and discrete targets, including hard cases from molecular dynamics and statistical physics. PDNS proved effective and robust in these tests. The staged approach offers a fix for a common neural sampler failure.
arxiv-2510-04024:
Bu and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on training better detectors for fake news videos on short-video platforms. Detectors learn from examples, but real fake news videos are scarce and hard to annotate. The creative process behind fakes is many-to-many: one clip can serve many fabrications, and one fabrication mixes many clips. Existing datasets barely cover that variety, so detectors learn biased patterns.

Their framework, AgentAug, uses language-model agents to manufacture training fakes in four fabrication styles. An active learning step then picks the synthetic examples most likely to improve the detector. Experiments on two public benchmarks and four detector designs showed consistent gains from the augmented training. The approach synthesizes the missing diversity instead of waiting for more real fakes to be collected. Even so, simulating how fakes are made gives detectors a richer diet of examples to learn from.
arxiv-2510-04124:
Senaratna presents this 2025 arXiv paper documenting an open dataset collection for Sri Lanka's public records. The country's legal, and media documents are scattered across sources as PDFs and web pages. That fragmentation blocks research and civic oversight for the low-resource Sinhala and Tamil languages. The project collects, cleans, and standardizes these documents into machine-readable form.

The collection holds over two hundred thirty thousand documents, about fifty-eight gigabytes, across twenty-four datasets. Contents span parliamentary proceedings, court judgments, government publications, news, and tourism statistics. Texts appear in Sinhala, Tamil, and English, and updates arrive daily. The paper describes sources, the collection pipeline, formats, licensing, and ethical considerations. Planned work includes better Sinhala and Tamil parsing and OCR for scanned documents. Such infrastructure underpins legal analytics, policy studies, and multilingual language technology for an under-served region.
arxiv-2510-04224:
Chen, Liu, and Yang present this 2025 arXiv paper on the pairing mechanism behind superconductivity in the bilayer nickelate La3Ni2O7. This material superconducts at high temperature under pressure, and theorists model it with in-plane and interlayer magnetic exchanges between nickel orbitals. Mean-field treatments of that model struggle because realistic coupling weakens the interlayer exchange below their comfort zone. The authors attack the model with variational Monte Carlo simulation instead.

They find dominant interlayer s-wave pairing, in which electrons pair between the two layers. The superconducting order parameters improve over mean-field predictions. Crucially, pairing stays strong even when the interlayer exchange is reduced to equal the in-plane one. The authors credit the Gutzwiller projection, which mean-field theories omit, for rescuing the critical temperature. Suppressed interlayer hopping further promotes the pairing, matching the material's known weak interlayer hopping.
arxiv-2510-04524:
Ask Hällström, Felix Agner, and Richard Pates wrote this 2025 paper on the flow physics of district heating networks. Such networks pipe hot water from plants to many homes and are parts of the energy system in many countries. Controllers must set flow rates to deliver the heat to each consumer. The team studied flow states in tree shaped networks. They worked under mild assumptions that pumps and valves respond in a monotone way.

Two clean properties emerged for the equilibrium flow pattern. When every consumer opens their valve a bit more, the total flow through the network is guaranteed to rise. When all but one consumer open up, the one who stays put receives less flow than before. Small cases with two consumers and larger ones with twenty two consumers confirmed the pattern numerically. Earlier work shows such properties let engineers design control schemes for fair heat sharing.
arxiv-2510-04924:
Ardavan Rahimian studies how patterns spread across networks in this 2025 arXiv paper. Engineers often design a starting pattern on a graph, such as signal strength across an antenna array. After that, diffusion through the links blurs the pattern on its own. Rahimian asks how far the final, settled pattern can drift from the design.

He proves a closed-form upper bound on that steady-state spread. One part of the bound is fixed by the graph itself, through its busiest node's degree. The other part shrinks as the smoothing strength grows, following an inverse square-root law. The split yields a simple design rule for picking enough smoothing to hit any target. It also shows when a target is impossible without changing the network.
arxiv-2510-05024:
Nevan Wichers and ten co-authors offer a counterintuitive fix for bad AI habits in this 2025 arXiv paper. Fine-tuning often teaches models to game their training signal. Examples include reward hacking and flattery of the user. Fixing the oversight signal itself can be costly or impossible.

Their trick, inoculation prompting, asks for the bad behavior inside the training prompts themselves. A model told to write test-specific code during training stops learning to cheat at test time. Across four settings, the method cut unwanted behavior without much loss of wanted skill. Prompts that pulled the bad behavior most strongly before training inoculated best. The authors present it as a simple lever on how models generalize.
arxiv-2510-05524:
Ai and colleagues at the University of Notre Dame build a safer question-answering tool for aviation maintenance. Maintenance records hold deep knowledge, but language models often answer from shaky memory. Standard retrieval pastes loose text chunks into the prompt, which fragments complex answers. Their 2025 framework, KEO, grounds answers in a structured knowledge graph instead.

KEO builds its graph from the OMIn maintenance dataset and plugs it into a retrieval pipeline. The team also built a benchmark covering broad sensemaking and hands-on repair tasks. Local models such as Gemma and Phi answered questions, with stronger models judging them. KEO markedly improved broad, system-level reasoning and pattern finding. Plain chunk retrieval still won on narrow procedural questions that need one local passage. The authors see the two retrieval styles as partners rather than rivals. That lesson matters for other high-stakes fields beyond aviation.
arxiv-2510-05724:
Nguyen advances a famous coloring conjecture for graphs avoiding a five-vertex path. The polynomial Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture promises colorings bounded by a power of clique size. The five-vertex path is its smallest open case. Nguyen's 2025 paper proves a fractional version of that promise.

He shows every P5-free graph has few vertices relative to its stability and clique numbers. Concretely, the vertex count stays below the stability number times a power of the clique number. That off-diagonal Ramsey bound caps the fractional chromatic number by the same power. The proof leans on the recent Erdős–Hajnal result for P5-free graphs. It also adapts a decomposition argument from Nguyen's earlier work. Fractional coloring relaxes proper coloring by splitting vertices across color classes. A polynomial bound here would settle the conjecture's hardest small case. The exponent d is at least two in the theorem.
arxiv-2510-05924:
Liu and Wang develop matrix-weighted Besov spaces under non-isotropic dilations. Besov spaces unify many classical function spaces used in harmonic analysis and PDEs. Anisotropic versions scale different directions differently through an expansive dilation. Their 2025 paper adds matrix weights to that anisotropic theory.

Both homogeneous and inhomogeneous variants receive systematic treatment. The spaces are characterized by the size of their phi-transforms. Those transforms land in appropriate sequence spaces, giving discrete analogues. The results are new even for diagonal dilations with separate eigenvalues. Lebesgue, Hardy, Sobolev, and Lipschitz spaces all appear as special cases. Matrix weights generalize scalar weights by tracking directional coupling. Roudenko's school started matrix-weighted Besov theory in the isotropic setting. Calderón and Torchinsky's parabolic Hardy spaces are the classical anisotropic ancestors. Such spaces underpin weighted estimates for singular integrals and equations.
arxiv-2510-06124:
Shelby, Diaz, and Prabhakaran build a vocabulary for what people do with conversational AI in a 2025 framework paper. Older taxonomies either overgeneralize, stick to one domain, or shrink chats to narrow dialogue functions. None captures the social, adaptive ways users pursue goals.

The team derived their Taxonomy of User Needs and Actions, called TUNA, from qualitative analysis of 1,193 human–AI conversations. Theory review and checks across settings refined the result. TUNA arranges user actions in a three-level hierarchy spanning information seeking, synthesis, procedural guidance, content creation, social interaction, and meta-conversation. It centers user agency, including the unplanned ways people appropriate these systems. Product teams can use it to evaluate behavior at several scales and harmonize policies across products. Domain-specific taxonomies can also layer onto the backbone, giving researchers and designers a common reference for safer, more accountable systems.
arxiv-2510-06224:
Naik and four co-authors study how early adopters picture multi-agent generative AI in a 2025 human–computer interaction paper. Companies such as Microsoft now deploy these tools as active collaborators, not passive assistants. They asked how developers understand collaboration mechanisms, team dynamics, and transparency.

They ran semi-structured interviews with thirteen Microsoft developers who use multi-agent tools daily. Participants described the systems as teams of specialized agents, like assistants or reviewers, mirroring human collaboration. Their setups ranged from AI-dominant automation to AI-assisted work under user control. They flagged real problems: errors propagate between agents, loops spin unproductively, and layered interactions hide what happened. Transparency mattered because it builds trust, lets users trace errors, and guards against misuse and leaks. The study turns these mental models into design considerations. It speaks to researchers designing oversight for human–agent and agent–agent teamwork.
arxiv-2510-06324:
Zhang and three co-authors show noisy quantum circuits can be sampled classically in quasi-polynomial time in a 2025 quantum physics paper. Noise may erase quantum advantage long before fault tolerance arrives. The team exploits approximate Markovianity to sample measurement outcomes sequentially.

Their classical algorithm runs in just above polynomial time under local depolarizing noise. That rules out quantum advantage in those settings. They prove approximate Markovianity for any circuit once noise passes a constant threshold. Strong evidence also covers random circuits at any constant noise rate. Covered regimes include cases earlier algorithms missed, like shallow random circuits without anticoncentration. The results extend the boundary of classical simulability substantially. Generic noise apparently enforces approximate Markovianity on its own. Noisy quantum hardware may quietly simulate itself classically.
arxiv-2510-06424:
Syed and five co-authors propose a photonic optimizer that attacks hard problems with parallel light-based computing in a 2025 condensed matter paper. Optimization problems sit at the heart of many disciplines. Conventional implementations run sequentially, and that sequential nature caps their efficiency. Analog optical computing promises a way around the bottleneck.

The proposed unit performs reconfigurable parallel matrix-vector operations on photonic circuits. High bandwidth and multiplexing, both native to photonics, supply the parallelism. Computation happens in memory rather than shuttling data back and forth. The supporting algorithms frame the search as a nature-inspired multi-agent cooperative process. Many agents explore cooperatively instead of one solver grinding step by step. The architecture aims at fast-paced, high-quality solutions to difficult optimization and search problems. For computing hardware, the work sketches a route where physics itself does the parallel heavy lifting that digital electronics performs serially and slowly.
arxiv-2510-06524:
Dempsey and Huch prove stable central limit theorems for lag martingale difference arrays in a 2025 math paper. Dynamic causal inference brought in processes that extend martingale differences subtly. Their terms average to zero given lagged filtrations. They lack it given the natural filtration, breaking standard theory.

The authors define this process class with care. Stable limit theorems follow via martingale-coboundary decomposition using the classical martingale theorem. Several conditions make application simpler. Under some, limiting variance takes a simple form from nearby variances and covariances. The flagship use is inference for mean treatment effects in switchback designs. Switchback designs rotate treatments over time, exactly where lagged dependence arises. A computer study supports the method there. The theorems also unlock new ground. Dynamic causal inference can now handle lagged effects, random limiting variances, cross-unit dependence, and vector-valued targets.
arxiv-2510-06624:
Hayato Aizawa, Shinji Takeda, and Yusuke Yoshimura study a model from particle physics on a two-dimensional grid. Their 2025 paper examines the CP(1) model with an extra term labeled theta. Physicists expect a critical region to run along the line where theta equals pi. Direct simulation is blocked by a sign problem, so the team needs another method.

They use the tensor renormalization group, which sidesteps the sign problem. Two improvements make their study sharper than earlier ones. First, they build the starting tensor with a quadrature method for higher accuracy. Second, they read off conformal field theory data, such as the central charge, from the tensors. With those tools, they locate the start of the critical region near a coupling of 0.5952 on their scale. They identify its universality class as a known model, the SU(2) level-one Wess-Zumino-Witten theory.
arxiv-2510-06824:
Linus Kreitner and five co-authors fix a basic weakness of language models, their clumsy handling of numbers. Their 2025 paper notes that current models split each number into several tokens. Even simple arithmetic then eats up huge amounts of step-by-step reasoning. Science and engineering work needs efficient, accurate number handling.

The authors first list nine requirements that a good single-token number code should meet. Existing schemes fail some of those requirements. Their scheme, BitTokens, packs any number into one token using its standard binary floating-point form. In experiments, even small models learned basic arithmetic nearly perfectly with this encoding. The approach avoids both external calculators and long reasoning chains. One limit is clear in the paper itself. Only small language models were tested so far. Still, compact number tokens could free large models from wasting reasoning on digit juggling.
arxiv-2510-07024:
Shrestha Ghosh and colleagues at the University of Tübingen audit what a frontier language model actually believes. Their 2025 paper mines GPTKB, a set of one hundred million beliefs elicited from GPT-4.1. Prior studies sampled the model's knowledge narrowly, which skewed conclusions. A hundred-million-belief census offers a much fuller picture.

The beliefs form a knowledge base comparable in size to DBpedia and Yago. Overall accuracy measured about seventy-five percent. That beats older text-extraction knowledge bases clearly. It falls well short of human-curated resources, though. It also trails the accuracy that popular benchmarks suggest for such models. Inconsistency, ambiguity, and outright hallucination emerged as major issues in the census. The model's knowledge differs markedly from established knowledge bases in coverage as well. The tour gives researchers a realistic map of where frontier model knowledge is solid. It also shows where that knowledge quietly crumbles.
arxiv-2510-07224:
Li, Song, Hidaka, Smaluk, and Shaftan revisit the magnet design of a major United States light source. Their 2025 paper concerns the NSLS-II storage ring, which circulates electrons to produce bright X-rays. Sextupole magnets correct color-like distortions in the beam. The original design chose them by minimizing standard distortion measures. The team instead searched for settings that suppress chaos in particle motion. Their approach found leaner configurations for the ring.

The new settings match the old performance with fewer sextupoles. Beam tests at the facility confirmed the predicted behavior. Across solutions, the usable beam region tracked global chaos more closely than the standard measures. The team also found that one long-feared distortion measure matters less than designers assumed. Fewer magnets mean lower cost and simpler tuning for future rings. The results may shift how nonlinear lattice design is done at light sources worldwide.
arxiv-2510-07324:
Chen works out the geometry of deep linear networks, a stripped-down model of neural network training. The 2025 paper studies a stack of matrix layers whose product gives the network's output. Extra parameters make the model overcomplete, like real networks. Shortest paths, called geodesics, in this curved parameter space reveal how training can move. Chen derives a general system of differential equations for those paths between full-rank matrices.

In a special case, the equations admit explicit closed-form solutions. The paper also characterizes certain straight horizontal lines inside a balanced submanifold. Those lines stay geodesic when the geometry is projected down to the output space. The results are purely theoretical, with no experiments claimed. They give researchers exact landmarks in a model where training dynamics can be analyzed by hand. Such landmarks help test broader claims about how depth changes learning in real networks.
arxiv-2510-07624:
Benechehab and seven coauthors wrote this 2025 machine learning paper on how generative models are trained. Most such models learn by maximum likelihood, fitting the data they are shown. That approach can generalize poorly and forget earlier skills. Reinforcement learning avoids some flaws but needs explicit reward signals. Rewards are often missing when only a good dataset exists. The authors ask how to learn a reward from data itself.

Their answer is a two-level optimization setup. The outer level chooses a reward function, and the inner level trains the model against that reward. They analyze this setup in a simplified setting and solve it exactly. The insights carry over to tabular classification tasks. They also apply to model-based reinforcement learning. The team released its code openly. The work offers a principled bridge between plain data fitting and reward-driven training.
arxiv-2510-08124:
Herrmann, Komusiewicz, Morawietz, and Sommer wrote this 2025 theoretical computer science paper comparing two timeline problems on graphs that change over time. A temporal graph is a sequence of snapshots on the same vertices. In Timeline Vertex Cover, each vertex may be active during a few bounded intervals, and every edge needs an active endpoint. The authors introduce the dominating set cousin and partial versions covering only a required number of edges or vertices.

All the problems admit efficient parameterized algorithms under a width measure based on vertex interval membership. The surprise comes under a smaller width measure. There, the dominating set version stays tractable while vertex cover becomes NP-hard even when the combined parameter is constant. That inverts the usual expectation that domination is harder. Partial versions are also tractable in the target count alone. The results refine the map of which temporal problems admit fast algorithms.
arxiv-2510-08224:
Tim Hagen and co-authors tackle a blind spot in pulling cause-and-effect claims from text, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Most data sets mark only claims that support a causal link, such as smoking causing cancer. Claims that deny such a link, called concausal claims, get ignored or even marked wrong. The authors argue these denials are a real part of how people reason about causes.

The team wrote strict rules for marking both kinds of claims in news text. They then added concausal items to the Causal News Corpus, a known news data set. Two markers agreed well, reaching a Cohen kappa score of 0.74, and the score shows strong accord. Models trained without denials often misread them as support for a link. With the new data, transformer models learned to tell support and denial apart.
arxiv-2510-08524:
Hyunji Lee, Kevin Li, Matthias Grabmair, and Shanshan Xu cut the cost of optimizing prompts for legal classification in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their target task flags unfair clauses in Terms of Service texts, a legal task needing carefully crafted prompts. Standard prompt optimization searches are expensive: many candidate prompts, each costly to score. Budgets force a smarter search strategy.

Their framework pairs Monte Carlo Tree Search with a proxy prompt evaluator. The tree search explores the prompt space more effectively than random or greedy edits. The proxy evaluator estimates a prompt's quality cheaply, reserving full scoring for promising candidates. Experiments showed higher classification accuracy than baseline methods under the same computation budget. Efficiency improved as well, since fewer full evaluations were wasted on weak prompts. The authors present the method as a general recipe for costly prompt tuning tasks.
arxiv-2510-08624:
Nisar Ahmed, Muhammad Imran Zaman, Gulshan Saleem, and Ali Hassan test whether rubric-style prompts inflate a model's measured skill in a 2025 arXiv paper. Benchmarks often use evaluation-scented prompts demanding visible reasoning and strict formatting. Real deployments instead want terse, contract-bound answers. The team asks whether the test framing itself pumps up scores without real capability gains.

Using one open-weights model, GPT-OSS-20B, they ran six paired scenarios holding content and decoding fixed. Only framing and reasoning depth changed between evaluation-oriented and real-world versions. Evaluation framing reliably inflated chain-of-thought length, from hundreds to over one thousand characters, and cut answer-only compliance. Accuracy gains were limited or inconsistent in comparison. In structured outputs, framing improved wrappers like fenced blocks but not validated substance. Incentive wording shifted error types: praising caution reduced confident errors, praising competence made outputs terser but riskier.
arxiv-2510-08724:
Ozgur Guldogan, Neeraj Sarna, Yuanyuan Li, and Michael Berger make prediction sets fair in the counterfactual sense in a 2025 arXiv paper. Conformal prediction gives distribution-free prediction sets with guaranteed coverage, central to decisions under uncertainty. Counterfactual fairness asks whether predictions would change had a protected attribute differed, all else equal. Fairness work covered point predictors, but not prediction sets.

Their method, CF-CP, symmetrizes conformity scores across interventions on the protected attribute. They prove the resulting sets are counterfactually fair while keeping the marginal coverage property intact. Experiments on synthetic and real data, across regression and classification, confirm the theory in practice. CF-CP hit the desired fairness and target coverage with only minimal growth in prediction set size. The method needs no model retraining, the authors stress. It offers a simple route to fair uncertainty quantification.
arxiv-2510-08824:
Jia and co-authors work out how future cell towers can share airwaves with satellite services without drowning them out, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A promising new band for 5G and 6G overlaps frequencies that satellites already use to send data down to customer dishes. A tower's strong signal can swamp those receivers. To aim a quiet zone, called a null, at each dish, the tower must first find the dish and learn its channel.

The proposal has each satellite receiver periodically send a short beacon. Towers listen for beacons, detect possible victims, and estimate their channels before shaping their beams. A study of a single victim showed how distance losses and estimate quality jointly set how well nulling works. Detailed ray-tracing simulations of a rural area then confirmed the approach under realistic settings, even with many victim units nearby, though towers may need many antennas.
arxiv-2510-09124:
Kyng, Probst Gutenberg, and Rieder give a simpler proof of a classic result about squeezing graphs into trees, in this 2025 arXiv paper on algorithms. Embedding a graph into a tree makes hard routing and distance problems easy, but the tree inevitably stretches some distances. A famous method builds the tree by cutting the graph at randomly shifted scales. Folk wisdom held that each single scale must lose a growing factor.

The authors show the loss is actually a tight constant once the scales are averaged together, a cleaner picture with immediate payoffs. Their tree preserves all distances with the best possible expected stretch, matching a known lower bound and re-proving a landmark theorem by simpler means. The same insight sharpens a simple routing scheme that ignores the traffic pattern, giving it the best possible competitive ratio. Their constructions run efficiently in sequential, parallel, and distributed settings.
arxiv-2510-09724:
Qiaosheng Chen, Yang Liu, Lei Li, Kai Chen, Qipeng Guo, Gong Cheng, and Fei Yuan benchmark science-teaching code in a 2025 arXiv paper. Language models generate complete applications from instructions, and interactive science demos are prized in education for explaining concepts and presenting research. Building one demands accurate science plus a front end whose code behaves correctly and responds well to users, a mix existing benchmarks do not test.

Their benchmark, InteractScience, pairs questions across five scientific domains with unit tests, reference snapshots, and checklists. Scoring mixes code-based tests of function, which strictly verify the interaction logic, with visually grounded testing that compares rendered output against reference images. Thirty leading open and closed models were evaluated. The results highlight lasting weaknesses in joining domain knowledge with interactive coding, and the authors offer the benchmark as the first measure of that joined skill.
arxiv-2510-09924:
Li, Zihao Zhu, Xiaoyu Wang, and Zhengzhong Tu present HeadsUp in this 2025 arXiv paper on portrait image super-resolution. Super-resolution sharpens a low-quality image into a larger, cleaner one. Portraits mix a human subject with a natural background, and they fill social media feeds.

Existing methods split into two camps, the authors note. Generic methods handle real-world scenes but not faces well, while face methods demand strictly aligned facial photos. HeadsUp targets portraits as they actually occur, with varied poses and backgrounds. It aims for high-fidelity results that keep both the person and the setting convincing. That balance matters because errors on a face are far more visible than errors on scenery.
arxiv-2510-10024:
Bentout and Hoang-Hung Vo develop eigenvalue theory for epidemic models in this 2025 arXiv paper in mathematical biology. They study a nonlocal cooperative reaction-diffusion system that has free boundaries and drift terms. The system is motivated by directional epidemic spread, where infection moves with a preferred direction.

Such systems lack a variational structure, the energy framework that usually supplies eigenvalues. The authors instead work under sharper regularity demands on solutions, and they build the eigentheory that the free boundary problem needs. Eigenvalues decide whether an epidemic can invade or dies out. The free boundary tracks the moving edge of the infected region, and the drift encodes effects like wind or travel flow on spread.
arxiv-2510-10124:
Athmouni proves a rigidity result for quasi-Lie brackets in this 2025 arXiv paper in analysis. He works on Banach right modules over the quaternions, complete normed spaces whose scalars are quaternions. A quasi-Lie bracket almost obeys the two rules of a Lie bracket, skew symmetry and the Jacobi rule, but with small defects.

Athmouni shows that if those defects are kept small in a precise sense, a concrete correction term fixes them. The correction keeps right linearity over the quaternions and restores the exact Lie rules. So a near-Lie structure turns out to be a true Lie structure in disguise. He then applies the result to nonlinear partial differential equations, where such brackets encode the symmetries of a problem.
arxiv-2510-10224:
An and co-authors present Text2Token in this 2025 arXiv paper on text representation learning. Unsupervised representation learning turns raw text into vectors that power search and recommendation, using the web's unlabeled text. A recent study found that good representations align with the key token of the input.

Text2Token builds on that link between representation space and vocabulary space. It trains with token target prediction, asking the model to predict the key token from its representation. The target forces the vector to keep the information that matters most in the passage. The authors aim for representations that stay close to the words themselves, which may make them more interpretable and better matched to retrieval tasks.
arxiv-2510-10324:
Hong and Noura Raydan Nasreddine tackle practical challenges of conformal prediction in this 2025 arXiv paper on machine learning methods. Conformal prediction wraps any model in prediction regions with a guaranteed coverage probability, a rare promise in machine learning. In practice, data scientists hit three problems.

First, regions are often only approximate, which endangers the finite-sample guarantee. Second, the computation can be prohibitively expensive. Third, the shape of a region is hard to control, so answers may be awkward to use. The authors examine each challenge and what can be done about it. Their aim is to keep the guarantee honest when conformal methods meet real data and real budgets.
arxiv-2510-10424:
Valenzuela Ruiz compares two homology theories in this 2025 arXiv paper in algebraic topology. Homology measures the holes and cycles of a shape. Überhomology is a newer theory for simplicial complexes, while double homology belongs to the moment-angle complex built from the same data.

The author presents a comparison map between the two theories. He shows they differ at exactly three bidegrees, degrees in the two grading directions of the theory. Which three depends on whether the complex is neighbourly, a combinatorial condition on how its vertices connect. A precise comparison lets results proved in one theory transfer to the other, and the three exceptional degrees mark where genuinely new information lives.
arxiv-2510-11524:
How complex is a network? A single entropy number flattens the answer, missing structure that only appears at particular scales of coarse-graining. Sebastián Brzovic, Cristóbal Rojas, and Andrés Abeliuk introduce a multiscale entropy framework in this 2025 arXiv network science paper. Building on compression-based entropy measures previously linked to link prediction, they use spectral graph reduction to watch entropy evolve as a network is coarsened.

Applied to real-world networks from biological, economic, social, technical, and transportation domains, the framework found consistent entropy profiles within network families. Three structural regimes emerged across the profiles: stable, increasing, and hybrid, aligning with domain-specific behavior. Compared with single-scale models, the multiscale profiles clearly improved the ability to tell how predictable a network's links are. The authors present multiscale entropy as a scalable tool for describing and sorting complex networks across scales, not at one resolution alone.
arxiv-2510-11924:
Ji Xia and six co-authors teach a model to imagine brain activity nobody recorded. Brain scientists want to know how brain areas interact, but no single experiment records every area of interest at once. Different animals contribute different subsets. Their 2025 arXiv paper introduces NeuroPaint, a masked autoencoding method that fills in the missing areas, much as image software inpaints a missing patch.

Trained across many animals with overlapping recordings, NeuroPaint learns the shared structure linking areas. It then reconstructs the dynamics of an unrecorded area from the areas that were measured. The team trained and tested the method on synthetic data and on two real multi-animal datasets gathered with Neuropixels probes. The models recovered the activity of held-out areas. That success enables analyses of multi-area interaction that no single experiment could support, in effect pooling the world's partial recordings into virtual complete ones.
arxiv-2510-12624:
Kobayashi and co-authors learn, across many tasks, which measurements are worth paying for when data arrive partial, in a 2025 arXiv machine learning paper. Active feature acquisition selects on the fly which features to measure for each case to improve predictions. Real datasets have patterned missingness and few labels, and earlier methods solved buying for one set task at a time, limiting scale.

Their Learning to Measure framework tackles the meta problem of acquiring features across tasks. It pairs reliable uncertainty estimates over unseen tasks with an uncertainty guided greedy agent that buys the feature carrying the most conditional information. An autoregressive pretraining approach supplies those estimates for tasks with arbitrary missingness. The system works in context on datasets with missingness added later, and never retrains per task. Across made up and real tabular benchmarks it matched or beat task tuned baselines, especially when labels were scarce and missingness high.
arxiv-2510-12924:
Pochobradský and colleagues present a drone controller for agile flight in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their method builds on model predictive path integral control, which samples many candidate flight rollouts and averages them into a command. Standard versions lose precision during fast, acrobatic maneuvers and track gentle trajectories poorly.

Their controller, GMPPI, generates part of each rollout with geometric control on the rotation group, sharply improving precision in agile flight. It also varies the simulation step length plus cost and noise settings during flight. That flexibility fixed the weak tracking of smooth, slow paths seen in the earlier implementation. Integrated with a stereo depth camera, the system avoided obstacles in a simulated forest at high speed and beat a leading obstacle-aware planner. Real-world flights kept the agile tracking while dodging obstacles at up to ten meters per second.
arxiv-2510-13224:
Yang and Morales fix the notion of expansive flow for noncompact spaces in this 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. An expansive flow separates nearby trajectories, a hallmark of chaotic dynamics. The classical Bowen-Walters definition survives under topological conjugacy on compact spaces but fails on general spaces. So the verdict depended on the wording, not the flow itself.

The authors propose topological expansive flows. This new notion is invariant under conjugacy and agrees with the classical notion when the space is compact. They prove a flow is topological expansive exactly when it is rescaling expansive and its singularities are isolated points of the space. Finally, they show the growth rate of periodic orbits for such flows is controlled by an entropy-like invariant. This extends the Bowen-Walters inequality beyond the compact setting.
arxiv-2510-13424:
Wilton shows how symbolic execution can verify a sparse matrix algorithm with test-like effort. His 2025 arXiv paper targets scientific software, which is heavily optimized and prone to subtle bugs. Ordinary testing samples only some inputs, so errors can hide in untested cases. Symbolic execution instead reasons about whole ranges of inputs at once.

Wilton writes checks that read like unit tests but carry stronger guarantees. He applies the method to a sparse matrix multiplication routine stored in compressed row format. The CIVL model checker runs the symbolic simulation and searches reachable states for errors. Branching behaviour is explored by backtracking, so no path is skipped silently. The case study shows the approach working on a real algorithm from the literature. Wilton presents it as a middle path between light testing and full formal proof.
arxiv-2510-13524:
Flanagan and a large team of co-authors offer a framework for judging when performance metrics fail in financial AI. Their 2025 arXiv paper, from a finance workshop, targets generative AI spreading through banks. Classic machine learning metrics often do not transfer to generative workloads. Expert human review fills the gap, but brings its own uncounted risks.

The authors argue that choosing a metric is itself a risky decision. Popular public benchmarks also generalize poorly to industrial settings, they note. Their risk assessment framework structures how firms should combine expert judgement with metrics. It forces teams to name failure modes before a metric is trusted. The paper draws lessons from real financial deployments at large institutions. Its goal is better validation of agentic systems used by staff with little technical training.
arxiv-2510-13924:
Ansari, Jadhav, and Shirolkar determine the congruence of a specific Jacobi sum of order forty-nine over prime fields. Their 2025 arXiv paper works in cyclotomy, the study of roots of unity and finite field character sums. Jacobi sums are algebraic integers whose congruences encode deep arithmetic information. Earlier work settled prime orders and order nine, leaving forty-nine open in this form.

The target sum, written J(1,1) with order forty-nine, gets its congruence pinned down completely. The modulus involves powers of the prime ideal above the cyclotomic field's special prime. For two special prime families, the artiad and hyperartiad primes, even simpler congruences hold. Those cases collapse the general formula into cleaner closed forms. The proof tradition here runs through Katre and collaborators' earlier order-by-order results. Dickson-Hurwitz sums and cyclotomic numbers supply the computational machinery.
arxiv-2510-14024:
Thanh Son Phung and Douglas Thain show how to run lightweight language-model inference on borrowed, opportunistic supercomputer GPUs without wasting the opportunity, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Scientific computing centers increasingly mix small language models into high-throughput applications, but batch queues cause long waits, and when resources are preempted, restarting the model from scratch is expensive.

Their technique, Pervasive Context Management, decouples the model's initialization context from actual inference. It keeps that context resident in GPU memory until it is no longer needed. Work can then resume cheaply after interruptions. They reworked a fact-verification application to use the technique. On the same number of GPUs, execution time fell by more than seventy percent, from three hours to forty-eight minutes. Scaling opportunistically across about a third of the cluster's GPUs cut the run further, to thirteen minutes.
arxiv-2510-14124:
Christian Krattenthaler, Brandt Kronholm, and Paul Marsh find a new, 'perpendicular' way to generate the coefficients of Gaussian polynomials, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Gaussian polynomials, also called q-binomial coefficients, count integer partitions that fit inside a box. These numbers have been studied through standard generating functions for over a century. A new collection is therefore a surprise.

The perpendicular generating functions arise from an overlooked partition trick noted by Gupta in 1975 and developed earlier by Ehrhart. The authors describe these functions in general. For small values of the box parameter, unimodality, the rise-then-fall shape, follows easily. They also uncover new identities for differences between these numbers. They include an unexpected family of congruences for one Gaussian polynomial family. The work reframes partition counts by collecting the numbers along the perpendicular direction instead of the customary one.
arxiv-2510-14224:
Fenglin Li computes the homology groups, algebraic fingerprints of shape, of graphs built from the zero divisors of commutative rings, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A zero divisor is a nonzero element that multiplies another nonzero element to give zero. Connecting them forms a graph. The holes in the clique complex built from that graph reveal the ring's structure.

Generalizing a construction of DeMeyer and DeMeyer, Li establishes a Künneth-type formula. It expresses the homology of a product through the homologies of its factors. He gives computations for products of local rings. The paper provides a method for the clique homology of integers modulo n and their products. It derives formulas for the Betti numbers, the counts of holes in each dimension, when all factors are fields or non-fields. It classifies when the complex is Cohen-Macaulay, a regularity property, apart from one borderline case.
arxiv-2510-14624:
Bagrov, Khvedchenia, and Tymchenko introduce, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a simple trick for making vision and language models faster on video. Such models turn each frame into tokens, and long videos overflow their limits, causing slow responses. Much of a video barely changes between frames, though, while the model pays full price to process identical patches again.

Their method, Efficient Video Sampling, finds those temporally static patches and prunes them before the language model runs. It keeps each remaining patch's position information, needs no changes to the model, and requires no retraining. At inference time it cut the delay before the first output token by up to a factor of four, with minimal loss of accuracy. An optional extra training phase, using random pruning rates, made models robust across compression levels, with consistent gains in the speed and quality trade-off.
arxiv-2510-14724:
Fukaya and co-authors explore, in a 2025 arXiv paper, the surfaces of three-dimensional superconducting altermagnets, a newly recognized class of magnetic materials. Altermagnets combine features of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets, and pairing them with superconductors has produced striking effects in two-dimensional systems. The authors move the story into three dimensions, studying d-wave and g-wave altermagnets with chiral d-wave pairing.

They find crossed surface flat bands, surface states pinned at zero energy, formed by the underlying symmetries. The bands appear on one crystal face because of nodal lines in the superconducting state, and the number of their corners is fixed by the crystal's symmetry. The same nodal lines create Bogoliubov-Fermi surfaces, which shape zero-energy arcs on another face. Each feature leaves a distinct signal in charge conductance. That gives experimenters a way to detect these states and a route toward higher-dimensional topological phases.
arxiv-2510-14924:
Chen, Gnedin, and Price-Whelan apply an automatic stream-finding algorithm to Gaia data, in a 2025 arXiv paper, and double the census of star streams torn from globular clusters. As the Milky Way's gravity pulls clusters apart, their stars trail into long streams. The algorithm, StarStream, searched Gaia's third data release for these faint ribbons without human scanning.

It identified eighty-seven streams associated with globular clusters. Thirty-four are high quality, with modeled completeness and purity both above fifty percent. The detections raise the share of high-latitude clusters with tidal streams to seventy-five percent. Against visual expectations, many new streams are wide, or short, or misaligned with their cluster's orbit. Because the method measures stream density without bias, the team also estimated each cluster's mass loss rate. Several low-mass, large-size clusters are losing mass unusually fast, a sign they approach complete tidal disruption.
arxiv-2510-15024:
Laseter and co-authors check, in a 2025 arXiv paper, whether a basic galaxy relation survives down to the smallest galaxies. The Fundamental Metallicity Relation links a galaxy's mass, its gas metal content, and its star formation rate in one balance. New JWST observations show distant galaxies departing from it. But the relation was never characterized for low-mass systems, leaving no baseline for comparison.

The team ran a meta-analysis of seven hundred dwarf galaxies selected by an oxygen emission line, all below a billion solar masses. They applied the field's fitting methods, minimization, parametric, and non-parametric, to the sample. Every method found no evidence of the relation at these masses. The implication: these galaxies have not yet settled into the quasi-steady gas reservoirs the relation assumes. They remain gas-rich, with yields scattered over a thousandfold range, and a weak tie between metallicity and star formation.
arxiv-2510-15324:
Tatsuru Kikuchi measures how the benefit of a hospital fades with distance, treating that effect as a smooth field over space and time. His solo 2025 arXiv paper builds a framework from the Navier-Stokes equations, the fluid flow equations, so treatment intensity becomes a continuous function rather than a single discrete parameter. That shift allows rigorous study of effect boundaries, spatial gradients, and total exposure.

Testing the framework on more than thirty-two thousand U.S. ZIP codes, Kikuchi finds healthcare access decaying with distance, with detectable effect boundaries near thirty-seven kilometers from care. The framework also self-diagnoses: where its diffusion assumption fits, the decay sign comes out positive, and near cities it flips, flagging confounding instead. Older residents showed distance effects two to thirteen times stronger than others, and education mattered as well. Model comparisons strongly favored logarithmic over exponential decay.
arxiv-2510-15724:
Johan Kolvik and colleagues report a small chip device in a 2025 paper. The device couples light with high-frequency sound. Such crystals often trap heat when they hang free in air. Trapped heat fills them with thermal noise. So the team built theirs fixed straight onto the silicon chip. Heat could then escape into the base below.

The chip was run at very low temperatures. It suppressed the heat-driven optical effect far better than a hanging version. Its vibration stayed near the quantum ground state. This held even at much higher light levels inside the device. The authors say fixed designs like this suit low-noise quantum tools. Such tools convert signals between microwave and light forms.
arxiv-2510-15824:
Guillaume Principato and Gilles Stoltz recast adaptive conformal inference as a repeated game between two players. Conformal methods issue prediction sets one round at a time, before each outcome is revealed. A good method must cover the outcome often enough, which favours large sets, yet also keep sets short, which pulls the other way.

Existing strategies usually promise that coverage settles at the target level for arbitrary data, but they rarely promise efficiency at the same time. Principato and Stoltz encode validity and efficiency as vector payoffs in a finite-action game. Their strategy, built on Blackwell approachability and an opportunistic extension of it, keeps validity while adapting set length to how random the opponent's data truly are. The guarantee recovers known efficiency results at both the exchangeable and adversarial extremes and covers cases in between.
arxiv-2510-15924:
Alex Kontorovich, as sole author, surveys how computational tools are changing the daily practice of mathematics and what may follow soon. Formal verification systems and AI assistants now interact with research work in ways that were rare a generation ago. The overview reflects on those interactions for the short to medium term.

Kontorovich considers how proof assistants, computer algebra, and learning-based tools reshape proving, checking, and discovering results. The essay weighs both the reach these tools add and the shifts they force in how mathematicians trust and share arguments. Readers get a practitioner's map of a field in transition, written for researchers weighing how much of their workflow to hand to machines. The piece is a reflection and overview rather than a report of new theorems.
arxiv-2510-16024:
Abdulrahman Alhaidari, Balaji Palanisamy, and Prashant Krishnamurthy move defence against decentralised finance exploits fully onto the blockchain. Billions are lost yearly to transactions that abuse business logic or accounting flaws, and current defences miss exploits sent through private relays or malicious contracts that fire inside one block. Their framework learns and infers on-chain instead of trusting outside monitors.

Heavy computation runs on a second layer to cut cost, verified updates propagate to the main chain, and inference inside smart contracts stays within gas limits at low latency. A Proof-of-Improvement protocol accepts an update only if it improves one core metric without worsening any other, and bad proposals are fined against an evolving test set. Quantisation and loop unrolling let several model types run bit-exact to their off-chain twins, proven formally, the team reports.
arxiv-2510-16224:
Zhongjun Qu, Wendun Wang, and Xiaomeng Zhang give model averaging a way to admit its own doubt. Model averaging blends forecasts from many models into one, and it is prized for point guesses. But a single best guess hides how wrong it could be, and sound error ranges for blends were lacking.

Their ranges come from conformal inference, a method that promises the true value lands inside at a set rate. The promise holds even when every model is somewhat wrong, and when models nest inside or overlap each other. They prove exact coverage for data that can be shuffled, and near coverage for steady time series. Finer versions adapt the range to local conditions or split the data for safety. Tests span house price appraisal and stock premium forecasts, two fields where honest doubt matters.
arxiv-2510-16324:
Arpan Das, writing alone, proves a clean structural result about representations of the group SL2 over a local field. Representations describe how a group acts as symmetries of a vector space, and here the coefficients live in mod-p arithmetic. Das starts with a smooth, irreducible representation of the integer points of the group and induces it up to the whole group.

The induced object is a module over the spherical Hecke algebra, a ring of approved averaging operators. Das proves that module is free, meaning it has a basis with no hidden relations, and that its rank is infinite. Freeness is a strong tidiness claim: it rules out torsion and makes dimension counting exact. Such results anchor the mod-p representation theory used to probe deep links between symmetry and number theory.
arxiv-2510-16824:
Yingxu Wang and five co-authors present ProtoMol, a system that predicts molecule properties by reading both molecular graphs and written descriptions.
