L. Schilcher, P. Waldert, B. Kantz, and T. Schreck build a dashboard for patient data. Their 2026 preprint is named Clusters in Focus. Exploring tables to find cohorts is key in biomarker discovery. Feature pairs split patients into groups in many such hunts.

Comparing clusters across many feature pair views is hard. A dashboard must keep detail on demand, simple and robust. The team's tool does just that for tabular patient data. Users can focus on one projection and pull detail as needed. Cohorts can then be checked across views with less strain. The work comes from Graz University of Technology. It aims at clinical data work that stays readable.
arxiv-2601-11724:
Muditha Fernando, Kajhanan Kailainathan, Krishnakanth Nagaratnam, Isuranga Senavirathne, and Ranga Rodrigo work on a hard learning task. A model must learn from few marked cases and still work on new domains it has not seen. This task is called semi-supervised domain generalization in the field.

Their method, named SemAlign in the work, is guided by language. Past work shows two chief risks in this task. One is wrong tags made for unmarked cases. The other is a model that fits its training data too well and fails on new data. The new method aims to cut both risks at once.
arxiv-2601-11824:
A. Brennan, L. Matrà, S. Mac Manamon, and the ARKS team report new views of the debris disk round the star HD 121617. Debris disks are rings of dust and rock left round young stars. About twenty such disks show carbon monoxide gas, split into gas-poor and gas-rich kinds.

HD 121617 is gas-rich, so it is a key case in the ARKS survey. That survey uses the ALMA array to map fine rings in such disks. Fine maps can show gaps and clumps made by unseen planets. The work adds one rich case to that map set.
arxiv-2601-11924:
Ming Shi studies shared bandit tasks where reward data can be spoiled. Many agents pick arms over many rounds and share what they learn. Each reward is a vector, so more than one goal is in play. A foe can spoil the shared data, but only up to a set total budget.

A check step can test some data, but checks are scarce. Shi links how much spoil is used with how checks are placed. The work aims for methods that still learn well under attack. Such guards help shared learning in open, risky nets.
arxiv-2601-12224:
Meng Wei, Kun Yuan, Shi Li, and a large team find surgical tools in video by how they move, from a text brief. Language-led work with surgical scenes could aid smart operating rooms and robot help. The task is to cut out the tool named in words.

Past tools rest on static visual cues and fixed tool names. Those fail on new tools and phrasing. Motion gives a strong extra cue, since the used tool is the one that moves with intent. The team's motion-led method aims to generalize better.
arxiv-2601-12424:
William Dorrell and James Whittington review a puzzle from neuroscience: grid cells. These neurons fire in a neat hexagonal pattern as an animal moves. For twenty years, that pretty code has raised a basic question. What computation does this pattern serve, and why does it take this curious form?

The first answer came fast: grid cells track position as an animal moves. That skill is called path integration. Dorrell and Whittington survey normative theories, which ask what an ideal system should do. Such theories try to derive the grid pattern from a goal, not just describe it. Their review weighs how well that project has worked so far.
arxiv-2601-12724:
Rishabh Iyer works on set functions that come from entropy, a core idea in the theory of data and codes. Shannon entropy is one such function, and it has a clean shape that math can use. But the set of all such entropy based functions is smaller than some had hoped. A newer frame stretches entropy style measures to a wider class of set functions.

Those wider measures have found many uses in the past few years. Teams use them to pick data, to guide learning, and to shift a model to a new domain. Iyer gives hands on forms of them for three classic tasks. The tasks are coverage, facility location, and graph cuts. Clear forms let users plug proven measures straight into real tools.
arxiv-2601-13124:
Donglei Du, Qizhi Fang, Bin Liu, Tianhang Lu, and Chenchen Wu sort the core of a broad class of games where pay offs bend. In game theory the core is the set of splits that no group can beat by breaking off. For straight line games the core is well known.

For bent games the core was far less clear. The team finds a fit loosening of the bent form. With it they give a full mark of when the core holds and what it holds. Their result grows the set of joint games that can be read in this way. It also links to games that spring from opt tasks, a rich source in trade and nets.
arxiv-2601-13224:
Michael Hanus and Steven Libby ease the work of tools that reshape code. Compilers, code probes, and proof tools all walk a code tree and change nodes as they go. To write such walks by hand is slow and prone to flaws. Each tool must loop the whole tree and act at the right nodes.

Hanus and Libby work in functional logic programming, a style that joins two code styles. They give ways to state code reshapes in a more brief and safe form. Their aim is less boiler plate for tool builders. For language tool teams, clean reshape rules mean tools that are more quick to build and more safe to change.
arxiv-2601-13424:
A. Martinez-Mendez and co-authors cut waste in the vast compute pool of the LAGO project. LAGO is a Latin American watch for high energy bits from space. It runs heavy sims on high performance clusters. Such sims eat time, power, and funds, so yield per run counts for both science and green aims.

The team counts where cluster time goes in the LAGO set up. They then tune how jobs are placed and run to lift yield. Their marks are tied to astroparticle sims, which have long runs and big data. For big sim teams, the work shows how yield checks pay off in more science per watt.
arxiv-2601-13624:
A team with Xin Zhang weighs two puzzles in the study of the early universe in 2026. One is cosmic birefringence, a slight twist in the light left from the Big Bang. The twist would link the two modes of that light in a new way. Such a link is a sign of parity violation, a break in mirror symmetry.

The team joins data from ACT, Planck, DESI, and PantheonPlus to set joint limits. They test birefringence next to early dark energy, a brief extra push in the young cosmos. New high-grade sky data make such fine effects worth a fresh look. Joint limits keep one puzzle from skewing the other.
arxiv-2601-14024:
Sergio López-Baños and co-authors boost a hybrid quantum-classical solver for hard planning problems in 2026. Mixed-integer linear programming, or MILP, is used widely in industry optimization. As problems grow larger, classical solvers struggle within practical time limits. Quantum annealers could in principle accelerate some of these tasks.

The problems map to quadratic unconstrained binary optimization instances for annealers. Limited annealer scale currently prevents practical speedups. The team enhances the hybrid Benders' algorithm, which splits a problem into parts. Better splits may bring quantum help closer to real industrial use. The split must be smart, or the gain is lost in extra work. Their tests show where the split helps most and where it does not.
arxiv-2601-14124:
Saad Mankarious and Ayah Zirikly use style transfer to build mental health text data in Arabic in 2026. Synthetic data promises a fix for data scarcity and demographic bias. Existing approaches rely largely on pretrained large language models. Those models may suffer limited output diversity in what they generate.

They may also propagate biases inherited from their training data. The team uses diffusion models for synthetic mental health text instead. Style transfer can recast real text in new voices while keeping content. Fair Arabic datasets could improve mental health tools for Arabic speakers.
arxiv-2601-14224:
Sahel Sharifymoghaddam and Jimmy Lin study where deep search agents should spend their compute in 2026. Deep research agents rely on iterative retrieval and reasoning to answer complex queries. Scaling test-time computation raises significant efficiency concerns for them. The team studies how to allocate reasoning budget in deep search pipelines.

Listwise reranking, which reorders a whole list of results at once, is their focus. They analyze reranking tradeoffs through effective token cost. Their title gives the advice: rerank before you reason. Spending tokens on better sources first may beat deeper thought on poor ones.
arxiv-2601-14724:
Haowei Zhang, Shudong Yang, Jinlan Fu, and their co-authors present a video understanding system in this 2026 paper. Streaming video understanding means answering questions about a video while it still plays. Long streams strain the KV cache, the memory a model keeps for past frames. HERMES treats that cache as a hierarchical memory.

HERMES is a training-free approach, so it needs no new model training. It reuses the KV cache and performs hierarchical management of the video tokens stored in it. Key tokens stay at fine detail, while older ones are compressed in tiers. Readers get stable, efficient inference for long videos, where naive systems run out of memory or forget the plot.
arxiv-2601-15024:
Nipun Agarwal reviews how to keep wireless links private when the listener stays silent. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with massive MIMO, a system where a base station uses a great many antennas. The tech drives 5G and later networks, with big gains in spectrum and energy use.

A passive eavesdropper never transmits, so the station cannot learn its channel. That makes secure links hard to promise. Agarwal surveys the known challenges at the physical layer. He also sets out open research directions for guarding these systems against such silent, hidden listeners.
arxiv-2601-15324:
Mark Wind bolts a memory onto a language model without touching its weights. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with a common problem: adding memory to a pre-trained model usually means changing its architecture or its weights. Prometheus Mind takes a different route.

The base model, a Qwen3-4B, stays frozen. Eleven modular adapters add the memory, at seven percent overhead, and removing them undoes the change. Building the system took four fixes. One finds semantic directions from minimal pairs with no labeled data. Another trains each adapter in stages, since end-to-end training collapses.
arxiv-2601-15424:
Juan Gomez Quispe, Matheus Medina, and co-authors tune carbon sheets to make hydrogen production cheaper. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with graphynes, carbon frameworks that mix two bond types. The mix gives distinct electronic regimes and site-selective reactivity across the sheet.

The team studies the hydrogen evolution reaction, a key step in splitting water. They dope two graphyne forms with boron, nitrogen, or both. Density functional theory and reactive molecular dynamics simulations judge each doped variant in turn. The goal is to control both the reaction's activity and the material's stability.
arxiv-2601-15524:
Ni An, Bhola Nath Saha, and Bidyut Sanki work on curves on hyperbolic surfaces in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their objects are filling pairs. A filling pair is two simple closed curves in minimal position. Cut the surface along both curves, and what remains is a union of topological disks. Nothing else is left over. Such pairs are basic tools in the study of surfaces.

The title names the paper's goal: length minimization for these pairs. Among all filling pairs on a surface, which ones are shortest? The abstract in the record states the definition and little more. Readers should expect a specialist geometry paper with proofs at its core. Short filling pairs give concrete ways to measure and compare surfaces.
arxiv-2601-15724:
Chenglin Li and a large team build video models that use tools in a 2026 arXiv paper. Long-form video remains a hard problem for video language models. Most models reason over uniformly sampled frames. That static approach weakens timing: they cannot pinpoint when things happen. It also loses much information in long videos. The team's system is called VideoThinker. It is built as an agentic VideoLLM.

Agentic tools let the model explore a video adaptively. The tools include temporal retrieval, spatial zoom, and temporal zoom. Guided by a language model, the system picks where to look closer. That mirrors how a person scans a long recording. For tasks like surveillance review or lecture search, active looking beats uniform sampling.
arxiv-2601-15824:
Joan Vendrell Farreny and colleagues at NeuralTrust propose a new security layer in a 2026 arXiv paper. They call it the Generative Application Firewall, or GAF. It is an architectural layer for securing language model applications. Existing defenses are fragmented, they argue. Prompt filters, guardrails, and data masking each guard one spot. GAF unifies them into a single enforcement point.

The model is the web application firewall. A WAF coordinates defenses for web traffic in one place. GAF aims to do the same for generative apps. It also covers autonomous agents and their tool interactions. Agent actions are a new attack surface that old tools miss. For security teams, one chokepoint is easier to audit than scattered patches.
arxiv-2601-15924:
Brainard Philemon Jagati and four co-authors fix learning on skewed class data in a 2026 arXiv paper. Deep networks degrade badly under long-tailed distributions. A few head classes dominate the training data. Tail classes get very few examples. The model then masters the common and fumbles the rare. Their method is class-confidence aware reweighting, per the title. Training examples are reweighted by class and by model confidence.

Reweighting shifts attention toward what the model gets wrong. Class awareness counters the head classes' bulk. Confidence awareness focuses on uncertain cases. Rare classes matter in medicine and safety, where the rare event is often the important one. Methods that lift tail performance without hurting the head are in real demand.
arxiv-2601-16324:
Rebecca Lopez and coauthors screen student minds with Fitbit data from the plague years. Their 2026 preprint deals with stress in college life. High stress drives high rates of fear and low mood in students. Wear gear gives quiet sense data through the day. Such data could flag ill minds at an early stage.

Past work used few mind tests and few body sense types. The team widens both the tests and the sense types in use. Wide data should give a more true screen of mind state. Early flags could guide help to students in time. The work uses data drawn in the COVID span.
arxiv-2601-16724:
Kevin Fan and Eric Yun study bias in machines that grade essays. Schools now use such tools for tests with high stakes. Tools trained on native speech can grade harshly. Students who learn English as a new tongue may lose marks. Their style traits get read as flaws. Their 2026 preprint seeks a fairer way to grade.

The team uses a learn-by-contrast trick in training. The trick pulls the tool's eye to real skill. It pushes the eye off surface traits of new learners. Fair grades guard life paths like school seats and jobs. This work shows one path to tame such bias in code.
arxiv-2601-16824:
Rongjun Ma, Shijing He, Jose Luis Martin-Navarro, Xiao Zhan, and Jose Such study love chats with AI. Apps now sell AI partners for romance and chat. Folks share deep, private woes with these bots. The risks of that share stay little known. Their 2026 preprint draws on talks with users of such apps.

The talks span first tries, close bonds, and break-ups. Users told what they share and what they guard. They also told who they think holds power in the bond. Their tales show where privacy lines blur with bots. The work can guide safe design for such apps.
arxiv-2601-17124:
Bin Lin and a large team fix a split in how AI makes shots. Shot bots come in two camps with a wall twixt them. One camp builds shots step by step from codes. The next camp spreads noise to shots in a smooth wash. Code roots split too, in VQ and plain forms. Their 2026 preprint heals one such code form, FSQ. A one-line code change does the work.

The fix is named iFSQ. It aims to lift shot grade from code-based bots. Fair tests twixt camps need such shared ground. Small fixes with big gains are prized in code work. The team shares the change for all to use.
arxiv-2601-17424:
Hanamichi Kawamura links two deep tools in the theory of multiple zeta values. Brown's lifting method solves double shuffle equations one level up. It builds full solutions from linearized ones, modulo products. Kawamura shows this method fits in Ecalle's dimorphic transportation frame. That frame moves structures between two unlike worlds while keeping their core.

A shared frame can make hard proofs shorter. It can also move results from one field to the other. Multiple zeta values sit at a crossroads of algebra and number theory. Tools that unify their study draw wide interest. Kawamura's link gives researchers a new path through old equations. It may spark fresh attacks on open cases.
arxiv-2601-17624: Sean McGuinness studies short rainbow circuits in regular matroids. His 2026 preprint takes up a conjecture of DeVos and co-authors. The setting colors the elements of a simple regular matroid with one more color than its rank, each color used at least twice. The claim under study is that a rainbow circuit, one using each color at most once, must exist with a bounded small size.
arxiv-2601-17824:
Saber Zerhoudi, Michael Dinzinger, Michael Granitzer, and Jelena Mitrović build a search tool that lets users set the bounds of what it reads. Their 2026 preprint presents OwlerLite, a browser-based system for retrieval-augmented generation. Such systems let a language model pull facts from outside sources as it answers. Most of them search a fixed index that can be stale, and users cannot choose the sources.

OwlerLite puts source scope and freshness at the center of the design. Users can say which sources count and how new the material must be. That control cuts the risk of answers that mix trusted and weak sources. It also cuts the risk of basing replies on old facts. The tool runs in the browser itself.
arxiv-2601-18024:
P. Brearley and T. L. Howarth give a method for writing hard operators as sums of easy ones. Their 2026 preprint deals with linear combinations of unitaries. Quantum computers can run unitary operators directly, but many tasks need non-unitary ones. Writing a non-unitary operator as a weighted sum of unitaries is a standard trick. The cost of the trick hinges on how fast the sum's error shrinks.

The authors base their split on a smooth periodic extension of the identity map. A Fourier extension gives a sine series whose terms decay very fast. Fast decay means fewer terms for the same accuracy. That saving matters for quantum algorithms that use the trick at their core.
arxiv-2601-19124:
Sang T. Nguyen, Nguyen Q. Pham, and Tho Quan build translation between Vietnamese and the Bahnaric language. The Bahnar people are an ethnic minority in Vietnam with a deep ancestral heritage. Their language holds great cultural and historical weight, and the state backs efforts to keep it alive and online across generations.

The team pairs sentence level data augmentation with a transformer based design. More training pairs, grown with care, help a model learn a low resource tongue. Machine translation for small languages is a preservation tool: it keeps the language usable in the digital spaces where young speakers live.
arxiv-2601-19324:
Zhen-Yang Peng and Mehdi Abdi propose a quantum device where a vibrating graphene sheet steers supercurrent. Graphene Josephson junctions join two superconductors with a graphene bridge. Here the bridge is a membrane that can flex, and its motion couples to the circuit.

The flexing of the membrane controls how Cooper pairs tunnel through, giving a strong, tunable link between motion and current. The link stays strong even at the level of zero point motion, the faintest jitter quantum rules allow. Such devices could turn tiny motions into readable signals, or cool and control motion with circuits.
arxiv-2601-19424:
Taylor J. Hoyt and five co-authors measure the home galaxies of two thousand Type Ia supernovae in one consistent way. Type Ia blasts serve as distance markers for the cosmos, judged from their light curves over time. The traits of the galaxy each blast lived in can shift that judgment, so they must be measured with care.

The Union3.1 work applies one self consistent method across the whole set. Uniform measures let cosmologists correct the distance scale without method noise. Sharper distances feed the long debate over how fast the universe expands and what drives that growth.
arxiv-2601-19924:
Yitian Chen and four colleagues probe the limits of language models at optimization modeling. Turning a word problem into equations a solver can crack is a skilled task. Language models have progressed fast at it, spawning new methods and benchmarks. Yet the boundaries of their ability remain poorly understood, especially as problems grow complex.

Their benchmark, OPT-Engine, scales problem complexity in a controlled way. Watching where models break reveals which ingredients defeat them: size, structure, or wording. Real-world tasks are exactly where benchmarks are thinnest. A scaling view helps users judge when to trust a model's formulation. It also directs research toward the failure modes that matter most.
arxiv-2601-20224:
Yi Zhang, Weicheng Lin, and Liang-Jie Zhang study how to adapt vision-language models like CLIP to new tasks with little labeled data. CLIP learns from images and text together and extracts features that transfer well. The challenge is to reuse that knowledge downstream without full retraining.

The authors propose feature projection learning as the adaptation route. Better light-weight adaptation would let small teams use strong pretrained models on their own tasks. It also cuts the compute and data needed to reach good accuracy, which widens access to modern vision-language tools.
arxiv-2601-20324:
Jingyuan Zhou, Haoze Wu, and Kaidi Yang work on formal safety guarantees for neural network controllers in large interconnected systems. Such controllers are hard to certify, above all when many units interact. The authors use neural certificates that capture cooperative behavior between units, expressing the idea of reaching a goal while avoiding bad states.

The challenge is twofold: the certificates must model cooperation, and they must be verified at scale. Existing methods fall short on both fronts, the authors argue. Progress here would let engineers deploy learned controllers in grids, traffic, and robot fleets with proof-backed safety.
arxiv-2601-20524:
Matic Fučka, Vitjan Zavrtanik, and Danijel Skočaj present AnomalyVFM, which turns vision foundation models into zero-shot anomaly detectors. Zero-shot detection must find and locate abnormal regions in an image with no training images from that domain. Recent methods lean on vision-language models like CLIP to transfer high-level concepts.

Methods based on purely visual foundation models, such as DINOv2, have lagged behind. The authors aim to close that gap. Strong zero-shot detection matters in medicine and industry, where defects are rare and labeled examples of each new fault cannot be gathered in advance.
arxiv-2601-20924:
Yuya Kusuki, Sridip Pal, and Hiroyasu Tajima build measures for how much a quantum state breaks a symmetry. Their 2026 paper works in quantum resource theory. That frame gives strict rules for such measures. The measures describe phases, far-from-balance dynamics, and open systems. The authors start with a warning case. One known measure, the second-Rényi entanglement asymmetry, can grow under symmetric steps.

A measure that grows under free steps cannot serve alone. It should not by itself capture the Quantum Mpemba effect. That effect is the odd faster cooling of some hotter states. The paper moves past the flawed measure toward stronger ones. Its title promises measures of both weak and strong symmetry breaking. The work sharpens tools used to grade quantum order.
arxiv-2601-21124:
Artem Dementyev and five co-authors give multimodal models ears that work on any device. Their 2026 paper presents PhaseCoder, a spatial audio encoder. Current multimodal LLMs process audio as a mono stream. That ignores the rich spatial information vital for embodied AI. Existing spatial audio models fix the opposite problem poorly. They are constrained to fixed microphone geometries. A model trained for one array fails on another.

PhaseCoder is a transformer-only encoder that ignores geometry differences. It reads phase cues that reveal where sounds come from. Any microphone layout can feed it. That frees spatial hearing from bespoke hardware. Robots and glasses with unlike mic arrays could share one model. The work brings direction-aware listening to general multimodal AI.
arxiv-2601-21324:
Mengqi Chen, Thomas B. Berrett, Theodoros Damoulas, and Michele Caprio make robust decision tools safer to use with messy data. Robust methods plan for the worst case inside a set of plausible data patterns. A classic way to model contamination lets a small share of points be arbitrary.

That freedom can blow the worst case up to infinity and make the whole exercise useless. The authors build ambiguity sets that can be calibrated in bulk. Their sets stay firm without demanding strong extra assumptions. The payoff is robust choices that remain fast to compute and honest about dirty data.
arxiv-2601-21424:
Anderson de Andrade, Alon Harell, and Ivan V. Bajić apply a classic idea from information theory to modern image coding. Many vision tasks share much of the same information in an image. Standard codecs ignore that overlap and store the same content again and again.

The Gray-Wyner network splits shared content from task-specific detail. The authors make that split learnable and lossy, tuned for real compression. A coder that stores shared parts once can serve many tasks from one stream. That saves bandwidth and storage for systems like camera networks, where the same scene feeds many different analyses.
arxiv-2601-21624:
Vasileios Sevetlidis and George Pavlidis survey the hidden memory inside deep learning training. Training is often treated as if each update stood alone. In truth, updates depend on optimizer state, data order, and a trail of auxiliary records.

The survey sorts these memory mechanisms by source, lifetime, and how visible they are. Teacher averages, contrastive queues, and normalization statistics all carry traces of the past. Staged augmentation and replay policies do too. Mapping this memory matters because it shapes results, reproducibility, and even privacy, yet it is rarely measured in a unified way.
arxiv-2601-21724:
Simon Woodruff gathers two decades of fusion power plant costing work into one framework. The work was done for a United States energy agency across several years. Early studies leaned on scaling rules from older designs to estimate the cost of a first-of-a-kind plant.

The framework later grew toward standards-aligned, auditable costing. A pilot study with industry partners checked the plant-level numbers for realism. Costing is where fusion dreams meet budgets, and weak estimates have burned the field before. A documented, checkable framework helps funders compare designs on equal terms.
arxiv-2601-21824:
Xinwei Qiang and co-authors address a quiet cost in training large language models: determinism. Training that gives the same result every run is essential for reproducibility, yet it often slows things down badly. In widely used attention code, the deterministic backward pass can cut throughput by a large share.

The slowdown comes because gradient accumulation steps must be serialized, done one after another, to keep the arithmetic exact. The team's 2026 preprint presents DASH, a deterministic attention scheduling method meant to win back that speed for high-throughput training. Faster deterministic training would help labs debug failures, verify results, and meet audit demands without paying a steep tax on every run.
arxiv-2601-21924:
Jinhang Chai, Enpei Zhang, Elynn Chen, and Yujun Yan study how a learning agent can borrow experience from related tasks. In online transfer reinforcement learning, the agent learns a new target task while data from similar source tasks sit nearby. The difficulty is a mismatch in how similarity is defined.

Tasks are usually called similar when their rewards or transitions match. But online algorithms learn from Bellman regression targets, a different yardstick. The team's 2026 preprint proposes optimistic transfer built on Bellman alignment, judging similarity in the terms the algorithm actually uses. Better transfer means robots and game agents could reuse past experience safely instead of treating every new task as a cold start.
arxiv-2601-22224:
Jia-Nan Yang and co-authors probe random quantum states with a superconducting processor. Quantum many-body systems are enormously complex, yet many of their features are universal. They depend not on microscopic details but on a few basics such as symmetries. The challenge is separating the universal features from the model-specific ones.

The team's 2026 preprint uses a superconducting quantum processor to probe entanglement and symmetries in random states. Random states act as a clean baseline: whatever structure appears there reflects the symmetries alone. Experiments like this turn today's processors into instruments for basic science, mapping the universal statistical laws that govern complex quantum matter.
arxiv-2601-22324:
Silas Ruhrberg Estévez, Christopher Chiu, and Mihaela van der Schaar turn strong health models into score cards a doctor can use at the bedside. Care runs on short rule lists that are easy to recall and check. Their 2026 preprint, AgentScore, builds such lists on its own.

Many smart models fail in real clinics because they clash with daily workflow. A good score card must be brief, clear, and quick to run by hand. The team frame the build as a search for rules that stay true to the data. Their work aims to close the gap between lab scores and ward use.
arxiv-2601-23124:
Angel Reyero Lobo, Bertrand Thirion, and Pierre Neuvial test whether two variables are independent given others. Conditional independence testing guards scientific discovery against spurious findings. Recent methods use machine learning models as stand-ins for the data distribution.

Model-agnostic versions must split data into train and test parts, which weakens statistical power. Their semi-knockoff method keeps finite-sample guarantees while using data more fully. Stronger tests help fields like genomics select real effects from noise. Finite-sample guarantees keep the error control exact rather than asymptotic, a distinction that matters in regulated science. Semi-knockoffs aim to recover the power lost when earlier model-agnostic tests split their data.
arxiv-2601-23224:
Xiangyu Zeng and a large team present Video-o3, a framework for reasoning over long videos. Models for long video usually sample frames uniformly and answer in one pass. That misses sparse but critical evidence buried in hours of redundant footage.

Video-o3 instead seeks clues step by step, in an interleaved loop. It inspects key segments closely and stops once enough evidence is gathered. Multi-hop reasoning over found clues suits surveillance review, lectures, and sports analysis. Adaptive termination is part of the design, so the system stops searching once the evidence is sufficient for an answer.
arxiv-2602-00224: Anatoly Dymarsky and Alfred Shapere extend mass formulas to TQFT boundary settings. Mass formulas count a class of algebraic structures, for instance lattices or codes, with weights. Here that count comes from averaging the TQFT partition function over closed 3D manifolds. That count can be read as TQFT gravity's renormalized partition function. For Abelian theories, the formula reduces to mass formulas for some code families, and the authors work it out for any bosonic theory.
arxiv-2602-00424: Philipp Hoellmer and Stefano Martiniani introduce open generation with inference time RL. Such models for crystal materials enable inverse design, but adding target properties into generation remains hard. That learning aligns models with downstream goals but typically requires access to the score, blocking use in flow models learning only velocity fields. Their system operates on learned fields and removes explicit score math. It uses random nudges to dynamics keeping base performance while enabling exploration and policy change.
arxiv-2602-00524: Erick Pastén and colleagues frame wormhole throat passage as a local, covariant null defocusing rule drawn from the Raychaudhuri equation. Because unimodular gravity leaves spacetime's local geometry alone, geodesic paths focus just as in general relativity. They show a traversable wormhole in unimodular gravity must break the null energy condition. The result is a local no-go theorem for such objects held up by normal matter in this framework.
arxiv-2602-00624: Hyekyung Yoon and colleagues study multivariate long-term time series forecasting, where embedding, backbone refinement, and long-horizon prediction rule. Backbone layers remain little studied, so they introduce layer sensitivity, a gradient-based metric of each time point's plus and minus effects on a layer's latent features. Applied to a three-layer MLP backbone, it reveals depth-specific specialisation in time dynamics. Their MoDEx mixture of depth-specific experts replaces backbones, ranking first in 78 percent of cases on seven benchmarks with far fewer weights.
arxiv-2602-00924: Ouns El Harzli and colleagues supervise decoder-only sparse auto-encoders to rebuild feature vectors by jointly learning sparse concept vectors and decoder weights. Sparse auto-encoders face non-smooth L1 penalty problems hurting rebuilds and scaling, plus mismatch between learned features and human meanings. They adapt free feature models from neural collapse theory and supervise the task. On Stable Diffusion 3.5, the approach shows compositional generalization, rebuilding images with unseen concept mixes and enabling feature-level edits for meaning-based image editing without prompt changes.
arxiv-2602-01124: Md Abrar Jahin and co-authors build ChronoSpike, a spike graph net for shifting graphs. Focus plans shine but cost square time, loop plans trip on slope ills and dense states, and spike nets lose bits through binary, local steps. ChronoSpike joins learnable leaky spike cells with per-channel cell tunes, wide focus over place, and a light time transformer. It beat twelve top baselines on three big tests while training far faster than loop plans, on a fixed small weight budget.
arxiv-2602-01224: Maor Ben Zaquen and Ron Holzman finish the axiom portrait of Random Serial Dictatorship for handing out indivisible goods. A random order is drawn, and each person in turn picks their top remaining good, a plan used for school seats and housing. For three people and three goods, past proof showed thrift, equal care for equals, and cheat-proofness pin the plan down alone. This work names just which market sizes keep that lone pin, builds rival plans where it fails, and asks if extra axioms could kill those rivals.
arxiv-2602-01724: Tushar Anand and colleagues build DenVisCoM, a Mamba block plus Transformer attention hybrid for joint real time optical flow and disparity estimation. Motion and multi view geometry tasks are deeply related, so one unified design tackles them together, with inference speed, memory footprint and accuracy in one. The authors analyze the accuracy versus real time tradeoff across many data sets. Their model estimates optical flow and disparity well in real time, with models and code released.
arxiv-2602-01824: Daniel Mwesigwa and colleagues study credit scoring in Nairobi, Kenya, through nine months watching digital lending. Telcos and banks use private data for loans, while new actors, techniques and regulations transform scoring. Practitioners build alternative data with workarounds, frame risk through readings, and negotiate performance by technical and political means. The authors argue scoring is done through alignment that steadies risk under uncertainty, in epistemic, modeling and contextual forms. Alignment works as translation: models are made safe for worlds, while worlds change to fit models.
arxiv-2602-02224: Georgi Ivanov and others develop a spectral theory of feature shape in neural networks, where more traits than sizes force sharing of representational space. The team analyzes spectra of weight-derived matrices through a frame operator, giving a spectral measure of how each feature allocates norm across eigenspaces. Earlier tools captured only pairwise contacts, while spectral methods capture global shape among all traits. In toy superposition models, the theory proves capacity saturation forces spectral localization, with traits collapsing onto single eigenspaces and organizing into tight frames.
arxiv-2602-02324: Andres Enrique Quintero Santander studies holomorphic and random motion of rank-two free groups generated by a pair of Hénon-type maps. In these simply constructed cases, he proves the Fatou set is non-empty and stationary measures rest on a compact set. With further care, the build yields cases having no stationary measures at all. These cases illustrate phenomena that can arise when studying holomorphic actions of groups on non-compact manifolds.
arxiv-2602-02424:
Ronaldo F. de Lima and 1 co-author develop the theory of translating solitons in hyperbolic space, in a 2026 arXiv paper. A translating soliton is a surface that moves under mean curvature flow, a process that shrinks surfaces toward their centers of curvature, while keeping its shape. The setting is hyperbolic space of dimension at least three.

The pair prove that horospheres, the hyperbolic versions of flat planes that touch at the far edge, are stable in motion as radial graphical solutions. Stability means nearby surfaces flow toward the same behavior rather than veering away. The proof builds wing-shaped translators that look the same after any turn, modeled on earlier flat-space examples. Those wings act as barriers inside a proof using the avoidance principle and the strong maximum principle for parabolic equations.
arxiv-2602-02524:
Olha Wloch and 3 co-authors argue that harmful content online cannot be judged from words alone, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The same sentence can be support in one community and abuse in another. Meaning depends on local norms, so detection models need community context built in.

Their system, GASTON, learns text and user embeddings grounded in those local norms. A contrastive pretraining step builds community embeddings from user membership patterns before any text is read. That lets the system tell a support group from a hate group by who gathers there, even when vocabularies overlap. On stress detection, toxicity scoring, and norm violation tasks, the embeddings beat state-of-the-art baselines. The design treats community identity as first-class evidence for moderation.
arxiv-2602-02824:
Removing unwanted knowledge from large language models is the problem tackled in a 2026 paper by Zhengbang Yang and 3 co-authors. Their method, called CALIBURN, aims to erase unsafe or private material. At the same time, it tries to keep the model's general ability intact.

CALIBURN measures how confident the model is in the unwanted knowledge. It then uses that measure to adjust the unlearning updates more precisely. Tests on benchmarks named MUSE and WMDP show effective removal. The authors report a better balance between forgetting and keeping useful knowledge than earlier methods, with less need for large retention datasets.
arxiv-2602-02924:
Xiaoyuan Cheng and 9 co-authors study how to keep reinforcement learning safe when policies use diffusion models, in a 2026 paper. Diffusion policies can represent varied action patterns, unlike simple single-mode policies. Most diffusion-based learning, though, targets offline reward maximization and ignores safety during online learning.

Their algorithm, ALGD, uses an augmented Lagrangian, a modified constraint penalty from optimization theory. The authors show the plain Lagrangian can be read as an energy guiding the diffusion process, but using it directly destabilizes training. The augmented version smooths the energy landscape locally. Theory and experiments across varied environments follow. Performance stayed strong and stable, without changing the optimal policy's distribution.
arxiv-2602-03124:
Children and neural networks learn categories in strikingly other ways, according to Fanxiao Wani Qiu, joined by 1 colleague. Their 2026 study uses a species-fair design, giving both learners novel object categories under identical cases. Each receives a mix of labeled and unlabeled examples, while the team varies label counts, target traits, and perceptual matching between examples shown during training.

Children generalized rapidly from very few labels. They also showed strong trait-given biases and sensitivity to matching. The networks behaved differently. More supervision helped them, but matching and trait form moderated that benefit in complex ways. The authors argue human-machine comparisons must examine such interactions, not overall score alone.
arxiv-2602-03724:
Switchbacks, sudden reversals of the solar wind's magnetic field, seemed to vanish in the slowest, sub-Alfvénic wind near the Sun. Nikos Sioulas and 8 co-authors show in a 2026 paper that the disappearance was an artifact of how the data were sliced. Measurements from Parker Solar Probe and Solar Orbiter supply the evidence.

Two diagnostic biases hid the events: instant wind-speed readings inflated by the rotations themselves, and short local averaging windows that tracked the rotations. Using rolling medians and event-independent backgrounds recovers sub-Alfvénic switchbacks systematically. Below the Alfvén point, mean deflection grows rapidly, consistent with expansion-driven amplification. Above it, growth turns scale-dependent under turbulent decay, tracing a formation pathway from corona to wind.
arxiv-2602-03824:
Jiao Sun measures bird shape with a neural network instead of a ruler in a 2026 paper on avian morphological evolution. Classic morphometrics needs hand-placed landmarks on homologous points, a slow and judgment-based craft that cannot capture plumage or texture. Sun instead extracts feature vectors from a convolutional network trained on images of over ten thousand bird species.

Placed into a high-dimensional morphospace, the embeddings recover classical taxonomy without being told any of it. They capture both homology and convergence, and their principal components correlate with known ecological and morphological traits. A new spherical method for rebuilding ancestral states reveals an early-burst pattern of disparity after the mass extinction that ended the dinosaurs. The pattern supports the niche-filling account of adaptive radiation.
arxiv-2602-03924:
One weather model for many jobs, with no retraining per job, is the aim of Michael Aich and 5 co-authors. Their 2026 paper introduces WIND, a foundation model pretrained by reconstructing atmospheric video from noise. At use time, each task is framed as an inverse problem and solved by sampling from the model.

The same system handles forecasting, sharpening coarse fields in space and time, and rebuilding full fields from sparse sensors. It can even enforce global dry air mass conservation. Tests extend to extreme weather under conditions outside its training range, a step toward unified climate tools.
arxiv-2602-04224:
Reasoning models can be taught to refuse, but jailbreaks still slip past. Zeming Wei and 3 co-authors blame shallow safe reasoning in a 2026 paper. Refusal training often produces safety checks too thin to withstand complex, disguised attack prompts.

Their Risk-Aware Preference Optimization trains models to size their safety reasoning to the risk at hand. Theory and experiments support the need for more sufficient deliberation against advanced attacks. Across diverse attack suites, the method generalized safe reasoning to several large reasoning models. The principle transfers beyond safety: the depth of a model's caution should scale with the threat it faces.
arxiv-2602-04724:
Chun Yu Ma and 7 co-authors study a noise source in ultra-stable lasers in a 2026 paper on crystalline mirror coatings. Coatings made from gallium arsenide alloys promise lower thermal noise than conventional ones. Yet several laser systems saw extra noise linked to birefringence, a direction-dependent optical property of the coating.

The team measured how light inside a cavity, and uniform external illumination at various wavelengths, changes that birefringence over time. A unified description emerged. Below a key photon energy, a two-photon process drives the effect; above it, a single-photon process dominates. Adding external light could balance two competing responses. That balance promises lower noise from laser power fluctuations at favorable operating points.
arxiv-2602-04824:
Samuel W. Flint, Robert Dyer, and Bonita Sharif test a common belief about programmers in a 2026 eye-tracking study: that developers read type notes in code as if they were docs. Statically typed code helps on many tasks even with no type checking, and reading the notes is the usual story for why.

Twenty-six students did code summary and bug hunting tasks in TypeScript while their eye moves were tracked. The team compared focus on lines with type notes or declarations, with and without types present. Developers did not look directly at those lines more often in either task. The authors discuss what this means for tool builders, shared standards on type use, and teaching students careful code-reading habits.
arxiv-2602-05124:
Hamilton-Jacobi equations govern optimal control and front propagation, but solving them in many dimensions defeats ordinary grids. Yesom Park and Stanley Osher propose a mesh-free method in this 2026 numerical analysis paper. Their approach leans on the Hopf-Lax formula, which turns the equation into a variational problem solved by repeated fixed-point steps.

Because the iteration needs neither a grid nor derivatives, both the solution and its associated control come out directly. Experiments reached problems in up to 100 dimensions, including control tasks and solutions with sharp kinks where smoothness fails. Accuracy stayed high and efficiency strong, and, most strikingly, computation time barely grew with dimension. That near-independence of dimension is the paper's selling point, since high-dimensional Hamilton-Jacobi problems are exactly where classical methods collapse under the curse of dimensionality.
arxiv-2602-05224:
Hard optimization problems can be phrased as finding the ground state of an Ising model, and quantum hardware is not the only place to borrow tricks from. Ryo Watanabe and 3 co-authors propose a quantum-inspired tensor network algorithm in this 2026 paper. The idea is spectral filtering: transform the cost Hamiltonian so its best solutions become its largest eigenvalues, then amplify them by repeated multiplication.

The transformed operator is stored as a matrix product operator, and enormous powers of it are built through truncated contractions, then embedded in a matrix product state for sampling candidate solutions. Unlike the density-matrix renormalization group, accuracy improves systematically by raising the bond dimension, and the method is less prone to local minima. Tests on a higher-order Ising problem over a heavy-hexagonal lattice, the layout used by some quantum processors, compare favorably with simulated annealing.
arxiv-2602-05324:
Computing equilibria in dynamic games is painful because every player's optimality conditions are tangled with everyone else's. Mahdis Rabbani and 2 co-authors restructure the problem in this 2026 game theory paper, submitted to RSS 2026. Joint solvers need every objective and constraint written out, while learning approaches decouple the players and lose equilibrium consistency.

Their formulation embeds a best-response map, computed offline or learned, as a feasibility constraint inside a reduced problem, stripping out nested optimization layers and derivative coupling. When the best-response map is exact, any converged solution is a genuine local Nash or generalized Nash equilibrium for that game. With a learned surrogate, the error tracks the surrogate's error. A large Monte Carlo study on a two-player game modeled on autonomous racing compares the method with leading joint solvers on solution quality, cost, and constraint satisfaction.
arxiv-2602-06224:
Tiny dwarf galaxies are hard to spot beyond our local neighborhood, so surveys risk missing most of them. Evangela E Shread and 4 co-authors use the TNG50 simulation to predict how many dwarfs should sit within a modest distance of Local Group-like settings. Their focus is the zone a few to a few dozen megaparsecs out.

The simulation holds thousands of dwarfs in that zone, split between lonely field dwarfs and satellites of larger galaxies. Comparing against a real galaxy catalog, the team estimates current observations catch only a small share of the faintest dwarfs. New wide-field surveys should reveal many more. The predictions give those surveys a target to aim at.
arxiv-2602-06324:
Antiperovskites copy the perovskite crystal pattern with the chemistry flipped, opening room for odd electronic phases. He Zhu and Turan Birol study a family built from tetrel elements (silicon, germanium, tin, lead) with alkaline earth metals and oxygen. Crystal structure trends in these compounds are far less mapped than in ordinary perovskites.

Using first-principles calculations, they show that a tolerance factor, a size-matching rule, predicts the structures in much the same way as for perovskites. They further show that ordering the cations in layers can switch on ferroelectricity, giving experimenters a knob for tuning electronic behavior. The electronic structure shows strong antibonding between face-center ions, a trait effective models should not ignore.
arxiv-2602-06724:
Tian Lan and nine co-authors reframe long research tasks for AI agents as filling in a table. Agents that search for information over many steps tend to lose focus, because their plans and findings pile up as fragile plain text. In their framework, each question becomes a table kept in an outside database, with rows for candidates and columns for the facts that must be found.

Filled cells record what has been verified, and empty cells form an explicit to-do plan, so the search state is never lost. One scheme covers three task styles: deep searches, wide searches, and a combined form that is hardest. In experiments the table approach beat strong baselines, including multi-agent systems and commercial products, and stayed robust on long tasks while remaining efficient and flexible.
arxiv-2602-06824:
El Mahdi Chayti and Mohamad Fakhouri work on a speed trick for training models. In momentum methods, the push from past steps lags behind the latest slope, and a second-order fix can close that gap. Old fixes, though, need either a smooth second slope or extra passes at a side point.

The pair let the step size vary at random, drawn from a spread with a set mean. A math link then turns one second-order product at the new point into a fair guess of how the slope changed, with no extra pass. Their method, RanSOM, works for plain, sign, and Muon-style steps, and a second form keeps Frank-Wolfe steps inside bounds. On a small image test it matched rivals on score while updating faster than the side-point method.
arxiv-2602-06924:
Abinitha Gourabathina and four co-authors fix a fairness flaw in models tuned for average score. Such models often fail in a patterned way on some subgroups, and in health care the hit subgroups may be unmarked or unknown ahead of time. Old robust methods usually need group labels for training, checking, or model choice, which this setting cannot supply.

Their method, MARLA, needs none of those labels. It starts from a plain trained model and scores how likely each held-out case is to be misclassified. From those scores it finds a low-size subspace where errors pile up, then learns a rank-limited correction to the classifier's outputs inside that subspace. Across seven real data sets and three levels of group knowledge, worst-group scores rose while the method stayed fast and lean, with settings picked from data alone.
arxiv-2602-07024:
Valerio Belcamino and five co-authors build a system that reads human hand acts for robots that work beside people. For such teamwork, a robot must sense what its human partner intends and adapt on the fly. Hand acts in contact with the robot carry much of that signal. Their system joins two sensors: a modular glove with inertial units, and a vision-based tactile sensor.

Tests ran in three modes. First, offline sorting of pre-cut sequences. Second, live sorting under still conditions. Third, a realistic teamwork scene. Scores stayed high in all three modes, which suggests many teamwork settings could gain from this mix. Fusing wearable motion sensing with tactile vision gives robots a fuller, more trustworthy read on what their partners are doing.
arxiv-2602-07324:
Static analyzers usually trade precision for soundness, which limits where they can be used.  Abdullah H.  Rasheed proposes an analyzer that accepts user-supplied assumptions local to program points, letting those assumptions counteract imprecision where it hurts most.

Because assumptions are taken non-deterministically, the analysis becomes a function from sets of accepted assumptions to results. The paper shows how to optimize over that assumption space in two demonstrations.  Program analysis teams get a principled way to spend human insight exactly where automation is weakest, widening the useful reach of static analysis.
arxiv-2602-07824:
Foundation models live or die by data quality, yet scientific text is notoriously hard for models to learn from raw. Yiwei Qin and seven co-authors introduce Data Darwinism, a ten-level taxonomy in which better models produce better data for the next generation, and test it by building Darwin-Science, a 900-billion-token corpus.

Generative refinement and cognitive completion, which spell out reasoning and terminology, bridge the learnability gap in raw papers. Models pretrained from scratch on the corpus, with contamination-free baselines, gain over two points across more than twenty benchmarks after continued training, and up to eight points on domain-aligned tasks. The paper argues data processing, not just scale, unlocks scientific value.
arxiv-2602-08324:
Long step-by-step reasoning makes language models smart but slow, and squeezing those steps usually costs accuracy. Yuntian Tang and ten co-authors propose Extra-CoT, a method that cuts reasoning tokens sharply while keeping answers right. Their 2026 arXiv paper starts by training a compressor that shortens math reasoning without losing its meaning.

A model is then tuned on compressed examples at many budgets, so it learns to reason under tight token limits, and a new training rule rewards solving problems with fewer tokens. On one math test with a small model, the method trims over 73 percent of tokens while slightly raising accuracy. Readers get a practical route to cheaper, faster reasoning that does not trade away correctness.
arxiv-2602-08724:
Inverse rendering splits a scene into shape, material, and light, but guessing material and light from radiance alone is deeply ambiguous. Geng Lin and Matthias Zwicker propose RotLight, a capture setup that rotates the object a few times to break that ambiguity. Their arXiv paper targets the baked shadows and wrong colors that plague albedo estimates.

As few as two rotations cut artifacts markedly. A proxy mesh added for 2D Gaussian splatting enables accurate light tracing, a residual constraint, and better global illumination handling. Tests on synthetic and real datasets show superior albedo estimates at efficient compute cost. Readers get a simple capture trick plus a mesh aid for cleaner relighting and editing.
arxiv-2602-08824:
At the heart of the Milky Way lies a dense, crowded zone of gas and dust, and S. M. King and six co-authors measure how fast it is turning that gas into stars. Using new carbon monoxide readings from the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope, plus earlier surveys, they map temperatures and gas mass across the Central Molecular Zone.

Typical gas sits near 11 kelvin, but pockets near the Sgr B1 and B2 clouds top 120 kelvin. The total gas mass comes to about seven million suns. Star birth looks modest today yet stronger in the cold, dusty ridges, hinting the region may be gearing up for a more active phase.
arxiv-2602-09124:
Some white dwarfs in supersoft X-ray sources burn accreted fuel steadily, growing heavier, spinning faster, and amplifying their magnetic fields. Mayusree Das and three co-authors model that coupled evolution with the MESA stellar code and compute the resulting deformation with the Einstein-Maxwell solver XNS. A tilted magnetic field distorts the star, making it radiate continuous gravitational waves.

The strongest signals come near the end of thermal-timescale mass transfer, close to the Chandrasekhar limit, falling in the deci-hertz band targeted by planned detectors like DECIGO and BBO. Well-studied sources such as CAL 83 and RX J0019+2156 could be detectable, while blind searches might reveal hundreds of hidden systems and even flag future Type Ia progenitors.
arxiv-2602-09224:
Starspots reveal how stellar magnetic dynamos work, and Mikko Tuomi and two co-authors map them on Kepler-411, a known exoplanet host, with two independent methods. One models how rotating spots dim and brighten the star, accounting for geometry, differential rotation, and spot evolution; the other maps spots through transits, as planets occult dark patches.

The spot models reproduce the observed brightness variations well and pin down spot distributions and motions. No differential rotation is found: the profile fits rigid-body rotation with a period of 10.52 days, plus or minus 0.34. Three spot occultations by planet c land exactly on larger spot structures from the modulation modeling, cross-validating both approaches.
arxiv-2602-09424:
Generative models for molecules and biological sequences aim at samples with high rewards, such as drug-likeness, but guiding discrete diffusion models by intermediate rewards works poorly. Reward functions in science are jagged, so halfway rewards mislead more than they help. Prin Phunyaphibarn and Minhyuk Sung propose a test-time sampler in their 2026 paper that guides generation without leaning on those noisy midpoints.

Their Clean-Sample Markov Chain sampler builds a chain of clean samples using the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm, targeting the desired distribution directly. A proposal distribution formed by running forward and backward diffusion in sequence keeps the acceptance probability tractable. On molecule and biological sequence generation under varied reward functions, the method consistently beats prior approaches that rely on intermediate rewards. Local search over clean samples, the authors show, guides better than reward signals from half-formed ones.
arxiv-2602-09524:
Factory checks need flaw spotting without defect cases, since faulty samples are rare by nature. Han Zhou and three co-authors propose HLGFA, a 2026 design that learns a normal look from cross-detail match rather than pixel remake. High- and low-detail views of normal samples pass through a shared frozen backbone, and high-detail structure and detail traits guide polish of low-detail traits.

Guided tuning and gated leftover fix carry that guidance. At use, flaws appear on their own as regions where cross-detail match breaks down. A noise-aware boost plan further damps nuisance noise common on factory floors. On standard benchmarks the method scores very highly at both pixel and image levels, beating typical remake- and trait-based rivals on the MVTec AD set.
arxiv-2602-09724:
Many European languages hold rich biblical translation histories, yet existing corpora stress linguistic breadth over depth. Maciej Rapacz and Aleksander Smywiński-Pohl offer Targum, a multilingual corpus of over six hundred New Testament translations, more than three hundred unique, spanning five languages. Their 2026 paper reports several times more translations per language than any prior corpus. English leads with nearly two hundred unique versions from nearly four hundred total.

The corpus draws on twelve online biblical libraries plus one prior corpus. Each translation carries metadata mapping the text to a standard identifier for the work, its edition, and its revision year. This mapping lets researchers define uniqueness for their own needs. Micro-level studies can trace translation families such as the King James lineage, while macro-level studies can deduplicate closely related texts. Targum fills a gap in the quantitative study of translation history.
arxiv-2602-09824:
Sensor nets have become vital with the rapid advance of net-of-things and edge compute, yet high rollout cost hinders large rollout. Xuhang Wu and four co-authors note that spatial filling adds virtual sensors guessing readings from seen sensors via graph structure. Current graph-based methods rely on ready-made models, lack tuning to larger unseen graphs at test time, and miss test data. Their 2026 paper offers PlugSI, a plug-and-play frame tuning the test-time graph.

Two new ideas drive the frame. An Unknown Shape Adapter adapts to each small batch's new graph structure, lifting spread of ready-made filling models. A Time Balance Adapter keeps a stable past accord guiding adapter updates and blocking drift from noise in the current batch. Wide tests show PlugSI joining smoothly into current graph-based filling methods with big gains, including about a tenth lower mean absolute error.
arxiv-2602-09924:
Running a reasoning model at full stretch on every question wastes compute, yet guessing which questions need the extra effort is hard. A 2026 paper led by William Lugoloobi, with three co-authors, asks whether a model already knows, before it writes, how likely it is to succeed. The team trains simple linear probes on the model's internal activations from before generation.

Those probes beat surface clues like question length on mathematics and coding tasks, and they reveal a model-specific sense of difficulty distinct from human judgment. Routing questions across a pool of models with these probes beat the best single model while cutting inference cost by as much as seventy percent. Internal signals, the paper suggests, can make inference both stronger and cheaper.
arxiv-2602-10024:
Reports built from multilingual sources pose a distinct challenge for retrieval and generation systems. A 2026 overview led by Dawn Lawrie, with five co-authors, describes the RAGTIME track at TREC 2025, built to study report generation from multilingual documents. Its collection gathers Arabic, Chinese, English, and Russian news stories.

The track ran three tasks: reports in several languages, reports in English, and retrieval across languages. Thirteen teams plus coordinator baselines submitted a hundred and twenty-five runs across the three tasks. The overview lays out the tasks and presents the available results, giving later systems a shared measuring stick.
arxiv-2602-10224:
Reinforcement learning with checkable rewards strengthens language model thought, but it lacks the error tracing and experience reuse of human learning cycles. A 2026 paper led by Shiting Huang, with nine co-authors, offers Meta-Experience Learning, which distills reusable knowledge from past errors into the model's stored memory. Self-checking drives side-by-side study of paired right and wrong paths, pinpointing where thought splits into error.

Those split points are summed up into broad meta-experience and built in by minimizing negative log-likelihood, creating a language-modeled reward signal linking right and wrong paths. Tests show steady benchmark gains of about four to five percent in Pass@1 across model sizes, showing useful knowledge reuse from mistakes.
arxiv-2602-10924:
James Neill and two co-authors present a Bayesian inference recipe for epidemic state-transition models in a 2026 paper. Fitting single-level disease data requires inferring unobserved disease statuses over time, a large and highly linked state space. Their recipe, Rippler, jointly estimates model settings and unobserved statuses through data-augmentation Markov chain Monte Carlo.

Rippler is a non-centred method applicable to any single-based state-transition model, a generality its competitors lack. Comparisons against state-of-the-art inference methods for random epidemic models show it performs better as the number of disease states grows. The paper gives epidemiologists a scalable inference tool for models where people, not just populations, carry the motion.
arxiv-2602-11224:
Agent benchmarks must balance control against realism. Hubert M. Pysklo and two co-authors present Agent-Diff, a frame for testing language-model agents on enterprise API tasks through code execution. It keeps real API interfaces while sandboxing the setting where calls run and are judged.

Two ideas drive it: a state-diff contract that defines success by the change in setting state, not by trace matching, and a sandbox of containerized replicas of enterprise APIs. Nine models were tested across hundreds of enterprise workflow tasks, with ablations on the value of API documentation. The paper offers a controlled yet realistic yardstick for agentic productivity software.
arxiv-2602-11424:
Fine-tuning usually weights every token equally, which misfires in two ways. Zecheng Wang and seven co-authors unify token-level fine-tuning objectives in a generalized deformed-log family, exposing a gate-times-error gradient structure. The gate controls how much the model trusts its current forecast.

A Cayley transform maps evolving doubt onto a continuous focus path, interpolating between novel concepts and established knowledge. Their Moving Entropy Fine-Tuning objective, setting-free, modulates the gate with a concentration measure as a proxy for predictive state. Tests show a better balance between exploration and exploitation, improving overall results without suppressing needed learning signals.
arxiv-2602-11924:
As language models join high-stakes choices, who does what in the partnership matters. Shreya Chappidi and two co-authors name the recurring patterns human-LLM archetypes: stable socio-technical shapes that set the roles of people and models in joint decisions. From a scoping review and thematic analysis of 113 papers on model-supported decisions, they describe 17 such archetypes.

They then test the archetypes on real clinical diagnostic cases to see how each choice shapes model outputs and final decisions. The analysis covers tradeoffs in decision control, social hierarchy, cognitive forcing, and information needs. The central finding is that picking an archetype is not neutral: it can shift outputs and outcomes, so designers of human-AI decision systems must weigh that choice with care.
arxiv-2602-12024:
Coordinating large robot fleets in warehouses demands planners that are fast, safe, and adaptable to surprises. Jiarui Li and three co-authors present Anytime Closed-Loop Conflict-Based Search, a closed-loop algorithm built on a finite-horizon variant of Conflict-Based Search with a horizon-changing mechanism borrowed from model predictive control. It adjusts its planning horizon to the available compute budget and reuses a single constraint tree across horizon changes.

That design yields high-quality feasible solutions quickly and approaches optimality as budget grows, showing anytime behavior. Case studies show a favorable balance among compute efficiency, solution quality, and execution flexibility, with online disturbances handled naturally by the closed-loop form. For safety-critical fleets, the combination of guarantees and responsiveness is the point: plans improve with budget yet remain usable at any moment.
arxiv-2602-12224:
Matching platforms must pair two sides who each know only a slice of their own tastes. Amirmahdi Mirfakhar led this work with four co-authors, studying markets where short interviews, profile views, or trial tasks give noisy hints before applications and offers. Firms, too, learn as they go and can hire too early.

The paper adds strategic deferral, a firm move to leave a post open for a round, fixing hasty hires and aiding decentralised learning from coarse, anonymous feedback. Methods are given for central and decentralised markets, and a constant number of interviews per round suffices for regret that does not grow with the horizon. That beats prior log-horizon bounds and sits near the best possible limits.
arxiv-2602-12324:
Some gas-rich early-type galaxies form stars far less than their gas supply suggests, and the reason is debated. Lori E. Porter led this work with three co-authors, running five high-resolution AREPO simulations: one Milky Way-like galaxy and four early-type galaxies. One early-type case forms far fewer stars despite a large molecular gas reservoir.

Applying a modified virial theorem to dense clumps, the team finds strong Coriolis forces from high galactic shear may block collapse in the suppressed galaxy. Its high central compactness drives that shear, offering a suppression path that needs no gas removal. Less compact early types host more gravity-led clouds and form more stars, yet the classic Toomre-Q measure barely moves, so a new suppression criterion may be needed.
arxiv-2602-12424:
Benchmarks rank language models, but most treat every question as equally hard, blurring real capability gaps. Ziqian Zhang led this work with ten co-authors, presenting RankLLM, a frame that scores both question difficulty and model skill together. Difficulty becomes the main lens for telling models apart, rather than a raw count of correct answers.

Scores flow both ways: a model earns skill credit for answering a question, while a question gains difficulty credit when it stumps a model. Tested on 30 models and 35,550 questions across domains, RankLLM agrees with human judgements 90 percent of the time, beating strong baselines such as IRT. It also shows stability, fast convergence, and high efficiency, making difficulty-aware ranking practical at large scale.
arxiv-2602-13024:
Federated learning lets parties train jointly without sharing data, but most methods iterate expensive deep networks and still leak information through gradients. Alejandro Dopico-Castro and four co-authors propose FedHENet, a frugal system for image sorting in mixed settings. It uses a fixed, pre-trained feature extractor and learns only a single output layer, avoiding costly local fine-tuning.

That layer is learned by combining client knowledge analytically in one communication round under homomorphic encryption, so data stay protected while updates combine exactly. Tests show competitive closeness against iterative federated plain rivals, superior calm, and up to 70% better energy leanness. The method is hyperparameter-free, removing the carbon cost of tuning sweeps. For privacy-sensitive vision tasks, frugality and closeness need not conflict.
arxiv-2602-13124:
Lattice gauge theories suffer sign problems, but tensor networks sidestep them, though extracting universal transition data remains hard. Adwait Naravane and four co-authors study deconfinement in (2+1)-D Z_N gauge theories on a lattice at finite temperature with thermal tensor networks. Partition functions become three-D tensor networks, contracted first in time, then coarse-grained in space to yield a renormalised transfer matrix whose spectrum encodes conformal field theory data.

Extracting central charge and scaling dimensions confirms the Svetitsky-Yaffe universality forecast for N equal to 2, 3, and 5. The Z_5 theory additionally shows an intermediate phase with emergent U(1) balance at finite temperature. Critical couplings from Gu-Wen ratios match Monte Carlo results, and extrapolating finite-temperature couplings finds zero-temperature deconfinement points for N equal to 2 and 3, a strong checks of the tensor-network approach.
arxiv-2602-13224:
Mirages in deployed language models can mislead calls in healthcare, legal, and money settings, yet live-use spotting sees only query, response, and sometimes a source document. Javier Marín argues that shape of the placing space offers clear spotting: wins and misses map to shape traits of contrast training. He puts forward three working types sorted by how the response placing sits against the trust region for grounded answers on the unit ball.

He derives one forecast per type from the line-up goal. First, an angular ratio detects query-near unfaith. Second, fibbing beyond the trust region leaves an aimed mark beating natural language inference on expert-tagged error. Third, factual errors sharing word list and frame with correct answers resist split by angular shape. Checked on 212 human-fibbed pairs across nine domains, created by prodded fibbing, the scheme's forecasts hold, showing shape predicts ease of spotting.
arxiv-2602-13524:
Reading features off singular vectors of attention matrices is common practice, but why that should work was not well justified. This paper asks why and when singular vectors line up with features, first demonstrating a robust match in a model where features can be observed directly. Theory then shows such a match is expected under a range of conditions, giving the empirical practice a principled footing.

The paper closes with a practical question: how can a match be spotted in real models where features are not directly seen? Sparse attention splitting is flagged as a testable prediction of a match, and evidence shows it emerging in real models as predicted. Together the results support singular-vector matching as a sound basis for finding features. Gabriel Franco leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14124:
Narges Tarakameh Samani and two co-authors build a 2026 arXiv model of non-linear effects in a tiny machine system. Control of such effects matters for sensing, signal work, and rate control. The device is a nano-string resonator with two vibrational modes, tuned by a DC voltage.

The voltage-tuned energy rule gives back a seen avoided crossing with no AC drive. It also gives tunable comb spectra when a parametric drive is on. Scanning the DC voltage maps comb birth and sharp regime edges to splits, multi-calm states, and attractor flips. Phase checks based on a Kuramoto order mark, plus auto-correlation and Poincaré checks, gauge coherence and slow-down near shifts, framing a design guide for nano devices.
arxiv-2602-14324:
Jinzheng Li and one co-author test a 2026 arXiv source for the nano-Hertz gravitational wave background. Pulsar timing arrays, including NANOGrav, EPTA, and PPTA, recently detected that background, opening a window on early-universe physics. The paper studies a supercooled first-order phase transition in a hidden sector whose U(1) gauge symmetry breaks on its own.

Thermal history of hidden and visible sectors proves crucial to the gravitational wave spectrum. The analysis shows supercooled transitions can generate waves strong enough to explain pulsar timing observations, while still satisfying Big Bang Nucleosynthesis constraints. The result keeps a hidden-sector phase transition alive as a candidate source for the observed background.
arxiv-2602-14524:
Ari Vesalainen and three co-authors weigh a 2026 arXiv pair of OCR systems on eighteenth-century printed texts. Old OCR is hard: worn print, old glyphs, and non-standard spelling test even strong systems. Overall gauges such as letter and word error rates tell little about trust for scholar use, so the paper adds guess-led error study.

A special OCR transformer, TrOCR, is weighed against a broad vision-language model, Qwen, on line-level old English texts using length-weighted exactness. Qwen hit lower error rates and greater toughness to worn input, but it showed picky language smoothing and spelling norming that may silently shift past-meaning forms. TrOCR kept spelling faith more steadily but suffered more cascading error spread, showing how design shapes error form.
arxiv-2602-14724:
Lukas Liehr determines, in any dimension, the Cheeger constant and Cheeger sets of a Gaussian mixture built from two Gaussians with weights p and one minus p. He characterises the Cheeger sets as specific half-spaces perpendicular to the line joining the two centres, confirming the conjectured solution to the Cheeger problem for such mixtures.

Liehr then studies the parameter regime in which the mixture admits a unique Cheeger set, pinning down when the optimal shape is single. The result turns a geometric optimisation problem into clean, explicit form. Isoperimetry for mixed Gaussians now has an answer in full generality.
arxiv-2602-14924:
Maurizio Piai and James Rucinski trace a light dilaton from top-down holographic confinement with magnetic fluxes. A two-knob clan of hard-coupled confining laws, with flux for two plain gauge groups, gains a twin that falls from top supergravity in eleven-space through seven-space answers.

Heat and cold steadiness tests show first-order shift lines that form a square in flux space, fencing confining answers in from others out. A light dilaton shows up near those shifts, the team reports. Holographic confinement thus gains a top-down, flux-tuned case with a light scalar.
arxiv-2602-15024:
Kwong and Mori model how isolated magnetars spin down, testing whether long-period radio transients are simply old magnetars. These transients form a new class of radio sources with long spin periods and highly variable emission, while known magnetars are young with clustered periods. The team runs a broad parametric study of spin evolution across several propeller spin-down models.

Higher starting magnetic fields and denser surroundings push stars into the propeller phase sooner, followed by gas intake from the interstellar medium or molecular clouds. A pulsar-to-propeller switch proves necessary to reach the observed transient period range. In Monte Carlo population synthesis, two propeller models account for most observed periods and period derivative limits. The models predict nearby radio-quiet neutron stars, fading accretion X-rays, and outbursts that standard pulsar emission cannot explain.
arxiv-2602-15124:
Xuan and colleagues tackle zero-shot human-object interaction detection. The task locates people and objects in images and names what they do together. Open-vocabulary object detection now handles finding things well. But naming pairings lags, since possible pairings combine in huge variety. Existing methods tie naming to one detector and lean on coarse vision-language features. That limits transfer to unseen pairings.
