Fiducial runs span three resolutions matching galaxy mass function and cluster gas fractions, while other runs vary cosmology and dark matter. A web service lets users explore and download datasets.
arxiv-2604-24924: Delepine and Khalil test the Left-Right Inverse Seesaw model through the decay tau to K pi nu-tau. In this model, TeV-scale right-handed neutrinos carry order-one Yukawa couplings while light neutrino masses stay protected by a violating scale. They identify a signal in the forward-backward CP asymmetry. They show the asymmetry is enhanced near K0-star-1430, reaching order 10 to the power minus 4, within reach of Belle II.
arxiv-2604-25124: Donohue and eight colleagues report on USEQIP, a two-week summer school in experimental quantum information processing. The school has run since 2009, paired with a summer internship program, to draw undergraduates from around the world into quantum research tools. The paper covers its structure, its hands-on lab work refined over many rounds and its outlook. It also tracks alumni careers, noting that many past students now contribute much to the quantum field.
arxiv-2604-25724: Prasad and Arora report a production deployment study of a modular inference architecture for compound AI systems. It was built at Salesforce for agent workflows such as Agentforce and code analysis with ApexGuru. Compound systems combine models, retrievers, and tools, demanding infrastructure that serves mixed, concurrent calls cheaply and quickly. Their platform uses serverless execution and dynamic autoscaling, plus machine-learning operations pipelines. Production results more than halved tail latency, raised throughput to almost four times the prior level, and cut costs by roughly a third.
arxiv-2604-25924: Verşebeniuc and six colleagues build a retrieval-augmented assistant for Maastricht University students facing bachelor project rules. Language models offer human-like answers to complex questions, but hallucination, missing facts, and context-specific accuracy remain problems in specialized domains. Their assistant grounds answers in up-to-date domain knowledge to raise accuracy and reliability. Tests with a robust evaluation framework and real-life trials show it meets student needs well. The work also points to open questions for LLM systems built for specific uses.
arxiv-2604-26024: Maxson and four colleagues fix bias in imbalanced classification with minority subconcepts. Class scores hide gaps across subconcepts in one class. Earlier scores favor larger minority subconcepts; true-label weighting helps, but such labels rarely exist at test time. The authors use predicted posteriors from a multi-class subconcept model. Weights are mean utility under that posterior, giving the soft predicted-weighted balanced accuracy (pBA) metric. On tabular, imaging, and text data, plain scores mislead in mixed classes, while pBA gives stabler reads.
arxiv-2604-26124: Ward and six colleagues report recent work on colliders. Their method improves infrared poles through amplitude-based resummation. It treats quantum electrodynamics and quantum chromodynamics jointly inside a larger gauge structure. It targets results precise enough for future machines. Uses span the Large Hadron Collider and its planned follow-up, linear machines, and other planned electron-positron machines, with new results and newly flagged issues for each setting.
arxiv-2604-26224: O'Brien studied weighted means from a positive Dunford-Schwartz operator on noncommutative Lp spaces, a setting where order of multiplication matters. He carried the classical subsequence argument into that setting and found many weighting sequences with a decay rule that the noncommutative individual ergodic theorem accepts as weights. The list covers sequences built from bounded independent draws and the Möbius function. Kindred results hold for T-admissible processes when the exponents meet a duality rule.
arxiv-2604-26424: Zapparoli and three colleagues built a two-stage stochastic scheduler for virtual power plants trading across energy and reserve markets under dynamic network tariffs. Detailed device and network limits join market and operational uncertainty, with conditional value-at-risk encoding risk appetite and Benders decomposition keeping large scenario sets tractable. Both cautious and bold strategies chased arbitrage, but risk aversion steadied profits by tracking physical dispatch more closely. Strong tariff signals cut expected profit by up to 65 percent with little extra flexibility gained.
arxiv-2604-26524: Bonança, Deffner, and Ingold traced Amir Caldeira's forty-year work on quantum Brownian motion. Starting from his early account of quantum Brownian motion, they stressed how dissipation changes tunneling out of a shaky state. They then followed his other routes past the Caldeira-Leggett model, through decoherence theory and quantum thermodynamics. The story shows how one physicist's frame kept shaping new fields across four decades.
arxiv-2604-26724: Li and six colleagues measure radial binary fraction profiles for 513 elliptical galaxies from the MaNGA survey, extending such studies beyond the Milky Way and its neighbors. After subtracting the effect of radial stellar-population variation, the median binary fraction turns approximately flat. For nearly all galaxies in the sample, the variation relative to the galaxy center at one effective radius stays under five percent. No clear link appears between the binary fraction gradient and stellar-population gradients, and UV-upturn and non-UV-upturn galaxies look comparable.
arxiv-2604-26924: Anderson and three colleagues test barium titanate films on silicon as a base for tunable acoustic resonators, filters for wireless bands. They excite symmetric Lamb modes in 120-nanometre membranes with a multi-cell electrode design that pairs strong coupling with workable impedance. Under DC bias, ferroelectric domains line up, letting voltage tune frequency and lift mode quality. The main resonance near 700 MHz shows a quality factor of 175 and coupling up to 25.1 percent, with modest series and parallel tuning.
arxiv-2604-27024: Bazarova and Alpay introduce the finite-horizon rank profile of a language: the smallest quantifier rank a first-order sentence needs to classify membership on words up to length n. They prove a rank calculus independent of regularity, bounding every language by ceiling log2 n plus 4. The supremum over n is finite exactly when the language is globally first-order definable, equaling the minimum rank of such a definition. For regular languages they prove a sharp gap: aperiodic monoids give bounded rank, others logarithmic rank.
arxiv-2604-27124: Sadashivaiah and three colleagues test sigmoid attention as a drop-in replacement for softmax attention in single-cell foundation models. Across six diverse single-cell datasets, sigmoid attention gives 25 percent higher cell-type separation, better cohesion, and lower validation loss, while training up to 10 percent faster. They trace the stability gain to bounded derivatives and a diagonal Jacobian structure, in contrast to the dense coupling of softmax, and stress-test large models without gradient clipping.
arxiv-2604-27724: Chen and seven colleagues propose MED-VRAG, an iterative multimodal retrieval system for medical question answering that reasons over document page images instead of OCR text. It couples patch-level page embeddings to a sharded MapReduce filter, scaling to about 350,000 pages with fast first-stage retrieval. A vision-language model then refines its query and banks evidence across up to three reasoning rounds. Across four medical benchmarks, MED-VRAG reaches 78.6 percent average accuracy, with retrieval adding about 6 points over no retrieval.
arxiv-2604-27824: Labib and three colleagues apply compressed sensing to gauge GHZ state fidelity, using their thinness to sharply reduce test load while keeping high care. They test the method on GHZ states using both quantum sims and Quantinuum's trapped-ion hardware. They add error catches during hardware tests, showing toughness and promise of compressed sensing for fidelity scores in noisy lab settings.
arxiv-2605-00024:
Ahmed Gamal Eldin presents evidence on the binding problem, the old puzzle of how scattered neural activity unifies into one conscious whole. His claim is that conscious unity relies on self-organized criticality maintained by brain-body resonance, placing human cognition among critical systems. The work uses recordings from a sixty-four-channel electroencephalogram.

He reports that standard cleaning of the recordings removes the very dynamics under study. Discarding bodily signals, usually treated as artifacts, sharply cuts the shared variance between global phase synchronization and stimulus-evoked responses. Raw data show heavy-tailed avalanche patterns of a near-critical regime, while cleaned data reject them. A resonance at a short time lag is reported to establish zero-lag synchronization with two-way causality, and spatial interference patterns are said to emerge after it, suggesting holographic encoding.
arxiv-2605-00224:
Abdulhady Abas Abdullah and 3 co-authors refine Direct Preference Optimization, a popular method for aligning language models with human choices. The standard method treats each preference as a flat win or loss. It also suffers when preferences are noisy, or when a fragile chain of thought produced the losing answer.

Their variant, TUR-DPO, also rewards how an answer is derived, not only what it says. It draws out light reasoning maps and mixes faithfulness, utility, and map quality into one uncertainty signal. That signal weights the training objective, with no reinforcement learning needed. On open models across math, factual questions, summaries, and dialogue, TUR-DPO beat the standard method on win rates, faithfulness, and calibration, and matched a heavier rival on reasoning tasks.
arxiv-2605-00524:
Aida Abiad, Stan van Hoesel, and Valentin Michaux study a classic spectral bound on graph structure and how hard it is to compute well. The inertia bound, dating to 1971, caps the independence number of a graph using eigenvalues of a weighted adjacency matrix. Recent extensions estimate independence and coloring numbers of graph powers, with applications in coding theory and quantum information.

Those inertia-type bounds hinge on choosing a polynomial and on the graph's eigenvalues, and optimizing them has meant solving several mixed-integer programs, which grow slow quickly. The authors improve those formulations, cutting the computational burden and running time significantly. They also settle the theory: for every fixed power, the optimization problems are solvable in polynomial arithmetic time given exact spectral input. The work makes a theoretically elegant bound practical to use at larger scale.
arxiv-2605-00624:
Brenno De Lucca and 5 co-authors model the L-H transition in tokamaks, the abrupt jump from low to high confinement that fusion reactors depend on. No one has explained it in over forty years. Their 3D, flux-driven simulations use a diverted geometry, the shape of real machines. The jump appears at lower power in the preferred field direction, matching the known asymmetry.

In the runs, electromagnetic drift-wave turbulence on its own creates a sheared flow that suppresses transport, the accepted signature of the high-confinement state. The field-direction asymmetry is traced to time-reversal symmetry breaking by finite collisionality, shown through a study of the momentum flux of the churning flow. From basic theory the authors derive scaling laws for the power threshold, the density minimum, and the minimum power. The laws match or beat the measured scalings engineers use today.
arxiv-2605-00824:
Yawen Qin, Ke Qiu, and Qin Zhang build tools for finding dance videos by describing the dance in words. Online dance content has grown fast, yet search must handle language, music rhythm, and full-body motion at once. The team releases TD-Data, a dataset of about four thousand short clips across twenty-two genres, with notes from professional dance experts.

On that data they build CustomDancer, which aligns text with dance through separate encoders for words, music, and motion, plus a module that blends music and motion. The system reaches top performance on TD-Data in their tests. Both benchmark scores and user preference studies point to better retrieval quality than prior methods.
arxiv-2605-00924:
Guantian Zheng presents StyleShield, a framework that exposes how easily AI content checkers can be evaded by style transfer. Checkers are used in high-stakes settings such as school honesty screening, yet the statistical gap between machine and human writing shrinks as models improve. StyleShield is described as the first flow matching method for conditional text style transfer, working in continuous token embedding space.

A single control parameter smoothly trades evasion against meaning preservation. On a multi-domain Chinese benchmark, evasion against the training checker and unseen checkers is very high while semantic similarity stays strong. A timing tool called RateAudit further shows detection-rate verdicts can be set to arbitrary values, questioning score-based evaluation.
arxiv-2605-01224:
Anjishnu Mukherjee and two co-authors argue that modern language models are multilingual only incidentally, and that this paradigm is fragile and misleading. Models appear multilingual because they train on massive, uneven web corpora, not because such competence was a core design goal. The authors contend this produces unequal, brittle, and opaque behavior across languages, with severe consequences for real and agentic deployments.

A focused study examines which languages models self-report as supported and which ones they actually respond in across prompts in many tongues. A simple language-change attack further surfaces hidden assumptions and failures. The authors call for multilingualism by design. Equitable performance, cultural grounding, and cross-lingual behavioral understanding should be first-class goals throughout the pipeline.
arxiv-2605-01424:
Richeng Zhou, Xuelin Zhang, and Liyuan Liu supply theory for multimodal metric learning, where a model learns distances from mixed inputs such as image, text, and sound. Real inputs often arrive with parts missing or duplicated, and how the choice of parts affects learning has been murky.

The authors order the model classes tied to each subset of modalities into a hierarchy, then measure the gap between learned maps and the truth. From pairwise complexity counts they derive fresh upper and lower bounds on generalization error, the gap between training and new-data scores. Both bounds show the same lesson: adding fine-grained features from more modalities can shrink the space of candidate models by making the parts back each other up. The results give builders a principled way to weigh extra modalities against cost.
arxiv-2605-01524:
Jingzhi Li, Zhiyong Cheng, Richang Hong, and Meng Wang add fairness for content providers to a recommender after it is trained, with no retraining of the main model. Providers need fair exposure to keep a platform healthy, but baking fairness into training means costly reruns whenever the goal shifts.

Their adapter learns small per-user score nudges from user and item embeddings and adds them to the frozen model's ranking, steering exposure toward a target spread. A plain global match can look fair overall while hiding gaps between and within provider groups, so a hierarchical alignment term balances both levels at once. A differentiable ranking loss guards accuracy while the adapter trains. On three public data sets the method wins large fairness gains at negligible accuracy cost, beating strong baselines throughout.
arxiv-2605-02024:
Uri Andrews, Luca San Mauro, and John Spoerl propose tenability, a new way to judge claims in a debate graph. In Dung-style work, a claim is sound if it can be defended against every attack. Weak forms relax which attacks count, but they still demand one defence that works against all fair attackers at once.

That demand can be too strong when the right reply depends on how the other side attacks. Tenability is based on dialogue. It states when a chosen claim, or a set of claims, can be held through such varied exchanges. The extended version gives the full definitions and compares tenability with past weak forms, aiming for a more strategic view of defence.
arxiv-2605-02124:
Rastegar works out what happens as a soft router hardens into a hard choice. In mixture-of-experts models, a router assigns each input to specialist sub-models, or experts. Softmax routing blends experts smoothly, while hard top-one routing picks a single winner; as temperature falls to zero, the soft gate should approach the hard one. That passage breaks down at ties, where the router is indifferent between two experts.

The key quantities are the margin between the top two experts and the share of inputs lying within a thin slab of the routing boundary. Under smoothness assumptions, geometric estimates show how that share scales with slab width, yielding uniform bounds between the soft and hard objectives. The main conclusion is precise: the zero-temperature approximation is governed by probability mass near the boundary, not by temperature alone.
arxiv-2605-02624:
Yu Lu Liu and three co-authors build a framework for judging how realistic simulated users are in multi-turn chats with chatbots. Simulated users could replace costly collection of real user data for testing chatbots, but only if their dialogues feel real. Older checks give a coarse score for a single dialogue, with no wider view.

Their framework, called realsim, compares real and simulated dialogues as distributions across eight dimensions. Those dimensions cover what the talk is doing, the user's state, and the surface form of messages. It is tested on a curated set of one thousand real task-focused dialogues across sixteen application domains. Simulated users, they find, miss the friction real users bring, which can make simulation-based tests too optimistic. Performance also varied by domain.
arxiv-2605-02724:
Yaxuan Wang and four co-authors present a method for rebuilding periodic time series after privacy noise has been added on the user's device. Periodic patterns drive many signals, from gait in video to rhythm in audio. Local differential privacy perturbs data before upload, which protects users, but the noise can corrupt spectral peaks and shift phase, wrecking period estimates.

Their framework first probes for the period at several scales and cross-checks candidates to suppress noise-made peaks. Samples are then grouped by matching phase within each cycle, stabilizing alignment across cycles. A denoising step that mixes an expectation-maximization method with density estimation recovers the per-phase values. On two real periodic datasets, the method kept periodic structure better and cut reconstruction error below standard privacy baselines, even under tight budgets.
arxiv-2605-03424:
Shalini Bhattacharya and Arathy Venugopal compute what happens to certain 2-adic crystalline Galois representations when they are reduced modulo 2. These representations, labeled V with parameters k and a2, encode deep arithmetic information. The authors work at small slopes, values in the interval from zero to one.

Using the compatibility between 2-adic and mod-2 local Langlands correspondences, they find the explicit form of the semisimplified reduction. Two parameter functions do the key work: one governs slopes strictly between zero and one, and the other governs slope exactly one. The result gives a concrete handle on objects that are usually described only abstractly.
arxiv-2605-03524:
Chiara Vercellino, Giacomo Vitali, Paolo Viviani, Edoardo Giusto, Alberto Scionti, Andrea Scarabosio, Olivier Terzo, and Bartolomeo Montrucchio present BBQ-mIS, a parallel hybrid algorithm for graph coloring on Rydberg atom quantum machines. Qubit counts limit problem size, so splitting across multiple small quantum resources is essential for real use.

The algorithm maps maximum independent set problems onto the machine Hamiltonian. Branch and bound then builds colorings, color by color. Emulated on an HPC cluster with MPI, the split preserved solution quality. The study also lists practical requirements for effective high-performance and quantum integration. The work shows how small quantum machines can team up on one hard task.
arxiv-2605-03824:
Vincent Degenhart and four co-authors test whether modern search systems truly satisfy complex queries built from conjunction, disjunction, and exclusion, or whether they take semantic shortcuts. They rerun earlier work across major retrieval families and reasoning-targeted methods on the QUEST benchmarks. They also introduce LIMIT+, a controlled benchmark where relevance depends on arbitrary attribute predicates rather than pre-trained knowledge.

On QUEST, the best neural retrievers more than doubled the recall of the classic BM25 method, though reasoning-targeted systems did not win uniformly. On LIMIT+, the strongest QUEST method collapsed to near-zero recall while lexical retrieval surged. Grouping by compositional depth showed consistent degradation for all methods, with sparse and lexical approaches more stable than dense ones.
arxiv-2605-04124:
Gerber fixes the standard errors of difference-in-differences estimators for survey data. These estimators compare changes over time between treated and untreated groups, and stay valid when effects vary across groups. Their theory, however, assumes simple random samples, while practitioners apply them to national surveys with cluster designs. Gerber shows that, under standard conditions, the estimators' influence functions satisfy Binder's smoothness conditions. The standard stratified-cluster variance formula then yields standard errors consistent with the design.

A Monte Carlo study with sixty-six thousand replications shows the stakes. Standard errors that ignore the design cover the truth as rarely as thirty-four percent of the time, and under eleven percent with informative sampling. Weighting plus clustering at the sampling unit restores near-nominal coverage. Full design detail adds precision. An NHANES illustration on the Affordable Care Act's dependent coverage rule shows conclusions can flip once the design is honored.
arxiv-2605-04224:
Shaun Swain, Tamanna Jain, and Llibert Aresté Saló study two black holes that fly past each other and scatter, rather than merging. Such close passes probe gravity in its strongest regime and offer another way to test Einstein's theory.

The team works in a modified gravity theory that adds a scalar field, running the first full nonlinear simulations of this kind of encounter. They compare the scattering angle with an analytic method that treats the pair as one body, and find the two agree well. That match supports future templates for signals from such systems.
arxiv-2605-04424:
Aditya R. Pujari and Amir A. Pahlavan combine experiments and computer models to study how a blob of colloidal particles spreads through a porous material when salt gradients are present. Such gradients are common in settings from cleaning contaminated ground to delivering drugs, and they push particles by a process called diffusiophoresis.

A joint blob of particles and strong salt is released into a medium with weak salt and a background flow. Common sense predicts attraction to the blob should hold particles together, but the opposite happens: attraction increases spreading along the flow, and repulsion reduces it. Computer models trace this reversal to particles exchanging between slow and fast regions.
arxiv-2605-04524:
Wang and eight colleagues rebuild a human head in 3D from a single photo, with topology fit for production. Single-image face reconstruction is ill-posed: many shapes could explain one flat image. Studios also need clean edge flow for rigging and animation, not just a good likeness. Their coarse-to-fine pipeline refines a rigged template through rig, joint, and vertex stages. It combines a normal-consistency objective with landmark alignment, plus geometry-aware constraints from curvature and conformal consistency. Those fix details like lip seams and eyelid breaks.

After geometry comes texture: UV-space texture and normal maps preserve appearance for downstream use. In a study with twenty-two professional technical artists, results approached industry-grade usability. Ninety-five percent ranked the method first. For digital humans and virtual reality, the framework narrows the gap between a quick reconstruction and a mesh an artist can actually use.
arxiv-2605-04624:
Yuelin Hu and four co-authors document a failure mode in leaderboards for automated program repair agents. Rankings shuffle when the evaluator is reconfigured. Part of that shuffling comes from methods that peek at evaluator-derived signals. They do so while choosing among candidate repairs. Such leakage makes leaderboard positions unreliable.

They release a paired-execution trace corpus with hundreds of thousands of registered cells. A large subset of those cells was executed. The corpus measures this ranking instability, inside a declared boundary of what can be observed. A modular screening architecture combines four different pathway-blocking checks into one posterior score. Validation on a hand-built set of channel-surgery cases anchors the corpus in real mechanisms.
arxiv-2605-04824:
Partha Kumar Paul, Narendra Sahu, and Shashwat Sharma connect three puzzles in particle physics: dark matter, tiny neutrino masses, and the excess of matter over antimatter. Their setting is a singlet-doublet dark matter model, a well-studied candidate for weakly interacting massive particles. Neutrino masses arise through a loop of new particles in their scheme.

The authors study two versions, one with Majorana particles and one with Dirac particles. In each, heavy new particles decay unevenly and out of equilibrium, creating the matter excess through leptogenesis. They find success below the tera-electronvolt scale in one version and at a few such units in the other.
arxiv-2605-04924: Jiaqian Yang and thirty co-authors demonstrate very fast two-way data transmission through a hollow-core fibre over a distance of sixty kilometres. Both directions used the same wavelengths across a wide band covering several standard optical windows. The measured quality matched the highest one-way rates reported for standard single-mode fibre in each direction.
arxiv-2605-05024:
Christopher Nemeth generates hypergraphs, structures where one link can join many points at once, with a diffusion model built directly on their incidence structure. Realistic generation is hard because pairwise reductions lose hyperedge sizes, overlap patterns, and linking detail. His model, HEDGE, noises the relaxed incidence matrix with a structured stochastic process instead.

The forward process mixes a hypergraph heat operator with a standard noise component, keeping structure near the data while ending at a known Gaussian law. Closed-form targets let an order-respecting network learn the reverse drift by direct fitting. Nemeth proves exactness in the ideal setting and stability over finite time spans, with better generation quality than strong baselines.
arxiv-2605-05224:
Bo Wang and four co-authors protect personal data from illicit training use by making example images unlearnable across more training styles than earlier work covered. Unlearnable examples carry tiny hidden perturbations that block feature learning. Most studies test them only when models train from scratch, while real practice often starts from pretrained weights and fine-tunes.

The authors show frozen pretrained layers filter out the noise-like edits, badly harming existing methods, and they explain why through semantic filtering. Their response, Shallow Semantic Camouflage, keeps the perturbation in a meaning-valid subspace so it survives that filtering. Wide experiments show the method restores protection across the diverse training styles they test.
arxiv-2605-05324:
Dovi Poznanski presents a compact, readable representation of light curves from the TESS space telescope, designed for exploring millions of stellar brightness records at once. The aim is not the best classifier but a map where nearby points genuinely vary alike, built without labels or known periods. Light curves are encoded by quantile graphs or scattering transforms, compressed, and projected onto a self-organising map.

After testing many configurations, Poznanski selects a quantile-graph model balancing readability, stability, and performance. Applied to about one and a half million light curves, the map organises stars mainly by variability size, signal quality, timescale, and curve shape. Repeat observations land in stable neighbourhoods, and an interactive web interface is provided.
arxiv-2605-05624:
Integrable systems have a classic device, the Hirota bilinear scheme, built on products of two tau functions. Takeshi Fukuyama studies the next step up, trilinear equations with three-slot couplings. His test case is the steady axisymmetric Einstein equations, written through the Ernst potential in tau-ratio form.

The nonlinear relation splits into a cubic sector carrying all second-derivative terms, plus a quartic shell. The cubic part matches a known YTSF-type trilinear kernel. Fukuyama states a general kernel test and checks it on Tomimatsu-Sato solutions, hinting the trilinear structure is a general feature of the system's highest derivatives.
arxiv-2605-06124:
Peng and Gao halve the cost of guided image generation. Classifier-free guidance is vital for high-quality conditional generation in flow matching, but it needs two forward passes per sampling step: one conditional, one unconditional. P-Guide instead modulates only the initial latent state, steering generation from the prior space in a single pass. Under a first-order approximation, the authors show this is equivalent to standard guidance, without explicit velocity-field extrapolation during sampling.

Both homoscedastic and heteroscedastic priors are treated, and jointly modeling mean and variance gives adaptive loss attenuation and better robustness to data uncertainty. Experiments show P-Guide cuts inference latency by about half while matching dual-pass guidance on fidelity and prompt alignment. For text-to-image systems, the saving matters at every step of every sample.
arxiv-2605-06324:
Florian Burnat and Brittany Davidson ask when a safety audit metric can still certify real harm reduction once platforms game it. Online safety laws increasingly treat scalar metrics as compliance evidence. Yet announcing a metric makes it a target. A platform can reroute recommendations through equivalent content variants and raise its score without lowering harm. The authors model the audit as a transformation graph whose connected parts form semantic classes, treating the metric itself as a security object.

Three results follow. Any metric scoring variants directly is manipulable once two equivalent variants in a harmful class score differently. A repair that assigns each variant its class maximum is the unique minimal conservative fix of its kind. A class stratified certificate then bounds true harm for every platform strategy, within stated error terms, and machine checked tests support the claims.
arxiv-2605-06424:
Luca Cocconi, Henry Alston, and Thibault Bertrand ask when the fastest control of a passive system is not the slowest, gentlest one. For systems in equilibrium, optimal control usually favors quasistatic, or near-endless, protocols. They study a Brownian particle held by a harmonic trap whose stiffness fluctuates randomly.

When those fluctuations break detailed balance, the controller itself exchanges work with the particle and changes what optimal means. The best protocols then have a finite duration, which shrinks to zero above a critical fluctuation strength. An endpoint constraint removes that collapse. The result shows finite-time optimality can arise under nonequilibrium control.
arxiv-2605-06624:
Ehsan Asadollahi, Calvin Hawkins, and Matthew Hale study repeated games where each player receives a payoff vector and judges it through a weighted sum, called a scalarization. Usually that weighting is fixed in advance by the modeler. Here the choice of scalarization is itself an online decision, treated as a control signal that shapes how play unfolds over rounds.

A two-level scheme runs an outer learner that picks the scalarization slowly and an inner bandit learner that picks actions quickly from the resulting scalar feedback. Algorithms based on stabilized online mirror descent carry sublinear regret guarantees. In a test game, convergence to the preferred equilibrium rises from about half under fixed weighting to about eighty percent under adaptation.
arxiv-2605-06924:
Do Xuan Long and four co-authors present A2RD, a system for generating long videos that stay consistent. Existing methods often drift in meaning or lose the story over long runs. Their design separates creative generation from consistency checking, and builds video segment by segment in a repeating cycle of retrieving, synthesizing, refining, and updating.

A multimodal memory tracks how the video progresses, while generation modes adapt to each segment. Self-improvement steps at frame and video level stop errors from spreading. On public tests and a new hard benchmark, the system beats leading baselines on consistency and story coherence. Human judges confirm smoother motion and transitions.
arxiv-2605-07024:
Delulu is a benchmark for catching code hallucinations, introduced by Mahdi Erfanian and six co-authors. Language models filling in missing code often invent methods, parameters, or imports that look right but fail at runtime. The benchmark holds nearly two thousand samples across seven languages and four hallucination types.

Samples were built adversarially, checked by several judge models, verified in containers, and reviewed by human experts. The strongest of eleven tested models still scores well below perfect, and every model family produces hallucination-like completions on some samples. The authors release the benchmark and tools, arguing the difficulty lies in the task itself, not one model family.
arxiv-2605-07124:
Bruno Carvalho, Jonas F. G. Santos, and Moises Rojas study tiny heat machines powered by measurements rather than by two heat baths. Their working substance is a double quantum dot, where electrons tunnel between two sites. A three-stroke cycle combines contact with one reservoir and two generalized measurement steps.

By tracking internal energy and entropy, the authors map when the device acts as an engine, refrigerator, heater, or accelerator. Tunneling shifts the borders between those modes and creates cooling setups absent in a simpler detuned model. Temperature, detuning, and tunneling together control the best regions for extracting work or cooling.
arxiv-2605-07224:
Jaydeep Goswami, Rupam Jyoti Borah, and Umananda Dev Goswami construct traversable wormhole solutions inside a modified gravity theory called f(Q) gravity. Using a power-law version of the theory with uneven matter, they derive a shape function. It meets the geometric demands of a wormhole a traveler could pass through.

Energy condition violations turn out unavoidable but stay confined near the wormhole throat, while outward anisotropic stress does most of the supporting work. Balance checks pass under two redshift choices. Perturbation analysis gives damped ringing frequencies, and time-domain simulations confirm the solutions stay stable, supporting the claim that this gravity theory admits consistent wormholes.
arxiv-2605-07524:
Yushi Tsubamoto and Takato Horii model how a parent and infant come to share inner representations while steering the infant's body state. Brain synchrony appears in real two-person exchanges, yet how alignment arises when each side sees the world differently was unclear. Their built model joins active inference with a naming game from collective predictive coding.

The parent judges the infant through outward bodily cues, while the infant senses its inner state at once, a one-sided gap built into their knowledge. That synchrony between their latent forms appeared well before their world models converged, and lasted despite their knowledge gaps. The result supports collective predictive coding as an explanation of inter-brain synchrony.
arxiv-2605-07724:
Ali Falahati and three co-authors revisit a feared failure of generative AI: models retrained on their own curated output collapse onto a narrow set of answers that over-serve one reward signal. Earlier work suggested this collapse is hard to avoid without mixing real data back in. The authors challenge that conclusion from an alignment perspective.

Tracking the dynamics of recursive training under several reward functions, they prove the model converges, under stated conditions, to a stable distribution. That distribution spreads mass across competing high-reward regions. Diversity survives the loop. The limiting distribution provably satisfies a weighted Nash bargaining solution, giving a formal reading of how plural values get combined in synthetic retraining.
arxiv-2605-07924:
Amin Karimi Monsefi and five co-authors argue that when a distilled text generator underperforms, the teacher's trajectory is to blame, not the student's capacity. Discrete flow matching needs hundreds of passes to turn noise into text, and distillation trains a student to shortcut a teacher trajectory built from blind random jumps. One bad early jump poisons everything after it, yet the student must imitate the result.

Their TS-DFM shapes the trajectory during training only: a lightweight energy compass scores candidate continuations at each midpoint and picks the most coherent, leaving inference cost unchanged. The shaped student, at eight steps, achieved perplexity well below its own thousand-step teacher while running more than a hundred times faster, and beat every discrete-generation baseline compared.
arxiv-2605-08024:
Wenxin Zhan designs a safer way to route glaucoma cases between an AI system and human experts. Screening tools can miss hard cases, and a deferral system must also respect which experts are free, how readers differ, and the unequal harm of each error type. Standard learning-to-defer setups ignore most of that.

The proposed router decides both whether to defer a case and which available expert should receive it. It fuses uncertainty, eye morphology, image quality, and out-of-distribution signals under a strict availability mask. Training uses asymmetric costs and a deferral budget, and the system was tested across three glaucoma cohorts from different countries.
arxiv-2605-08624:
Dawid Tarłowski revisits Cusick's conjecture, a claim about counting ones in binary expansions. Adding a fixed number to n changes its count of ones, and the conjecture says counts more often rise than fall, for every shift. Tarłowski reorders the odd numbers to turn the density question into a growing tree process with an attached stopped random walk.

That view yields a clear structural account of the densities, covering support, symmetry, variance, and when normal or almost sure behavior rules. The conjecture itself reduces to a special case of a broader claim about uneven tree growth, which numeric work supports. Number theory gains fresh machinery for a stubborn digit problem, though the conjecture stays open.
arxiv-2605-08724:
Weiren Zhao, Yi Dong, and Cheng Chen unite medical image understanding with medical image generation in one model, SynerMedGen. Earlier unified medical models treated the two jobs as separate goals with no real synergy. The authors ask what kind of understanding actually helps generation, and build training around that answer with three understanding tasks aligned to generation plus a two stage schedule.

Understanding training alone already yields strong zero shot results across twenty two synthesis tasks and fresh datasets. Adding generation training then beats both specialized synthesizers and recent unified rivals. A large released dataset pairs a million synthesis samples with two million derived understanding cases. Medical AI gains a working recipe for synergy, not just coexistence.
arxiv-2605-08824:
Haimin Luo, Min Ouyang, Lan Xu, and Jingyi Yu grow true to life 3D hairstyles strand by strand. Hair is both fluid and built, which makes it hard to model. Past plans based on fields blur the whole shape with fine strand traits. HairGPT treats strands as the base units, like words in a line of text. Growth splits two ways. It splits by scalp zone. It also splits by scale, from broad layout down to fine style.

A shape code and zone tags guide each strand as it forms. This allows part by part edits. It allows rare and hard styles, and styled looks too. Hair work turns into a clear, guided craft with strong grip on sense and form.
arxiv-2605-08924:
Xiao Fei and seven coauthors write of protein pair acts in free text, not fixed tags. Pair work in the main stops at class calls. New multi mode models can tell of one protein. They can not yet tell of a pair. PPI2Text codes each protein with a sequence model. It builds a map of all residue pairs twixt the two. It then writes with a language model. A place code lines each map axis up with its protein's residues.

A shared set holds a vast count of pairs with free text acts. The text comes from ten kept data banks, plus made text with tiers of proof in the prompt. The model beats strong base lines on word scores and on truth.
arxiv-2605-09024:
Adrian Azzarelli, Nantheera Anantrasirichai, James Pollock, and David Bull relight virtual production scenes captured as Gaussian splats, freeing film sets from fixed lighting. LED wall stages light actors with the background itself, which looks right on the day but locks editors into that lighting later. Classic inverse rendering leans on low resolution environment maps that assume distant light, a poor fit for near, detailed wall illumination.

Their framework conditions relighting on the known background imagery instead, turning compositing into background editing. Each splat carries coordinates, intensity, and resolution controls that sample the background texture directly, mimicking reflections without full physical rendering. Reconstruction quality and relighting control beat baselines at modest memory and near real time rates.
arxiv-2605-09124:
Tamer Abdelaziz, writing alone, surveys where smart contract security research is heading. Work on these blockchain programs began with simply spotting known flaws, but the field now reaches toward deeper goals, and the author organizes the frontier into four directions for student capstone projects.

The four directions cover language-model reasoning about contract meaning and flaws, automatic repair with formal guarantees, adversarial learning for spotting malicious contracts and transfers, and real-time detection of exploits as transfers happen. Two recent studies anchor the account: one diagnoses where current analyzers fall short, and one shows a system for flagging malicious Ethereum transfers at scale. Each direction is framed as measurable and buildable.
arxiv-2605-09624:
Mei and two colleagues argue that AI schooling for materials work must move past tool access toward workflow aligned skill. AI models now aid property guesses, experiment ranking, and new ideas in materials science. But the bottleneck is whether students and teachers can use them with domain specific scientific judgment. Their workshop informed paper links AI literacy to materials informatics skills. These include data origins, feature building, model checks, uncertainty measures, physics informed reasoning, and experiment feedback.

Equity, they stress, must be judged by outcomes, not just access. Gains, transfer, confidence match, persistence, and research readiness should match across student subgroups. The paper flags risks like letting tools do the thinking, where learners hand judgment to the tool. Its dual track course plan and scoring plan aim to make better scientists, not merely faster AI users, across courses, bootcamps, and program reform.
arxiv-2605-09724:
Song and Ye explained grokking, the odd pattern where a model masters training data long before it generalizes, through a race between two speeds. Earlier accounts invoked circuit efficiency or shifts in learning dynamics, but left open how model size shapes the effect. On modular arithmetic tasks, the authors measured a memorisation speed and a generalisation speed, each as a function of parameter count.

Grokking did not start the moment a model grew large enough to memorize the training set. It appeared near the size where the two speeds crossed. The framework also yielded a model for predicting memorisation speed from capacity and data complexity, recovering the known finding that larger models memorize faster. Timing, the paper argues, is the missing lens on grokking.
arxiv-2605-10024:
Liu and seven colleagues simulated wind production from hot accretion flows in tidal disruption events, where black holes tear apart stars. Wind is a key mechanism for supermassive black hole feedback to host galaxies. In tidal disruption events, black holes spend most time accreting at highly sub-Eddington rates, so feedback from persistent sub-Eddington winds could matter. The study varied black hole mass, viscosity parameter, and stellar debris temperature.

More massive black holes yielded a higher accreted fraction and faster winds, while debris temperature barely influenced the accretion flow. For viscosity α = 0.1, mildly relativistic unbound winds near 0.1c launched mainly from outside the accretion flows along the equatorial plane, with kinetic energy near 10^-4 of the Eddington luminosity. For α = 0.01, convective bound outflows dominated instead, unlike true winds in active galactic nuclei and X-ray binaries. The results bear on delayed radio brightening near 10^3 days and on hunting intermediate-mass black holes.
arxiv-2605-10624:
Ramesh Arvind Naagarajan and two colleagues explain model predictive control with hierarchical causal abduction. MPC operates safety systems by predicting future paths and tuning actions. But nonlinear motion, hard safety constraints, and tuning often make control moves opaque to staff. Their 2026 paper presents Hierarchical Causal Abduction, or HCA.

HCA combines physics reasoning from knowledge graphs with tuning evidence from Karush-Kuhn-Tucker multipliers. It adds causal discovery via the PCMCI algorithm. That generates faithful reasons for actions made by MPC. Across greenhouse climate, building HVAC, and chemical plants, HCA beats LIME scores by 53 percent. The scores are 0.478 versus 0.311, with expert checks. Domain-specific KKT tuning over 2 to 3 days lifts scores to 0.88 on tests. Cutting tests confirm each source is key, with a 32 to 37 percent drop when any part is removed.
arxiv-2605-10824:
Four researchers present StartFlow, a 2026 method that helps people without design training sketch early product prototypes for software startups. They are Guilherme Corredato Guerino, João Pedro de Souza Olivo Tardivo, Renato Balancieri, and Gislaine Camila Lapasini Leal. StartFlow turns planned features into wireflows, diagrams that join screen sketches with the paths users follow through them.

Work runs in three moves: sorting features, drawing the wireflows, then checking and revising them against usability rules of thumb. A focus group of researchers called the method plain and flexible, while a small trial with experts tested it in practice. Startup teams short on design help get a structured route from an idea to a testable early prototype.
arxiv-2605-11124:
H. Bora and five others link neutrino masses, dark matter, and leptogenesis in one model built on Delta(54) flavor symmetry, two Higgs doublets, and a triple inverse seesaw. Neutrino oscillations prove at least two neutrinos have distinct nonzero masses, which the Standard Model cannot explain.

The model makes neutrino masses through the triple inverse seesaw. It predicts shifts from tribimaximal mixing, with a nonzero reactor angle and an upper-octant atmospheric angle, and it fits the CP phase and Jarlskog invariant to oscillation data. Its dark-matter part is checked against relic abundance and neutrino-dark-matter mixing under cosmic limits, while resonant leptogenesis at the tera-electronvolt scale with flavor effects yields the observed baryon asymmetry. Particle physicists get one symmetry frame spanning three open problems.
arxiv-2605-11224:
Bulat Maksudov and three colleagues introduce ABRA, an agent benchmark for radiology applications. Existing medical-agent benchmarks hand agents pre-selected images, never an environment to navigate. ABRA hands the agent control of an OHIF viewer plus an Orthanc DICOM server, worked through twenty-one function-calling tools.

Tools span slice navigation, windowing, series selection, pixel-coordinate annotation, and structured reporting. ABRA holds 655 generated tasks across three difficulty tiers and eight types, drawn from LIDC-IDRI, Duke Breast Cancer MRI, and NLST New-Lesion LongCT. Automatic scorers grade each episode on Planning, Execution, and Outcome. Ten models, five closed and five open-weight, reach at least 89 percent Execution on real annotation but only 0 to 25 percent Outcome. On the paired oracle variant with a simulated detector, Outcome reaches 69 to 100 percent. The gap points to perception, not tool orchestration, as the bottleneck. Builders get a benchmark testing navigation, not just answers.
arxiv-2605-11324: Yinan Li, Tuan Nguyen and Kwang-Sung Jun study fixed-budget max-min action identification in depth-two trees, a key case of Monte Carlo tree search. The learner samples leaves, then recommends a subtree whose worst leaf is best, accepting any subtree within epsilon of optimal. Their epsilon-agnostic algorithm needs no epsilon input yet reaches instance-dependent error bounds for every meaningful epsilon, with misidentification probability decaying exponentially in budget over a hardness measure. It is the first provable fixed-budget guarantee for this problem.
arxiv-2605-11424: Tang and seven colleagues present VidSplat, a training-free framework that rebuilds complete three-dimensional scenes from sparse views using video diffusion priors. Gaussian splatting degrades with few views and cannot infer unseen or occluded regions. VidSplat iteratively synthesizes novel views to fill missing coverage, guiding denoising toward underlying geometry with rendered colour and mask images, then refining through confidence-weighted training on sampled camera paths. It stays robust even from a single image.
arxiv-2605-12024: Jonathan McLennan, Jay Farihi, and Steven Parsons survey, in 2026 work, 879 dwarf carbon stars by their light curves in search of pairs left after shared-envelope evolution. Strong wobble under 15 days showed in 31 objects, matching starspots and spin in tidally locked pairs. One clear halo star dims every 1.224 days with a 30 percent depth that rules out a white dwarf blocker, the first dimming pair among carbon-rich stars. Four stars show multi-year trends hinting at magnetic cycles.
arxiv-2605-12224: Rodney Sanchez, Ferat Sahin, Alex Ororbia, and Jamison Heard present vicarious conditioning as an intrinsic reward for learning. Drivers use direct training and limit how agents learn from the world and from others, while learn-by-example methods need the teacher's policy or rewards. It needs neither, drawing on psychology and biology through four steps: attention, retention, reproduction, and reinforcement. Tests in MiniWorld Sidewalk and Box2D CarRacing show it lengthens runs by steering agents away from final states toward good ones. It suits single-life and ongoing learning.
arxiv-2605-12324: Eschen and colleagues report two planets around the cool dwarf TOI-4311. The inner world is a super-Earth circling in under a day, while the outer world is a sub-Neptune taking about fifteen days. Both came from TESS data, refined by CHEOPS and HARPS. A third wobble hints at a possible outer planet near thirty-eight days, though no transit has been seen. The inner planet proves unusually dense for its star's chemistry.
arxiv-2605-12424: Langford and three colleagues update a method for sizing the Milky Way's central bar from star orbits. They compute orbit frequencies in simulation-based models, classify stars by bar-supporting orbits, and map their farthest reach. A refined rule isolates warm inner Lindblad resonance orbits, including looped x1 orbits that shape the bar's shoulders and radial extent. Applied to over two hundred thousand stars from Gaia, APOGEE and OGLE, the method leaves several bar lengths and spin rates consistent within five percent.
arxiv-2605-12524: Arkoudas and Batzoglou introduce ProofGrid, a benchmark suite that judges language-model reasoning by machine-checkable proofs, not by final answers alone. ProofGrid holds fifteen tasks spanning proof writing, checking, masking and gap-filling. Tasks use minimal formal notation, notably NDL, a compact natural-deduction language fitting short prompts and supporting precise, auditable verification. The design yields mechanical, reproducible and fine-grained evaluation. It covers a calibrated difficulty spectrum up to challenge tasks no current model solves.
arxiv-2605-12624: Huang and eight colleagues present MindVLA-U1, a unified streaming vision-language-action architecture for autonomous driving. Driving VLAs have often trailed vision-to-action models on planning quality, suggesting the gap lies in how semantic reasoning, temporal context and continuous control join, not merely in model scale. Their design uses one shared backbone to produce language tokens and flow-matching action trajectories in a single forward pass, preserving each modality's natural output form. A full streaming design processes video frame by frame rather than as fixed clips.
arxiv-2605-12824: Zhao, Pham and Vincent ask what makes an agent-based model explanatory. Language models make diverse patterns without coded rules, and appear in agent-based models and social simulations. But power, forecast and accounts differ: an account shows how a pattern is produced by parts. The team joins agent-based models with philosophy, setting plausibility as a scale. Their Mechanism Plausibility Scale separates sufficiency, copying a pattern, from how it is produced, and marks roles.
arxiv-2605-12924: Balazadeh and four co-authors bound causal effects when hidden confounding rules out exact point values. Their IV-ICL method learns the effects' posterior at once via amortised Bayesian in-context learning, then reads bounds off as quantiles. A mass-covering goal nets the full identified set, where standard variational inference falls to one mode. On synthetic and semi-synthetic tests it gives more valid, sharper intervals far faster.
arxiv-2605-13024: Wang and five co-authors tackle few-shot molecular property prediction, key in drug discovery where labelled data are scarce and costly. Their ReCoG method learns on a relational and compact context graph. One module models structural context across properties, while a bottleneck module cuts irrelevant side signals. The pair aims for rich molecule vectors from thin context, and theory backs joint relational and compact extraction in context graphs.
arxiv-2605-13424: Divij Khaitan and Ashish Tiwari propose last-mile fine-tuning, a pipeline for turning messy clipboard text into clean tables. A pre-trained large language model first extracts an initial table. A fine-tuned small model then repairs errors in that table. On a benchmark of 2,596 tables, the pipeline matches or beats end-to-end fine-tuning. It needs as few as 1,000 training examples and resists format changes. At that level it beats end-to-end fine-tuning by as much as 0.144 TEDS points.
arxiv-2605-14024: Baqer and Said study lone waves under a longer KdV equation that keeps energy, aimed at shallow-water shock waves. The longer model comes from full shallow-water Euler equations once surface tension and stronger nonlinear effects count, under weak nonlinearity and long waves. Past plain KdV it adds four terms: one quadratic nonlinear term, two mixed terms, and one fifth-order term. A variational method based on mean Lagrangians tests how true lone waves stay.
arxiv-2605-14324: Alshahrani analyzes convergence rates of norm-minimization methods for convex vector optimization with l_p scalarization. He proves Hausdorff approximation error of order k to the 2 over 1 minus q for every p between 1 and infinity, where q counts objectives and k counts iterations. The proof uses a Euclidean middle step on the inner product structure. It gives a quadratic hyperplane bound, dodging the l_p smoothness limit. Norm equivalence converts this to any l_p metric at only a dimension-dependent constant. Experiments confirm the rate.
arxiv-2605-14424: Payra and colleagues report spontaneous formation of nitrogen-bearing PAHs in an ion trap, a new pathway in the interstellar medium. N-PAHs are key precursors to complex organic molecules in space and in nitrogen-rich atmospheres, yet their formation pathways remain open. Ion trap work with electronic structure maths reveals barrier-less reactions between gas-phase pyrimidine cations and acetylene. They form a new endocyclic N-PAH. The results bear on astrochemistry in Titan's air and the interstellar medium.
arxiv-2605-14524: Zhou, Li, Cheng and Lin extend large-dimensional kernel ridge regression to a broad new family of product kernels. Earlier work focused on inner-product kernels on spheres. They derive convergence rates for generalisation error. The results recover phenomena previously tied to spherical kernels. These are minimax optimality when the source condition is at most one, a saturation effect above one, and a periodic plateau with multiple descent as sample size grows.
arxiv-2605-14624: Afifi defines an amortised efficiency threshold for comparing neural and heuristic solvers in combinatorial optimisation. Training a neural solver costs a large fixed sum of GPU energy. A heuristic costs a little CPU energy per instance. The two become comparable only once deployment volume is fixed. The threshold marks the volume above which the neural solver breaks even on energy or carbon at fixed solution quality. For vehicle routing it is measured near forty-five hundred instances.
arxiv-2605-14724: Singh, Tapender, Singh and Verma reconcile TM2 neutrino mixing with LMA and dark-LMA data using small corrections from the charged-lepton sector. A Wolfenstein parametrisation of the charged-lepton mixing matrix adds two parameters and brings TM2 predictions in line with current data. For the LMA case, one parameter is capped by the atmospheric mixing angle. Sizeable CP violation is predicted. The inverted hierarchy region is claimed to sit within the reach of future tests.
arxiv-2605-14924: M. Y. Abd-Rabbou and Cong-Feng Qiao propose a nonlocal Maxwell demon that moves usable energy, called ergotropy, between distant quantum batteries. Alice encodes a logical qubit in a shared surface code and sends only a classical syndrome note that Bob decodes to charge his battery. No energy crosses the channel directly. Active error monitoring suppresses logical faults, and the authors find net work extraction becomes impossible beyond a size near 78, whatever the code distance.
arxiv-2605-15124: Karoline Romero and four others survey 92 people on prototypes made by generative AI tools versus humans, with authorship hidden. Using the UEQ-S survey, they measure use traits like usability and efficiency plus hedonic traits like originality. AI prototypes score well on use quality but neutral to poor on hedonic quality. The authors conclude that generative tools produce working interfaces yet reinforce visual and structural patterns that dampen seen originality.
arxiv-2605-15324: Chenghong Bian, Meng Hua, and Deniz Gunduz propose P-WRFGS, a wireless radiance-field framework built on 3D Gaussian splatting for guessing channel state across transmitter spots. A learnable mask per Gaussian primitive marks importance and guides pruning of trivial units, weighing drawing quality against speed through a weighted loss. On the NeRF-squared dataset it reaches up to 100-fold storage cut and 7-fold drawing speedup with only mild loss in structural similarity and reached rate. Point-cloud initialization lifts the tradeoff further.
arxiv-2605-15424: Po-Chien Luan and three others present Social-Mamba, a trajectory-forecasting architecture that treats social interactions as structured sequences instead of attention patterns. Attention captures complex dependencies but costs fast in neighbor count, while stepwise state-space models misfit unstructured social dynamics. The Cycle Mamba block enables smooth two-way information flow, and social triplet factorization splits exchanges into temporal, egocentric, and goal-centric scans, fused through a learnable social gate. Five benchmarks show true and fast prediction.
arxiv-2605-15524: Bruno Trentini, Jacob Hume, Vincenzo Antonio Isoldi, Philipp Misof, Ekaterina S. Ivshina, and Kelly Maggs launch neural point-forms, learned shape traits for point clouds. Point clouds lack a tangency frame, so the team builds discrete form comparisons from diffusion geometry. They prove comparison matrices settle under standard sampling rules. The payoff is a compact layer blind to point order that yields a learned form-comparison matrix. Tests on toy and biology data show it competes well. Gains are biggest where labels hinge on sample density or manifold shape.
arxiv-2605-15924: Jan Henry Belz reflects on synced realities for context-aware AR in mobility settings. Matching what users see, hear and feel matters for immersion in virtual reality, but real-world elements often lie beyond user control in AR. Generative AI now enables on-demand content creation. Combined with context data, it allows cases that align smoothly with the user's setting. Belz presents synced cases, compares their shared traits and differences, and discusses the upside and risks of syncing AR with the real world.
arxiv-2605-16924: Malik's team uses Faraday rotation readings from SPICE-RACS DR2 and the DESI catalog to probe magnetized halo gas near redshift 1. They compile 2,483 lines, including 612 with in-between Mg clouds marking galaxies and 1,871 controls. After cutting Milky Way rotation and capping to low H column and H-alpha glow, 757 quasars remain. Mg lines show a 4.5-sigma excess in rest spread of 4.13 plus-or-minus 0.91 radians per square meter over controls. That implies halo field strengths near 0.4 to 0.8 µG over 20 to 150 kpc, showing magnetism by redshift near 1.
arxiv-2605-17124: Boasso and colleagues derive a curved-boundary expansion for a massless scalar field's nonlocal effective action, working to second order in extrinsic curvature with heat-kernel methods. The framework recovers earlier results for simple Monge-patch surfaces and extends them to surfaces lacking such a description. As a check, they compute particle creation for a wobbling deformed ring and sphere.
arxiv-2605-17224: Iwakiri, Miyata and Mori spot thermopolarization in a wide set of insulators. That is electric charge split made by a heat gradient. Heat swell under a gradient makes strain gradients that split charge through flexoelectricity. The effect shows up in crystals, plastics and glass alike. The size of the response tracks heat swell, and thin samples or phase shifts boost it more than tenfold.
arxiv-2605-17324: Udari Madhushani Sehwag and colleagues show that asking an agent to clarify ambiguity sharply raises its vulnerability to prompt injection. Their ASPI benchmark of 728 task-attack cases compares matched execution and clarification settings across ten frontier models. Attack success jumps from under 2 percent to about 34 percent for o3 and to about 36 percent for Gemini-3-Flash. The gap reflects both a state shift in processing and the clarification channel itself.
arxiv-2605-17624: Miquel Martí i Rabadán and colleagues test invariant and equivariant semi-supervised learning for multi-task models on partial labels. They use FixMatch for the invariant case and its extension Dense FixMatch, tested on Cityscapes and BDD100K for detection and scene parsing. Varying size and overlap of per-task labeled subsets, both approaches beat plain baselines in most cases, with the largest gains when few labels exist and better results for the latter approach. Both approaches thus look promising for multi-task learning from limited data.
arxiv-2605-18024: Sunwoo Lee and three colleagues propose interaction-breaking adversarial learning, a framework for robust multi-agent reinforcement learning. Cooperation is central to multi-agent learning, yet coordination can break when attacks disrupt agent links. Prior methods tried value-based attacks, leaving a gap when interaction links are broken. IBAL takes an information view to build attacks breaking coordination by perturbing what agents see and do, and trains agents to perform well under attacks. Tests show IBAL improves strength over rivals across attack settings, with stronger results under agent-missing cases.
arxiv-2605-18324: Jaskirat Singh's 2026 paper improves representation autoencoders, which swap old variational autoencoders for pretrained vision encoders. Three design insights simplify and strengthen the recipe. Summing the last k encoder layers, rather than the final layer alone, greatly improves rebuilds without encoder fine-tuning or special data. Autoencoders and alignment, which distills the same code into middle layers, prove complementary, so one representation serves as both encoder and target. Viewing alignment as a guess in latent space lets the model supply guidance for free, without a second weaker model.
arxiv-2605-18724: Yuki Ohnishi and Fan Li develop, in a 2026 paper, sensitivity analysis for causal mediation. Mediation splits a total effect into a mediator path and a direct portion. Finding natural direct and indirect effects rests on sequential ignorability, unverifiable in practice. They define the bridge score from two treatment densities at a common value. Given the bridge score, they derive a sharp variance envelope on unidentified outcome confounding. A residual budget calibration makes the bound usable, with Bayesian g-computation handling inference.
arxiv-2605-18824: Mohammed Saidul Islam and seven colleagues offer a framework that builds fine-grained benchmarks for foundation models from reference books. Aggregate scores hide gaps, and most benchmarks lack the coverage and metadata for detailed diagnosis. Their multi-agent pipeline writes problems grounded in textbooks and checks answers through a solution graph. Three benchmarks cover personal finance, corporate finance, and machine learning, and show lower ground-truth error than older tests and reveal model gaps that aggregate scores miss.
arxiv-2605-18924: Milan Rosko proves, with machine-checked formalization in Rocq, an obstruction to excluded middle for primitive regulators over a small logical fragment. A regulator assigns each formula a proposition, and excluded middle would demand it affirm either every formula or its negation. Rosko shows that if the regulator is closed under modus ponens, consistent, and admits a formula equivalent to its own negation, then excluded middle fails. Consistency alone rules out both the formula and its negation, so the argument needs only that single instance.
arxiv-2605-19224: Aditya Vaidya, Richard Antonello, and Alexander Huth show slow fMRI data can train models of fast brain recordings. Intracranial ECoG gives fine space and time detail, but only patients with implants can provide it. The team fine-tuned spoken language models on fMRI, then built ECoG models from them, gaining prediction even in bands fMRI never measures. Halving fMRI time resolution still gave comparable prediction, and ECoG gains grew steadily with more tuning data. The work suggests slow data can power models of fast brain signals, aiding decoding.
arxiv-2605-19324: Siddharth Viswanath and colleagues model brain activity with BrainDyn, a graph network built on a cellular sheaf. Standard message-passing nets force every brain region into one shared feature space and add neighbor messages as plain sums, which fits biology poorly. BrainDyn instead lets learned maps between regions, refreshed from each forecasting window, steer how activity evolves over time. Tested on resting brain scans, EEG, and simulated activity, it beats rivals at forecasting and generating transients, and its learned features stay interpretable and biologically sensible.
arxiv-2605-19724: Maassarani shows that not every symmetric 2-cocycle is a coboundary. For many finite groups a symmetric 2-cocycle with values in the nonzero complex numbers is a coboundary. Yet the author proves by a theory argument and GAP work that a group of order 64 carries such a 2-cocycle with a nontrivial cohomology class. The result marks a limit for the common hope that symmetry forces a cocycle to be trivial there.
arxiv-2605-20024: Soonho Kwon and four co-workers study South Korean parents of LGBTQ+ children, and how trauma and healing reshape their identities. After the shock, fear and isolation of learning a child's queer identity, parents encounter queer-related information, true and false, as a way of coping. Through that process many rebuild as supportive parents, judging such information more critically, guarding against harmful narratives and challenging misinformation for others. The authors argue tackling misinformation must look beyond individual fact-checking to its relational, cultural and emotional dimensions.
arxiv-2605-20124: Erik Fitzner and six co-workers quantify spin diffusion for the square-lattice quantum spin-one-half XY model at finite temperature. Theory uses a recently developed dynamic high-temperature expansion to capture the long scales of the hydrodynamic regime. Experiments use a hard-core boson quantum simulator in an optical lattice. Theory and experiment agree closely on spin diffusion constants, a breakthrough for spin transport beyond one dimension and for validating quantum simulation platforms. The authors also predict dynamic spin conductivity and anisotropy-induced integrability breaking for future experiments.
arxiv-2605-20224: Akiva Groskin presents the first implementation of the Connes-van Suijlekom Galerkin matrix at 16 cutoffs. The Weil form's ground state has Fourier-Mellin zeros on the critical line. Convergence to Riemann zeros as the cutoff grows is open. Across cutoffs 13 through 67, the first-zero error shrinks from ten to the minus fifty-five to ten to the minus one hundred sixty-eight. The smallest-positive even eigenvalue reaches about ten to the minus three hundred thirty-four at cutoff 100, size 250. It recovers ten Riemann zeros.
arxiv-2605-20324: Ahmadain, Frenkel and Yin refine Zwiebach's closed string field theory for non-critical backgrounds at genus zero. A special string state encodes the failure of worldsheet BRST invariance, paired with a metric-dependent descent operator. They build the mixed moduli spaces for the classical BV action, prove they exist, and extend background independence to first order off the conformal locus. The formalism is then applied to near-critical cases, including flat space just below 26 dimensions.
arxiv-2605-20524: Kelvin Alves, Rogerio Cavalcanti, and Santiago Perez Bergliaffa study how the twist of light bends its path around black holes. In plain geometric optics, light rays stay in one plane. Once the coupling between light's spin and curved space is kept, rays deflect out of that plane. The authors trace this spinoptic bend in two round black-hole geometries and test whether one parametrized model can mimic the other.
arxiv-2605-20624: Taesung Kwon and three colleagues speed up video inverse-problem solvers with autoregressive diffusion models. Diffusion priors help restore video without task-specific training, but full-video restoration brings high first-frame delay and repeated passes hurt throughput. Their AVIS solver restores video in a streaming way, starting reverse diffusion from a measurement-consistent guess. It cuts initial delay from 114 seconds to 4 seconds and lifts throughput from 0.71 to 1.18 frames per second.
arxiv-2605-20724: Rajendra Narayan Jena, Rajan Padmanabhan, and Sankar Arumugam present CALMem, an application-layer dual memory for conversational AI. Language models work within fixed context windows, so long talks lose history when compaction discards it and sessions reset memory to zero. CALMem needs no model change and pairs an episodic layer of sliding-window vector embeddings with a semantic layer of agent-written structured facts. Together they give assistants virtually unbounded effective context.
arxiv-2605-20824: Abdullah X introduces Markovian Circuit Tracing, a diagnostic pipeline for checking whether transformer activations hold coarse state-transition patterns. Many sequence computations are simpler to study as motion through internal states than as lone local circuits. The benchmark uses synthetic Hidden Markov Model tasks where latent states, shift matrices, belief vectors, and optimal predictions are known exactly. Across six model families and three seeds each, tiny causal transformers find near-Bayes next-token models, and extracted state patterns recover coarse transition signal.
arxiv-2605-21124: Dongjin Oh and colleagues report orbital motion in a chiral tellurium crystal that carries no spin. Using light-based measurements that resolve electron bands, they find well-separated s-orbital bands whose orbital angular momentum comes only from electrons hopping between atoms, not from motion within an atom. Spin-sensitive checks confirm no spin momentum is present, pointing toward pure orbital currents for future orbitronics.
arxiv-2605-21324: Farhad Pashakhanloo and Jacob A. Zavatone-Veth show that stimulus symmetries can confound similarity analyses of neural codes. Similarity tables are popular summaries of neural codes, but symmetries in inputs make many codes functionally equivalent while yielding varied tables. Those tables reflect varied code shapes, from disentangled to maximally mixed codes. Gradient descent or energetic regularization can generate sparse, drifting codes, leading to drifting tables, and the effects appear in networks trained on image data.
arxiv-2605-21524: Amirali Fatehizadeh generalizes the Erdős-Sierpiński conjecture. He studies solutions to sigma of n plus one equals k times sigma of n, for integer k greater than one. Solutions relate closely to k-layered numbers, a generalization of Zumkeller numbers. In the analytic core, he uses probabilistic number theory and an extension of the Kubilius model. Truncation and the Chinese Remainder Theorem reduce the problem to a measure space with independent random variables.
arxiv-2605-21724: Lyubinin proposes a new way to build manifold-constrained hyper-connections, which mix multiple residual streams in neural networks. Residual streams carry data past layers, and mixing them blends traits from paths. Prior methods forced double stochasticity by Sinkhorn normalization, paid factorial cost for exact rules, or kept mixing on a submanifold. His transportation Birkhoff polytope build gives exactly doubly stochastic matrices with a quadratic count of free parameters. It keeps full expressivity with no normalization loop, and tests on model training show it works well and stays stable.
arxiv-2605-21824: Ze Sheng and co-authors present QuartetFuzz, a maker of quality-assured fuzz harnesses, bridging fuzzers and library APIs. No current tool ensures harness correctness, so logic errors, API misuse, and life-cycle breaks slip through. Four Principles defines correctness as logic correctness, API protocol compliance, security boundary respect, and entry point adequacy, with specs and checks. An agent makes harnesses meeting all four via a generate-check-fix loop. On twenty-three projects it filed forty-two reports, twenty-nine fixed, three of them CVEs, and two rejected.
arxiv-2605-21924: Ruiqi Liu and co-authors tackle a flaw in on-policy distillation for vision-language models, where a student can improve without leaning more on what it sees. On vision-critical tokens, the student's outputs barely change when visual detail is removed, though the teacher's do. Their visual-advantage method rewards reliance on vision during distillation. It was trained on two math datasets and tested on eight benchmarks. Across three Qwen3-VL teacher sizes, it beats on-policy distillation on all of them, with gains growing with size and scale.
arxiv-2605-22024: Wei Yi Yeoh, Bo Lan, and Michael Lowe present a reciprocity-based compensation method for ultrasonic backscatter measurements in heterogeneous scattering media. In varied materials, distance effects can hide true microstructural variation with depth. Their cross-directional method corrects those effects while keeping local scattering patterns. Tests cut the cross-directional mismatch from 0.367 to 0.120 and the fitted gradient from 0.171 to 0.0067, beating standard methods.
arxiv-2605-22224: Hiramatsu studies parallel surfaces of cuspidal cross caps, a basic type of sharp-edged surface that is not a front. He gives a test for when the squared distance function breaks down. The test uses known shape measures, and he charts the pattern of sharp points that results. In most cases the parallel surface stays a cuspidal cross cap. At set distances, though, it turns into a degenerate S1 point. Those distances act much like principal radii of curvature.
arxiv-2605-22524: Woo and team offer EnCoR, a phone design moving mobility out of the core. Phone networks give seamless roaming, but raise delay and bloat. Modern apps bear roaming, so in-network work is revisited. EnCoR uses end-to-end links, dropping IP anchoring while keeping logins, charging and QoS. It works with plain phones and matches LTE speed. Operators cut delay and build cost by over 90 percent versus 3GPP networks, per FCC data. Handoff signals fall, letting the core handle more events, with 2.6 times lower delay under load.
arxiv-2605-22724: Weihs and Schaeffer study Multiple Neural Operators, an architecture for learning collections of operators across tasks that share representations. For broad classes of Lipschitz operator maps they derive near-optimal bounds on approximation and generalization, plus a curse of parametric complexity and matching minimax rates. The upshot is that shared representations add no extra cost: multi-task operator learning follows the identical scaling laws as single-operator learning, and a DeepONet variant matches those rates.
arxiv-2605-23224: Koo and three coauthors study binomials Fr(x) over finite fields, focusing on characteristic 3, where extremely low boomerang uniformity arises more often. They identify and prove two classes of binomials Fr that are locally-PN with boomerang uniformity 0. These classes use exponents from the APN build and the differentially 4-uniform exponent r.
