They also study Fr with r equal to 3 to the power n minus 3, proving it is locally-APN with uniformity 1 when n at least 5 is odd.
arxiv-2605-23324: Cruz and four coauthors study Hybrid Quantum-Classical Neural Networks for blood cell sorting. They propose a modular setup joining a ResNet-50 backbone with a latent neck and a varied quantum circuit, to compare quantum-enhanced and classic changes. Tests on two open blood cell datasets, the Blood Cell Images and PBC datasets, show that HQNNs achieve better or more balanced scores across metrics. For the Blood Cell Images Dataset, the approach lifts overall F1-score by up to 3.7 percent over classic bases.
arxiv-2605-23424: Salehi proposes Dijkstra-pruned in-network learning, a leaner way to train distributed neural modules that swap activations and errors over a communication graph. The method keeps only a capacity-aware shortest-path tree rooted at the fusion node, dropping all other links, and treats local routing as a finite-rate stochastic gate. A rate-distortion-generalization bound backs the design. In a distributed classification test, training traffic falls by 70.4 percent versus the dense version with accuracy intact, and added rate regularization cuts the latent rate by 45.7 percent.
arxiv-2605-23524: Giacomelli and colleagues lay foundations for data-enabled predictive control of piecewise affine systems, which DeePC had not yet reached despite their wide use and universal approximation power. They characterize system behavior from raw data. They extend Willems' fundamental lemma to show that behavior. They analyze coherence of DeePC strategies with a linear predictor and shrinkage regularizers, and study how misclassification errors shape data for prediction. Tests on a simple example back the theory. Good control actions need more than a plain DeePC baseline, and stay explainable.
arxiv-2605-24024: Cheng and three co-authors trace vision-language hallucinations to route competition, where text can dominate the choice despite attention. Their training-free fix splits each attention head into visual and text routes, estimating token-level effects with a one-forward, one-gradient approximation. That reveals within-head route conflict and prior-dominant heads, so only the text route is suppressed while the visual route stays intact. Across five benchmarks in discriminative and generative settings, the method cuts hallucination errors with little harm and modest inference overhead.
arxiv-2605-24224: The MINERvA Collaboration reports high-statistics measurements of muon-neutrino charged-current single-pion production on scintillator at Fermilab. Combining track-based pion reconstruction with pions spotted only through Michel electron decays, the team measures kinetic energies from zero to 350 MeV. Differential cross sections in pion and muon variables are compared with several event generators. Modern models mostly agree with data at the edges of the probed regions but stray by up to 15 percent for muons and up to 20 percent for pions. No model describes any variable well.
arxiv-2605-24424: Wu and five co-authors study four-party entanglement in a Dicke state of four qubits under relativistic motion, with one detector accelerating uniformly. Entanglement does not fall steadily: it first drops, then climbs back toward a finite value as acceleration grows. Against the usual view that the Unruh effect only degrades multipartite entanglement, the results show it can instead strengthen entanglement within a finite parameter range. Dicke states thus look like sturdier multipartite resources against Unruh-driven decoherence, with possible advantages for relativistic quantum information tasks.
arxiv-2605-24524: Xinyu Zhang and colleagues audit non-invasive brain-to-language retrieval, asking how much reported accuracy comes from real stimulus evidence rather than shortcuts. Signal-blind noise alone reached 66.3 percent Rank at 1 under variable-length decoding. It collapsed to near chance once fixed windows and identity splits were enforced. Under those controls, fixed-window retrieval recovered genuine MEG-audio discriminability, though most Top-1 errors picked the wrong sentence. A Group Context Bias intervention lifted Rank at 1 from 44 to 52 percent on Gwilliams and 22 to 29 percent on MOUS.
arxiv-2605-24624: Chris Ge and three colleagues show that in FLUX.2 in-context image generation, text tokens quietly absorb visual reference content and carry it into the output. Three causal interventions surface the binding: a text-to-image lens decoding text activations, attention knockout severing edges, and patching text activations between runs. Across 2,875 editing tasks, reference color, style, and scene setting travel through text tokens. Pixel-exact traits like a face or identity bypass text and flow directly image to image. Padding tokens of the text sequence host the binding.
arxiv-2605-24824: Rei Sakuma and co-authors propose an ancilla-free hybrid method for point-group symmetry analysis of many-electron wavefunctions. Point groups are sets of spatial symmetry operations, key tools for molecular orbitals and spectroscopy. Their method works out weights for irreducible representations by applying orbital rotations from matrix eigenvectors. It works for abelian and non-abelian groups and arbitrary basis functions. Benzene and ferrocene tests show it, and an IBM run reproduces benzene weights within a few percent.
arxiv-2605-25124: Cassandra Mussard and Stéphane Mussard extend multidimensional scaling, a way of turning dissimilarities into spatial layouts, to a Gini-based distance built from values and their ranks. A tunable parameter lets the layout adapt to the data. The method resists noise and outliers better than the standard Euclidean version. Tests on sixteen UCI data sets with outliers and noisy MNIST images favor the Gini approach, while a PyTorch version runs it fast on graphics hardware.
arxiv-2605-25324: Juan Scarpetta and colleagues automate the hunt for nondispersive wave packets, long-lived quantum states that ride resonant orbits without spreading in driven helium. Finding them usually demands close study of phase-space structure across wide ranges. The team computes quantum states with a Floquet description, feeds their distributions to a convolutional network, and clusters the embedding. Geometric checks, parameter inspection, and time studies then tag clusters as frozen planet states and nondispersive packets. The method recovers known packet regimes with no prior labels, showing the features carry physical structure.
arxiv-2605-25624: Wang and colleagues present CUA-Gym, a pipeline scaling verifiable training data for computer agents. Hand-curated benchmarks verify well but cover little. Their pipeline builds reward functions, environment states and task instructions. A generator builds initial and golden states, a discriminator writes rewards, and an orchestrator runs rounds. A filter of majority voting and agent rollouts keeps quality high. It synthesizes CUA-Gym-Hub, mock web applications. It builds 32,112 verified training tuples across 110 environments, with models reaching 62.1 and 72.6 percent on OSWorld-Verified.
arxiv-2605-26124: Fauzi, Latief and Sulaksono study a black hole environment in braneworld theory, where our universe is a brane in a bulk. The black hole is sourced by localised bulk matter, covering regular and Schwarzschild-like cases. With an Einstein cluster description, cluster anisotropy plus finite brane tension weakens gravity through quadratic and nonlocal corrections. That weakening prevents horizon formation inside the environment itself. With brane-tension limits from neutron star data, the effect matters most for sub-stellar-mass black holes in compact settings.
arxiv-2605-26224: Mohamed Anber's 2026 paper studies Maxwell theory for A-type asymptotically locally Euclidean spaces, asking how Abelian S-duality behaves there. The path integral splits into theta-function blocks, read as components of a boundary state. That reading turns an apparent failure of modularity into vector-valued modular covariance. An explicit test glues Eguchi-Hanson space to its reversal, recovering the standard partition function on the sphere product. Electric and magnetic one-form backgrounds turn the blocks into sections of a line bundle, showing these spaces act as chiral building blocks.
arxiv-2605-26424: Ge Fan and eight colleagues offer Uniboost, a single scheme for splitting traffic across rival business goals in recommendation systems. Current blending stages tangle plans, inflate scores, and hide reasoning, so Uniboost first lines raw scores up against anchor measures with plain business meaning. It then boosts each plan on its own linear track, letting teams see what each plan adds. Live trials show lighter weighting curbs stray business meddling. A new Effective Completion Score gives a cheap, steady anchor for content pipelines.
arxiv-2605-26524: Yuxu Lu and four colleagues predict vessel paths with CmIVTP. AIS tracks run sparse for small vessels, while CCTV alone misses full dynamics. Their framework adds a target scene encoder and a cross-modal transformer fusing AIS motion, CCTV environmental, and scene features. Cross-modal attention captures within-mode and cross-mode links at once, keeping predictions consistent and feasible. A trajectory bank from clustered past AIS tracks supplies candidate paths, and Maritime-MmD+ syncs AIS and CCTV data. Tests beat multimodal benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-26824: Bianco and three colleagues tighten Big Bang nucleosynthesis limits on heavy, long-lived relics beyond the Standard Model that decay into ordinary particle pairs. Their analysis adds fresh helium measurements, current nuclear rates, and refined treatments of neutron-proton swaps and light-element breakup during nucleosynthesis. The result is a set of updated exclusion curves for relic lifetime, mass, and abundance across each decay channel studied.
arxiv-2605-27024: Shi, Zhao, and Feng present NeR-SC, a neural representation framework tailored for screen content video, which has sharp edges, limited palettes, and strong temporal redundancy. Three modules handle discrete color structure, dense attention-gated fusion, and frame skipping for static frames. On DSCVC and VCD benchmarks, NeR-SC reaches average PSNR above 40 decibels on both, beating neural rivals and, at low bitrates, surpassing H.264 and H.265. Frame skipping enables real-time decoding with no quality loss.
arxiv-2605-27224: The LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA Collaboration describes the methods behind the fifth release of the gravitational-wave transient catalog. Building a catalog from detector data takes signal modeling, transient detection, and data quality checks. It also takes glitch mitigation, parameter inference, and comparison with waveform models for compact binary mergers, plus handling of the large result sets these steps produce. The paper covers the later part of the fourth observing run, laying out the full pipeline that turns raw detector output into catalog entries.
arxiv-2605-27424: Julio C. F. Silva, B. F. Rizzuti, and Cristhiano Duarte revisit the Wigner's Friend paradox as an inference problem. Their radically Bayesian reading finds no contradiction between Wigner and his Friend, classically or quantumly, with compatibility and agreement at the core. Extending the setup with the benefit of the doubt lets either description be driven to match the other.
arxiv-2605-27524: Alejandro Uria-Alvarez and Roser Valenti study disorder-driven insulating phases in the interacting Haldane model. Beyond standard Chern-2 phases, they find an antiferromagnetic Chern-1 phase matching the clean model's Hall insulator at finite staggered mass. Tests with a neural network show that a clear charge imbalance, made by disorder rather than staggered mass, brings on the Chern-1 phase.
arxiv-2605-27724: Kevin Lin and colleagues generate humanoid loco-manipulation data with whole-body planning instead of teleoperation. Their HumanoidMimicGen transfers contact-rich whole-body skills from a few source demonstrations to new object poses, interleaved with locomotion and manipulation planning. Whole-body visuomotor policies co-trained on the generated data beat real-data-only policies by 20 percent on a nine-task benchmark.
arxiv-2605-27824: Phuong Minh Nguyen, Tien Huu Dang, and Naoya Inoue hunt for the parts of a language model that carry out step-by-step logical reasoning. Aligning each reasoning step with the model's token scores, then testing attention heads by causal mediation, they find about three percent of heads handling individual factual and rule-based subtasks. Higher layers, by contrast, stitch those pieces into overall strategies such as graph traversal.
arxiv-2605-27924: Zhuang and colleagues turn the flood of public image-editing examples into training data for spotting manipulated pictures. Their SIGMA annotator compares original and edited images in a vision model's feature space, guided by the edit instruction, to draw masks of changed regions. It beat existing auto-mask tools and produced a million-scale set that lifted four detectors.
arxiv-2605-28224: Xinzhe Li and Yaguang Tao ask when memory truly helps tool-using agents that try many reasoning paths. They test four memory methods under three search styles on four benchmarks. The search style confounds the verdict. Reflection counts only under one style, sibling injection helps only starved beam search, and fact extraction shortens runs with no accuracy change.
arxiv-2605-28524: Zhixing Zuo and three colleagues detect fraud with a framework joining language models and graph neural networks through soft prompts. Most graph methods lean on rich text attributes, which fraud data often lack, and hard prompts that verbalize graph structure distort features. Their LGSPF bridges graph structure and semantic space with soft prompts, while a parallel graph encoder turns multi-relational topologies into graph tokens. End-to-end training aligns the two sides deeply, and benchmarks show state-of-the-art fraud detection plus clearer interpretation of fraud behavior.
arxiv-2605-29124: Juha Vierinen and colleagues track the February 2025 re-entry of a Falcon 9 upper stage with 43 meteor cameras in central Europe and multistatic radar. Optical data rebuild 30 fragment paths from 85 to 36 km, peaking near 60 km, while radar echoes from 55 to 75 km match them. Two radar echo types appear: strong specular echoes from dense wake plasma, and short-lived non-specular echoes delayed one to two seconds. Both fade in about one second, and flows point to shock-driven plasma, suggesting smaller craft like Starlink satellites could be tracked likewise.
arxiv-2605-29224: Aditya Nawal and colleagues ask how web retrieval weakens the safety alignment of language-model agents. They introduce AgentREVEAL, a diagnostic framework that studies both how retrieval is wired into the agent and what the retrieved content looks like. Binding tool calls and answer generation into a single step amplifies harmful outputs. Strikingly, even safety-oriented sources such as warning pages can raise harmful compliance, a pattern they call the Safe Source Paradox. They also release HarmURLBench, a benchmark of real-world URLs paired with harmful behaviors.
arxiv-2605-29524: Yijia Fang and three colleagues present KBF, a black-box audit checking which model serves a relay or reseller endpoint. Users cannot see behind such endpoints, so KBF probes steady recall near the knowledge boundary, counting wrong answers that repeat. It calibrates decisions against the reference model's own variation. Across sixteen production endpoints it catches all 155 relevant substitutions without rejecting any same-reference controls. Field audits flag seven of twenty-eight endpoints as inconsistent, at under a dollar per audit after enrollment.
arxiv-2605-29624: Ryo Ohashi studies plane quintic curves with automorphism groups of order greater than 10, and those with cyclic groups of orders 8 and 10. The latter two cases form one-value families, where superspeciality can be described in full through a truncation of certain Gaussian hypergeometric series. Using this characterization, he counts the isomorphism classes of superspecial plane quintic curves with automorphism groups isomorphic to Z/10Z. He also gives an efficient algorithm to enumerate such curves with groups isomorphic to Z/8Z, for primes between 13 and 10000.
arxiv-2605-30024: Kristoffer Hedegaard Aden and Alexander Kies test spreading Europe's clean power capacity more evenly across regions. Standard least-cost models pile plants where wind and sun are best, which can strain politics and security. Using a 37-node model of the European grid with a new cap on local renewable capacity, they run 105 scenarios. Full cleaning raises costs by about four fifths, yet a middle setting captures most of the fairness gain for a small extra cost.
arxiv-2605-30124: Wen Chen and An Min Wang apply the many-interacting-worlds method, a deterministic reading of quantum mechanics proposed in 2014, to smooth models of singular potentials beyond the harmonic oscillator. They treat Coulomb-like spikes and finite trap potentials in bounded systems, extended to two dimensions, using a gradual smoothing trick. Still states are found with the method's step-by-step algorithm. Their results agree with the standard matrix Numerov method for bounded systems, suggesting it could handle harder systems.
arxiv-2605-30524: Yichen Liu and nine co-authors study whether chained post-training slowly squeezes internal vectors into low-rank, uneven, and same vector spaces. They define a test set for hidden states, logits, token paths, and LoRA updates, across post-training stages. The central idea is that too much vector clumping predicts reduced flex during later tuning, weaker out-of-domain general use, and poorer tuning. They further test light fixes, like replay, refresh, and varied rules, as ways to preserve future learning without giving up behavior gains of post-training.
arxiv-2605-30724: Sun and colleagues survey quantum neural networks and quantum machine learning, a field using quantum mechanics to enhance machine learning. They examine fully linked, convolutional, and equivariant quantum neural networks, quantum Hopfield networks, quantum Boltzmann machines, and quantum reservoir computing. They also cover composite networks for quantum reinforcement learning, quantum generative learning, and quantum transfer learning. For each type, they summarize performance, including learning accuracy, training time, and resource requirements. Each type has unique strengths and weaknesses, giving diverse solutions for varied applications.
arxiv-2605-30924: Choi and colleagues build a safety guardrail for embodied agents that separates risk reasoning from agent policy. Agents powered by models can miss physical hazards or over-flag risks, stalling deployment. EMBGuard judges a visual observation plus an action, flags hazardous setups, and explains the risk in words. Alongside it come a training set of over fifteen thousand action-conditioned pairs and a test set of hundreds of checked scenes across seven risk types. Despite its small size, EMBGuard matches proprietary models while cutting false alarms.
arxiv-2605-31124: Pan, Hesong Wang and Huan Wang shrink a bulky 3D vision model so drones and phones can run it. Their QVGGT method compresses the Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer, which reads camera angles, depth and point clouds from single images. Fragile blocks keep higher precision, stray tokens are filtered out, and scale choices are checked against all three prediction heads. Tests show nearly no accuracy loss, with memory down several-fold and speed up to 2.8 times.
arxiv-2605-31224: Figliè and colleagues test a chat-style AI agent against a dashboard for factory decision tasks. Twenty people tried both tools on four made-up tasks of mixed difficulty. Workload, speed and decision accuracy were scored, and interviews were read for themes. The chat agent cut the effort of getting facts, while the dashboard stayed best for overviews and double-checking. Gains shifted from task to task, the authors note, so bigger trials are still needed.
arxiv-2605-31424: Accardi and colleagues unveil CJ26, a fresh worldwide QCD fit. It folds in all JLab 6 GeV DIS data plus the earliest released JLab 12 GeV data. The work zeroes in on large x, where 12 GeV data separates higher-twist effects from off-shell nucleon shifts. It pins down the n/p and d/u ratios well, cutting errors by 30-50% and 5-10% respectively. Linked systematic errors play a starring role in that precision, the team notes. NLO PDFs and structure functions come out in LHAPDF form for all to use.
arxiv-2605-31524: Abate and team connect certification of stochastic systems with reinforcement learning for omega-regular tasks. Certification gives proof rules from real-valued supermartingale certificates for almost-sure satisfaction of omega-regular properties. Learning methods for such tasks usually lack formal guarantees outside finite spaces. Under the right reward, the value function of a policy that meets the spec almost surely encodes a Streett certificate.
arxiv-2606-00024:
Qiu and co-authors speed up long-context language model generation by stopping wasted cache reads early, in this 2026 arXiv paper. During decoding, each token attends over a key-value cache of past tokens, and reading that cache dominates cost. Existing pruning methods decide which entries matter using keys alone, because checking values too is expensive. Their mechanism, Attention Run-time Termination, watches the attention output accumulate during computation and halts traversal once entries contribute negligibly.

A stability criterion monitors the size and direction of intermediate outputs, and the authors characterize the truncation error in theory. The method layers on top of sparse attention policies rather than replacing them. On LongBench and the RULER needle-in-a-haystack tests, which hide a fact inside long text, generation throughput rose by up to about 20 percent over existing cache methods. Result quality stayed intact, the key requirement for such shortcuts.
arxiv-2606-00124:
Mannes asks how place codes shape what a vision model learns inside. Vision models split an image into tiles and add a code for each tile's spot. Past work showed these codes change scores and strength. Their role in the inner map of space was less clear.

Mannes builds a score that tracks how much space form stays in the tile codes. Models trained with no place codes still form some space map. That map rests on image content and breaks when tiles are shuffled. All three code types he tests tie the map to tile index instead. Such models stay firm when content is scrambled. Strength seems to come from a fixed frame, not from one code type.
arxiv-2606-00224:
Cheng and co-authors free a trove of old clash data in a form AI tools can use. The data come from the SLD test at the SLAC site. That test ran in the late years of the last century. Its beam of light-charged bits was strongly spun.

The set holds near 660,000 rebuilt clash events. They were caught at an energy near the Z mass peak. Old store forms are now turned into fresh, wide-used forms. AI agents helped with the shift. A stack of in-house notes was also scanned into text. The team shows checks that prove the data are sound. They sketch uses for both clash science and machine learn work.
arxiv-2606-00324:
Xiangyi Chen and co-authors argue that semantic codes in shop tools need their own encoder. Such codes stack in layers to name goods for dream-based picks. A code chip means one thing in one stack and a next in the next. Stock tools just add chips to the word list.

Their tool, PrefixMem, reads each chip in light of its stack so far. Small n-gram note boards hold those stack-based traits. The tool can train on its own, then plug into any big model. Tests use large Pinterest data across model lines. Deep chip scores jump by up to near half in fair terms. Full-code hunt marks rise too, most on hard cases where fast picks fail.
arxiv-2606-00424:
Jin and co-authors use weak critics to coach strong models past what weak judges can grade. As models grow strong, weak guides fail at firm tags or picks. Yet a weak guide may still nudge a strong reply the right way. That nudge needs no full solve of the task at hand.

They call this weak-critic strong oversight in their frame. Weak notes lift frozen strong models at use time, when notes are sound. Their plan, OPCD, sifts top notes from the weak critic pool. Those notes are then taught back into the strong model as self-guide marks. Marks adapt as the strong model's own line shifts. Tests on thought and fit sets show gains that grow with rounds.
arxiv-2606-00624:
Oliveira and co-authors feed big-picture money traits into market calls through a tiered watch net. Deep tools show flair for trade calls, yet their broad skill is thin. Small sets, noise, and shift-prone runs all drag them down. Scant past money regimes are the core bind they name.

Their net, HANET, nests day trade marks in month money frames. A cross-watch step joins slow money marks with fast day marks. No day grain is lost in that join, they stress. Regime pick acts as watch weight on past money frames. Tests span 55 liquid trade lines in more than one class. Gains swell most in wild times, with loss cuts to match. A kin tool with the same money marks but no tiers falls flat.
arxiv-2606-00924:
Zhou and co-authors organize trial wavefunctions for fermions by locality in this 2026 physics paper. Correlated fermions are hard to simulate: their wavefunction must respect both quantum rules and rich interactions. Backflow wavefunctions bend single-particle states by the crowd around each particle. The team asks what principle should rank those bends.

Their answer is locality itself. They build hierarchical backflow states, ranked by a path depth K that sets the range of backflow effects. More depth means more expressive power, in a controlled ladder. At half-filling, depth one already gives energies within about 0.5 percent for grids up to 10 by 10. At hole doping of 0.125, the method scales to 16 by 16 and shows a clear stripe phase. Energy accuracy grows with K, as the ladder promises. The states stay compact and bridge toward neural quantum states, the authors note.
arxiv-2606-01024:
Yu and co-authors adapt a masked diffusion language model to denoise in a smooth space in this 2026 paper. Masked diffusion models write text by unveiling tokens step by step. With few steps, they face a trade: short clean text, or long text that repeats itself. Smooth denoising in embedding space can dodge the trade, but training such a model from scratch is unsolved.

The team starts from LLaDA-8B-Instruct and adapts it lightly. One thousand extra training steps swap hard masks for soft Gaussian noise per token. The result, DSL-LLaDA, evolves all positions at once and commits to tokens only at the last step. On zero shot summarization with at most 16 passes, it posts the best ROUGE-1 score on all four benchmarks, they report. It largely skips the early stop and repeat traps of plain unmasking. It also fixes corrupted tokens while leaving clean ones alone.
arxiv-2606-01324:
Dhuheir, Vu, and Chatzinotas manage spectrum for drone-aided 6G networks. Drones extend coverage and add resilience for ground users. Open-RAN design makes the network more open and flexible. But spectrum and resource choices shift fast in such settings. Mobility reshapes the topology as drones move. Tight latency and energy limits add more strain. A digital twin assists deep reinforcement learning here.

The problem splits into two linked parts. Particle swarm optimization steers drone trajectories. Multi-agent learning handles spectrum, power, and user association. The twin supports context-aware calls across the drones. Simulations show gains in spectral efficiency and data rates. Energy use also improves in their tests. The path points toward self-evolving 6G service.
arxiv-2606-01424:
Koh and Sanguanmoo study how to regulate a new technology over time. Firms learn about a technology in two ways. They learn by doing, as they scale it up. They also learn by waiting, as time passes. A regulator must set rules amid that private learning. Their answer is an adaptive speed limit. It caps how fast the technology can grow per unit time. The cap adjusts as learning unfolds.

This mechanism gives optimal worst-case guarantees. The guarantees hold over all learning processes and preferences. It is also the only time-consistent mechanism that does so. The result frames speed limits as a robust policy tool. It speaks to debates on pacing risky new technologies.
arxiv-2606-01724:
Ehsani, Pallakonda, and Mishra map how severe weather hurts Starlink performance. LEO constellations now carry much global broadband traffic. Their reliability is sensitive to local weather dynamics. Weather varies strongly in space and time, which complicates study. Their work is a continental-scale analysis for the United States. A unique dataset holds over 870,000 terminal hours of telemetry. Minute-level data come from 1,292 Starlink terminals across the country.

High-resolution weather records join the telemetry in the analysis. Ping latency, drop rate, and signal quality are the tracked metrics. Spatial joins and time-aligned correlation link weather to performance drops. Storms with heavy rain or snow hit performance hardest. Over 55 percent of affected terminals saw substantial degradation. Impairments lasted from minutes to multiple hours at a time.
arxiv-2606-01824:
Wu and co-authors track moving objects in 3D from range data. Their DisFlow method works online, frame by frame. It finds an object's pose and speed as it moves. It also rebuilds the object's surface over time. The scene is stored as a smooth distance field.

Surface normals add slope facts to that field. Flow is read from how the field shifts in time. New point clouds are fit with a closed-form step. Fusion takes place in the object's own frame. In that frame, the object stays fixed in shape. The authors report dense shape, normals, and pose paths. The tight space-time link is the core of the design.
arxiv-2606-02024:
Xue and co-authors locate where blazar jets produce high-energy neutrinos. Those production sites remain poorly constrained today. Radio data constrain the jet properties used here. The team track the external-to-magnetic energy density ratio. That ratio is the Compton dominance along the jet.

Efficient neutrino production needs that ratio far above one. Large values boost photohadronic interactions in the jet. They also suppress synchrotron light from secondary pairs. That avoids excess hard X-ray emission in models. Such values arise near the broad-line region most readily. One emission region cannot fit the full spectrum then. The neutrino site is thus distinct, they argue. Multi-zone jet models gain support from the result.
arxiv-2606-02324:
Nguyen and co-authors work in pure mathematics, on a class of functions called rational necklace functions. Necklace polynomials show up in counting problems, Lie theory, and work on finite fields. The new functions join two known families in one frame. These are necklace polynomials and Fekete polynomials.

The authors show how cyclotomic polynomials arise as factors of the new functions. They give several routes to this result. The results unite and extend earlier work on both families. One finding stands out as a surprise. Certain Galois groups play a hidden role in some new factors. Earlier work did not cover those cases. Readers gain a wider theory with cleaner links between its parts.
arxiv-2606-02624:
Gao and co-authors build TadA-Bench, a benchmark for protein engineering that replays a real lab campaign. Agentic systems should pick future wet-lab experiments, not just fit old data. The bench replays 31 rounds of TadA directed evolution. It holds a million variants. Chronology is preserved. Models see earlier rounds and must rank variants that appear only later.

DNA, RNA, and protein views are aligned for each variant. A pipeline called Seq2Graph unifies noisy enrichment measures. It produces consistent activity labels across rounds. Random-split controls show strong interpolation skill. Future-round ranking is much weaker. Finite-budget candidate selection is weaker still. Controlled tests suggest evolutionary coverage beats local data density as a signal. Data and code are released on Hugging Face and GitHub. The bench gives agentic protein engineering a reproducible test bed.
arxiv-2606-02724:
Wang and co-authors build a dataset for tracking active speakers in complex real scenes. Audio-visual speaker tracking locates who is speaking. It uses sound and vision together. Video editing, surveillance, and human-computer interaction all need it. Existing datasets use simple scenes with coarse annotations. Evaluation then rewards static audio-visual matching. Robust modeling of dynamic scenes goes untested.

Their dataset, AVTrack, targets human-centric audio-visual instance segmentation. Scenes include camera motion, occlusions, and position changes. Conditions are diverse and hard by design. Representative methods lose substantial performance on it. That drop establishes AVTrack as a tough benchmark. A simple yet effective baseline is also provided. The authors aim to push audio-visual scene understanding toward real-world complexity.
arxiv-2606-02824:
Good and co-authors show that an accelerated charge can radiate with a spectrum that looks fermionic. Photons are bosons, and their occupation numbers are not capped at one. Yet a special class of acceleration kinematics makes the emitted spectrum follow Fermi-Dirac form. The effect is apparent, not thermal. It does not rely on thermal equilibrium. It does not need horizons or statistical ensembles.

The distinction matters for how spectra are read. A Fermi-Dirac shape is usually taken as a signature of fermions or of hot equilibrium. Here it arises from motion alone. The charge is a point charge with the right acceleration profile. Bosonic radiation then mimics a fermionic spectrum in form. The result is a caution and a tool for radiation theory. Kinematics can forge statistical-looking signatures without any statistics underneath.
arxiv-2606-03224:
Asadi and Sheikhi sort galaxies into early and late types with a fast machine learning method. The data come from the COSMOS2025 catalog, at redshifts from zero to three. Past routes need image labels or slow structural fits. This team trains on simulated galaxies instead, with labels from a semi-analytic model.

Labels rest on bulge-to-total mass ratio and star formation rate. Real-style photometric noise is added to bridge the gap to true data. A CatBoost model trained on 66 broadband colors did well in the simulated domain. It caught late types at about 98 percent precision and recall. Early types scored lower but still well. Applied to 44,132 real galaxies, the model put about 94 percent of cases at high confidence. Checks against bulge-disk fits gave 70 percent overall accuracy. The whole pipeline runs in under 30 minutes on standard hardware.
arxiv-2606-03424:
Druel, Pereira, Pym, and Touzet prove Bondal's conjecture for five-dimensional Fano manifolds. The conjecture comes from Poisson geometry. It gives lower bounds on the sets where a Poisson structure loses rank. Those sets are called degeneracy loci. Prior work had settled the claim for dimensions up to four.

The proof gives the first result in dimension five. It also yields partial results for all odd dimensions. Three tools carry the argument. One is an algebraic integrability test for codimension-one foliations on weak Fano manifolds. Another is the modular residues of Poisson structures, introduced by Gualtieri and Pym. The third is a cohomological bound on invariant subvarieties for Pfaff fields. That bound extends earlier work by Esteves and Kleiman to a harder case. Geometers get a new foothold on a long-open conjecture. The tools may serve other problems in Poisson geometry as well.
arxiv-2606-03524:
Torregrosa Abellán and co-authors track how fast droplets cloak themselves on lubricated polymer brushes. A wetting ridge grows at the drop's edge as lubricant gathers there. Cloaking spreads a thin lubricant film over the drop. The team mixes experiments, molecular dynamics simulations, and theory. Three systems are compared, with water and a DMSO mix on swollen brushes and on PDMS.

Ridge growth drains lubricant from zones below and outside the drop. That drain slows growth over time, since lubricant must travel through the brush. At high swelling, oil separates from the brush inside the ridge itself. That split adds a second drain path. A continuum diffusion model ties brush free energy to the contact line. It matches ridge growth at middle and late times well. The kinetics are thus governed mainly by diffusion inside the brush. Surface scientists get a predictive frame for these soft coatings.
arxiv-2606-03624:
Zhao and co-authors help large reasoning models follow many instructions at once. Such models often drop single constraints or fail to balance rival ones. The challenge is named the Constraint Adherence Problem. Their framework, CRGC, turns instructions into a structured knowledge graph of constraints. Relationships between constraints are modeled directly.

The graph reveals where adherence will strain. It also finds bridge constraints, extra instructions that make the main ones stand out. Bridges make primary constraints more salient and more compatible with each other. The method uses the model's own knowledge to build better generation paths. No general retraining is involved. Across three instruction-following datasets, violations fall by 39 percent versus standard prompting. Reasoning skill stays intact while satisfaction rises. The result offers a targeted fix for a common failure of reasoning models.
arxiv-2606-03724:
Tai argues that a robot policy is more than its model weights. Vision-language-action policies are often treated as checkpoint-defined. Same weights, prompt, and benchmark are taken to mean the same deployment. Robot execution breaks that idea. One normalized output can become a different physical action after unnormalization and controller rules apply. Safety review can thus certify the checkpoint yet miss the real policy.

The executable policy includes the model, the action form, the unnormalizer picked by metadata, and controller conventions. Identical checkpoints can be executable-inequivalent under this view. A closed-form transform quantifies drift from metadata mismatch. An ExecSpec certificate measures action-space drift without running the model. On LIBERO replay tests, swapping one metadata key cuts success from perfect to near zero. The checks rule out simpler explanations for the drop. Deployment teams should treat action metadata as part of the policy itself.
arxiv-2606-03824:
Parker and co-authors open the CRIMSON survey with silicon chemistry in a directly imaged companion. Silicon governs magnesium-silicate clouds in giant planet air. It also records how much silicate a planet gathered while forming. Volatile species like CO and water have dominated past spectra. M-band spectroscopy with CRIRES plus reaches the SiO band head near four microns. TWA 5 B is the first target.

Gaseous SiO is detected strongly in the companion's atmosphere. Its abundance implies little silicate cloud condensation there. Nearly all silicon sits in the observed gas phase. Carbon monoxide and water are also detected with high confidence. Ratios point to a stellar carbon-to-oxygen value. Silicon over hydrogen runs above the stellar level. The mix fits core accretion past the CO snowline, or gravitational collapse with later solid enrichment. SiO gives a new probe of clouds in hot giants.
arxiv-2606-03924:
Park and Jo ask if fact editing works in masked diffusion models. These models build text in both directions and clean it step by step. Most editing tools were made for models that write one token at a time. The pair move a locate-then-edit method into the new model class. They then compare matched pairs of the two model types.

They find the best edit site is shared by both types. It sits in an early to mid layer at the last subject token. Short edits work in both, they report. Long edits fade much faster in diffusion models. The cause is half-masked states that the edit never trained on. A fix that trains on such states restores much of the lost skill.
arxiv-2606-04124:
Facundo Pérez Paolino, Lynne Hillenbrand, and Jeff Bary track in 2026 how the magnetic fields of nine young T Tauri stars change with rotation and over years. These pre-main-sequence stars are still contracting toward stable burning, and their fields steer much of their early evolution.

From nearly five hundred high-resolution infrared spectra, the team fit each observing epoch with magnetic model spectra. Six stars showed linked magnetic and thermal variability, and all six yielded their known rotation period in at least one season. Both field strength and the size of the rotational signal drifted over the years, sometimes vanishing, meaning the surface pattern itself rearranges. Magnetic regions also covered more of the surface than the cool starspots alone suggested.
arxiv-2606-04224:
Tomáš Dohnal and co-authors study in 2026 the spectrum of waves at the interface of two materials. One side is a standard medium. The other is dispersive: its response depends on the wave's frequency, as in plasmas and some engineered materials.

Without assuming any specific material model, they pin down which frequencies behave tamely. Those form the resolvent set, where waves pass in a controlled way. The rest splits into parts tied to radiation escaping to infinity and to waves bound at the interface. The split is sharp and complete for the cases covered. The work extends older results for simpler media. It gives a firm base for later work on sensing and waveguides at such interfaces.
arxiv-2606-04724:
Kachkachi builds a two-scale theory of how chains of nanomagnets heat up under an alternating magnetic field, in a 2026 arXiv physics paper. Each nanomagnet is a heat source governed by its magnetic response, dipolar interactions with neighbors, and coupling to the matrix. After spatial averaging, he derives a coarse-grained equation with heating terms and a loss coefficient, then solves both equations exactly.

The framework gives conditions for a crossover between local heating, where magnets run hot, and global heating, where the chain warms. The crossover is quantified through a spatial correlation length and variance. For magnetic systems, nanomagnets in water, parameters land firmly in the collective regime, with local variations around a microkelvin.
arxiv-2606-04824:
Führer, Grasegger, Hametner, and Roche-Newton resolve part of a question about a two-player game on graphs, in a 2026 arXiv combinatorics paper. In the Maker-Breaker Domination Game, players alternately claim vertices. The Dominator aims to claim a full dominating set, while the Staller aims to prevent it. The question: for a given minimum degree d, how small can a graph be, in vertices, while still making the first-moving Dominator lose?

The answer is denoted beta of d. The authors determine its precise value for d up to three. For general d, the known lower bound from the Erdős-Selfridge theorem and the upper bound from a construction left a wide gap. They improve the lower bound to two-to-the-(d-plus-one) plus two, narrowing the gap from below.
arxiv-2606-04924:
Velutharambath and colleagues survey whether human data collection can survive workers quietly delegating to chatbots, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Crowdsourcing supplies the free-text data that language research runs on, but crowdworkers may outsource tasks to large language models, challenging the data's validity as human data. The authors surveyed 155 researchers about their experiences.

Forty-four percent of respondents reported observing model usage in their crowdsourced data. Nearly all of them had anticipated it, yet half were unsure what precautions to take. The most prevalent detection strategies are textual style patterns and fast completion times. Overall, the community is aware and taking measures, but efforts remain insufficient to fully address the problem. Models are evaluated and trained on human data, so undetected model output in that data quietly corrupts the yardstick itself.
arxiv-2606-05124:
Hongyu Zhou and Zorah Lähner decouple appearance from geometry in Gaussian splatting in this 2026 arXiv paper. 3D Gaussian Splatting renders new views of a scene quickly and well, and many groups want to reuse it for geometric surface reconstruction. Pulling accurate geometry out of it is hard, though, and attempts often degrade the rendering quality instead.

The authors first show, by training with complete ground-truth texture and geometry, that the default method is inherently unsuited to representing texture and geometry at the same time. The splats that best explain appearance are not those that best describe surfaces. Their fix is simple: give each splat one additional geometry opacity parameter, with an optional transparency-curated optimization pipeline. Experiments with both ground-truth and vision-foundation-model geometric input showed improved rendering and geometry across a wide variety of datasets. Complex scenes containing transparent objects benefited significantly from the change.
arxiv-2606-05224:
Jiamin Li and Jianya Liu prove a theorem interpolating between Chen's theorem and the Goldbach conjecture in this 2026 arXiv paper. Goldbach says every large even integer is a sum of two primes, still unproven, while Chen's theorem allows one summand to be a product of two primes. The authors use a scale of propositions in which one prime can be multiplied by a small extra factor. The endpoint cases recover Goldbach at one extreme and Chen at the other.

They prove unconditionally that the proposition at level 1.9 on that scale is true, and assuming the Elliott-Halberstam conjecture the exponent improves to 1.4, closing much of the gap toward Goldbach. A twin prime scale yields an unconditional result at level 1.75, improving to 1.4 under the same conjecture. The breakthrough comes from new weighted sieves and new analytic tools, building the first connecting pathway across a divide that had persisted for six decades.
arxiv-2606-05624:
Tengjiao Sun and colleagues add path control to text-driven motion models in a 2026 arXiv paper. Such models animate a figure from a sentence, with plausible style and gait. Real work also demands paths: follow this route, touch that target. Bolting on control usually means copying the generator or slow test-time fixes. The team instead slips control into the model's attention memory.

Their method, KV-Control, injects path data as keys and values at every attention layer. The frozen generator's weights and text handling stay untouched. A body-part coding scheme gives each frame and limb its own addressable slot. The add-on trains only about one and a half million parameters. It tracked root and joint paths to sub-centimeter accuracy. Text-based motion quality held up at the same time. Control, the authors argue, can ride as memory rather than as a rebuilt model.
arxiv-2606-05724:
Qiuyu Tian and colleagues answer questions about long stories with a narrative-shaped memory in a 2026 arXiv paper. Story questions hinge on shifting goals, character states, and causes spread across a whole book or script. Chunk retrieval finds passages but misses how evidence works inside a plot. Their Narrative Knowledge Weaver aligns text, atomic facts, a canonical graph, and character profiles. Episodes and storylines sit in the same structure.

At query time the system mixes text search, graph tools, and narrative tools. A reading stage then audits who acted, what scope applies, and when events fall. Three benchmarks tested the design: STAGE, FairytaleQA, and QuALITY. The weaver was strongest on screenplay-level story questions. It stayed competitive on the more passage-centered sets. Breakdowns by question type showed joint gains for character, scene, time, cause, and plot progress reasoning.
arxiv-2606-05924:
Zhihao Lin and colleagues create their training data to teach models literary translation in a 2026 arXiv paper. Literary texts starve models: good annotated translations are scarce, and fluency fights with artistic effect. The team deploys specialist translator models, each honing one quality aspect like metaphor or style. Their revision loop yields reference translations and preference pairs.

Those references beat the human ground truth as fine-tuning material by a wide margin. Reinforcement learning then split two ways. Direct preference tuning hurt results here. An explicit reward model driving GRPO added a further clear gain. The resulting LitMT models, at eight and fourteen billion parameters, scored near a leading commercial system on an English-to-Chinese metaphor benchmark. The larger model edged slightly ahead of it. Tests on O. Henry stories showed the skill travels to unseen authors. Synthetic supervision, well staged, can substitute for scarce gold data.
arxiv-2606-06124:
MacCallum redraws a famous diagram of the rotating black hole and finds a missing region in a 2026 arXiv paper. The Kerr solution's ring singularity is usually pictured as one disc. MacCallum argues the region spanning the ring is better described as two flat discs. That viewpoint changes what the standard worldsheet depiction shows.

The usual conformal diagram of the equatorial slice, he shows, omits the negative-radius region entirely. Multiple copies of that region should appear, representable as a triangle in the diagram's style. The fix sounds small but touches the maximal analytic extension, relativists' complete map of the solution. Generations of students have learned Kerr geometry from the incomplete picture. The paper grew from a talk honoring Brandon Carter, a founder of black hole theory, and is dedicated to him. Textbook diagrams, MacCallum reminds readers, are arguments, and arguments can drop pieces.
arxiv-2606-06324:
Mengzhuo Chen and co-authors fix the scaffolding around language model agents in this 2026 arXiv paper. The harness is the runtime layer that gives an agent its tools, context, and execution rules. When an agent fails, the fault often sits in that harness, not the model. Self improvement methods that only see final outcomes tend to patch blindly, making broad changes in the wrong place.

Their framework, HarnessFix, starts from the execution trace. It compiles raw traces and harness files into a structured representation that links each runtime step to the harness artifact that shaped it. Failures are then attributed to the responsible steps, and recurring problems are grouped into flaw records. Scoped repair operators generate patches under those records, checked by regression aware validation. On four benchmarks, performance rose over the initial harnesses by six point three to eighteen point four percent, beating human designed and self evolving alternatives.
arxiv-2606-06724:
Machine learning needs lots of example data, and real physics measurements are often too few. Vepsalainen builds a way to manufacture believable stand in data in this 2026 arXiv paper. His method, called Synthics, learns the algebraic shape of real physics equations. It then samples brand new equations with the same habits. A grammar assigns probabilities to each building block.

Inputs are drawn only from ranges where each equation makes physical sense, found by probing, and mixed to mimic real lab conditions. Checked against the Feynman equation collection, the synthetic sets matched the real corpus on all eight structural traits studied, while a simpler grammar managed only two. In a practical test, tuning on the fake data picked the sixth best model setting out of twenty on real data. That matched tuning on real data itself. It also far beat random stand ins.
arxiv-2606-06824:
Symmetry groups of trees are a testing ground for ideas born in geometry. Du studies two generator subgroups of those symmetries in this 2026 arXiv paper. The tree is trivalent, meaning three edges meet at every branch point. The subgroups must be discrete and faithful: no bunching up, and no hidden kernel.

He gives a partial classification under a restriction. The restriction bounds a small geometric quantity tied to the generators. Graphs of groups provide the language for the classification. When the restriction is relaxed, full classification slips away. Du instead describes the possible quotient graphs. He constructs infinite families of examples on each of them. The paper also generalizes a classic algorithm. The Poincare style test decides whether given tree symmetries generate a discrete subgroup. The problem descends from Fuchsian groups, where discreteness criteria are classical.
arxiv-2606-06924:
Choosing which language model should answer each question saves money, but routers learn from shaky labels. Lai, Hu, Chen, Li, and Ye expose that shakiness in this 2026 arXiv paper. A router is usually trained on one sampled answer per model. Generation is random, so one answer is a noisy snapshot.

Their framework, DARS, builds labels from distributions instead. It watches how a model behaves across reworded questions. It also samples repeated generations for the same question. Both input and output randomness enter the estimate. Experiments across varied tasks showed single shot labels mislead model selection. Distribution aware labels stayed more stable. Routers trained on them behaved better in practice. The authors argue that capability is a distribution, not a coin flip. Routing supervision should reflect that spread.
arxiv-2606-07124:
Two agents each see half the features of the same samples and must jointly estimate how the halves covary, over a thin channel. Tan and Han find the fundamental limits of that task in this 2026 arXiv paper. The model is vertical split distributed estimation: features, not samples, are divided. The cross covariance between the two halves is what the server needs.

Imposing sparsity on that matrix changes the problem's economics. The authors prove minimax lower bounds on communication and sample needs. With very sparse structure, the cost collapses from a product of dimensions to a logarithm of that product. That is an exponential saving over the dense case. A matching protocol built on covering nets and hard thresholding achieves the bound up to small factors. Earlier work on mean estimation had suggested sparsity never helps. Covariance estimation plays by different rules.
arxiv-2606-07424:
Sinha and co-authors speed up the design of a robot's body and brain in this 2026 arXiv paper. Tuning morphology and control together beats tuning either alone, but testing each candidate body requires retraining its controller with reinforcement learning, which is expensive. Universal policies that accept the body design as input avoid retraining, yet they collapse to one compromise behavior that suits no design well. Their framework, Gaussian Evolutionary Specialists, assigns specialist policies to evolving regions of design space instead.

Specialists are trained, probed, and allowed to expand territory where they excel, then plugged into design sampling as scorers. On BALLU, a buoyant balloon-legged robot testbed, the method found designs 5 to 25 percent better than universal-policy baselines in simulation. A hardware build of the optimized design cleared an obstacle three times taller than the baseline robot could manage in their tests. Design time fell by over a third.
arxiv-2606-07524:
Wang and co-authors fingerprint language models by how they attend, not by what they say, in this 2026 arXiv paper proposing ABLE. Hundreds of open models circulate with poor documentation, complicating provenance auditing, security analysis, and model selection. Methods reading weights fail when architectures differ, while output-based methods confuse models that behave alike and clash across tokenizers. ABLE aggregates gradient-based attributions, measures of which input words drive a model's responses, aligned at word level so tokenizers cannot distort the comparison.

The embedding captures a model's input-sensitivity pattern. Theory supports it: under assumptions the map from parameters to embedding is stable, with finite-sample convergence guarantees. Experiments across 200 models showed the training-free method matching or beating rivals at predicting model relationships, routing queries to models, and forecasting benchmark scores. The authors frame attribution space as an underexploited middle ground between weights and outputs for mapping the ecosystem.
arxiv-2606-07624:
Xie argues that the study of sequences, not single responses, is the missing field for trustworthy language model deployment, in this 2026 arXiv essay. Deployed models are queried again and again, shaped by evolving contexts, fed user and tool feedback, and changed by updates and shifting data. Treating each prompt-response pair as a lone draw misses all of that. Xie builds the statistician's part around three tasks: representation, validity, and monitoring.

Representation means modeling model traffic as dependent stochastic flows. Validity means uncertainty guarantees, like those from conformal prediction, that survive dependence, repeated use, and change rather than counting on new samples. Monitoring means stepwise alarms and change-point detection watching calibration, hallucination rates, refusal behavior, and fairness traits, as statistical process control watches a factory line. The view complements surveys by reframing the setup as a process to be controlled, with drift the normal case rather than an exception.
arxiv-2606-09024:
Nakayashiki and Watanabe ask how much of a person shows through in their highlights, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Social highlighters let readers mark what matters to them. The authors separate three forces behind a mark: generic salience (structure), crowd salience (others' marks), and personal salience. Their control: many users highlight the same document, and the test is whether your history predicts your marks better than another reader's does.

Highlighting turned out to be mostly social. The crowd predicted a person's marks better than structure or personal models, and the personal signal was tiny, an identity gap of 0.017. Individuality instead lived in selection: choosing which already-salient passages are yours was strongly personal, with a gap of 0.14, and popularity hurt there. The selection signal was mostly topic taste, shrinking about eightfold against a topically matched peer. The authors show naive evaluations leak, inflating personal scores, so their leakage-free design matters.
arxiv-2606-09124:
Kim and colleagues argue that human choices are statements about regret, and retrain language models on that basis, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Reinforcement learning from human feedback treats a preference as a reward signal: this answer scores higher. But people judge by imagining outcomes and comparing against what could have happened. A preference often encodes relative regret, how much worse one behavior is than another.

Their method, Regret-based Preference Optimization, models them as behavior-based judgments of suboptimality. Under KL-regularized learning they derive a closed-form regret decomposition, making the objective trainable. Experiments on math reasoning and human preference data showed consistent gains over DPO-style baselines. The claim: regret captures what a human comparison says better than a scalar reward, and training on it yields stronger, better aligned models.
arxiv-2606-09424:
Takao Obi and his colleagues test whether turn-taking prediction tools built for speech can work for sign language in this 2026 arXiv paper. Social robots need to anticipate who will act next, and Voice Activity Projection already does this for spoken conversation. For signing users, though, the relevant cues are visual rather than acoustic.

The team adapted the framework using recordings from the Public DGS Corpus of German Sign Language interaction. They derived streams of signing activity from lexical annotations and represented each signer with pose-based features from the hands, eye region, and mouth. Two tasks were tested: judging whether a turn shifts or holds after a pause, and predicting a coming shift during activity. The first task proved promising, especially when hand cues were used, while predicting shifts remained difficult. The authors conclude that sign language needs its own event definitions, not just categories borrowed from speech.
arxiv-2606-09524:
Prashun Kumar gives an explicit structural description of a restricted class of finite groups in this 2026 arXiv paper. A group is quartic-free when its order is divisible by no prime raised to the fourth power. It is an A-group when all its Sylow subgroups, the maximal prime-power pieces, are abelian, meaning their elements commute.

Kumar's first main theorem handles the solvable case: every solvable quartic-free A-group decomposes as a nested semidirect product of four abelian quartic-free subgroups. The second theorem covers the non-solvable case, splitting the group into a solvable part acted on by a simple group. If that action is non-trivial, the simple part must have order divisible by five and in fact be the alternating group A5. Along the way, it classifies relevant subgroups of small general linear groups and finds the derived length for the solvable case.
arxiv-2606-09724:
Hudson de Martim argues that the standard fix for shaky legal AI is mismatched to how law is built in this 2026 arXiv paper. The fix is retrieval-augmented generation: a model looks up text, then answers from it. Courts still see fake cites and stale law passed off as current. De Martim says scale will not cure them.

Law, he notes, has three deep traits. It is layered, with parts nested in wholes. It shifts over time while staying a closed system. And each norm must trace to an institution that can justify it. Plain similarity search is blind to all three: it misses part-whole links, mixes old and new law, and hides sources. He names these flaws and gives tests to spot them. The fix he urges is built in from the start: law-first data shapes, events as records, two-time stamps, and strict exchange rules.
arxiv-2606-10024:
Stiskalek and his team find a cheap way to reuse expensive cosmology simulations at new settings, in a 2026 arXiv paper on computational cosmology. Learning cosmology from galaxy surveys needs many runs across parameter values, but full runs are costly. The team extends cosmological rescaling, a technique that stretches one simulation to mimic another universe, to work directly on merger trees.

Running a semi-analytic galaxy model on the rescaled trees produces galaxy populations at tiny extra cost. A halo-profile fix, tuned by one free parameter, keeps rescaled halo mass bias below the percent level. As few as sixty-four base simulations, rescaled into about one thousand samples, matched the parameter accuracy of seven hundred fifty dedicated runs. Rescaling trees from one simulation costs about a tenth of a CPU hour, versus several thousand to run it.
arxiv-2606-10124:
Zhang and colleagues fix a failure mode in federated learning, where many clients train a shared model without sharing raw data, in a 2026 arXiv paper on distributed machine learning. When clients participate inconsistently, servers often reuse stale updates from inactive clients to reduce variance. Their method, FedSteer, builds a gradient subspace from a cache of recent client gradients, representing the current optimization landscape in low dimensions.

An active client's true gradient is projected onto that subspace to find optimal coordinates. For an inactive client, FedSteer reuses those coordinates with the subspace as it has since drifted, effectively steering outdated gradients toward the current global objective. A selective caching strategy picks a representative client subset to form the subspace, reducing server memory. Experiments show FedSteer prevents performance collapse in challenging scenarios and delivers accuracy gains of over seven percent in others.
arxiv-2606-10424:
Ye and colleagues study swirling flows in active matter in this 2026 arXiv paper, asking how slip at a container wall affects whether a steady vortex survives. Active matter consists of small units that use energy to move on their own, like bacteria. In an active nematic, rod-like units share a direction, and their internal stresses stir the surrounding fluid.

Using a continuum model of a circular chamber and linear stability analysis, which tests whether small disturbances grow or fade, the authors reach a counterintuitive result. Letting the fluid slip more freely along the boundary makes the vortex more stable, because extra slip weakens the flow-driven reorientation that normally tears a single vortex apart. Their explicit stability criterion combines slip velocity with activity, system size, and flow alignment, giving boundary slip a clear role as a design knob for steady active flows.
arxiv-2606-10624:
Latour and a large collaboration re-examine a young planetary system in this 2026 arXiv paper in astronomy. The star HD 135344B hosts a protoplanetary disk with three spiral arms, a dust gap, and a filament crossing that gap, all signposts of a forming planet. A twist in one spiral had hinted at the planet driving the pattern. The team reprocessed a decade of archival images from the Very Large Telescope and the James Webb Space Telescope with careful algorithms.

They measure the spirals rotating at 0.81 degrees per year, give or take five hundredths, matching earlier estimates. Modelling confirms the twist moves with its spiral, fitting a planet at sixty-nine astronomical units, give or take four. A previously claimed protoplanet candidate dissolves into a processing artifact. One puzzle remains: the spirals' distance from the star shifts with wavelength.
arxiv-2606-10724:
Cankaya and colleagues design an audit for AI data centres in this 2026 arXiv paper on AI governance. If nations ever agree on limits for AI training, they need verification without trusting the operator. The proposal fingerprints all information entering and leaving a cluster: taps on wires hash the traffic, so an auditor can challenge the operator to reveal the data behind a hash. The goal is to make covert exfiltration of undisclosed workloads infeasible.

Hashes cannot stop side channels, so a gateway device scrubs them, erasing steganography in protocol headers and re-timing packets to kill timing and analogue channels. The architecture needs no processor trusted by both sides: passive optical splitters and coin-flip protocols supply shared randomness, grounding trust in physics, not device integrity. A device is estimated at a few engineer-months, and the approach scales to clusters of 100,000 accelerators.
arxiv-2606-10824:
Blaser and colleagues rethink how a topological descriptor is fed to neural networks in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Euler Characteristic Transform profiles a shape by sweeping it along directions and tracking how its Euler characteristic, components minus holes plus voids, evolves. Networks usually receive this as a discretised curve, a choice that is itself an inductive bias. The authors propose a continuous encoding: per direction, each vertex contributes a token carrying its net Euler change, and a transformer turns the tokens into features.

Across 6 classification benchmarks spanning point clouds, graphs, cubical complexes, and meshes, the encoding improves accuracy on five, with gains up to 0.120 on Letter-high and 0.094 on SwissBuildings. Control experiments attribute the gain to the tokenisation itself, not the transformer capacity. Six architectures for combining them are also compared: architecture matters less than that choice, and a feedforward network, fragile under discretisation, performs best with the new tokens.
arxiv-2606-11024:
Croft presents a self-completing modeling tool for particle physics in this 2026 arXiv paper. ALETHEIA builds foundation models over collision events for effective-field-theory content, here four dimension-six operators in neutral-current Drell-Yan. Two jobs are kept apart: active learning picks the simulation points that pin down coefficients fastest, while the physics itself, ordered by power counting, decides which new operator to switch on.

A residual fingerprint watches for missing directions; when one dominates, the encoder grows by that direction and refits. The first such extension cuts the peak residual about thirty-one-fold, and across four extensions about a hundred-and-fifty-fold, until the trace falls below the noise floor: the signature that the representation is complete.
arxiv-2606-11524:
Rongrueangkul and eleven co-authors probe what binds electrons into pairs in the record cuprate superconductor in a 2026 arXiv paper. The pairing mechanism in cuprates remains a basic open problem: magnetism and lattice vibrations both govern electron behavior, but their working together has never been directly observed. The team studies Hg1223, the cuprate with the highest transition temperature at ambient pressure, as a magnifying glass.

Using resonant inelastic X-ray scattering, they find the charge response is led by dynamic charge density fluctuations extending up to several hundred milli-electron-volts, where magnetic excitations reside. At the momentum where they are most intense, the paramagnon, a spin excitation, shows pronounced softening. The result reveals a strong interplay of charge, lattice, and spin. The authors argue dynamic charge fluctuations mediate the coupling of lattice, charge, and spin, pointing to a shared pairing mechanism.
arxiv-2606-11624:
Jimmy Lederman and Aaron Schein introduce a new family of probability distributions in this 2026 arXiv paper on statistics. The setting is regression for outcomes trapped between zero and one, such as proportions. The usual beta distribution struggles here: it reacts badly to outliers, cannot handle exact zeros, and lacks simple partner priors for Bayesian updating.

Their distribution, named in the title, is built by randomising the beta parameters with three linked negative binomial variables. A median, a concentration and a boundary parameter describe it, and genuine zeros and ones are allowed. A construction using Gaussian hidden variables makes the Bayesian updates closed-form, so a Gibbs sampler, a standard simulation routine, stays simple. Tests show better effective sample size per second and held-out predictions than standard beta regression, especially with outliers. A forest canopy study shows it handling spatial structure and exact zeros.
arxiv-2606-11924:
Alexander I Tyulenev describes what functions look like when restricted to rough sets in this 2026 arXiv paper on analysis. Sobolev spaces collect functions with integrable derivatives; their trace problem asks what boundary values such functions can take on a lower-dimensional set. The limiting exponent case, where derivatives are merely integrable, is the hardest and least understood.

Tyulenev works in that case for weighted spaces, where a Muckenhoupt weight distorts the measure, and for Ahlfors-David regular sets, fractal-like sets with controlled mass at every scale. He gives a complete intrinsic description of the trace space: a characterisation using only quantities measured on the set itself. He also constructs a new family of nonlinear extension operators that lift trace data back to the whole space with bounded norm. Finally, he finds conditions on the weight sufficient for a bounded linear extension operator to exist.
arxiv-2606-12524:
Tang and co-authors ask whether outer gas giants sculpt the small planets closer in. They find the chisel marks only in rich systems, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Gas giants can dam the flow of building blocks in a young disk, starving or enriching inner worlds. The team assembled forty-three systems holding sixty-eight small planets, each with mass and radius. Correcting for how sensitive each system was to detecting giants, they computed giant occurrence rates by planet density and composition.

Overall, nothing: giants appear as often beside dense planets as fluffy ones, whatever the core mass. Restrict attention to metal-rich stars, though, and a hint emerges. There, giants preferentially accompany lower-density planets whose core masses look alike. Larger samples split by the radius valley or by mass show hints. The reading: metal-rich disks assemble cores fast and start gas accretion, changing what planets become.
arxiv-2606-12724:
Chao develops a block algebra notation for morphing circuits, a hardware-lean approach to quantum error correction, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Morphing circuits extract error syndromes from a stabiliser code using only the code's own qubits as the measurement workspace. They replace extra ancilla qubits with contraction rounds that shrink the code, measure some qubits, and restore it.

Grouping qubits and checks into blocks, Chao expresses the parity-check matrices with entries drawn from algebras generated by permutation matrices. So a CNOT layer becomes a column operation and each contraction a Gaussian-elimination pattern. He presents 4 constructions for CNOT-based CSS morphing circuits with explicit qubit connectivity degrees. The first 3 rewrite known surface-code and colour-code morphing circuits in this notation, recovering a published circuit for 2-block group algebra codes. The fourth is new: a 3-round construction modelled on the 6.6.6 colour code whose connectivity degree is just 3.
arxiv-2606-12824:
Soliman shows that CT acquisition settings act as a hidden variable that distorts AI lung-nodule measurement and detection in different ways, invisible in image metadata, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Clinics monitor imaging AI through outputs and DICOM metadata, the header information attached to scans.

Using a MONAI RetinaNet detector trained on LUNA16, the study checks 155 lung nodules scanned with soft and sharp reconstruction kernels. Kernel choice shifted AI size readings by 0.27 millimetres on average and flipped the Fleischner size category in 5.2 percent of nodules, while detection confidence stayed the same. Shifts in LIDC-IDRI scans dissociate the axes: noise degrades detection confidence, notably for nodules under 6 millimetres, but not sizing, while the frequency or kernel axis corrupts sizing but not detection. A 4-feature fingerprint built from the pixels finds the reconstruction identity with area under the curve near 0.95, where the DICOM kernel tag, reading STANDARD for each, says nothing.
arxiv-2606-12924:
Duraj and colleagues at eBay present a 2-agent simulation framework for evaluating conversational shopping assistant architectures, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their framework pairs a buyer agent, configured with personas, missions, and patience levels, with an interchangeable responder connected to an e-commerce search API, so responder designs face identical scenarios.

Using 2,011 conversations across 14 persona buckets, they establish 4 findings. First, rolling-window memory outperforms intent-extraction memory on all quality metrics while being 35 percent faster per query. Second, failure analysis of one responder version enabled targeted fixes that reduced failure and near-failure rates by 62 percent across the full dataset. Third, swapping the responder's model backbone from Gemini 2.5 to Llama 3.3 70B costs between 0.16 and 0.45 points despite identical architecture. Fourth, judge selection is consequential: Gemini and Claude judges disagree on 30 percent of conversations by 2 or more points despite identical prompts, so evaluation conclusions depend on who grades them.
arxiv-2606-13024:
Liu and colleagues propose CausalMoE, a billion-scale multimodal foundation model for Granger causal discovery in time series, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Granger causality infers causal links from temporal prediction, but current neural methods use a one-size-fits-all model that struggles with distribution shifts and regime changes, making entangled encodings and spurious causal graphs. CausalMoE instead models patch-level heterogeneity.

Its pattern-routed mixture of experts spots latent temporal patterns and routes time-series patches to specialised experts, decoupling regime-specific mechanisms from shared dynamics. A causality-aware self-attention mechanism acting across variables, paired with proximal optimisation, yields sparse Granger causal graphs. It is the first in this line to integrate language and vision-language models, matching numerical signals with textual and visual priors. Tests show CausalMoE sets a new state of the art on supervised benchmarks while reaching few-shot settings where methods fail.
arxiv-2606-13124:
Boardman and colleagues show that galaxy sizes encode the link between long-term gas inflow histories and metallicity, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Gas metallicity rises with stellar mass along the mass-metallicity relation, and its residuals anti-correlate with star-formation rate, gas mass, and size. No single analysis had treated all 3 trends. The authors combine MaNGA integral-field spectroscopy, HI-MaNGA gas masses, and MaNGA DynPop dynamical masses for about 1,500 star-forming galaxies.

From estimated inner gas masses, they find inner gas mass is the most important parameter after stellar mass in predicting gas metallicities. They also report results for stellar metallicities and nitrogen-to-oxygen ratios, linking inner gas reservoirs to chemical evolution. Chemical evolution models explain the results through differences in long-term inflow histories: compact galaxies accreted earlier, leaving lower gas masses and more rapidly declining reservoirs at late times, hence higher metallicities.
arxiv-2606-13424:
Sójka and colleagues study how iron doping changes the light emitted by gallium selenide in this 2026 arXiv paper. Gallium selenide is a semiconductor whose properties can be tuned for devices. Doping, adding impurity atoms, is the standard lever for tuning. The team uses photoluminescence spectroscopy, shining light on the crystal and analysing the glow it returns, while varying excitation power, temperature, and magnetic field. Iron adds multiple sharp emission lines beside the intrinsic excitonic transitions, the marks of bound electron-hole pairs.

Their power and heat response identifies the lines as excitons bound to iron-related centres in the crystal. Field data reveal two families of g-factors, numbers describing how energy levels split in a field. Those families separate excitonic transitions from iron-induced defect states. The results show iron doping creates active centres with their own signatures, a step toward engineering emitters by design.
arxiv-2606-13524:
Víctor Blanco, Camacho-Vallejo, and Hinojosa design city waste systems as one problem in this 2026 arXiv paper. Urban collection faces pressure from population growth, waste streams, traffic congestion, and the need to recover resources.
