Citations of the term grew from about 400 in one year to over 8,000 in another. The authors sort the field into ten working categories. The gains stay modest, often 30 to 60 percent above normal. That range, they argue, marks the limits of biological flexibility. Many cell tasks rise together, from DNA repair to clean-up systems. The frame should help plan and read future studies. Readers get a refined map of a fast-growing concept.
europmc-pmc5615924:
Geyer and co-authors rethink blood biomarker hunting in Molecular Systems Biology. Blood tests are medicine's most common diagnostic tool. Yet good protein markers are few and often vague. New ones appear at a crawl. Mass spectrometry can now read the plasma proteome in depth.

The old plan was triangular. Small groups yielded single candidate markers. Antibody tests then checked them in large groups. Most candidates died on the way. The authors propose a rectangular plan instead. Profile the full protein pattern of large cohorts first. Then match patterns against health and disease states. The shift would change how labs build diagnostic choices. Early steps toward that practice are already visible. Readers get a strategy paper for systems medicine.
europmc-pmc5622124:
Clarke and co-authors scan the genome for drinking habits in Molecular Psychiatry. Alcohol links to over 200 diseases worldwide. How much people drink varies for genetic reasons too. Known alcohol-gene variants are rare in Europeans, though.

The study used 112,117 white British UK Biobank members. Self-reported drinking was the trait under study. Fourteen loci reached genome-wide significance. Alcohol-processing genes appeared, as expected. So did two spots in KLB, a newer drinking gene. Fresh loci included GCKR, CADM2, and FAM69C. Gene-level tests flagged DRD2 and PDE4B, both tied to substance use. Common variants explained about 13 percent of drinking variation. Male and female results overlapped strongly. Genetic links also tied drinking to schooling, cholesterol, and smoking. Readers get the widest map yet of inherited influences on consumption.
europmc-pmc5665524:
Bazzano and co-authors map how human-centred design is used in global health. Their scoping review gathers studies that apply design thinking to health work. Health projects have begun to use this approach, but no summary of the field existed. The team asked why and how design can help health research.

The review found design used in a wide range of health settings. It covered research, design, rollout, and evaluation work. The authors note that global health and design use distinct terms and models. That gap can cause friction in joint projects. Clear talk and careful records can ease the strain. Lessons for future projects close the review.
europmc-pmc5666824:
Zhuo and co-authors present a review in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. It covers SELEX technology and aptamer use in biomedicine. Aptamers are short DNA or RNA strands that bind targets tightly. SELEX selects them from huge random libraries over repeated rounds. More than 2,000 aptamers have been generated so far. Targets range from metal ions to whole cells.

Few aptamer products have reached clinical or industrial use. Only one aptamer drug has won approval to date. Selection stays slow, with low success rates. Performance inside the body also remains uncertain. The review weighs limits and recent advances in selection. It compares methods for measuring binding strength. Clinical progress and hurdles get full discussion.
europmc-pmc5760624:
Fellows and co-authors study a histone mark called crotonylation in the gut lining. This mark links cell metabolism to gene control, but its rules were unclear. The team focused on one form, on histone H3 at lysine 18. It proves abundant in the small intestine and colon.

The mark shifts with the cell cycle and tracks with gene activity. Three class I deacetylases, HDAC1, 2, and 3, remove it. Butyrate, a fatty acid made by gut microbes, slows that removal. Wiping out gut microbes changed the mark across the colon. The work ties gut microbes to chromatin through these acids.
europmc-pmc5785724:
Oberbeckmann, Kreikemeyer, and Labrenz study bacteria that settle on microplastics in water. Plastic bits drift through seas and rivers, but their role as carriers of microbes is unclear. The team soaked plastic and wood pellets for two weeks along a gradient. Sites ran from Baltic Sea water to a waste water plant.

Plastic specific communities formed only under some conditions, they report. Low nutrients and higher salt favored them. One genus able to use oil related compounds favored plastic across much of the gradient. No enrichment of likely pathogens appeared on the plastics. Setting shapes these biofilms most, they conclude.
europmc-pmc5802524:
Terpos and co-authors review bone disease in multiple myeloma. Multiple myeloma is a cancer of plasma cells in bone marrow. Most patients develop holes in their bones. Fractures and pain then cut quality of life.

The review explains how myeloma tips the bone balance. Bone-eating cells speed up, and bone-building cells slow down. Signals like RANKL and Wnt drive that shift. Bone cells called osteocytes also play a new-found role. The authors then survey targeted drugs, including denosumab. Readers get the biology behind a common and harmful cancer effect, plus the main treatment leads.
europmc-pmc5817324:
Alelign and Petros update current thinking on kidney stone disease. Stones are hard crystal masses that form in the kidneys. The disorder affects about 12 percent of the world population. It also raises the risk of kidney failure.

The review covers causes, stone types, and how stones form. Calcium oxalate stones are the most common kind. Formation runs through saturation, nucleation, growth, and clumping of crystals. Cell injury helps crystals stick to kidney surfaces. No drug yet cures or prevents repeat stones well. The authors point to prevention paths that need study. Readers get a full primer on a painful, rising disorder.
europmc-pmc5837124:
Chen, Liu, and Qin review the long hunt for drugs against Myc, a master switch of cancer growth. Their review appeared in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. Myc runs wild in over half of human cancers. Its flat protein shape has defied direct blockers for decades.

So the field attacks from the flanks. Some drugs choke off MYC transcription or translation. Others speed the protein's breakdown. A third group breaks the Myc-Max partnership it needs to work. Synthetic lethality offers a fourth route, striking partners that Myc-driven cells cannot live without. Early results keep the target in reach.
europmc-pmc5852624:
Sluijter and co-authors present a position paper on extracellular vesicles and the ischaemic heart. It comes from a working group of the European Society of Cardiology. Vesicles are tiny membrane sacs that cells release into blood and other fluids. They carry RNA, lipids, and proteins to other cells. The paper sets out shared advice for work in this fast-growing field.

The authors cover how to isolate vesicles and how to describe them. They review vesicle roles in new vessel growth and heart protection. They also weigh vesicles as disease markers and as a therapy option. Methods vary widely between labs, which clouds results. The advice aims to make studies robust and fit for patient care.
europmc-pmc5863824:
Alemayehu and co-authors review barriers to clinical trials in developing countries. Their systematic review appeared in the International Journal for Equity in Health. These countries carry most of the world's disease burden. Yet they host few of the world's clinical trials. The team searched major databases plus grey literature. They kept ten studies, reported across fifteen papers.

Five themes grouped the barriers they found. Money and trained staff were often short. Ethics and approval systems posed further obstacles. Weak research settings and daily operational problems added strain. Competing demands on local teams also hindered trials. The authors urge wider support for trials led by local researchers. Such trials fit local needs and can shape local policy.
europmc-pmc5900024:
Schmidt and Varga review CD8 T cell responses to respiratory viruses. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Viruses covered include influenza, RSV, and coronaviruses. Some cause mild colds, while others cause pneumonia or death. Most vaccines aim at antibodies that fade with time. CD8 T cells clear infected lung cells directly.

Memory CD8 cells can guard against later infections, the authors note. Pairing them with antibodies may give the best protection. The review sums what each virus teaches about these cells. It gives special weight to RSV vaccine design. Gaps in lasting vaccine success are addressed plainly. Readers get a basis for next-generation vaccine plans.
europmc-pmc5924024:
Findlay wrote a historical note on rickets and its presence in ancient times. The note appeared in the Glasgow Medical Journal in 1919. Findlay was a physician at Glasgow's children's hospital. Rickets is fostered by poor housing, crowding, and lack of air. Many authors placed its first appearance in fairly modern times. He asked whether it existed far earlier.

He searched ancient Egyptian medical papyri for any trace. He found no reference that suggested the disease. Excavated bones from Egypt and Nubia also lacked clear signs. Experts he cites doubt claims made for ancient remains. Captive apes in temples may have shown it, though. The note weighs sparse proof with care.
europmc-pmc5972624:
Panjkovich and co-authors present CHROMIXS, a program for analysing chromatography-coupled small-angle X-ray scattering data. Their software note appeared in Bioinformatics. Inline SEC-SAXS is used more and more for studying molecules in solution. One run yields thousands of scattering profiles. Finding buffer and sample regions among them is slow, manual work. CHROMIXS speeds that reduction and analysis up.

The program works both automatically and interactively. It ships free to academic users inside the ATSAS suite. The note explains the task the tool solves. It also places the tool among standard SAXS practice. Structural biologists gain a faster route from raw frames to results.
europmc-pmc5985424:
Briggs and co-authors argue for action to cut the global burden of musculoskeletal conditions. Their paper appeared in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization. These conditions cover more than 150 diagnoses of the locomotor system. They bring pain and reduced physical function. They also raise the risk of mental decline and early death. About one in three people worldwide lives with such a condition.

Back and neck pain, osteoarthritis, and fractures are among the most disabling. They strike children and workers as well as older people. Lost productive years in the workforce top other chronic diseases. The authors set out why health systems must respond.
europmc-pmc6025724:
Anastasiadi and co-authors study DNA methylation in the first intron. Their research article appeared in Epigenetics and Chromatin. Methylation is a chemical mark that helps control genes. Marks near gene starts can silence a gene. The first intron sits just inside the gene.

The team compared tissues from a modern fish. They found a steady inverse pattern genome-wide. More methylation in the first intron meant lower expression. The same pattern held in pufferfish, frog, and humans. First introns also held many tissue-specific marked regions. Some marks sat in spots where control proteins bind. Readers get evidence that this gene region matters across vertebrates. Future gene studies, the authors argue, should focus there.
europmc-pmc6041724:
Salisbury and co-authors trial a new care model for multimorbidity. Their trial report appeared in The Lancet. People with several chronic conditions strain single-disease systems. Expert consensus favors patient-centered care for them. Proof that such care helps was still thin.

The trial ran in general practices in England and Scotland. Thirty-three practices joined the cluster design. Adults had three or more chronic conditions. The 3D approach gave full reviews every six months. Reviews covered health, depression, and drug burdens together. After fifteen months, quality of life matched usual care. The gap was zero on the main measure. Deaths were judged unrelated to the intervention. Readers get a sobering test of a favored care model.
europmc-pmc6133624:
Janelidze and co-authors present a research article in Neurology on spinal fluid markers in early Alzheimer's disease. The study uses the Swedish BioFINDER cohort. It covers 508 healthy older adults, 256 people with mild impairment, and 57 with Alzheimer's dementia. The team measured markers of brain inflammation and blood vessel trouble.

Several markers were high at all stages of the disease. They include YKL-40, ICAM-1, VCAM-1, IL-15, and Flt-1. High levels tracked with higher tau, a core Alzheimer's marker. They also tracked with thinning of the cortex. Some predicted later decline and dementia onset. The authors say inflammation and vessel harm start early in this disease.
europmc-pmc6148624:
Eriksen and Frandsen offer a systematic review in Journal of the Medical Library Association on the PICO search model. PICO breaks a question into patient, intervention, comparison, and outcome. Many searchers use it to plan literature searches. Whether it lifts search quality was not clear.

The team searched nine databases and catalogs. Of 2,163 records found, just three studies qualified. Those studies compared PICO with rival models or with unguided searching. The models differed too much for pooled analysis. The authors say too few studies exist to judge PICO's effect. Well-designed trials are needed before practice advice can be given.
europmc-pmc6154824:
Newcombe and co-authors wrote a review in Journal of Neuroinflammation on inflammation as a link between other diseases, genes, and Alzheimer's disease. Most Alzheimer's cases have no single clear cause. That makes the disease hard to define and diagnose. Some cases are genetic, but many lifestyle and health factors raise risk.

The review lists those factors, including head injury, diabetes, high blood pressure, obesity, and aging itself. Chronic inflammation runs through many of them. The immune system defends the body, yet long-term inflammation is tied to several age-related diseases. The authors argue this shared thread could sharpen diagnosis and lead to better treatments.
europmc-pmc6186824:
Smulski and Eibel wrote a review in Frontiers in Immunology on BAFF and its receptor in B cell selection and survival. The BAFF receptor is one of the main survival receptors on B cells. A human genetic deletion shows its force. People lacking it almost stop making B cells at an immature stage.

That deficiency leaves very few B cells in blood and very low IgM and IgG antibodies. Yet IgA levels stay normal or high, and IgA-secreting plasma cells still form. The review explains the receptor's structure and where it appears. It also covers how this pathway selects which B cells live. Drugs that block BAFF, used in autoimmune disease, are part of the story.
europmc-pmc6207324:
Wang and co-authors present RAVEN 2.0, a software toolbox. The toolbox builds genome-scale models of cell metabolism. Such models list all chemical reactions in a cell. They help predict how cells react to change. The work appeared in PLoS Computational Biology. It includes a case study on a soil bacterium.

The new version can build models from scratch. It uses the MetaCyc database for that task. It also has a rebuilt KEGG-based pipeline. The team built fresh models for Streptomyces coelicolor. That bacterium makes antibiotics. Their models matched most of a hand-built gold standard. They then used the fresh model to improve that standard. The result, Sco4, is the fullest model yet for this species.
europmc-pmc6231624:
Rodrigues and co-authors measured burnout among medical residents. Burnout combines emotional exhaustion and detachment. It also includes a sense of low personal achievement. Residents face long hours and high stress. The review appeared in PLoS ONE. It followed PRISMA guidelines.

The team searched five major databases and grey sources. They screened thousands of studies. In the end, 26 papers with 4,664 residents were kept. Overall burnout prevalence was about 36 percent. Surgery and anaesthesia specialties showed the highest rates. Ear, nose and throat plus neurology showed the lowest. Rates differed by which burnout trait was counted. The authors call for action to protect resident health.
europmc-pmc6250824:
Hanada and co-authors review why bacterial pneumonia often follows viral chest infections. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Flu and other chest viruses are the most common acute chest infections. A bacterial infection on top often runs a far worse course. The Spanish flu pandemic showed that pattern at huge scale. Many of its deaths came from later bacterial pneumonia.

Healthy microbe communities in the gut and airways help defend the host. Viral infection disturbs those communities, a shift called dysbiosis. The antiviral response itself can change which microbes thrive. Harmful bacteria may then grow out and invade. The authors gather fifteen years of work on these links. The review maps how virus, microbes, and host defences interact. That map may guide new ways to prevent the second infection.
europmc-pmc6270724:
Mierziak, Kostyn, and Kulma review flavonoids as tools plants use in their surroundings. Their review appeared in Molecules. Flavonoids are small plant compounds, with over nine thousand known forms. They colour flowers and fruit. They also shield plants from sun, pests, and grazers. Most of their jobs flow from strong antioxidant power.

Inside plants, flavonoids shape growth and stress responses. They guard against ultraviolet light and heat. They also help plants talk to microbes and animals. Some attract pollinators, while others repel pests. Soil microbes respond to flavonoid signals too. The review stresses that medicine and food uses are only half the story. Plant life itself depends on these compounds. Knowing their plant roles can guide breeding and farming.
europmc-pmc6294524:
Didelot and co-authors present a faster Bayesian method for dating bacterial family trees. The method appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. It is packaged as an R tool called BactDating. Dated trees show when shared ancestors of strains likely lived. Such dates can reveal when a key lineage first emerged.

Older tools built the tree and its dates in one slow step. BactDating instead takes a tree built by standard methods. It then infers the ancestor dates on that fixed tree. This design also lets it handle bacterial recombination. The team tested the method on simulated data sets. They also applied it to three real bacterial studies. Results support its speed and accuracy.
europmc-pmc6324024:
El-Gebali and co-authors report the Pfam protein families database in 2019. The article appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. Pfam groups proteins into families by shared domains. Release 32.0 holds 17,929 families. Each family starts from a seed alignment. A statistical model then finds matching sequences. Recent years brought big changes to the resource.

Existing families got refined domain boundaries. Families were sorted into broader clans. A comparison with a structural database spawned 825 new families. Those came from sets of uncharacterized proteins. Pfam types now map to Sequence Ontology terms. Work with RepeatsDB sharpened tandem repeat families. Contributors can claim credit through ORCID links. Curation authorship is now tracked for every entry.
europmc-pmc6326824:
Müller and co-authors trace how the RNA-binding protein IGF2BP1 boosts a cancer gene program. Their study appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. IGF2BP1 appears in fetal tissue and returns in tumors. It binds the regulator SRF, which switches genes on. The team worked with cancer cells in the lab.

IGF2BP1 raised SRF levels in an m6A-dependent way. It shielded the SRF message from microRNA-driven decay. More SRF meant stronger activity at its target genes. Two targets, PDLIM7 and FOXK1, helped tumor cells grow and invade. A set of 35 linked genes marked poor survival. The pattern showed in ovarian, liver, and lung cancers. The authors name this network a shared driver of cancer growth.
europmc-pmc6341724:
Liu and Wang improve computer prediction of microRNA target genes. Their paper appeared in Genome Biology. MicroRNAs are tiny RNAs that tune gene activity. Guessing their true targets is error-prone. The team first measured targets experimentally at scale. They sequenced RNA after adding 25 different microRNAs.

Genes that fell in those tests marked real targets. Public binding data added a second evidence layer. Features shared by both data types stood out. A machine learning model combined those features. It beat older prediction models in validation tests. All predictions were released through the miRDB website. The work helps labs choose which targets to test. It also clarifies what makes a target site functional.
europmc-pmc6352924:
Holbrook and co-authors review tumour necrosis factor signaling in health and disease. Their review appeared in F1000Research. TNF is a master inflammatory signal in the body. It shapes the first, fast phase of immune defense. It also drives cell growth and programmed death. Two receptors pass its messages into cells.

The wider TNF family holds 19 ligands and 29 receptors. Over forty years of work mapped their roles. The same signals that defend us can go wrong. TNF is implicated in rheumatoid arthritis. It also features in Crohn's disease and a spine condition. Drugs that block TNF grew from this knowledge. The review sums the pathways and their disease links.
europmc-pmc6359724:
Nagao and co-authors present a review in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences on how cancer cells rewire glucose use. The focus is HIF-1, a protein that helps cells respond to low oxygen. The authors explain how HIF-1 drives the Warburg effect, where tumors favor fast glycolysis even when oxygen is present.

The review covers how HIF-1 turns on glycolysis and a linked pathway that supplies building blocks for growth. It also links this metabolic shift to antioxidant defenses and resistance to radiation. The authors add their own findings on a factor that raises HIF-1 activity in cancer cells. Readers get a clear map of these pathways and of possible treatment targets.
europmc-pmc6372724:
Spitzer and co-authors report a research article in Neuron on cells that make myelin in the brain. Oligodendrocyte progenitor cells are the main dividing cells in the adult brain. They mature into cells that wrap nerve fibers in myelin.

Young progenitor cells looked much alike in their electrical traits. With age, the cells grew varied, both inside one brain region and between regions. Those electrical differences matched how well each cell could mature. The authors link this growing variety to why myelin repair fails in some regions. The work changes the old view of these cells as one uniform group.
europmc-pmc6381624:
Lagkouvardos and co-authors study a gut bacteria family in Microbiome. The family, now called Muribaculaceae, fills much of the mouse gut. It stayed unnamed for years because its members were hard to grow in the lab.

Joining gene surveys with grown cultures, the team inferred about 685 species. They mapped where these bacteria live and which hosts they favor. The study also probes what the bacteria do for the host gut. Naming and sorting this group clears up confused records. It gives gut researchers firmer ground for future mouse and animal studies.
europmc-pmc6414424:
van der Kant and co-authors report a cell study in Cell Stem Cell on cholesterol and Alzheimer's disease. Genes and population data link cholesterol handling to the disease. The team grew neurons from Alzheimer's patients' stem cells and screened them for tau buildup.

Compounds that lowered cholesteryl esters, the storage form of cholesterol, also lowered tau. The same axis controlled amyloid-beta through a separate route. Gene-edited cell lines confirmed the split control. The authors name cholesterol metabolism as a drug target in its own right. Hitting it early may slow both hallmarks of the disease.
europmc-pmc6434624:
Assefa and co-authors review fifteen years of Ethiopia's Health Extension Program, a community scheme launched in 2003 to carry primary care into rural villages. Trained health extension workers staff village health posts and visit households. The reviewers searched three databases for studies from the program's full span and synthesized them interpretively.

Gains were broad: maternal and child health, control of communicable disease, hygiene and sanitation, and care-seeking all improved, helped by strong community participation. The program repeatedly adapted, shifting tasks between health centers and villages. Remaining problems include worker productivity and living conditions, thin health post capacity, and social factors beyond the health system. A closing framework aims to guide the push toward universal coverage.
europmc-pmc6455124:
Zhao and co-authors characterize the first African swine fever virus isolated in China, from the outbreak strain Pig/Heilongjiang/2018. The disease entered China in August 2018 and swept the country, threatening a national herd holding over half the world's pigs. The isolate, grown in porcine macrophages, belongs to genotype II by its p72 gene.

In specific-pathogen-free pigs, doses produced acute fever and hemorrhagic disease after a three-to-five-day incubation. Every inoculated pig died between days six and nine; contact pigs sickened later and died around days thirteen to fourteen. Virus appeared in blood by day two and in swabs within days. The strain is judged highly virulent and transmissible.
europmc-pmc6497624:
Wilkinson and co-authors validate whether routine health records can be trusted to find dementia cases inside UK Biobank, the cohort of over 500,000 adults. From 17,198 Edinburgh recruits, they pulled everyone carrying a dementia code in primary care, hospital, or death records and had clinical experts adjudicate the full charts of 120 participants as ground truth.

For all-cause dementia the codes held up well, positive predictive values of 86.8 percent in primary care, 87.3 percent in hospital data, and 82.5 percent across all sources. Subtypes were shakier: Alzheimer's codes scored 71.4 percent combined and vascular dementia only 43.8 percent. Three algorithms balancing accuracy against case capture are offered for researchers building studies on linked records.
europmc-pmc6515324:
Nguyen and Soulika review the dynamics of the skin's immune system. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Skin guards the body with physical, chemical and microbial barriers. It also holds a network of resident immune cells. Those cells defend the tissue and keep it in balance.

The authors describe skin structure across its three layers. They then detail the resident cells and their daily roles. After injury, the same cells help prevent infection. They also guide tissue rebuilding and wound closure. When immune responses go off track, healing suffers. Scarring and poor restoration can follow. The review ties cell types to each phase of repair.
europmc-pmc6664124:
Garg and co-authors review new work on chitosan nanoparticles for drug delivery. Their review appears in the Advanced Pharmaceutical Bulletin. Chitosan is a natural polymer from crustacean shells and fungi. It breaks down in the body and is low in toxicity. US regulators list it as generally safe. Its surface amine groups invite chemical tailoring. Particles made from it release drugs slowly. They also carry drugs to chosen sites.

The review describes how the particles are formed. Methods include ionic cross-linking and reverse micelles. Rain-out and emulsion methods feature as well. Uses span eye, lung, nose, and gut delivery. Gene and vaccine delivery are covered too. Poor solubility at neutral pH remains a drawback.
europmc-pmc6715724:
Jadiya and co-authors studied how faulty calcium handling in mitochondria may drive Alzheimer's disease. Mitochondria are the cell's power units, and calcium signals help run them. In brain tissue from people with Alzheimer's, the team found the calcium exit machinery remodeled. A mouse model of the disease showed the same flaw early.

The exit route is a protein called NCLX. Deleting it in mouse neurons sped memory loss and raised amyloid and tau damage. Restoring it did the reverse, protecting memory and cutting pathology. Calcium overload, they show, fuels harmful oxygen byproducts and cell death. The exit protein is put forward as a drug target.
europmc-pmc6723624:
Tooke and co-authors review beta-lactamase enzymes and the drugs that block them. Beta-lactam antibiotics hold a central place in fighting bacteria. Many bacteria resist them by making enzymes that split the drug's key ring. These enzymes spread on mobile DNA between species such as E. coli and Pseudomonas.

The enzymes fall into four classes. Three use a serine site, and one uses zinc. New crystal structures and computer simulations have clarified how each class breaks drugs down. The review gives special weight to carbapenems, the last-line drugs now under threat. It also surveys new inhibitor pairings entering clinical use.
europmc-pmc6734524:
Fu and co-authors review the tumor immune microenvironment in liver cancer and its treatment. Hepatocellular carcinoma is the most common primary liver cancer. Fewer than 40% of patients qualify for possibly curative therapy. The tumor grows out of chronic inflammation, and its surroundings suppress immune attack.

Immunotherapy has worked well in lung cancer and melanoma, raising hopes here. The review gathers recent progress from lab and clinic. It covers how the liver tumor evades immunity and how new treatments try to provoke a stronger response. Dendritic cell vaccines are among the options surveyed. The authors end with advances and challenges ahead for this approach.
europmc-pmc6912224:
Dewidar and co-authors update the story of TGF-beta in liver scarring, in the journal Cells. Liver fibrosis, the build-up of scar tissue, can end in cirrhosis and liver cancer. No approved drug attacks the scarring directly. The signal TGF-beta is the master switch: it wakes hepatic stellate cells, which then lay down scar. Blocking it, though, harms other jobs the signal does.

The review summarises discoveries of the last five years on this pathway. It traces how the signal is stored in tissue, released, and read by stellate cells, and what feeds back on it. That detail is the point: hitting a side branch may spare the signal's useful roles. The authors aim at safer antifibrotic designs.
europmc-pmc6923224:
Gschwandtner and co-authors review the chemokine CCL2 beyond cell movement. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. CCL2 is also called MCP-1. It is famed for drawing myeloid cells to tissues. That pull matters in defence and in disease.

New data show a far wider scope. CCL2 can shape cell adhesion and polarization. It can alter effector release, autophagy, and killing. It can also affect cell survival. Effects depend on context and partner signals. The authors link CCL2 to arthritis and multiple sclerosis. They also cover atherosclerosis, diabetes, obesity, and cancer. Drugs against CCL2 have so far disappointed in clinic. Better insight into these actions may improve future therapy.
europmc-pmc6952324:
Watanabe and co-authors review recent progress in combined treatment for oesophageal cancer. Their review appeared in Surgery Today. This cancer is among the most aggressive gut cancers. Removing the oesophagus is a major operation that can impair quality of life, so gentler options are prized.

The authors cover eight topics in team-based care. Endoscopic removal of early cancer, paired with chemotherapy and radiation, can preserve the organ. For stage I disease, that drug-radiation route matched surgery in long-term outcome. Locally advanced cancers gain from treatment before or around surgery. Keyhole surgery may improve results further. Radiation with salvage surgery offers another organ-saving path. Immune checkpoint drugs, already effective in this cancer, are entering practice.
europmc-pmc7013824:
Wright and co-authors measure microplastics falling from the air over central London. Their study appeared in Environment International. Plastic waste persists for decades before crumbling into particles under five millimetres. Such particles were long treated as a sea problem; now they turn up in rivers, soils, and city air.

Samplers on a London rooftop caught a steady rain of plastic. Fibres dominated, averaging over 700 particles per square metre per day, with polyacrylonitrile the commonest polymer, likely shed from clothing and fabrics. Non-fibre particles added a smaller share. Matched by size, London levels ran about twenty times those at a remote site. Nearby source areas swayed the counts, while weather showed no clear link. As global plastic output heads toward a projected 25 billion tonnes by 2050, the authors frame airborne plastic as a pollution route in its own right.
europmc-pmc7025524:
Henke, Nandigama, and Ergün review the extracellular matrix in tumours for Frontiers in Molecular Biosciences. A solid tumour is more than cancer cells. It also holds blood vessels, immune and stromal cells, and the matrix, a scaffold of proteins between cells. That matrix often forms the larger part of the tumour mass and differs greatly from matrix in healthy organs.

The matrix shapes signalling, transport, metabolism, oxygen levels, and immune activity inside the tumour. By doing so it influences growth and also how well radiation, chemotherapy, and immunotherapy work. The review explains the physical and molecular routes behind those effects. It then surveys strategies that target or remodel the matrix to improve treatment response, an approach gaining ground in cancer care.
europmc-pmc7081524:
Shi and co-authors studied which patients with COVID-19 outside Wuhan were most likely to become severely ill, in Critical Care. Their group reviewed 487 confirmed cases in Zhejiang Province, China. Records, lab results, and lung scans were checked for each patient.

Of the 487 patients, 49 were severe cases at admission. Severe patients were older and more often male, and high blood pressure was far more common among them. The team combined such factors into a host risk score meant to flag high-risk people early. Readers get an early-pandemic picture of how doctors tried to spot danger before a patient's condition worsened.
europmc-pmc7092824:
Chen and co-authors analysed the structure of the new coronavirus binding domain and how it grips the ACE2 receptor, in Biochemical and Biophysical Research Communications. The 2019-nCoV binding domain shares 72% of its amino acid sequence with the SARS virus version. Computer models showed the two structures look highly similar, with one key difference.

The new virus carries a flexible loop where SARS has a rigid one, and a phenylalanine at position 486 reaches deep into a pocket in ACE2, strengthening the grip. ACE2 is similar across many animals, from fish to mammals, so many species could host the virus. Blocking this contact is proposed as a route for antibodies and small drug molecules.
europmc-pmc7096724:
Emami and co-authors pooled data on underlying diseases in hospitalised COVID-19 patients, in the Archives of Academic Emergency Medicine. Their systematic review and meta-analysis searched four databases for studies published up to 15 February 2020. Ten articles covering 76,993 patients met their rules.

High blood pressure was the most common underlying condition, at 16.37% of patients. Cardiovascular disease followed at 12.11%, then diabetes at 7.87% and smoking history at 7.63%. Chronic lung disease, cancer, and chronic kidney disease also appeared often. Knowing which conditions cluster in hospital patients helps staff judge risk and plan care, though the figures come from the outbreak's first weeks and early hospitals.
europmc-pmc7145624:
Alcock and co-authors describe the 2020 update of CARD, a database of antibiotic resistance in bacteria, in Nucleic Acids Research. CARD holds reference DNA and protein sequences. It also holds models that detect resistance genes in new samples, plus software to run those checks. A shared set of terms keeps the data in order.

Since 2017 the team has added over 500 new detection models. They also revised how entries are sorted and built a new module on resistomes and variants. That module sums up predicted resistance from 82 pathogens and over 100,000 genomes. The sums expose trends in how resistance spreads between bacteria and between places. New tools let outside experts help curate the data, so the reference set stays current as new resistance genes are found.
europmc-pmc7145824:
Ribeiro and co-authors train a deep neural network to read standard 12-lead ECG heart tracings automatically, in Nature Communications. Computer ECG reading has long been too inaccurate to trust alone. Their network learned from more than 2 million labelled exams collected by the Telehealth Network of Minas Gerais in Brazil.

The model recognised 6 types of abnormality and beat cardiology resident doctors on the test set, with F1 scores above 80% and specificity over 99%. Earlier deep learning ECG work used a single lead; this study shows the approach carries to the full clinical 12-lead exam. The authors caution that other conditions, such as acute coronary syndromes, were not tested and cannot be assumed covered.
europmc-pmc7228924:
Huang and co-authors introduce a gold-assisted method for peeling large, clean sheets of two-dimensional crystals. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Atomically thin materials opened new physics after graphene's isolation. The standard peeling method, mechanical exfoliation, gives fine flakes. But they stay small, few, and often contaminated.

The new one-step method uses a gold surface to lift the layers. It worked across 40 types of single-crystal monolayers. The catch included magnets and superconductors, not just simple materials. Most flakes reached millimeter size with high quality. Measurements could run without transferring the flakes elsewhere. Tuning the metal layer's thickness even allowed device building in place. The authors present the method as universal for this materials family.
europmc-pmc7235224:
Johnson and co-authors show that fats made by gut bacteria enter the host's own metabolic pathways. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. The fats are sphingolipids, a class that includes ceramides. Ceramides are tied to insulin resistance and fatty liver. Mammals get these fats from food and make their own.

The gut's dominant bacteria group, Bacteroidetes, can also make them. Their genomes carry the needed starting enzyme. Experiments in cell culture and animals traced bacterial fats into host tissues. Those fats influenced the liver's sphingolipid pools. The finding adds a microbial source to a disease-linked fat supply. It may help explain links between gut microbes and metabolism. The work opens a new route for studying metabolic disorders.
europmc-pmc7241824:
Azlan and co-authors survey public knowledge, attitudes, and practices toward COVID-19 in Malaysia. Their study appeared in PLoS ONE. An online survey reached 4,850 Malaysian residents. It ran from March 27 to April 3, 2020, under movement control orders. Lockdowns work only if the public cooperates, the authors note. What people know and believe decides that cooperation.

Most respondents reported strong hand hygiene habits, at 87.8 percent. Mask wearing told a stranger story. People with higher knowledge scores were less likely to have worn masks in the week before the order began. Attitudes toward government measures were also recorded. The authors judge public readiness overall as good but uneven. Health authorities gain targets for clearer messaging. The snapshot captures a society adjusting to emergency rules.
europmc-pmc7268724:
Zhang and co-authors study a ring-shaped RNA molecule, circSATB2, that helps non-small cell lung cancer grow and spread. Their study appeared in Molecular Cancer. This cancer type accounts for 85% of lung cancer cases, and outcomes remain poor. Circular RNAs are a newer class of molecules whose roles in cancer are still being mapped.

CircSATB2 was strongly overproduced in lung cancer cells and tissues. Working through a small RNA called miR-326, it raised levels of FSCN1, a protein that helps cells move. Cancer cells package circSATB2 into tiny vesicles called exosomes, which spread its growth-promoting effect to other cells, even healthy bronchial cells. Levels in blood exosomes from patients were high enough to suggest a diagnostic marker tied to metastasis.
europmc-pmc7271924:
Kell, Heyden and Pretorius review lactoferrin, an iron-binding protein found in milk and other body fluids. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Lactoferrin moves iron between cells and fluids and supports immune defense. It can kill bacteria and interfere with viruses.

Of special interest, lactoferrin can attach to some of the same cell-surface molecules that coronaviruses use to enter cells. Those include heparan sulfate chains and possibly ACE2, the main doorway for SARS-CoV-2. By blocking attachment, lactoferrin might stop infection before it starts. The authors argue that lactoferrin, especially in coated forms that survive digestion better, deserves study as a preventive or added treatment during the COVID-19 pandemic.
europmc-pmc7273324:
Diggle and Whiteley profile Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a bacterium that is both a health threat and a lab model. Their short profile appeared in Microbiology. The germ lives in soil and water and in places touched by people. It rarely harms healthy people. It can cause severe illness in people with weak immune systems or chronic disease.

The profile covers the germ's shape, growth needs and family tree. It describes the two main lab strains, PAO1 and PA14. Genome size and gene sets are summarized. The authors stress drug resistance and sticky biofilms, which make infections hard to treat. The profile suits readers who need a quick, reliable overview.
europmc-pmc7285724:
Sung and Kim survey new work on polymer-based drug delivery. Their review covers systems that carry a drug into the body in a polymer package. Polymers that break down safely in the body have opened many new designs in the past two decades. The field is now moving fast toward real use in pharmacies.

The team covers natural polymers such as chitosan and hyaluronic acid, and man-made ones such as dendrimers. Uses range from cancer drugs sent to a target, to systems that copy body materials, to large molecules that act as drugs on their own. Gene delivery gets its own part, with virus-based and non-virus carriers set side by side. Gains with body-safe polymers, they say, are bringing these systems close to daily medical use.
europmc-pmc7376924:
Tonkin-Hill and co-authors introduce Panaroo in Genome Biology, a tool for building cleaner bacterial pangenomes. A pangenome is the full gene set of a species, and bacteria swap genes so freely that members differ widely. Automated genome annotation makes errors, and those errors pile up across hundreds of genomes.

Panaroo works on a graph of gene relationships, so it can spot and correct common error sources: fragmented assemblies, contamination, and mis-annotation. The result is a polished gene catalogue for population comparisons. The software is freely available online. Readers in bacterial genomics get a practical fix for a quiet problem, since dirty pangenomes can invent genes that do not exist and hide ones that do.
europmc-pmc7383524:
Williams and co-authors test saliva as a COVID-19 sample in a letter to the Journal of Clinical Microbiology. Nasopharyngeal swabs are uncomfortable, need special supplies, and put collectors close to possibly infectious patients. At a Melbourne screening clinic, 622 patients were swabbed, and 522 also gave saliva.

Saliva caught the virus in patients whose swabs were positive, though with somewhat lower sensitivity. One swab-negative patient even tested positive by saliva. The authors argue that saliva works as a first-line screening sample in many settings, with swabs saved for strong-suspicion cases. Self-collection also eases shortages of swabs and protective gear. Readers get a short, practical report from a busy clinic at the pandemic's start.
europmc-pmc7402624:
Mathew and co-authors deeply profile the immune systems of COVID-19 patients in Science. Severity varied wildly between patients, and the immune reasons were unclear. Using high-dimensional flow cytometry on hospitalized patients, the team built an atlas of immune cell states during infection.

Three distinct immunotypes stood out, each tied to disease severity and clinical measures. Some patients showed strong activation of particular T cell groups, others a quieter or different pattern. These immune fingerprints suggest different treatments could suit different patients, rather than one immune therapy for all. Readers get a roadmap from immune measurement to tailored intervention, drawn while hospitals were still learning the disease.
europmc-pmc7409324:
Cornel and co-authors review how cancers hide from killer T cells in Cancers. Immunotherapy has transformed blood cancers, but solid tumors resist. One main trick is lowering MHC class I, the display platform that shows tumor fragments to CD8 T cells. It is reported in 40 to 90 percent of human tumors and tracks worse prognosis.

The loss usually comes from reversible controls, chemical marks and regulators such as NFkB, IRFs, and NLRC5, rather than from broken genes. Reversible means restorable. The review catalogues the mechanisms and then the strategies to switch display back on and reawaken adaptive immunity. Readers get a hopeful angle on a major escape route: the tumor's invisibility cloak is held by clips, not welded shut.
europmc-pmc7462924:
Chadt and Al-Hasani review glucose transporters in fat tissue, liver, and skeletal muscle. A family of carriers, the GLUTs, moves glucose into tissues. Their work keeps blood sugar steady across the body.

GLUT2 is the main controller of sugar flow in the liver. GLUT4 does the heavy lifting for insulin-driven uptake in muscle. When transport activity falls, fuel use goes wrong. That failure links with insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. How insulin commands transport across cell membranes is still not fully clear. Blood-borne signals and extra transporters fine-tune flow between organs as energy needs shift. The review gathers what is known and marks the open gaps in the mechanism.
europmc-pmc7490424:
Zhao and co-authors review chitinase-3 like-protein-1, a protein known as CHI3L1, and its roles in disease. It binds chitin, heparin, and hyaluronic acid but has no enzyme action. Many cell types make and release it, from macrophages to tumor cells.

CHI3L1 helps steer tissue injury, inflammation, repair, and remodeling. It links with asthma, arthritis, sepsis, diabetes, liver fibrosis, and heart artery disease. In cancer it is overproduced in many human tumors and animal models. Its signals drive tumor growth, spread, vessel growth, and immune skewing. Several receptors for it are now known. Targeted treatments based on CHI3L1 are in study for glioma, colon cancer, and rheumatoid arthritis. The review maps paths and treatment ideas.
europmc-pmc7502724:
Ganguli and co-authors build a rapid, portable test system for SARS-CoV-2 that skips the central lab. Standard RT-PCR is the gold standard but needs lab steps to free and clean viral RNA. Those steps cost time and hands.

Their system uses isothermal RT-LAMP, which copies RNA at one steady heat. A printed cartridge holds the sample work. A smartphone-based reader reports the result at the point of collection. The design cuts the labor and gear of lab testing. It aims for speed, accuracy, and ease in one package. Such tools could widen testing in clinics, airports, and field sites. The authors frame it as a proof of a new testing class for outbreaks.
europmc-pmc7511224:
Ramaswamy and co-authors compare patient satisfaction with video visits and in-person visits during COVID-19. New York City was the pandemic's early epicenter. Clinics shifted fast from office visits to video calls.

The team analyzed 38,609 Press Ganey survey outcomes at one large urban medical center. Video visits numbered 620 against 37,989 in-person visits in the data set. Video visits scored higher on satisfaction than office visits did. Both video format and the pandemic period linked with higher scores after adjustment. Younger age, female gender, and new visit type linked with lower scores. The authors say satisfaction is no barrier to wider telemedicine use. More quality measures should guide the shift, they add.
europmc-pmc7518324:
Zhang, Parmigiani, and Johnson present ComBat-seq, a batch fix for RNA-seq count data. Joining data batches boosts power, but batch effects add unwanted variation. Technical gaps between batches drive the problem.

Many fix methods assume smooth, bell-shaped data curves. RNA-seq counts are skewed and over-dispersed, so that assumption fails. ComBat-seq uses a negative binomial model instead. It keeps the integer nature of the counts intact. That makes fixed data fit standard differential expression tools. In realistic simulations, it gave better power and false positive control than rival methods. On real data, it removed batch effects and recovered the true signal. The authors offer it for large merged genomic studies.
europmc-pmc7610724:
Munafò and co-authors set out a manifesto for reproducible science. Unreliable research wastes effort and slows discovery. Their paper argues for changes across the research process.

Measures target methods, reporting and dissemination first. Reproducibility, evaluation and incentives are also covered. Threats include low power and publication bias. Data dredging and poor sharing add to the problem. One estimate says 85% of biomedical effort is wasted. A survey found 90% saw a reproducibility crisis. The authors review proof for each proposed fix. Wide adoption needs funders, journals and institutions to act. Stepwise testing of the measures is urged. The goal is more credible published science.
europmc-pmc7645624:
Chen and co-authors build a deep learning model to detect COVID-19 pneumonia on chest CT scans. CT is a favored imaging route for this pneumonia. Fast and accurate reading can aid busy clinicians.

Training used 46,096 images from 106 admitted patients. Cases included 51 confirmed COVID-19 pneumonia patients. Controls numbered 55 patients with other diseases. Per-patient accuracy reached 95.24% in the test set. Per-image accuracy reached 98.85% in that set. A prospective test covered 27 consecutive patients. There the model matched an expert radiologist in performance. An outside hospital test gave 96% accuracy overall. With model help, radiologist reading time fell by 65%. The system may speed clinical work in pneumonia care.
europmc-pmc7688124:
Alsoufi and co-authors survey medical students in Libya on online learning during COVID-19. Their study appeared in PLoS ONE. Students came from more than 13 medical schools across the country. The survey asked about knowledge, attitudes, and daily use of electronic learning. It also covered devices, study status during the shutdown, and mental health.

In all, 3,348 valid replies came back from the students. Most doubted that e-learning could be rolled out with ease in Libya. Few had joined an online medical program during the pandemic months. Most also doubted that online tools could teach hands-on clinical skills. Yet 65% used the internet to join study groups and talks with peers. The authors see a lasting disruption that schools must plan for.
europmc-pmc7731724:
Landrigan and co-authors examine how ocean pollution harms human health. Pollution overall causes an estimated nine million early deaths each year. Ocean pollution is a large but poorly tracked part of that toll. It mixes toxic metals, plastics, chemicals, oil, and sewage.

More than 80% of it comes from land, by rivers, runoff, and direct discharge. An estimated 10 million metric tons of plastic enter the seas each year. Mercury from coal burning and small-scale gold mining is the metal of chief concern. The authors urge leaders to act and set clear priorities for control and prevention.
europmc-pmc7745124:
South and co-authors engineer tobacco plants to waste less energy in the field. Their study tested synthetic paths for handling glycolate, a toxic byproduct of photosynthesis. In C3 crops such as soybean and wheat, this cleanup, called photorespiration, can cut yields by 20 to 50%. The team placed new paths inside the leaf's chloroplasts.

They also blocked export of glycolate into the old path, to force flow through the new ones. The best designs raised photosynthetic efficiency by 20%. In repeated field trials, many plant lines grew 19 to 37% more biomass. The authors say such redesign could lift yields of major C3 crops under real farm conditions.
europmc-pmc7816624:
Bayati and co-authors show that SARS-CoV-2 enters cells through clathrin-mediated endocytosis. The virus first grips the cell surface with its spike protein. What happens next was unsettled. Many coronaviruses get pulled inside the cell. Whether SARS-CoV-2 needs that step was unknown.

The team used pure spike protein and harmless test viruses wearing spike. After surface contact, uptake was rapid. It ran through the clathrin pathway, a standard cell entry route. Viral RNA likely passes to the cell interior from inside those compartments. Blocking clathrin heavy chain cut infection sharply. The authors name this entry step a key part of infectivity. It is also a possible drug target.
europmc-pmc7895824:
Ochocka and co-authors report a single-cell study of immune cells in brain tumours called gliomas. Microglia are the brain's own immune cells. Other immune cells enter from the blood. Both kinds gather in gliomas and can help the tumour grow. Their full variety has been unclear.

The team used single-cell RNA sequencing on immune cells from healthy and glioma-bearing mouse brains. They found distinct groups: microglia, invading monocytes and macrophages, and border-associated macrophages. Each group had its own gene profile and place in the tumour. Male microglia switched on more immune-display genes than female ones. The same pattern showed in human glioma data. The authors suggest sex-linked immune differences may help explain why gliomas are more common in men. The work maps targets for future treatment research.
europmc-pmc7898624:
Tilg and co-authors present a review that revisits a leading theory of fatty liver disease after ten years. Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease affects about one quarter of the world's population. It ranges from simple fat build-up to inflamed, scarred liver and cancer. The multiple parallel hits idea tried to explain that wide range.

The idea holds that many insults strike the liver at once, rather than one cause acting alone. Diet, gut signals, fat tissue, and genes can all hit in parallel. The authors review how the idea has held up over a decade of new data. They weigh fresh evidence on inflammation, fibrosis, and metabolic links. The review also notes that noninvasive scans have cut the need for liver biopsy. Readers get an updated frame for a very common disease.
europmc-pmc7933824:
Litchfield and co-authors report a meta-analysis of what makes tumours respond to checkpoint inhibitors. These drugs free the immune system to attack cancer. Some patients gain lasting benefit, while others gain none. The team pooled genetic and clinical data to weigh the rival explanations for that split, inside both the tumour and its T cells.

The data covered more than 1,000 treated patients across seven tumour types. Clonal mutation burden was the strongest predictor of response. Total mutation burden and one immune signal, CXCL9, followed. Several favoured markers failed to hold up across cancers. Two gene changes also stood out: one loss tied to response, one gain tied to resistance. Single-cell work named two further T-cell markers of sensitivity. The study gives trial designers a ranked list of what to measure.
europmc-pmc7945924:
Burget presents a biographical study of Stephen Hales, who lived from 1677 to 1761. The paper was read before a medical history club in Portland in November 1924. Hales was born at Bekesbourne in Kent on September 7, 1677. He was the sixth son of Thomas and Mary Hales. Little is known of his early years, Burget admits.

In 1696, at nineteen, he entered Bennet College, Cambridge. He took his first degree and won a fellowship around 1702. A friendship with William Stukeley shaped his student days. The two roamed the countryside with a plant catalogue in hand. Fossils, butterflies, and dissections of frogs and dogs all drew them. Chemistry lectures by Vigani added a further pull. Burget traces how a country parson became a founder of experimental physiology.
europmc-pmc8005924:
Page and co-authors present the PRISMA 2020 statement, an updated guideline for reporting systematic reviews. It replaces the PRISMA statement from 2009. Systematic reviews answer questions that single studies cannot settle. But their value depends on clear, complete reporting of why the review was done, what the authors did, and what they found.

The statement gives a 27-item checklist for review reports. An expanded checklist spells out the guidance for each item. The authors also supply an abstract checklist. Revised flow diagrams cover both new and updated reviews. The new guidance reflects advances in how studies are found, chosen, appraised, and combined.
europmc-pmc8027624:
Wauters and co-authors profile single immune cells from lung washes to separate mild from critical COVID-19. How innate and adaptive immunity miscommunicate in severe disease stayed murky. The team sampled bronchoalveolar lavage from 5 patients with mild and 26 with critical illness. Samples from non-COVID pneumonia and healthy lungs served as comparisons. Pseudotime methods traced how T cells and monocytes matured.

In mild disease, resident-memory CD8 and helper-17 CD4 T cells expanded late and worked well. In critical disease, those cells stayed naïve-like. Helper-1 and exhausted-like cells showed stress signs in critical cases. Harmful hyperinflammatory monocytes built up, while protective alveolar macrophages thinned out. Monocytes also left a signaling footprint tied to lung fibrosis. Viral RNA turned up in epithelial cells, neutrophils, and macrophages.
europmc-pmc8041624:
Nayfach and co-authors assemble a genomic catalog of Earth's microbiomes. Most microbes have never been grown in a lab. Genome-resolved metagenomics rebuilds their genomes from environmental DNA instead. The team applied it to more than 10,000 metagenomes. Samples spanned every continent and ocean, plus human and animal hosts. Soils, farms, and engineered systems joined the haul.

The catalog holds 52,515 metagenome-assembled genomes. They represent 12,556 novel candidate species-level groups across 135 phyla. Known diversity of bacteria and archaea grows by 44%. The resource supports comparative analysis, metabolic modeling, and bulk download. The authors show its value in two test cases. They mine secondary-metabolite potential across the genomes. They also resolve thousands of new links between viruses and their hosts.
europmc-pmc8062524:
Huang and co-authors review the extracellular matrix and its promise as a cancer treatment target. The matrix gives tumors their physical frame and much of their signaling. Its amount and cross-linking set how stiff a tissue feels. Tumors often stiffen their matrix, and cells read that stiffness as a growth cue. Faulty force sensing then feeds further malignant change.

The review starts with the main matrix parts and their jobs in health and cancer. It then traces the two-way talk between cancer cells and matrix. Key force-sensing receptors and their shifts during cancer come next. The closing section surveys drugs aimed at the abnormal matrix. Some attack its building blocks, others its stiffness signals. The authors frame the matrix as part of the disease itself. Treating the tumor's scaffold may slow the cells it holds.
europmc-pmc8080624:
Baik reviews how stress bends the brain's dopamine reward system toward depression. Dopamine runs reward behavior through the mesolimbic pathway. Stress shifts dopamine levels and the firing of its neurons. Such tuning helps an animal pick the right response to threat. Both reward and harsh events can excite the system, which complicates the picture.

Acute stress sharpens reward sensitivity and aids coping. Chronic stress does the opposite, dulling the sense of reward. That blunting shows up as anhedonia, a core mark of depression. The review weighs animal and human evidence line by line. It asks which circuits flip the system from coping to collapse. Receptor-level changes in the reward path get close attention. The author frames the reward system as a stress sensor. Protecting its tuning may guard against stress-born depression.
europmc-pmc8128724:
van Leeuwen and co-authors catalogue 100 commercial AI products for radiology and audit their evidence. All carried the CE mark for clinical use in Europe. They came from 54 different vendors in the team's census. Tasks spanned image types, body regions, and reading jobs. Deployment and pricing models varied just as widely. The science behind the sales pitches varied most of all.

For 64 of the 100 products, no peer-reviewed efficacy evidence existed at all. The other 36 products shared 237 papers between them. Most of those papers, 65%, stopped at diagnostic accuracy. Only 18 products showed evidence of real clinical impact or beyond. Half the evidence was independent of the vendors involved. The sector, the authors conclude, is still in its infancy. Hospitals are buying promises faster than proof. Buyers should demand outcome data, not accuracy alone. Regulators may need to raise the evidence bar.
europmc-pmc8131624:
Zhang and co-authors build a light-activated nanoparticle that both kills tumors and degrades a shield protein. The particle, SPNpro, pairs a semiconducting polymer with a PROTAC unit. Under near-infrared light it makes singlet oxygen on command. That burn kills tumor cells in an immunogenic way. Dying cells then advertise themselves to the immune system. A second weapon wakes only inside cancer tissue.

A tumor marker, cathepsin B, switches the PROTAC part on. The switched-on unit targets IDO, an enzyme tumors use for cover. IDO normally drains tryptophan to paralyze effector T cells. Destroying it reopens the metabolic road for attack. In living mice the double action shrank tumors and curbed spread. Always-on degraders risk damage at healthy sites. Gating the degrader by tumor signals fixes that flaw. The platform points toward smarter protein-degrading drugs.
europmc-pmc8139424:
Zhang and co-authors solve the structural puzzle of the D614G spike change that swept the world early in the pandemic. One letter of the spike protein flipped at position 614. The G form outran the D form on every continent. Oddly, it binds the human ACE2 receptor less tightly. The team built the full-length G614 spike trimer. Cryo-EM tests compared it with the old form.

New contacts inside the G614 spike hold its S1 subunit in place. S1 carries the receptor-binding machinery of the virus. In the D form, S1 sheds too early and is lost. Stabilized spikes therefore stay armed far longer on the surface. More working spikes per virus means easier infection overall. The variant won by durability, not by grip strength. That lesson guides how later variants get judged. Small structural mercies can move a pandemic.
europmc-pmc8249424:
Luu and co-authors show that microbial short-chain fatty acids boost cancer-killing T cells. Gut microbes make these fatty acids during digestion. The team tested pentanoate and butyrate on cytotoxic and CAR T cells.

Both compounds reprogrammed the cells through metabolic and epigenetic routes. They raised mTOR activity and blocked class I histone deacetylases. Treated cells made more CD25, IFN-γ, and TNF-α. Their tumour attack grew markedly stronger in tests. The effect held for antigen-specific cells and engineered CAR cells. Feeding T cells these molecules may sharpen adoptive therapy. The strategy needs no genetic change to the cells themselves.
europmc-pmc8356424:
Wu and co-authors survey data mining in clinical big data, its databases, steps, and models. Public sets such as SEER, NHANES, TCGA, and MIMIC feed many studies. Their data are rich but messy, sparse, and uneven in time.

Mining methods help turn that mass into patient risk scores. They also aid diagnosis and treatment choices. The paper lists the databases most often used. It then lays out the mining workflow stage by stage. Model families are compared for clinical tasks. The authors stress how much value sits unused in these sets. Better mining could free it.
europmc-pmc8480024:
Hu and co-authors review ways to target mutant p53 in cancer therapy. The TP53 gene is a key tumor suppressor, mutated in over half of human cancers. Mutations do not just switch off its guard role. The faulty protein gains new cancer-driving powers of its own.

Direct drugs try to restore normal p53 action or wipe out the mutant form. Their success turns heavily on tumor shape and drug type. Indirect paths attack the backup systems mutant cells lean on. Synthetic lethality is one such idea, where paired gene losses kill the cell. Noncoding RNAs add fresh angles. The review sorts these direct and indirect strategies.
europmc-pmc8557524:
Jiang and co-authors sum up work on CD47 as a target for cancer immunotherapy. Blocking this protein helps immune cells attack tumors. Much progress has come in solid tumors and blood cancers alike. The review analyzes the trial landscape in the United States and China.

As of August 28, 2021, a registry held 23 related agents in 46 clinical trials. Most trials sat in early phases. Designs split between single-target and dual-target agents. Tumor types ranged from stomach cancer to leukemias and lymphomas. New-generation CD47 antibodies have shown promising results. The authors expect some agents to reach clinic use and meet urgent patient needs.
europmc-pmc8604724:
Feng and co-authors search for immune markers that predict protection from SARS-CoV-2 infection. Data came from a United Kingdom trial of the ChAdOx1 nCoV-19 vaccine. If a marker level can stand in for protection, new vaccines can be judged faster. The team measured binding and neutralizing antibodies 28 days after the second dose.

Higher levels of all markers linked to lower risk of illness with symptoms. A set level of binding antibodies matched 80 percent vaccine efficacy. The markers did not predict infection without symptoms at the set test level. Most cases in the trial were the alpha variant. The authors say these levels can help extend results to new vaccines and groups.
europmc-pmc8612924:
Karvelis and co-authors show that a transposon protein called TnpB can cut DNA under RNA guidance. Transposons are DNA pieces that move within genomes. Their TnpB gene was not needed for movement, and its job was unknown. Clues hinted it might be an early form of CRISPR enzymes.

Tests used TnpB from the bacterium Deinococcus radiodurans. An RNA from the transposon end guided the protein to a DNA site. It cut next to a short motif with the letters TTGAT. The team then reprogrammed TnpB to cut chosen sites in human cells. The work supports TnpB as a forerunner of CRISPR cutting tools.
europmc-pmc8660024:
Markello and co-authors introduce abagen, a software toolbox that standardizes work with brain gene expression data. Gene activity shapes the structure and function of the human brain. Open atlases let teams study this link in living people. Yet each group processed the data its own way, so results varied.

The team tested 750,000 distinct processing pipelines on one atlas. Pipeline choice had a large effect on findings. Some choices swung result correlations by a full point or more. Steps that set gene normalization mattered most. The toolbox gives the field one shared, open route. The authors argue this base will make imaging transcriptomics more sound.
europmc-pmc8664924:
Kozlowski, Crook, and Ku review ways to grow organoids without Matrigel, the gel most labs now use. Organoids are small cell clusters that copy organ function. They serve as stand-ins for organs such as liver, gut, and brain. Matrigel comes from mouse tumor cells and is poorly defined.

That vague mix hides which factors guide organoid growth. The review covers defined options to replace it. Teams can use processed tissue matrix from real organs. Synthetic gels offer a second path with known content. Gels made from engineered proteins form a third. The authors weigh each path for growth and care of organoids.
europmc-pmc8718224:
Wolchok and co-authors report 6.5-year outcomes from a trial of immune drugs in advanced melanoma. Patients with untreated, inoperable disease were split into three groups. One got nivolumab plus ipilimumab, one got nivolumab alone, and one got ipilimumab alone. Group sizes were near equal, at just over 300 each.

Median survival was 72.1 months in the combo group. It was 36.9 months with nivolumab and 19.9 months with ipilimumab. Survival rates at 6.5 years also favored the combo. Gains held in tumors with and without the BRAF mutation. The authors frame the combo as a durable gain for this cancer.
europmc-pmc8728224:
Varadi and co-authors introduce the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database, a free store of predicted protein shapes. The system uses DeepMind's AlphaFold v2.0 to predict structure from sequence. This has vastly widened the share of known proteins with a structure model. Each entry gives atomic positions plus confidence scores for the model.

The first release holds over 360,000 predicted structures. They span 21 model organism proteomes. Plans call for growth to most of the 100 million-plus reference sequences in UniRef90. Users can view models in an interactive display. Programmatic access is also offered for large-scale work.
europmc-pmc8866424:
Wei and co-authors review smart biomaterials that respond to signals while healing bone. Bone defects often come with tumors, infection, or other disease. Standard grafts can bring complications of their own. Worse, the diseased surroundings can sabotage regrowth. A material that treats disease and rebuilds bone at once is the goal. Stimuli-responsive designs promise exactly that.

Some materials answer outside triggers. Light, electric and magnetic fields, ultrasound, and force all serve. Others answer the defect site itself. Tumor acidity, bacterial enzymes, and excess reactive oxygen species can flip the switch. Multi-responsive designs combine both logics. The authors explain how each design is built. They clarify the mechanisms and clinical uses so far. They also state the limits plainly. The review serves bone engineers and clinicians alike.
europmc-pmc8935224:
Wang and co-authors test forsythoside A, a plant compound, against Alzheimer's-like disease in mice and cells. The compound comes from Forsythia suspensa. It is known for calming inflammation and oxidation. Alzheimer's involves both ferroptosis and neuroinflammation. The team used APP/PS1 transgenic mice as the disease model. Three cell systems probed separate mechanisms. Memory tests tracked the animals' cognition. Brain tissue was read for amyloid and tau.

Treatment eased memory and thinking deficits in the mice. Amyloid deposits and phosphorylated tau fell. Iron buildup and fat oxidation in brain dropped. Inflammatory factors fell while calming factors rose. In cells, the compound blocked ferroptosis and inflammation. A pathway through Nrf2 and GPX4 proved key. Dopamine signaling also strengthened. The authors propose the compound as a drug lead. Human proof, they note, is still to come.
europmc-pmc9039924:
Masyita and co-authors review terpenes and terpenoids, the main active compounds in essential oils. These plant oils show antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and anticancer effects in studies. The review covers green methods for extracting and purifying the compounds. It also explains how the body absorbs them and how well they reach target tissues. Compounds named include linalool, limonene, and eugenol.

The authors then weigh essential oils as natural food preservatives, a use backed by their microbe-fighting action. Limits remain, including dose control and stability in food. The review maps where these natural compounds could realistically replace synthetic preservatives.
europmc-pmc9134924:
Zhang and co-authors demonstrate that neutrophil extracellular traps drive a form of cell death in sepsis-linked lung injury. Traps are DNA webs that neutrophils cast out to fight microbes. The team found more traps in patients and mice with sepsis-linked acute lung injury. A death process called ferroptosis rose alongside them.

Experiments in cells and in a mouse sepsis model pinned down the chain. The traps raised an enzyme-driven mark on RNA, called m6A, through the protein METTL3. That mark lowered GPX4, a guard against ferroptosis, in lung lining cells. Mice lacking METTL3 fared differently, confirming its key role. The findings name a new target chain for a lung injury with few good treatments.
europmc-pmc9287124:
Banta and co-authors explain why blocking both TIGIT and PD-1 works better than either alone against tumors. Both are brake receptors on T cells, and dual blockade shows early promise in patients. The team studied how each brake controls the gas-pedal receptors CD28 and CD226. Tests ran in mouse tumors and in lung cancer patient samples.

PD-1 was found to damp both CD226 and CD28 signals directly. TIGIT instead blocks CD226 by stealing its shared binding partner. Either drug lost effect when CD226 was absent. CD226 levels also tracked with patient benefit from anti-PD-L1 therapy. Full revival of CD226 signaling needs both brakes off. That gives a clear reason for combined treatment in the clinic.
europmc-pmc9442924:
Hambleton and co-authors give a rapid review of the psychiatric and medical conditions that occur with eating disorders. Eating disorders are severe and can be life threatening. Death rates run high, driven by medical complications and suicide. The review aimed to sum up the evidence and find gaps.

The team searched three databases for studies from 2009 to 2021. A total of 202 studies entered the review. Of these, 58% dealt with psychiatric conditions and 42% with medical ones. Anxiety reached up to 62% and mood disorders up to 54% among patients. Substance use and post-traumatic stress each reached up to 27%. Medical problems spanned hormone, bone, gut, dental, and reproductive systems. Early spotting of these added conditions may improve care, the authors argue.
europmc-pmc9499024:
Brown and co-authors build mobileOG-db, a curated database of proteins from bacterial mobile genetic elements. These elements carry core and accessory gene modules. Accessory genes often look like ordinary immobile genes. That likeness floods older databases with false positives.

The team analyzed 10,776,849 protein sequences from eight source databases. From them they built 6,140 manually curated protein families. Each family ties to a step in an element's life cycle. Steps span entry, copying, transfer, and defense roles. Entries carry tiered notes and an element class label. The finished database holds over 700,000 deduplicated sequences. They sort into five major and more than 50 minor categories. Users can pull custom subsets from the web portal. The tool aims to make element annotation simple and sound.
europmc-pmc9640124:
Bass sets out the sources of hookworm infection and how infection takes place, in a paper read in May 1910. Knowing the worm's life facts is the base for tracing each case. Two species infect man, he notes. One is the Old World kind and one the New World kind.

The New World species was first found in material from Porto Rico. It proved to be spread wide across the Southern United States. Adult worms live only in the human gut, where they lay eggs. The eggs leave the body in feces and cannot hatch inside the gut. Hatching takes twenty-four to thirty-six hours in the open. Young worms then need at least four or five days to reach the stage that can infect. Every case thus traces back to the waste of an infected person. One heavy case was estimated to pass over 4,000,000 eggs in a stool.
europmc-pmc9646524:
Bera and co-authors show that thicker extracellular fluid makes cells move faster and helps cancer spread. Cells answer physical cues such as stiffness and fluid shear. Viscosity shifts in health and in cancer states. How cells sense those shifts was unknown until now.

Higher viscosity raised cell motion on flat surfaces and in tight spaces. It also pushed more cells out of tumor spheroids. Thick fluid loads the cell surface with more force. That load builds a dense actin web through the ARP2/3 complex. The web lines up the exchanger NHE1, which swells the cell. Swelling raises membrane tension and opens the TRPV4 channel. Calcium flows in and RHOA driven grip power climbs. Breast cancer cells kept a memory of thick fluid exposure. That memory raised their spread in fish, chick, and mouse tests.
europmc-pmc9991924:
van Lengerich and co-authors describe a TREM2-activating antibody built to cross the blood-brain barrier. Loss-of-function TREM2 variants raise Alzheimer's disease risk. That fact suggests that switching TREM2 on could help patients. A normal antibody reaches the brain poorly, so delivery needed work.

The team fused a high-affinity TREM2 antibody to a transferrin receptor binding site. This transport vehicle carries it across the barrier in mice. Brain exposure and signaling beat a standard anti-TREM2 antibody. In human stem-cell-derived microglia, the antibody switched on cell programs. It enhanced microglial metabolism in disease models. The design shows how brain delivery can unlock immune targets. It offers a template for other barrier-blocked antibodies.
europmc-pmc9995824:
Hu and co-authors review the JAK/STAT pathway, a central route for signals from outside the cell. The pathway carries cytokine and growth signals to the cell nucleus. It shapes immunity, blood formation, and tissue growth. Faults in its parts link to cancer, immune disease, and inflammation.

The hosted text for this record is dominated by the article's reference list. That list spans trials of JAK inhibitors such as tofacitinib and fedratinib. It also spans work on STAT signaling in tumors and immune cells. From the title and record, the review covers extracellular signals, disease links, and immunity.
