The expulsion of the Jews from Vienna in 1670 drove him out. He became rabbi at Rausnitz in Moravia, then in 1673 at Krotoschin. There he served sixteen years as rabbi and district head, and he built a school that drew students from across Poland. His commentary on part of the Shulḥan 'Aruk, "'Aṭeret Zekenim," was printed at Dyhernfurth in 1720.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-azriel-ezra-ben:
Azriel, also called Ezra, was a founder of the speculative Cabala. He was born at Gerona in 1160 and died in 1238. Men called him the Saint. Drawn to the mystic studies spreading in Spain, he went young to southern France. There he studied under Isaac the Blind, the famed cabalist of Posquières.

Azriel then traveled across Spain preaching the Cabala. He tried to win the philosophers over and failed, as he admits in his own preface. Thinkers, he says, believe only what logic can prove. He came home to Gerona and founded a school. Naḥmanides learned the Cabala there from him. His works include a commentary on the Ten Sefirot, written as questions and answers. Two other commentaries of his long went under Naḥmanides' name. His system rests on God as En Sof, the Endless One, from whom all things flow.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baena-juan-alfo:
Juan Alfonso de Baena was a Spanish troubadour of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, born at Baena in Cordova. He worked as a notarial secretary at the court of John II. His fame rests on a song-book he gathered, the "Cancionero del Judino Juan Alfonso de Baena." It holds poems from the courts of John I, Henry III, and John II of Castile.

The entry calls that book the oldest Castilian court song-book and the only one of its kind. It holds work by fifty-five authors of the Sevillan school, friars, knights, masters of theology, and others. Their verses picture court life and were meant to amuse the king. The book was first printed at Madrid in 1851.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bamberg-samuel-:
Samuel of Bamberg was a halakist and liturgist who lived about 1220. Born in Metz, he was taught by his father, Baruch ben Samuel, and by Eliezer b. Samuel of Metz. He became one of the best known German Talmudic scholars of his day. Meïr of Rothenburg was his pupil and, it seems, his kin. Of his private life nothing is known, beyond two daughters, Yiska and Gentil.

As a legal scholar Samuel leaned toward a liberal reading of the Law where no direct Bible command stood in the way. His famous pupil sometimes called him to account for it, yet praised him in verse. No book of his own on Halakah survives. His rulings live in the works of others. The entry clears him of two false credits, then quotes his saying that a gift for teaching the young outranks a gift for keeping up the synagogue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barges-jean-jos:
Jean Joseph Leandre Bargès, honorary canon of Notre Dame of Paris, was an abbé and Orientalist born in 1810 at Auriol and died in 1896 near Marseilles. From 1835 he belonged to the Asiatic Society of Paris. He lectured on Arabic at Marseilles, then traveled widely in Algeria. In 1842 he became professor of Hebrew in the faculty of theology at the Sorbonne. He held the chair until the faculty was abolished in 1885.

Bargès put his Arabic at the service of Hebrew literature. With Beer Goldberg he published Judah b. Koreish's letter to the Jews of Fez in 1857. His other works include the Book of Ruth with two French translations (1854), "Les Samaritains de Naplouse" (1855), and Japheth b. Heli's Psalms in 1861. He also wrote on Hebron and Abraham's tomb, on a Hebrew-Samaritan Pentateuch fragment, and on six Phenician inscriptions. A study of Marseilles' Arabic inscriptions came in 1889.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bashyazi-moses-:
Moses ben Elijah Bashyazi was a Karaite scholar born at Constantinople in 1537. He was a great-grandson of Elijah Bashyazi. At sixteen he already showed deep learning and skill in foreign tongues, and he traveled in Palestine and Syria to gather old manuscripts.

Moses died in 1555, yet he left many works. Four survive in manuscript. They deal with barred marriages, the Passover rite, the history of the Karaite split, and points of belief. The entry names the cities where copies are kept. His travels were made, the entry says, for the love of knowledge alone, not for office or gain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beddington-maur:
Maurice Beddington was an English communal worker born in 1821, who died at Carshalton on Sept. 9, 1898. All his life he stayed tied to London's Jewish institutions. He helped found the Board of Guardians and chaired its inquiry board.

Beddington also helped found the Central Synagogue and sat on the United Synagogue council for life. He gave freely to the Jews' Hospital and Orphan Asylum as its vice-president. Beyond Jewish work, he sat as a justice of the peace for Surrey and for London. He also served the Anglo-Jewish Association and societies for the blind and for the spread of religious knowledge.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-belle-assez-or-:
Belle-Assez, also called Rachel, was a daughter of Rashi, the famed commentator who lived from 1040 to 1105. She married a rabbi named Eliezer. Like her sisters, she was well versed in Hebrew and in rabbinic books, the entry reports.

An old claim held that she or a sister wrote down Rashi's legal answers. Zunz showed that claim rests on a misreading and points to a grandson instead. A ruling by her nephew Jacob Tam shows her marriage was unhappy. She gained a divorce from her husband. That claim about the daughters was held for a time by the historian Graetz, the entry reports.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benedict-xiii-p:
Pedro de Luna, called Benedict XIII, was an antipope born in Aragon about 1334. Elected on Sept. 28, 1394, he was deposed by the Council of Constance in 1415 and died at Peñiscola in 1424. The entry stresses his drive to convert the Jews and the suffering it caused.

He summoned Jewish leaders to a forced debate at Tortosa, which ran from Feb. 6, 1413, to Nov. 12, 1414. His bull of 1414 then banned Talmud study, seized copies, and barred Jews from offices and crafts. It also forced badge wearing and attendance at Christian sermons three times a year. Two converts had urged him on. One was the former rabbi Pablo de Santa Maria. The other was the physician Geronimo de Santa Fé. Both claimed they could prove his case from the Bible and the Talmud.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berachah-blessi: Berachah is a name that the entry treats in two separate senses. First, it was a Benjamite who came to David and joined his forces at Ziklag, as First Chronicles records. Second, it was a valley where Jehoshaphat and his men gathered after despoiling the Ammonites and Moabites. That valley is identified with the modern Berekut, west of Tekoa. The entry is a short double identification, one person and one place, each with its biblical citation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernhardt-marti: Martin Bernhardt, a German nerve doctor and medical author, was born at Potsdam on April 10, 1844. He studied at Berlin under Virchow and Traube and took his degree in 1867. Posts at Königsberg and at the Charité in Berlin followed. War service with the Landwehr in the Franco-German war won him a medal for bravery under fire. From 1872 he taught medicine at Berlin as a specialist in nerve disease. He also edited a central medical journal from 1885 and wrote on skin feeling and brain tumors.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bethesda-3224: Bethesda was a pool in Jerusalem. John is the only source that mentions it. He places it by the sheep market. That puts it north of the Temple-hill. Its exact spot cannot be fixed firmly. Early writers describe a double pond. Its water was reddish in color. Five colonnades surrounded it. That matches two ponds near the Sisters of Zion. In the Middle Ages another pond was favored. It lay by the French church of St. Anne.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-births-3324:
Births compares birth-rates among Jews and Christians. Its tables cover many lands and decades. At first sight Jews show fewer births per thousand. Algeria and Hungary are exceptions in the table. The entry calls the result surprising. Jewish population still grows faster almost everywhere. Fewer deaths under age five explain much of it.

That survival swells the share of children. Rates reckoned on all people thus dip. Later tables treat the sex ratio at birth. Boys predominate among Jews more strongly. Russia shows 129 boys to 105 girls. St. Petersburg shows an even wider gap. Scholars' proposed causes remain unproved.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blumenfeld-aron: Aron Wolff Blumenfeld was a German composer. He was born at Kurnik, Posen, on February 29, 1828. In 1846 he went to Berlin. Rungenhagen taught him composition there. He settled as teacher and composer. His opera "Künstlerleben" is his largest work. A cantata was first performed in 1851. His piano pieces are mostly salon morceaux. Titles include "La Fée Dansante" and "L'Espérance." His "Blumenlese" is a curious compilation. It arranges concert music for six to twenty instruments. Ninety-six separate books hold its contents.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brainin-simon-3:
Simon Brainin was a Russian physician born at Riga, Livonia, on July 15, 1854. He studied medicine at Dorpat and Berlin. He served as physician to the Jewish community of Riga and as a director of it.

Brainin sat on a government committee on Jewish rights in Riga in 1885. In 1892 he went as a delegate to a rabbinical conference at St. Petersburg. In 1895 he emigrated to New York and practiced medicine there. His books include a Hebrew work on popular medicine, printed at Wilna in 1883. A guide for physicians and a study of kefyr followed in the next three years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-briviesca-not-b: Briviesca, the ancient Virovesca, is a city in Old Castile, not far from Burgos. A Jewish community dwelt there and was taxed 11,700 maravedis in 1290. Ferdinand III. gave the taxes of several named Jews there to a Burgos convent for ever. In the civil war that followed, Jews defended the city walls bravely. Attack from the rear killed or captured them all, one account says. Of two hundred heads of families, none stayed alive in that telling.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-california-3924:
California, a Pacific coast state, has no firm record of Jewish life before 1849. In that gold year large numbers of Jews rushed to the new fields. They came from the eastern and southern states and from as far as Australia. First services met on Kippur Day 1849 in a San Francisco tent, with about ten people present.

Mining camps across Placer, Amador, and Yuba counties formed congregations and aid societies. When many camps failed, their Jews moved into San Francisco, whose community dated from 1850. The long entry then follows cities, synagogues, and charities across the state. Its tail notes Jewish officers in the Spanish American War era and in the state militia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-carcassonne-ado: Adolphe Joseph Carcassonne was a French poet born at Marseilles in 1826. He died on Sept. 22, 1891. The entry is almost all a list of his works in print order. Poems came first, in a first volume of 1852 and a later one of 1869. Stage works fill most of the list: an opera, dramas in verse, and a siege play on Marseilles. Much of his later output was theater for the young, with short comedies and pieces for girls and teens. One verse piece marks the loss of Alsace in 1871.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-castelli-david-:
David Castelli, an Italian scholar, was born at Leghorn, in Tuscany, on Dec. 30, 1836, and died in 1901. He trained at the rabbinical college of Leghorn. From 1857 to 1863 he taught Hebrew and Italian in the Jewish schools there. He then served as secretary of the Jewish congregation in Pisa.

From January 1876 until his death, Castelli held the chair of Hebrew at an institute of higher studies in Florence. His many books, all in Italian, treat Ecclesiastes, Talmudic legends, the Messiah in Jewish thought, and biblical poetry. He wrote a history of the Israelites in two volumes, issued at Milan in 1887-88. Later works cover the Song of Songs, the Book of Job, and a short political and literary history of the Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chamberlain-hou: Houston Stewart Chamberlain, an Anglo-German musical critic and antisemitic writer, was born on September 9, 1855, at Portsmouth, England. Schooled in France and in science at Geneva, he settled in Austria and taught philosophy at Vienna. His chief work, issued at Munich in 1899, reads all history as a clash between Aryans and Semites. It casts the Jew as a type of the Semite and fears Jewish world rule. It even denies the Jewish origin of Jesus, whose character he admired.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cloud-4424:
Cloud gets a word study first. Hebrew holds five terms for it, from the everyday anan to the heavy dark arafel. The entry gives chapter and verse for each and notes which books favor which word. Poetic books lean on ab and shahak, the last often standing in for the heavens themselves.

Palestine's climate made clouds matter. Rain fell from October to May, then skies stayed clear for months. A rain cloud rose slowly from the sea in the west before the downpour. Later sections gather cloud images in speech and lore: clouds over Sarah's tent, a cloud that carried Moses upward, and rabbinic wordplay tying each Hebrew term to a trait. Glory clouds at death close the survey.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohn-leopold-45:
Leopold Cohn, a German author and philologist, was born on Jan. 14, 1856, at Zempelburg in West Prussia. He took his philosophy doctorate at Breslau in 1878. He became a privat-docent there in 1884, a librarian in 1889, and gained the professor title in 1897.

Greek literature fills his first book list, on Aristophanes of Byzantium, the Plato scholia, and the proverb collectors. His Jewish work centers on Philo of Alexandria. He edited Philo's work on the making of the world in 1889. With Paul Wendland he then issued Philo's surviving works in four volumes from 1896 to 1902. Essays on the latest Philo research and on Greek word study close the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cozbi-deceiving: Cozbi, whose name is glossed as deceiving, was a Midianitish woman. The entry gives only a few facts about her. She was a daughter of Zur, the leader of a tribe. She was put to death along with the Israelite Zimri. Phinehas carried out the killing. The entry cites Numbers, chapter twenty-five, verses 14 to 18, for the account. No family story, speech, or further act of hers is recorded here. Readers get her parentage, her partner in the story, and her death, and nothing more.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cypros-4824: Cypros was a woman of a noble Arabian family. About 75 B.C. she married Antipater, the Jewish governor. She bore him five children: Phasaelus, Herod, Josephus, Pheroras, and Salome. When Herod had to go to Augustus, he placed his mother and sister in his brother's care at Masada. His wife Mariamne went elsewhere, since she looked down on them. Herod built a fortified retreat near Jericho and named it Cypros for his mother. That stronghold was destroyed at the start of the Jewish war under Nero.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-4924: David was an Oriental rabbi who lived at Mosul toward the end of the twelfth century. He was a nephew of the exilarch Daniel ben Solomon, who died in 1175 leaving no male offspring. David claimed the office of exilarch against his cousin Samuel, but Samuel ben Ali ha-Levi stepped in ahead of both and obtained the post. Some writers identify this David with David ben Hodaya, exilarch of Mosul. The traveler Pethahiah reported finding the nasi David at Mosul in 1176.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-disna-5224: Disna was a town in the government of Wilna, Russia. The census of 1897 counted 6,739 people there, about 5,600 of them Jews. The entry says most of those Jews worked as traders, while about 265 were day-laborers. A few families farmed rented land, and Jews owned some 437 deciatines nearby. The town had the usual charities and a Jewish public school for boys and girls, with 170 pupils on its register.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-edel-judah-low-:
Judah Löw ben Moses ha-Levi Edel was a Russian preacher born at Zamoscz, in the Lublin government. He studied under Elijah of Wilna, the famed Gaon. He showed great gift as a preacher. He was also a Hebraist and a sound Talmudic scholar. He died at Slonim in 1827.

Edel's first book was a short Hebrew grammar for beginners, printed at Lemberg in 1793. His Afike Yehudah gathered his sermons, though only one volume came out, in 1802. It held twenty-four sermons. Two commentaries of his treat the laws of purity in Maimonides and the Mishnah. His son Solomon later edited his essays on the Haggadah at Ostrog in 1835.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eleazar-b-abina: Eleazar ben Abina was a Palestinian haggadist of the fourth century C.E. He belonged to the fourth amoraic generation. He was a younger peer of Aha the Third, whose sayings he repeats. A later teacher, Yudan, in turn reports sayings in his name. The entry gives one of his homilies in full. In it he argues that keeping the Sabbath equals all other commandments joined. He builds the proof from all three parts of the Bible. He cites Exodus, Ezekiel, and Nehemiah in turn.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eliezer-ben-sam: Eliezer ben Samson was a rabbi and prayer poet of Cologne. He lived in the twelfth century. He was kin to the tosafist Eliezer ben Nathan. He studied at Speyer and at Mayence. He sat among the leaders of a great synod of rabbis. That synod drew 150 rabbis under Jacob Tam and Rashbam. Two of his prayer poems are still in hand. One is for the Feast of Tabernacles and runs to seven stanzas. The other, in Aramaic, runs to thirty-two verses.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-embezzlement-57:
Embezzlement is the false use of goods held in trust. A man turns to his own ends what was left in his care. It differs from theft in one key way, the entry says. In theft the holding itself breaks the law from the start. The Law of Moses treats the crime in a narrow case. A man denies goods left with him and swears to the lie. He must pay back the whole sum if found out. He must add one-fifth of its value on top. He must also bring a ram as a guilt gift.

The Mishnah takes the topic up in one of its tractates. It sets rules for keepers who swear false oaths on a loss. If he swears to a loss that would clear him, he is caught. The entry works through those cases in set order.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-evora-5924:
Evora was a Portuguese city and seat of the rabbi of the Alemtejo province. In 1490 its Jews met a royal bride-elect in solemn march and gave her cows, sheep, and hens. Seven years later King Manuel decreed there that all Jewish children under fourteen be seized on Easter Sunday. They were to be scattered and raised as Christians.

In April 1506 the crowd tore down Evora's synagogue. Many rich Marranos lived there when the Inquisition was proclaimed on October 22, 1536. Its work began in the city in 1542. Among the first brought to the stake was David Reubeni. The entry rests on Kayserling's history of the Jews in Portugal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-farissol-judah-: Judah Farissol was an Italian mathematician and astronomer who worked at Mantua at the end of the fifteenth century. In 1499 he wrote Iggeret Sefirah, a description of the astronomical sphere with diagrams. That book and its date are the whole factual core of the entry. No birth or death dates, teachers, or other works are named. The entry rests on two sources: Steinschneider on Jewish literature and Neubauer's catalogue of Hebrew manuscripts in the Bodleian Library. A reader learns his field, his city, his century, and his one book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-finzi-6124:
Finzi is an old Italian family whose name likely comes from Pinehas, through the Latin Finea. The earliest known bearers helped set up the first Jewish money-lending office in Padua in 1369. Sons of that line bought land in 1380. One of them may be the Isaac Finzi who spoke for his congregation at Bologna in 1416. A family Bible held the line's genealogy.

Branches spread to many Italian towns over the centuries. Members served as rabbis, bankers, printers, and poets. One Mantua physician of the fifteenth century also won note as a mathematician and astronomer. His tables of the length of days were printed at Mantua. Later Finzis taught noted pupils and wrote responsa, sermons, and legal works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-franklin-jacob-:
Jacob Abraham Franklin was an English journalist and philanthropist born at Portsmouth in 1809. He died on August 3, 1877. On retiring from business he moved to London and took an active part in its Jewish affairs. He set up a weekly paper, the first organ of the Anglo-Jewish community. In it he stated his views against the Reform movement of 1842. He spoke for the Manchester community at the Board of Deputies. He helped found the Anglo-Jewish Association.

Franklin cared deeply for Jewish schooling. He worked to set up a Jewish board school in London. He also won a share of state grants for the Jewish schools. He read papers on decimal coinage and on education. At his death he left most of his property for school projects. Works on natural religion and Jewish history came out under his fund.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fundam-isaac-64: Isaac Fundam, a Spanish author and publisher living in Amsterdam about 1723, issued a volume of plays and pleasant pieces there that year. He also wrote a treatise on the world from its start up to Moses the prophet. That work survives only in manuscript. With Aaron Hezekiah Querido he edited a communal order book. In 1724 he printed a catalogue of Spanish and Portuguese books and manuscripts at Amsterdam.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gambling-10124:
Gambling means playing games, above all games of chance, for money. Ancient Israel names no such games and made no rule against them. Dice play came in with foreign ways late in the Second Temple age. Rabbis hated the new habit. The Mishnah barred a gambler from giving witness in court. They classed gambling as a form of robbery, though losses could not be sued for in court.

Dice, lotteries, bets, and cards spread among Jews in medieval Europe. Towns passed many bans against them. Even scholars fell to the habit. Venice rabbis in 1628 banned card play for six years under pain of the ban. Play for pastime, though, was allowed, even on the Sabbath for women and children.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gaster-moses-65:
Moses Gaster, haham of the Spanish and Portuguese congregation in London, was born in Bucharest on September 16, 1856. He took a degree at home in 1874, then studied at Breslau. There he won a doctorate in 1878 and rabbinic leave to teach in 1881. His great work is a Rumanian reader and word book that spans the tongue from its dawn to 1830.

Rumania drove him out in 1885, and he settled in England. In 1887 he became haham in London. He led the two hundredth year feast of Bevis Marks Synagogue. His books treat Jewish folk lore, an old magic text, and chronicles. He also stood high in the Zionist cause and sat as vice president at the first Basel Congress.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gershon-ben-sol: Gershon ben Solomon ben Asher, a French Talmudist who flourished at Beziers in the twelfth century, wrote a case-law work called Sefer ha-Shalmon. His son Samuel finished that book after him. Isaac ben Sheshet quotes it in his Responsa. A second title, Sefer ha-Shulhan, may name the same work. Gershon also left a set of legal replies, cited by Abudarham. The entry records no birth or death dates for him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gottheil-gustav:
Gustav Gottheil was an American rabbi. He was born at Pinne in Prussian Posen on May 28, 1827. He died in New York city on April 15, 1903. He studied under Plessner, Holdheim, Zunz, and Steinschneider. In 1860 he left Berlin to serve progressive Judaism in new fields. Manchester's Reform congregation took him as rabbi for thirteen years.

In 1873 New York's Temple Emanu-El chose him as assistant. He soon became its senior rabbi. He rebuilt its religious school and helped found a theological training school. His 1886 hymn-book was the first Jewish one printed in America. It fed the later Union Hymnal. In 1889 he started the first Sisterhood of Personal Service. He also helped found the Jewish Publication Society and the Federation of American Zionists.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hast-marcus-732:
Marcus Hast, born at Warsaw in 1840, was a London cantor and composer. He went to Germany in 1864 to study music. At Breslau he became cantor of the chief Orthodox synagogue. There he taught many pupils who later won fame as cantors. In 1871 he moved to London as chief cantor of the Great Synagogue.

Hast printed many settings of Hebrew melodies and much music of his own. His works include a sacred cantata, an oratorio, and a piece on the death of Moses sung at Queen's Hall in 1897. Another work marked the fall of Jerusalem in 1901.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hazor-7424:
Hazor was a fortified city on high ground above Lake Merom, between Ramah and Kadesh. Its king Jabin led a league of kings against Israel. Joshua beat the allied force and burned the city to the ground. The entry calls Hazor the head of all those kingdoms.

The city rose again. A second Jabin ruled there in the days of Deborah and Barak, and Israel fell under his power for a time. Hazor later went to the tribe of Naphtali. In the end, Tiglath-pileser carried its people off to Assyria. Four lesser places of the same name are also listed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heldai-7524: Heldai is the name of two men in the Bible. The first was a captain in the Temple service for the twelfth month in David's time. He came from Netophah and traced his line to Othniel. A parallel list calls him Heled instead. The second Heldai returned from exile with Zerubbabel. With others he gave Zechariah gold and silver for making crowns as memorials. In one verse his name shifts to Helem. Other old versions give still other forms of it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ma-arabi-nahum-:
Nahum Ma'arabi, a Moroccan Hebrew poet and translator, is the subject of a 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry. His surname means the western one, or the Moroccan. He worked in the thirteenth century. His poems survive only in Moroccan collections, and two liturgical pieces were printed by L. Dukes.

The article values him most as a translator from Arabic into Hebrew. He rendered Maimonides' Letter to Yemen under the title Petah Tikwah, adding a preface in verse. He also translated a commentary on the Sefer Yezirah and Joseph ibn Zaddik's Microcosmos. A fourth translation covered Saadia's notes on the thirteen rules of Rabbi Ishmael. Some of these works are anonymous, and the entry weighs the evidence for his hand in them. It preserves the name of a poet who carried Arabic Jewish thought into Hebrew.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-malaga-10324:
Malaga, a Spanish seaport on the Mediterranean, is given a Jewish history in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Said to be founded by the Phoenicians, it was a trading town under Rome with Jews from a very early date. Under Moorish rule its Jews enjoyed full equality. In Samuel ibn Nagdelah's time they were held in high esteem.

The article admits its sources are scanty, then tells a grim end. When Spanish forces took the city in August 1487, converted Jews who had fled there were tortured and killed. The town's own Jews, some 450 souls, were enslaved with the rest of the population. Young Solomon ibn Verga raised 20,000 gold doubloons across Spain for their ransom. They were redeemed and shipped to Africa. After 1492 no Jews could live in Malaga at all. The entry also claims the city as the birthplace of Solomon ibn Gabirol.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marks-david-woo:
David Woolf Marks, called the father of Anglo-Jewish Reform, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born in London on November 22, 1811, he studied at the Jews' Free School. He taught at a Hammersmith boarding school, then served synagogues at St. Alban's and Liverpool. At Liverpool he refused to read the Law on second festival days.

The article follows that stand into a movement. About 1840 London's founders of a Reform synagogue noticed his sympathy. At twenty-nine he became minister of the West London Synagogue of British Jews. His ministry there ran for sixty years. He furthered education, regular preaching, and decorum in public worship. From 1848 to 1898 he held the Hebrew chair at University College, London. He published three volumes of sermons and compiled the Reform order of service. The entry honors the man who gave British Reform its pulpit.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mazzah-plural-m:
Mazzah, the unleavened bread of Passover, is explained in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906 by Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein. It is dough kneaded with water alone, without yeast, and baked in haste so it cannot ferment into hamez. The article calls it the primitive form of bread: leavening made loaves tastier, but mazzah stayed the poor man's bread, since the poor could not wait a day for dough to rise.

Scripture gives it two great roles. It is the bread of sudden hospitality, served to Abraham's angel guests and baked by the witch of Endor for Saul. And it is the bread of the Exodus, eaten with the Passover lamb and through the festival's seven days to recall the flight from Egypt. The article adds its symbolism: purity in the sacrifices, where leaven figures the evil impulse, and, in the Zohar's phrase, a sign of freedom.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-ben-eli:
Menahem ben Elijah was a Turkish liturgical poet of the fifteenth century. He came from Kastoria. Richard Gottheil and M. Seligsohn catalogue him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His surviving hymns are feats of construction. Two of them spell out in acrostic his own name, his father's, and his town's. One runs twelve strophes. Each strophe begins and ends with the same letter.

The marvel is his prayer "Shirat ha-Yad ha-Hazakah." It is also called "Malkiel." The prayer has 140 lines of five words apiece. The first ten lines all begin with one letter, the next ten with the next, and so through his name fifty times over. The entry also weighs another claim. Some would identify him with a Menahem ben Elijah of Crusade times. That man's letter, full of Salonica, survives among the Egyptian fragments. Neubauer published those fragments. Zunz rejects the identification.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mi-kamokah-who-:
Mi-Kamokah, Hebrew for Who is like unto Thee, names the verse from Exodus chapter fifteen sung as a response in Jewish daily services. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on its music in 1906. The verse, with the chapter's closing line, sits between the Shema and the Shemoneh Esreh prayers.

Most days the verse takes the melody pattern of the service around it, the article explains. But for the penitential evening service between New Year and the Day of Atonement, its own later, major-key setting sets the tone for everything else. The entry prints that melody and traces how such tunes became signature themes reused across the northern liturgy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-morrison-lewis-:
Lewis Morrison was an American stage actor born in Jamaica, West Indies, in 1845. His Jewish Encyclopedia entry, written by Cyrus Adler and Edgar Mels, follows a career that began in uniform. When the Civil War broke out he joined the Federal Army and served four years as an officer.

Morrison went on the stage in 1865, appearing with Lawrence Barrett in New Orleans. He played Iago opposite Salvini's Othello and supported stars such as Edwin Forrest, Edwin Booth, and Charlotte Cushman. Later he toured with his own company in Faust, and his Mephistopheles became his best known role. The sketch also notes his wife, the actress Florence Roberts, and his daughter Rosabel, also an actress.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-munsterburg-hug:
Hugo Münsterburg was an American psychologist born at Danzig on June 1, 1863. Cyrus Adler and Joseph Jacobs wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He took a philosophy doctorate at Leipsic in 1885 and a medical degree at Heidelberg in 1887. In 1892 Harvard made him its professor of psychology.

Münsterburg wrote many papers for the specialist journals and a shelf of books for wider readers. They include Psychology and Life, the Grundzüge der Psychologie, and American Traits. Die Amerikaner, his two volumes on the Americans, appeared in 1904 in German and English. In 1898 he was president of the Psychological Association of America.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nard-11324:
Nard is an eastern Asian plant whose root gave the ancient world its prized spikenard perfume. Joseph Jacobs and Immanuel Löw wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on it. In the Bible the word occurs only in the Song of Songs. The plant never grew in Palestine; it belongs to the poet's imaginary garden there.

Costly spikenard ointment appears in the Gospels, poured out at Bethany. In the Mishnah nard is a constituent of the sacred incense, under a name meaning an ear of grain. The article traces that name through Hai Gaon, Maimonides, and Rashi. It is a small study in how one perfume crosses languages and rites.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nehemiah-of-bet:
Nehemiah of Beth-Horon was a scholar of the third century. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Beth-Horon is a small town northwest of Jerusalem. His true name seems to have been Nehunya. Other sources call him Hunya or Hanina of Beth-horon.

He was prized as both a scholar and a pious man. Jerusalem often sought his advice on the calendar. A saying claimed the waters parted when he traveled there. Only a few of his legal rulings survive today. Johanan hands some down as very ancient tradition. A few of his haggadic sayings survive as well. His learned son Uzziel bore his grandfather's great name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nicholas-of-dam:
Nicholas of Damascus was a Greek historian at Herod's court. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Damascus to a respected father. Wealth freed him from needing any prince's service. He stayed a faithful follower of Aristotle's philosophy.

Herod found him through shared studies in rhetoric and politics. Nicholas urged Herod to write, and wrote much himself. At Rome he won back Augustus's favor for Herod. In Asia he defended the Jews' ancient rights successfully. He advised against executing Herod's sons, in vain. After Herod's death he served Archelaus as adviser. His great history ran to 144 books, now mostly lost. Josephus built his Herod story largely upon it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nunes-robert-11:
Robert Nunes was a Jamaican magistrate of public weight. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Montego Bay in 1820. He died at Falmouth on Jan. 31, 1889. Medicine was his first intended calling in life.

Three years of study under two doctors followed. England rounded out his schooling before commerce claimed him. Politics drew his vigor, retrenchment his advocacy. In 1850 he started the Political Eagle newspaper. It later continued under the County Union name. Falmouth made him partner in a banking agency. Trelawny sent him to the Assembly in 1863. He served as custos, then senior resident magistrate. Consular posts for three nations rounded his career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oppenheim-11724:
Oppenheim is a German family that sprang from that town. Gotthard Deutsch wrote the family entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its best known man here is Bernhard Oppenheim, a rabbi. He was born at Strassnitz, in Moravia, about 1790. He died at Eibenschütz on December 26, 1859.

Bernhard learned first from his father Hayyim, a rabbi at Strassnitz. He then read with Baruch Fränkel, a rabbi in Leipnik. About 1830 he was called as rabbi to Eibenschütz. He stayed in that post till his death came. Two of his sons, David and Joachim, became rabbis. His girl Hinde wed Isaac Hirsch Weiss, a scholar. The entry goes on to treat David Oppenheim at length. David was born at Leipnik in December 1816.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oven-11824:
The oven of the East was a tool for the baking of bread. Emil G. Hirsch and Wilhelm Nowack wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Stoves built in a room for heat are not known there. A brazier, a pot of coals, serves in their place. It is set in the room in cold months of the year.

The Hebrew word for oven is tannur in the texts. It names a large, open pot or jar of clay. The jar is half filled with small bricks of clay. When hot, the bricks bake the dough laid on them. Dough is spread on the bricks or stuck to the sides. Dung of horse or sheep serves as the fuel there. The bread bakes in a few minutes in such heat. It is oft a bit burnt by the quick fire.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-partridge-kore-:
The partridge, called kore in Hebrew, gets a short entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote the article. They note the bird is named only twice in the Bible. It appears in First Samuel and in Jeremiah.

The writers list the kinds of partridge found in Palestine. The chukar is the most common one. Another kind lives near the Dead Sea and the Jordan valley. A third kind lives in the low plains. They also cite Talmud passages about the bird. One passage forbids crossing it with a cock or a peacock.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-peretz-isaac-lo:
Isaac Löb Peretz was a writer in Yiddish and Hebrew. He was born at Samoscz, in Poland, in 1851. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. As a boy he was famed as a Hebrew prodigy.

Peretz first worked as a lawyer in his home town. Rules against Jews ended that career for him. He moved to Warsaw and clerked for the congregation. There he gave himself to writing full time. His tales speak in the voice of common people. His Hasidic sketches mix warmth, fantasy, and deep insight.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-phrygia-12124:
Phrygia was a province of Asia Minor with many Jews. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Antiochus the Great moved two thousand Jewish families there. They came from Mesopotamia and Babylonia by royal order. The entry traces the Jews there across many ages.

The families settled chiefly at Laodicea and Apamea. Jews from Phrygia appear in the Acts of the Apostles. Christian teaching found easy entry among them there. In Byzantine times Jews held power in Amorion. A place in the region was called Jews' Castle.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-poggetti-jacob-: Jacob Poggetti, also called Pavieti, was an Italian Talmudist born at Asti in Piedmont. Gotthard Deutsch and Schulim Ochser wrote his short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. His only known work shortens the Reshit Hokmah of Elijah de Vidas. The short version came out at Venice in 1600. It was reprinted at Cracow, Amsterdam, and Zolkiev. Its aim was to teach a strict and moral life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-prado-moses-123:
Moses Prado was a Christian scholar who took up Judaism. Gotthard Deutsch and Isaac Broydé wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His Christian name was Conrad Victor. He taught classic tongues at the University of Marburg. He lived in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

Prado could not accept two church teachings. He could not hold the Trinity or the godhood of Jesus. In 1607 he went to Salonica in Turkey. There he became a Jew and took the name Moses Prado. After seven years he asked leave to go home. He begged the Duke of Hesse to let him return. The entry tells what came of that strange plea.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ptolemy-v-surna:
Ptolemy the Fifth, surnamed Epiphanes, was king of Egypt. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He reigned from 205 to 182 B.C. He was a child of five when the crown came to him. The long fight for Palestine ran through his reign. It ended in favor of Syria at last.

Antiochus the Great took the land in the year 202. The Egyptian general Scopas tried to win it back. He was beaten at the sources of the Jordan. His army was wiped out at Sidon soon after. Josephus says the Jews of Jerusalem helped Antiochus. They even opened the city to him, by that account.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-radin-adolph-m-:
Adolph M. Radin was an American rabbi of Polish birth. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Neustadt-Schirwindt in 1848. He learned Talmud at Volozhin and at Eiseshok. He read at the universities of Berlin and Königsberg. At Königsberg he edited a Jewish paper of the frontier.

Radin took his doctorate at Greifswald in Germany. He then held rabbinates at Mewe, Kempen, and Kalisz. A post at Lodz came to him after those. He crossed to America for the rest of his career. There he led a congregation at Elmira, New York. A New York congregation took him on after that.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rheinhold-hugo-:
Hugo Rheinhold was a German sculptor born on March 26, 1853. Isidore Singer and S. Mannheimer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Oberlahnstein in Prussia. He died at Berlin on October 2, 1900.

The article says he first entered a mercantile career at sixteen. Four years in San Francisco prepared him for trade in Hamburg. After his wife died in 1882, he retired to Berlin. He studied science and philosophy at the university. In 1886 he entered a sculptor's studio. His first shown work drew wide attention in 1895. It shows a chimpanzee pondering a human skull. A compass rests under one of its feet. His figure Am Wege then secured his reputation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-roquemartine-da:
David Roquemartine was a French Jewish scholar of the fourteenth century, born in the town of Roquemartine. His entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia was written by the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Isaac Broydé. He is remembered for works that read Bible stories in symbolic terms.

His main work, Zekut Adam, treats the sin of Adam as an allegory, not a literal event. Part of it was printed in Paris in 1866, with notes by Senior Sachs. Sachs showed that Isaac Abravanel had used the book in his own commentary. Roquemartine also wrote notes on Isaiah chapter 53 and Haggai chapter 2, which survive in manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rubinstein-niko:
Nikolai Rubinstein was a Russian pianist born in Moscow on June 2, 1835. Herman Rosenthal and A. Porter wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was the younger brother of the more famous Anton Rubinstein.

Their mother took both boys to Berlin in 1844 for serious study. Nikolai trained there under Kullak for piano and Dehn for composition. In 1859 he founded the Moscow Musical Society in his home city. Under it the Moscow Conservatorium opened in 1864, with him as director. Anton himself often said Nikolai was the better pianist of the two.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salem-shaloam-d:
Salem Shaloam David was a Chinese convert to Judaism born at Hankow in 1853. Joseph Jacobs and Ezekiel Moses Ezekiel wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born to Chinese parents and named Feba, he lost his family young.

Rebels of the Taiping rising murdered his family and held the boy captive. Freed near Shanghai, he found shelter with the Sassoon firms there. In 1862 he was sent to Bombay and admitted to the Jewish faith. Educated at the David Sassoon school, he joined E. D. Sassoon and Company in 1872. He became a trusted communal worker in Bombay's Jewish life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-salvation-12624:
Salvation, in the English Bible, renders several Hebrew words for rescue and deliverance. Joseph Jacobs and Emil G. Hirsch wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. The entry first sorts the Hebrew terms one by one.

Behind them all stands one idea: help made real in need and danger. One word means to keep alive, another to deliver from an enemy's hand. Padah means to free by paying a ransom price for another. Ga'al means taking up a duty that first fell on someone else. Yasha pictures widening: the sufferer moves from a narrow place to a wide one.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ha-kohen:
Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Samuel ha-Kohen di Pisa, a Portuguese scholar. He lived across the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Samuel wrote a commentary on two hard books of the Bible. Those books are Ecclesiastes and Job.

His commentary takes up the hardest passages in both books. In it he argues about whether the soul lives on after death. He also asks whether Job denied that the dead would rise again. The work runs to fourteen chapters. It was printed at Venice in 1650. The entry points readers to the old catalogs that record his book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saul-13224:
Joseph Jacobs, Ira Maurice Price, Isidore Singer, and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Saul. He was the first king of all Israel. Saul was the son of Kish, a Benjamite of valor. Israel had long been ruled by judges. The Philistines pressed hard on the tribes. The people demanded a king like those of their neighbors.

Two accounts tell how Saul was chosen. In one, he seeks Samuel while hunting his father's lost asses. Samuel anoints him in secret, by God's command. In the other, the lot falls on him at Mizpah. Saul hides among the baggage in modesty. His chance came when Nahash besieged Jabesh-gilead. Saul raised all Israel and marched through the night. He crushed the Ammonites and saved the city. The victory made his kingship secure.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schulhof-isaac-:
Alexander Büchler wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It profiles Isaac ben Zalman Schulhof, an Austrian rabbi. He was born about 1650 at Prague. He died there on January 19, 1733. Schulhof settled at Ofen as rabbi of a small congregation. In 1686 disaster struck his family.

That year imperial troops stormed Ofen. Schulhof's wife was murdered in the assault. His son died in prison at Raab. Schulhof himself was jailed and barely escaped death. He got free on September 3, 1686. His family marked that day each year as Schulhof Purim. He wrote elegies for the Jews delivered at Ofen. He also told his own sufferings in a megillah, a scroll-like account. David Kaufmann published that account in 1895.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-senior-phoebus-:
Phoebus ben Jacob Abigdor Senior was a Talmudic scholar of the early eighteenth century. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. His main work explained all six orders of the Mishnah. He called that commentary Melo Kaf Nahat.

For his notes Senior gathered views from Rashi, Maimonides, and other classic voices. He drew most on Isaac ibn Gabbai's Kaf Nahat. His work was printed with the Mishnah text in six volumes at Amsterdam in 1732. A German edition followed at Berlin a century later. The entry keeps alive a teacher whose notes guided many later readers of the Mishnah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-she-eh-ne-esar-: She'eh Ne'esar is a response hymn sung in the prayers for the fast of the Seventeenth of Tammuz. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Its acrostic signs the name Shelomoh, for Solomon ibn Gabirol. The hymn recalls four disasters tied to that fast day. They are the breaking of the Law's tablets and the end of the daily Temple offering. They also include the breaching of Jerusalem's walls and the burning of a Torah scroll.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shylock-13624:
Shylock is the Jewish moneylender in Shakespeare's play The Merchant of Venice. Joseph Jacobs wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the character. Shylock lends Antonio, a Venetian merchant, three thousand ducats. The bond sets a pound of Antonio's flesh as the forfeit.

Antonio fails to repay the loan on time. Meanwhile Shylock's daughter Jessica elopes with a Christian lover. In court Shylock insists on his pound of flesh. Portia, disguised as a lawyer, defeats the claim cleverly. The bond grants flesh but no blood, she argues. Taking it would also plot against a Venetian's life. That crime carried death under Venetian law then. The doge spares Shylock only if he converts and surrenders half his fortune. The entry retells a plot that shaped images of Jews for centuries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-b-zabdai:
Simeon ben Zabdai, also Zebid, was a Palestinian amora of the third century. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He taught the son of Assi, the entry notes. A few of his readings of Scripture have been preserved.

One reading explains Hezekiah's postponed Passover feast in Chronicles. A Jebusite skull was found under the altar, he said. That find made the altar unclean for the feast. Another reading of his stands beside a rival by Samuel. Two more readings treat sayings of Hanina and Resh Lakish. On Ecclesiastes he judged learning in this world vain. What one learns here fades beside the world to come. There, he taught, nothing learned will ever be forgotten. The entry gathers fragments of a thoughtful interpreter.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-societies-learn:
Learned societies existed in nearly every Jewish community of the past. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Groups formed to study the Talmud, called hebrot shas. Others studied the Mishnah or works like En Ya'akov. Members gave a few hours each day to joint study.

In some towns the Talmud society split the work by treatise. Each member finished his set tractates within the year. Then the whole Talmud was done by the group together. Under Mendelssohn a new kind of society arose in 1783. It joined modern culture with ancient Judaism at Königsberg. A Berlin society of 1823 took up that same broad aim.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sonnino-sidney-:
Sidney Sonnino, Baron Sonnino, was an Italian politician born in 1849. Isidore Singer and Sigmund Münz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Alexandria, in Egypt, that year. His father was a Jewish emigrant from Leghorn, Italy. His mother was an English Protestant by birth and faith.

He grew up in Florence among scholars and historians. With Leopoldo Franchetti he studied the peasants of Sicily. His treatise on Sicilian peasants showed deep economic knowledge. He also wrote on the leasehold system of Tuscany farms. Since 1882 he has sat in the Italian Parliament. From 1893 to 1896 he held the finance portfolio under Crispi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-stern-adolf-140:
Adolf Stern was a German poet and historian of literature born in 1835. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. Stern was born at Leipsic on June 14 of that year. He studied philosophy and history at Leipsic and Jena. In 1868 he settled in Dresden as a teacher.

Stern became professor of literature and art history at the Dresden polytechnic in 1869. His output was huge across poems, plays, and novellas. He wrote histories of German and world literature too. His fifty years of German poetry survey appeared in 1871. He edited collected works by Hauff, Herder, and Körner. The entry lists a scholar who shaped how Germans read their own literature.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tamid-in-full-o:
Tamid is a Mishnah treatise on the daily Temple offerings. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Its full name, Olat Tamid, means the continual burnt offering. The treatise covers the morning and evening sacrifices. It stands ninth in the order Kodashim.

Seven chapters hold thirty-four paragraphs in the treatise. Chapter one describes the priests' night watch in the Temple. Three posts were guarded through the night. Lots chose which priest cleared the altar ashes. A ritual bath came before that duty. Chapter two follows the altar's cleansing and fuel. Ashes were piled in a hillock as an adornment. Other chapters cover priestly and Levitical rites. The entry walks readers through a lost daily service.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-te-omim-joseph-:
Joseph ben Meïr Te'omim was a Galician rabbi born at Lemberg in 1727. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Young, he succeeded his father as preacher there. He also taught in Lemberg's yeshiva. He died at Frankfort-on-the-Oder in 1793.

Te'omim spent several years studying in Berlin. Daniel Jafe's house of study hosted him there. He then resumed his Lemberg posts for a time. In 1782 he became rabbi of Frankfort-on-the-Oder. His Peri Megadim comments twice over on the Orah Hayyim. One part glosses the Ture Zahab commentary. The other glosses the Magen Abraham instead. He also wrote seventy rules for understanding the Talmud. The entry honors one of his age's foremost rabbis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-todesco-hermann:
Hermann Todesco was an Austrian financier and philanthropist born at Presburg in 1792. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He began in the silk trade, then grew rich in cotton. At Marienthal he built one of the first machine-run cotton mills. In 1835 he bought the Legnaro estate near Padua.

His mill at Legnaro ranked among Europe's most important. Yet charity was his main activity, the article stresses. In 1843 he funded a primary and infant school at Presburg. The school opened the next year before an archduchess. He also helped found a Jewish hospital at Baden. His son Eduard later headed the family bank. Eduard entered the Austrian nobility in 1869.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vaez-14624:
Vaez was a prominent Lisbon family whose four brothers lived as Maranos. Gotthard Deutsch and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Immanuel, Pedro, Ayres, and Salvador Vaez head the entry. Abraham Vaez served as hakam at Bayonne later. His Arbol de Vidas treats Jewish ritual law in Spanish.

Ayres Vaez was physician to King John III of Portugal. The King of Fez begged his cure for a dangerous illness. Ayres healed him and returned to study astronomy at Lisbon. A fulfilled prediction of a royal child's death cost him favor. The king handed him to the Inquisition as a secret Jew. The papal nuncio rescued him to Rome instead. Pope Paul freed him and protected the whole family.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vogelstein-herm:
Hermann Vogelstein was a German rabbi and historian. He was born at Pilsen, Bohemia, on January 8, 1870. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His father was Heinemann Vogelstein, rabbi of Stettin. Hermann studied at Berlin and Breslau. He earned his doctorate and rabbinate in 1894.

In 1895 Vogelstein became rabbi in Oppeln. Since 1897 he has served at Königsberg. His first book studies farming in Palestine in Mishnah times. With Rieger he wrote a history of the Jews in Rome. Its first volume won a prize from the Zunz Foundation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weil-henri-1482:
Henri Weil was a scholar of Greek and Latin. He was born at Frankfort on August 26, 1818. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He studied at Bonn, Berlin, and Leipsic. He then continued his work in Paris. He took his doctorate there in 1845.

Weil taught ancient literature at Besançon. In 1872 he became dean of its faculty. In 1876 Paris called him to two teaching posts. The Academy of Inscriptions elected him a full member in 1882. He received the Legion of Honor in 1887. He edited Aeschylus, Euripides, and Demosthenes. His books treat word order and Greek drama.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wilderness-wand:
The wanderings in the wilderness fill a generation of Israel's story. Emil G. Hirsch wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Next to the Exodus, the desert march shapes Israel's memory. The Bible often calls the region simply the wilderness. It matches Arabia Petraea of Greek and Roman maps. Three text blocks tell the journey.

Exodus and Numbers give the march in narrative order. Deuteronomy retells it without strict chronology. Numbers chapter thirty three lists the camps in a catalogue. That list adds eighteen stations the stories omit. Other small gaps appear between the accounts. The entry compares the lists station by station. It shows where the records agree and part.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-worms-baron-sol:
Solomon Benedict de Worms (1801-1882) was an English money man from Frankfort. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Frankfort, he was brought to England as a boy. He later went out to Ceylon to seek his fortune.

In Ceylon his good sense helped the colony grow fast. He gave with a free hand to Jewish good causes. He sat for life on the board of the United Synagogue. He served as trustee for more than one London synagogue. In 1871 Austria made him a baron for his service. Three years later the queen let him use that rank in England. The grant named his work in Ceylon with his brothers. The entry honors a rich man who gave back in kind.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-young-men-s-heb:
Young Men's Hebrew Association is a group for the growth of Jewish youth. Joseph Jacobs and Percival S. Menken wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Such groups rose in town after town in the United States. They aim at mind, soul, social life, and body.

The first group was formed in New York in 1874. It met first at the house of a town doctor. Its first board held names of weight in that town. Lewis May served as its first chief for two years. In 1876 the group moved to rooms on Sixth Avenue. Its work was one of aid and good will at base. Talks by top men drew crowds to its hall. Free classes taught Bible, Hebrew, and trade skills there. A book room grew into a free town book store.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zeitlin-joshua-:
Joshua Zeitlin (1742-1822) was a Russian scholar and friend to learned men. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Shklov, he died at Kherson in the south. He was a pupil of the author of Shaagat Aryeh.

He knew the craft of state funds with rare skill. Prince Potemkin, the pet of Catherine, held him close. In the Turk war he fed the Russian host with goods. He ran that work so well he won a court rank for it. In his last years he lived on his own estate in peace. Rabbis came to him there for his word on the law. He gave cash aid to more than one poor sage in need. He kept a fine house of study at his own cost there.
journal-of-discourses-vol-24:
Maximum pressure bears down through Volume Twenty-Four, issued in 1884. Much of the kingdom's leadership sits behind bars or in hiding. The government's full weight rests on one small, stubborn people.

Discourses of endurance preach patience when the heavens seem like brass. Hidden apostles surface to bless the flock, then vanish once more. Wives run farms, shops, and wards while their husbands dodge marshals. Faith stays unbroken under a strain few churches have ever borne. kafka-ein-hungerkunstler-1924:
Ein Hungerkunstler, A Hunger Artist, was Kafka's last story, published in 1924 in the collection of the same name that he corrected on his deathbed. Its hero is a professional faster, once a star of fairs and circuses, whose art the world has stopped wanting.

Caged and forgotten, he fasts on, and at the end confesses his secret: he never found a food he liked, so fasting was no feat at all. A panther takes his cage, fed and glorious. The story is Kafka's bleak joke on art, fame, and appetite, written as he himself starved of breath.
laclos-liaisons-dangereuses-aldington-19:
Choderlos de Laclos, a French army officer, published Les Liaisons dangereuses in 1782. Richard Aldington translated the novel into English in 1924 as Dangerous Acquaintances. The whole story unfolds in letters between two cold, clever aristocrats and the people they set out to ruin.

The Marquise de Merteuil and the Vicomte de Valmont plot seductions as moves in a game. Their targets include a virtuous married woman and a convent-bred girl. Letter by letter the plots tighten, until pride and revenge turn the players on each other. Laclos builds the trap with icy control and no wasted scene. The novel remains the sharpest portrait of desire used as a weapon.
lawrence-boy-in-bush-1924:
The Boy in the Bush, published in 1924, is Lawrence's Australian novel, written with Mollie Skinner. She ran the guest house where the Lawrences stayed in Western Australia. She supplied a draft; he rewrote it into his own fierce idiom.

Its hero, Jack Grant, is an English boy sent to the colony, who grows up in the outback among settlers, stockmen, and Aboriginal people. The bush tests him toward a hard, free manhood outside English rules. The collaboration gives the book a double texture: local knowledge under Lawrence's prophetic voice. It remains the most Australian of his novels.
lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-literat:
Lippincott's April 1875 number concludes its Australian papers. Scenes and adventures from Australia end their run here. W. A. Baillie-Grohman writes of the golden eagle and his eyrie. William Black advances Three Feathers through Mabyn's dreams.

The exile returns in chapter thirty-two of that serial. Russian sects, the Raskol, receive a three-part examination. Kate Hillard studies Shakespeare's sonnets for the issue. Emma Lazarus contributes a poem, A March Violet, among others. Nice, conclaves, and Monsur Pacha fill Trollope and Davey's pages. Faust in Poland and artists' models enliven the gossip section.
lowie-primitive-religion-1924:
Robert Harry Lowie, a leading Boasian anthropologist, wrote this 1924 survey to give religion among stateless peoples a clear, systematic treatment. Rather than ranking beliefs as stages, he described them as living systems that deserved study on their own terms.

Lowie covers awe and the sense of the extraordinary, prayer, sacrifice, shamans, visions, and myths across many peoples. He draws heavily on his own fieldwork with the Crow and on reports from every continent. His tone is dry and skeptical of grand theories. The book became a founding textbook of the anthropology of religion, used for decades.
machen-ornaments-in-jade-1924:
Arthur Machen wrote short prose poems late in his career, and Ornaments in Jade, published in 1924, gathers them in one slim book. Each piece is brief. Each one tries to catch a flash of awe, fear, or joy in plain, rich words.

Readers meet brief scenes rather than full tales. A street, a face, or a scrap of song can open onto a vast hidden world. The book shows Machen at his most pure and spare. Fans prize it as the heart of his strange, bright style. Late in life Machen still held that the world hides bright, dread truths. Each short piece gives that faith a sharp, clear shape.
mann-magic-mountain-1924:
Thomas Mann published The Magic Mountain in 1924, a German novel set in a sanatorium in Davos, Switzerland. Hans Castorp visits his sick cousin for three weeks and stays for seven years. The Berghof sanatorium cuts its guests off from normal time. Illness, idleness, and talk fill their days.

Two guests argue over Castorp's soul: Settembrini, a humanist, and Naphta, a radical critic of the West. Love, music, seances, and snow deepen the spell of the mountain. Castorp at last leaves as the First World War begins. Mann turns a health resort into a mirror of European thought. The novel is vast, ironic, and humane.
mead-gnostic-john-the-baptizer-1924:
A living Gnostic community, the Mandaeans of Iraq and Iran, still honors John the Baptist as its greatest prophet. G. R. S. Mead presented their scriptures to English readers in The Gnostic John the Baptizer, published in 1924. The book offers selections from the Mandaean John-Book in translation.

Mead, a tireless student of forgotten religions, treats the texts with care and sympathy. Hymns, teachings, and the Baptist's story appear in a form few Western readers had ever seen. The volume opened a window on a faith that never died out, unlike its ancient cousins. Scholars and seekers both took notice of his pioneering English treatment. The tradition he introduced still draws researchers to the marshes of southern Iraq.
melville-billy-budd-1924:
Herman Melville left Billy Budd unfinished at his death, and it first saw print in 1924. The novella was his final word on justice, innocence, and martial law. Its spare, grave tone differs sharply from his wild early sea tales of youth.

Billy Budd, a fine young sailor, is pressed into a British warship's crew. The master-at-arms Claggart hates his goodness and charges him with mutiny plots. Billy, tongue-tied, strikes and kills him, and the law demands his death. Captain Vere hangs him though he believes the lad is guiltless of intent. The tale asks hard questions no court at sea can settle.
moore-observations-1924:
Marianne Moore published Observations in 1924, a book of poems marked by precision and restraint. Moore wrote about animals, art, sports, and American scenes. Her lines often use syllable counts rather than a steady beat. Quotations from other writers appear inside the poems themselves.

Pangolins, ostriches, and baseball players share space with paintings and gardens. Moore looks closely and judges with dry wit. She avoids grand claims and favors exact detail. The book helped define American modernist poetry at its most disciplined. Later poets learned from her care with facts and form. Her work rewards slow reading and a second look.
nasa-tm-19640005950-motion-of-the-sub-sa:

openalex-w2774787224:

Their tally gave long COVID a shape that clinics and researchers could plan around, turning scattered case reports into one measured picture.

openalex-w4401164724:

openalex-w7212598424:

physiologus-carlill-1924:

The writer mixes real habits of animals with legend and reads both as lessons in faith. Monasteries copied and expanded the text for a thousand years. Every later bestiary, with its painted lions and dragons, flows from this spring.
pigafetta-first-voyage-round-the-world-1:

He kept a log of all: straits, storms, trade, fights, and the death of his chief in the far isles. His tale is the chief source on the first such voyage in man's past.

Midst the log stand the giants of Patagonia, men so tall, he says, that his mates stood waist high to them. That tale launched years of giant lore. The book is a prime trek text.
plaw-118-121-2024: Oceanside, California is the city covered by Public Law 118-121, approved on November 25, 2024. The law states that the postal facility at 517 Seagaze Drive shall be known as the Charlesetta Reece Allen Post Office Building. It adds that any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, record, or other paper counts as a mention of the new name.
plaw-118-201-2024: Public Law 118-201, approved on December 23, 2024, renames a post office in Bastrop, Texas. The law states that the postal facility at 1106 Main Street shall be known as the Sergeant Major Billy D. Waugh Post Office. Any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, record, or other paper counts, under the law, as a mention of the new name.
plaw-118-46-2024: Public Law 118-46, approved on March 22, 2024, renames a federal building in Detroit, Michigan. The law states that the building at 985 Michigan Avenue shall be known as the Rosa Parks Federal Building. Any mention of that building in a federal law, map, record, or other paper counts as a mention of the new name. The law also repeals two older laws from 2005 that had named the site before.
plos-pbio-0020024:
Sidarta Ribeiro, Damien Gervasoni, Ernesto S. Soares, and their team recorded brain activity during sleep for PLOS Biology in 2004. Rats that had explored new objects showed replays of brain patterns in several forebrain areas during slow-wave sleep. The replays lasted far longer than many expected.

Sleep replay is thought to help move new memories into long term store. Finding it spread across many areas, and lasting for hours, hints at a broad, slow process of memory fixing. The study gives weight to the idea that sleep is active work for the brain, not rest alone. It also offers a model for testing how poor sleep might weaken learning and recall.
plos-pone-0000024:
Taisheng Li, Jing Xie, Yuxian He, and co-authors checked the immune memory of people who had recovered from SARS, in work published in 2006. SARS, the severe lung disease that spread in 2003, left a key question behind: how long does protection last after infection? The team drew blood from recovered patients well after their illness.

They found robust responses still in place: antibodies against the virus and cytotoxic T cells, the killer cells that destroy infected cells, had both persisted long-term. Lasting immunity of this kind shapes vaccine hopes and tells doctors whether survivors can be reinfected. For a virus that vanished, the study also left a template for judging immunity to its later cousins.
plos-pone-0000124:
Ilaria Roato, Giacomina Brunetti, Eva Gorassini, and colleagues published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2006. It looks at patients with solid tumors and examines a signaling protein called IL-7. The team reports that IL-7 raises the activity of osteoclasts, the cells that break down bone, through a pathway tied to TNF-alpha.

Bone loss is a serious problem when cancer spreads or when the immune system runs hot. The authors connect an immune signal to the cells that erode bone. That link matters for understanding why some tumor patients lose bone strength, and it may point to ways of slowing that damage.
plos-pone-0000224:
Servane Blanvillain, Damien Meyer, Alice Boulanger, and colleagues published this microbiology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Bacteria that live on plants or in water need to scavenge carbohydrates for food. The authors show these bacteria share a route for that scavenging: TonB-dependent receptors, gates in the cell surface that pull in nutrients.

The receptors were best known from other bacteria, so finding them as a shared feature broadens the picture. Both plant pathogens and aquatic bacteria use this system to harvest plant sugars. The work identifies a possible weak point in bacteria that damage crops, since blocking food intake can stop growth.
plos-pone-0000324:
Gareth A. Wilson, Edward J. Feil, Andrew K. Lilley, and colleagues published this comparative genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Taxonomically restricted genes are genes found in only one group of organisms, with no known relatives elsewhere. The authors carry out a large-scale ranking of such genes across bacterial and archaeal genomes.

Orphan genes like these are often ignored because nothing is known about them. Ranking them by properties such as length and conservation highlights which ones look genuinely functional. The paper gives microbiologists a shortlist of mysterious genes most worth the cost of experiments.
plos-pone-0000424:
Cristiana Cavina-Pratesi, Melvyn A. Goodale, and Jody C. Culham used brain scanning to separate grasping from seeing, in PLOS ONE in 2007. People can judge an object's size and also reach out and size their grip to it, and the two abilities may use different brain systems. The fMRI study used real three-dimensional objects rather than pictures.

The authors report a dissociation: brain activity for grasping an object split apart from activity for perceiving its size. Using real objects matters because flat images can mislead studies of the hand. The finding supports the idea that the brain runs a dedicated system for guiding actions, distinct from the system that builds what we consciously see.
plos-pone-0000524:
R. David Shankar and colleagues described a teaching experiment from a medical school in Nepal, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Students practiced personal drug selection, the skill of choosing the right medicine for a condition from evidence rather than habit, through problem-based learning in pharmacology. The authors reported their experience running the course.

Choosing drugs well is a core clinical skill, and prescribing habits formed at school persist for careers. Problem-based learning makes students defend choices on real cases instead of memorizing lists. A report from Nepal carries weight. Settings with few resources must teach economical prescribing. Each rupee spent on the wrong drug is care someone else does not get.
plos-pone-0000624:
Martin R. Miller, Andrew White and Kenneth Wilson modeled what happens when parasites hit males harder than females. Their 2007 PLOS ONE study starts from growing evidence that male hosts tend to carry higher levels of parasitism. What that bias does to the host population as a whole was not yet understood.

The team built on an established two-sex model and ran it under different mating systems. Mating patterns change how a male-skewed parasite burden feeds through births, deaths, and population growth. Modelers and disease ecologists get a framework for asking when male-biased infection stays a detail and when it reshapes the whole host population.
plos-pone-0000724:
Mark S. Bretscher and Margaret Clotworthy improved a genetic trick in a social amoeba, writing in PLOS ONE in 2007. Dictyostelium discoideum amoebae are haploid, carrying one gene copy, and share many features with animal cells. That makes them ideal for studying basic processes such as cell locomotion. But isolating mutants had largely been limited to non-essential genes.

Their method uses single loxP sites to enhance homologous recombination, the swapping of DNA at matched sequences. Temperature-sensitive mutants in the Sec1 gene are the demonstration case. Mutants in essential genes, which kill cells when fully removed, need gentler tools. A better recombination method widens what this model organism can teach.
plos-pone-0000824:
Alexander Moffett, Nancy Shackelford and Sahotra Sarkar mapped malaria risk across Africa from the mosquitoes' point of view, in PLOS ONE in 2007. A central goal of epidemiology is building spatial models of disease prevalence and risk, including maps for the potential spread of infectious disease. Malaria risk depends on which vector species live where, and each species has its own ecological niche.

The team provides three continent-wide maps of relative malaria risk in Africa, based on ecological niche models of the vector species. Risk maps built on mosquito habitat can anticipate transmission where case data are sparse. They also show where risk could shift as environments change.
plos-pone-0000924:
Michael Lodes, Dominic Suciu, Jodi Wilmoth and colleagues built an electronic test to name the germs behind throat and lung infections, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Upper respiratory infections from bacteria and viruses look much alike at the bedside. Symptoms alone cannot name the culprit, yet the right treatment depends on knowing it, since antibiotics do little against viruses.

Their method uses an oligonucleotide microarray, a chip of short DNA probes, with electrochemical detection to flag matches. Naming the pathogen fast and correctly could cut wasted antibiotic use. It could also speed care for patients whose infection turns serious. The paper presents the test as a working system, not just a concept.
plos-pone-0001024:
Martina Bielaszewska, Robin Kock, Alexander Friedrich and colleagues challenged how a severe gut illness is diagnosed, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Hemolytic uremic syndrome is a dangerous condition caused by certain E. coli that make Shiga toxin. Diagnosis looked for the toxin genes and a second marker called eae.

The team report cases where stool samples held E. coli lacking the toxin genes yet positive for eae. If toxin genes can be lost during infection, tests that demand them will miss real cases. The authors ask whether the diagnostic paradigm needs to change. For a syndrome that can damage kidneys fast, a missed call is costly.
plos-pone-0001124:
Museums and herbaria hold centuries of records on where species live, and a global effort is digitizing them. Chris Yesson and colleagues audited that effort in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their subject is the Global Biodiversity Information Facility, the largest single gateway to this occurrence data.

The authors ask how global the facility's coverage really is. Gaps matter: records cluster in some regions and taxa while others stay sparse, which can skew studies of how life is spread across the planet. Their check gives data users and collectors a clearer picture of what the archive holds and what it still lacks.
plos-pone-0001224:
Detecting a specific molecule quickly and cheaply is a basic need in medicine and research. William Chiuman and Yingfu Li engineered fluorescent sensors from catalytic DNA in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Most sensors built from nucleic acid enzymes pair an RNA-cutting catalytic motif with an aptamer, a receptor piece that grabs the target.

Their design, called MgZ, rests on a non-classic allosteric scheme, where target binding switches the catalyst's activity through a shape change. When the sensor fires, it produces a fluorescent signal. DNA-based sensors are cheap to make and stable, so better designs widen their use.
plos-pone-0001324:
Dog genetics is powerful because breeds are closed populations, but that structure can also fool association studies. Pascale Quignon and colleagues assessed population structure within breeds, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Studies usually sample cases and controls from a single breed, often from one country, to control structure.

The authors examine intra-breed stratification, hidden subgroups within a breed, and its impact on SNP-based association studies. If cases and controls come disproportionately from different subgroups, false associations follow. Their assessment tells dog geneticists how finely they must match their samples.
plos-pone-0001424:
Morgane Rolland and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on immune responses and HIV control. Certain gene variants help some people hold the virus at low levels. The team asked whether the breadth of the killer T cell response explains that control. Past work had given mixed answers on breadth alone.

They found that broad responses, with a bias to one virus protein, went with lower virus levels. The protein bias mattered as much as sheer breadth. That nuance helps shot design, since it names which targets to favor. Shots that train the right breadth on the right protein may copy what natural control does best.
plos-pone-0001524:
Laura Wesolowski and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on fast HIV tests that clash. Fast tests on blood or mouth fluid that react must be checked with a lab test. When the lab check says no, the results clash. The team drew on watch data after the tests reached wide use.

They set out how often such clashes occur and what repeat checks show. Clear rules for repeat testing spare people long waits in doubt. The data help clinics write those rules on proof, not habit. They also show the worth of tracking test performance once tests leave the lab.
