For project owners and governments, the lesson is practical. Pay down the cost of sharing and prove its usefulness, and partners will build data value together.
plos-pone-0342424:
Ghazal Khalili and Manaf Zargoush led a vast study of aging veterans. It asked how loss of daily function plays out over time. Most past work crushes that story into one score. This team kept the order and timing of change. They mined more than a million checks on daily tasks. The checks came from US veterans' nursing homes. More than two hundred sixty-five thousand residents were in the data.

Thirteen clear path types stood out. Short, harsh paths carried the worst death risk. The worst group lost near half its members in year one. Long, mild paths were far more stable. Mild loss might touch just walking or bathing. The team says path type can guide care plans.
plos-pone-0342524:
Zifeng Li led a team of seven authors setting out a review protocol on nurse burnout, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Nurses who absorb the suffering of others can develop compassion fatigue, a deep exhaustion that harms both nurse and patient care. Many models claim to predict who is at risk, with mixed quality.

Li's protocol plans a systematic review that will appraise those prediction models critically. Sorting models that work from those that do not helps hospitals act early, before a nurse is in crisis. Publishing the plan in advance keeps the review honest. With nurse shortages worldwide, tools that truly predict fatigue, and trigger support in time, have clear practical value.
plos-pone-0342624:
Sarah Yeoh and Mai Stafford use routine health records to measure how poor English affects health in England, in this 2026 study. More than a million people in the UK speak English poorly or not at all, yet their health burden is rarely quantified. The authors drew on a linked database of GP, hospital, and social care records for the London borough of Brent, comparing residents by language proficiency.

People who were not proficient in English had higher rates of heart and metabolic conditions after accounting for age and sex. They also used both primary and hospital care more heavily than proficient speakers. The authors present the work as the first large, representative quantification of this gap in a UK setting. They call for language support to start at GP registration, and for records to capture language properly.
plos-pone-0343224:
Shahriar Afandizadeh, Saeid Abdolahi, and Hamid Mirzahossein set out to forecast traffic on Kandovan Road, a mountainous recreational route in Iran where holiday crowds, weather, and terrain make flows hard to predict. Their 2026 study trained eight different machine learning and deep learning models on traffic, weather, and calendar data spanning 2017 to 2023.

A random forest model won the comparison, tracking actual traffic most closely, ahead of several fashionable neural networks. Blending weather and event data with traffic counts clearly sharpened every model's forecasts. The team also built working software that shows live predictions, giving road authorities a planning tool for congestion, safety, and holiday surges on difficult mountain roads.
plos-pone-0343624:
Gustavo Vieira Veloso and co-workers compare ways to draw soil maps for farming in the Brazilian state of Minas Gerais. Good maps of nutrients and texture guide planting and fertilizer choices. Their 2026 study pits two classic gap-filling methods against several machine learning models, using map position and grid layouts as inputs, and weighs accuracy against computing time.

Learning models clearly beat the classic methods at predicting soil traits such as clay and phosphorus. One forest-style model led on most traits, while another led on sand. Classic methods were faster to run, and learning models slowed as grids grew finer. For farms and agencies, the trade is clear: better maps cost more computing.
plos-pone-0345524:
Zeinab Ebrahimian and co-workers build a small bench-top model that lets liver and fat tissue talk to each other without pumps. How these tissues exchange signals drives obesity and diabetes, but animal tests are slow and costly. Their 2026 device rocks four linked chambers so fluid flows between liver-like and fat-like cells grown side by side.

Cells stayed alive through four days of drug testing. A drug known to cause weight gain raised fat storage and sugar and fat levels in the shared fluid. Two other compounds, one natural and one a standard diabetes drug, blunted those effects. The simple setup could screen drug side effects earlier and cut animal use.
plos-pone-0345724:
Nobuhito Muramoto and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It concerns metastatic renal cell carcinoma, kidney cancer that has spread. The authors assess prognosis, the likely course of the disease, using two blood-based scores combined: one built on the systemic immune-inflammation index, the other on a ratio of C-reactive protein to albumin.

Both scores are built from routine blood tests, one reflecting inflammation and nutrition, the other immune cell balance. Judging whether the pair beats either alone helps doctors sort patients by risk cheaply. Oncologists treating advanced kidney cancer are the readers who could fold such combined scores into treatment planning.
plos-pone-0346324:
Yifei Huang, Zhiyuan He, and Cheng Ding teach a neural network to forecast trade balances. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. It covers two hundred twenty-nine countries. Trade links form a web, so the team used a graph network. Such models learn from webs of linked points. Rival methods included deep networks, attention models, and tree ensembles.

The graph model won by a clear margin. It explained most of the spread in trade balances. Its errors stayed low across test runs. The team also ranked which inputs mattered most. That gives the forecast some explanation, not just a number. Sharper trade forecasts help exporters, importers, and policy makers plan.
plos-pone-0346424:
Jiajun Zhu and colleagues built a featherweight vision system that lets drones spot rooftop solar panels. Counting panels from the air helps cities track solar growth, but panels vary hugely in size and drones carry weak computers. Their 2026 paper adapts a popular detection network with a finer-grained detection layer and an attention block that adjusts to cluttered rooftops.

On their test set of drone images the system reached precision and recall above ninety-five percent while weighing only a few megabytes and running at over one hundred frames per second. That balance of accuracy and speed makes it realistic to run directly on the drone. The authors offer it as a practical tool for solar inspection work.
plos-pone-0346624:
Alexander Karner and co-authors tested a computer-based way to measure fear of spiders without bringing a real spider into the room. In their test, people slowly sharpen three blurred spider pictures, stopping at the point where looking still feels comfortable. The team compared scores from this task with trusted questionnaires and with a real-life approach test in which volunteers move toward an actual spider.

The computer scores lined up moderately well with both the questionnaires and the live test at first, though the link with the live test faded at a later follow-up. Karner and colleagues judge the test quick and easy but limited, since avoidance on a screen may not capture the full force of fear. They propose a refined version that keeps the simple task while mimicking real encounters better.
plos-pone-0346824:
Sheng Jin and six colleagues improve how unmanned tracked vehicles follow a path. Their 2026 study attacks two headaches at once. Such control is accurate but heavy to compute. Hydraulic drive systems, meanwhile, resist tidy physical modelling. Their framework splits control into two layers. The upper layer plans motion with a lean planning method using Laguerre functions. That slashes the work. The lower layer learns each hydraulic motor's behaviour from data instead of equations.

Simulations showed the planning layer's speed gain plainly. A single optimisation took about a quarter of the time conventional control needed. Real-time performance improved without surrendering control quality. A standard feedback controller in the lower layer added resistance to disturbances. Field tests on a real tracked vehicle followed. Speed and trajectory tracking both confirmed the design works outdoors, not only in simulation. Cheaper computation means smaller onboard computers can steer heavy machines precisely.
plos-pone-0346924:
Welelaw Necho Mulatu and a large team interviewed twenty-three supply chain workers and experts across Ethiopia about why contraceptives, maternal, newborn, and child health goods run out at small clinics. National reforms improved the upper levels of the system, but the last mile, health centres and tiny health posts, still fails patients. Interviews were coded into themes by setting, farming regions and pastoral regions alike.

Six bottlenecks recurred: erratic deliveries, poor data that nobody uses, sloppy stock keeping, weak forecasting of need, too few staff, and broken infrastructure. Pastoral areas added bad roads and thin cold storage, while health posts often fetched goods themselves. Extra hand-offs through district offices added delay everywhere. The authors map these frictions so reform money can be aimed at the exact points where supplies stall.
plos-pone-0347324:
R. Srivats and his team fused four known image nets to find landslides in shots from space and drones. One net can miss a faint slide or blur its edge. Bad maps can slow aid when hills fall. The fused net adds a fifth part, a rival pair that sharpens the edge of each slide it finds.

On three test sets, the scores ran from near ninety-four to near ninety-seven per cent. The sets span fine drone shots, mid space shots, and quake slides. The fused net beat each lone net by a clear gap. It also draws map-ready charts fast, fit for use right after a slide.
plos-pone-0348124:
Nigar Sultanova, Rasim Bayramov, and Narmin Maharammova measured face soft tissue thickness on three hundred CT scans of adults in Azerbaijan. Thickness at twenty landmarks, midline and paired, was split by three age bands, sex, and body weight class. Such tables guide face reconstruction from skulls in forensics and surgery.

Averages, spreads, and ranges were tabled for every landmark, with differences by age, sex, and weight reported. The set forms the first such database for Transcaucasia populations. Using tables from distant populations can distort a reconstructed face; local data give investigators and surgeons a truer starting point for Azerbaijani adults.
plos-pone-0348624:
Felipe do Carmo Jorge, Gabriel Politzer Couto, and Berndt J van Rensburg spent nights listening to an Australian open forest. Or rather, they let recorders listen. Then they asked whether simple sound measures can stand in for biodiversity after dark. Night ecology is understudied because sampling in the dark is hard. The team compared several acoustic indices, numbers that summarise a recording, against hand-counted insect sound types.

No single index did the job, but a blend of four, covering activity, evenness, and how full the soundscape is, tracked the richness of insect sounds well. Index patterns also matched how sites differed from each other. The authors caution that the recipe will not transfer unchanged to other habitats, yet they offer their procedure as a cheap way to watch nighttime ecosystems over long stretches.
plos-pone-0348724:
EDITORIAL NOTE: This notice updates an earlier Expression of Concern about a published study of virus communities found in fluid around the heart of patients with unexplained heart inflammation. The PLOS One Editors explain that the journal investigated whether the original study, which used samples from patients including minors, had proper ethics approval.

A university ethics representative in Marseille reported that an internal investigation found the study met ethical standards, since it only reanalysed samples taken during routine care. The journal, however, found that one of the study's authors sat on the very ethics board that approved the work. Because of that conflict, the editors say they cannot confirm the study received independent ethics review.
plos-pone-0349024:
Wenyan Xiao, Lin Zhang, and Yangshuyi Xu built a network that reads feelings from video by letting the words lead. Judging emotion from face, voice, and speech together trips many systems, because the channels disagree in quality and timing. Their design uses the transcript as an anchor: a gated attention step aligns sound and image against the text while damping noise. A second gating stage balances each channel's contribution before merging.

A contrastive learning scheme, also anchored on text similarity, keeps the merged representation honest to both shared and unique signals. On the two standard benchmark collections for this task, the system set new best scores for accuracy and robustness. The authors argue that giving text the anchor role, rather than treating all channels as equals, is the design lesson.
plos-pone-0349124:
Matthew M Harper and Nickolas A Boehme tested whether repeated short spells of low oxygen could shield mouse eye nerve cells from blast injury. Blast waves can harm the retina cells that carry vision signals to the brain, leading to slow nerve loss. Mice received six low oxygen sessions over two weeks, then a blast or sham blast, with eye function, structure, and cell counts checked a month later.

Blast mice lost signal strength and nerve layer thickness versus sham mice. Mice pretreated with low oxygen spells looked like sham mice on both measures, and surviving cell counts held up. Training the body with mild oxygen stress beforehand, the authors conclude, can at least partly protect vision nerves from blast harm.
plos-pone-0349224:
Tao Luo, Qingpeng Huang, and Jingyan Mai studied young people who have newly taken up farming in Guangdong Province, China, asking how their job skills are developing. Drawing on interviews and questionnaires across twenty-one cities, they traced three stages of a farming career: entering the field, putting down roots, and growing a business. Skill needs differ at each stage.

Young farmers' abilities fell into three layers: hands-on professional skills, general abilities useful anywhere, and core qualities such as judgment and commitment. Each layer grows best with its own kind of training. As more young people enter farming, matching training to career stage could help them stay and help villages renew their workforce.
plos-pone-0349624:
Ryo Murata and Kenji Tanaka propose a way to fill the gaps in pedestrian flow data by blending real measurements with simulation. Cities track crowds to plan streets and marketing, but sensors miss people, while simulations are complete yet ignore real human quirks. Their method borrows data assimilation, the fusion trick used in weather forecasting, and applies a particle filter to an agent-based crowd model.

Virtual pedestrians are continually nudged toward whatever the real sensors did capture, so the finished picture is both complete and realistic. The team tested the approach against three kinds of missing data. Better crowd pictures matter for evacuation planning and station design, where decisions are only as good as the flow data beneath them.
plos-pone-0350024:
Wenxin Jiang and Peng Liu compared two chemotherapy regimens for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, a fast-growing blood cancer, in patients whose tumors showed a high growth marker. One regimen adjusts doses upward over cycles, and the other is the long-standing standard. Earlier records from three hundred seventy-six patients set the marker level that counts as high.

Twenty-nine patients received the dose-adjusted regimen in a forward-looking study, matched against similar patients who got the standard one. Survival without the disease returning, and overall survival, did not differ meaningfully between the groups. Enrollment stopped early because benefit looked unlikely and recruitment was slow. For doctors, the result argues against choosing the harsher regimen on growth marker alone.
plos-pone-0350124:
Qiuyu Li led a study of two skills in Chinese undergraduates. One skill is computational thinking: breaking hard tasks into clear steps. The other is AI literacy: grasping what AI can and cannot do. Past work linked the two at one point in time. This team tracked two hundred sixteen students over time. They asked if the first skill builds the second.

Both skills grew across the study span. The modeling showed a clear push from the first skill to the second. The link held steady as both rose. The team says courses that teach step-wise problem solving lay real ground for AI smarts. They offer the design as a guide for course planners.
plos-pone-0350224:
Mohammad Abdul Karim Khan and four colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on blood flow and aneurysms. It is a computational investigation of nanoparticle effects on hemodynamics, the forces of moving blood, inside patient-specific aortic aneurysms, ballooned sections of the body's main artery shaped from individual patients' scans.

Alongside simulation, the authors use machine learning to predict those effects more quickly. Nanoparticles are studied as possible drug carriers, so knowing how they alter flow inside a weakened aorta matters for safety. Biomedical engineers and vascular specialists share the audience for a model built on real patient anatomy.
plos-pone-0350624:
José Alejandro Valdevila Figueira and co-authors tested what Ecuadorian health students know about Alzheimer's disease in 2026. With populations ageing, tomorrow's doctors, nurses, and psychologists will all meet dementia, and training gaps are easiest to fix early.

More than a thousand students, mostly nursing, took a standard knowledge scale. Average correct answers sat near fifty-five percent, a limited level. Medical students scored highest, with nursing and psychology behind. The authors call the gap urgent and propose stronger dementia teaching across all three programs. Knowing the baseline by discipline lets universities aim the remedy where it is weakest.
plos-pone-0350824:
Brown and colleagues compared gut microbes of Eastern indigo snakes, wild and captive, in a 2026 study. The snake is a threatened species native to the American Southeast. Samples from the rear opening stood in for gut samples across three groups: captive snakes with a gut parasite, captive snakes without it, and wild snakes.

Gene sequencing measured microbe variety and mix in each group. Captivity and infection each can reshape a reptile's gut community, and separating their effects matters for breeding programs. Knowing the normal microbe profile helps keepers spot illness early and may guide release choices for captive-bred snakes.
plos-pone-0350924:
Hai Huang and co-authors built a way to score how much cultural value a heritage building holds, working in Longxing Ancient Town in Chongqing, China. Conservation teams often argue about value without a shared yardstick. The team reviewed two decades of writing on cultural value, then interviewed shop owners and visitors in the town and convened heritage experts to shape the criteria.

The finished scale sorts value into five kinds: local, historic, sustainable, scientific, and aesthetic, with twenty-four finer measures beneath them, weighted by a structured ranking method. Because owners, visitors, and experts all fed into it, the scale reflects how a town actually experiences its old buildings, not only how specialists do. Other historic towns could adapt the same scaffold when deciding which buildings to protect first and why.
plos-pone-0351124:
Rudy Brogi and colleagues asked whether the ways scientists catch wild chamois quietly filter which animals get studied. If bold animals walk into nets more easily, behavior research built on caught animals would lean bold. The team compared two methods, drug darts and drop nets, in an Alpine herd, then watched twenty-five tagged adults alongside untagged herd mates.

Key behaviors like eating, standing, and resting proved consistent within each animal, so they could fairly test for bias. Neither capture method ended up over-sampling the risk-takers: shy and bold chamois alike turned up in the caught group. That all-clear matters because personality studies across wildlife rest on the assumption that traps do not pick personalities. At least for this large herbivore and these two methods, the assumption held.
plos-pone-0351224:
Cecilia Camacho-Hubner and seven colleagues survey doctors across Latin America about a stealthy heart disease. Their 2026 study concerns transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy, where misfolded protein stiffens the heart. The disease is progressive, fatal, and badly under-recognised. Four hundred seventy physicians in eight countries answered questionnaires during 2023. They described their knowledge, attitudes, and the barriers they hit in diagnosis and treatment.

Knowledge was thin. Only about half the doctors understood the disease's basic mechanism. Patients reportedly consulted four or five physicians before anyone confirmed the diagnosis. Cardiologists carried most day-to-day management. Genetic testing for the transthyretin gene was available to barely a quarter of respondents. The key drug's cost and access blocked treatment often. Most local practice simply borrowed international guidelines. The authors map a fixable problem: train front-line doctors to suspect the disease sooner, and widen access to testing and therapy.
plos-pone-0351324:
Linking power grids flexibly lets regions share electricity and cuts waste, but planners must first forecast demand well. Xiaoyan Zhao and colleagues paired a hybrid forecasting network with a chaos-driven search method to design such links, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

The forecaster reads past load at several time scales, mixing pattern-spotting and memory layers. A new measure scores how well regions' demands complement each other hour by hour. The search algorithm then tunes the system's layout against balance, reliability, cost, and that complementarity score. Tests showed very small forecast errors, and the authors claim the combined approach designs cheaper, steadier interconnections.
plos-pone-0351424:
James Dickson Fiagborlo, Mexoese Nyatuame, and Stella Ahone Ntoko surveyed just over one thousand farm households across five areas of Ghanas Volta Region. Land wear harms soil and deepens rural poverty, yet uptake of better land care stays uneven. The survey asked how training and farm size shape what farmers would pay for such care, split by gender.

Training raised willingness to pay, and the effect ran stronger for men. Larger farms also paid more, since owners had more means to invest. Women started lower but gained fast when land access and training improved. Gaps thus look driven more by blocked access than by lack of interest. Fair training and land rights, the authors argue, are central to wider uptake.
plos-pone-0351624:
Justin Ofosu-Dankwa, Cristina Sisu, and Rhona Anderson examine the genomes of British nuclear test veterans in this 2026 study. These men served at Cold War nuclear test sites decades ago. Many worry the radiation left marks on their DNA. The team compared thirty veterans with thirty age-matched control veterans. Whole-genome data were processed with standard best-practice pipelines.

Somatic mutations, the small DNA changes gathered over a lifetime, were counted and classified. No variant type appeared more often in the test veterans. Tight mutation clusters, a suspected radiation fingerprint, were also no commoner. The dominant mutation signatures in both groups were the usual ones left by ageing itself. The null result cannot rule out every possible harm. Still, it offers these veterans evidence that their genomes carry no obvious excess burden.
plos-pone-0351724:
Rules against sexual harassment are clear on paper at a large Swedish university, yet Jack Palmieri, Frida Pilgaard, and Anette Agardh found daily norms tell another story. Their 2026 PLOS One study ran ten staff discussion groups, split by whether members managed others.

One theme covered everything: harassment is viewed through silence, power, and shifting boundaries. Staff described limits being negotiated on the spot, with women often checking with peers while men called the same behavior harmless. Prestigious senior researchers were seen as untouchable, and managers felt unsure how to act. Silence, many said, protected careers more than honesty would.
plos-pone-0351924:
Wonil Chung and Keonwoo Koo studied how GPT language models handle focus, the spotlight inside a sentence. Focus tells a listener which piece of news is at issue. The team used cut-off sentences with two possible completions. A question before the sentence set one spotlight. The small word only set another, placed before different items. Word-by-word surprise scores showed which ending each model expected.

The question's spotlight ruled in the first tests. It beat even a competing only. When only stood before the second object, the word-level spotlight grew stronger. It began to bend the expected endings its way. The models weigh the two cues in a graded tug-of-war, not by fixed rules. That matters wherever emphasis changes meaning in a text.
plos-pone-0352024:
Magreth Theophil, Ally Lyimo, and Joel Ambikile surveyed four hundred twenty-six adults on HIV treatment in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, asking whether their kidneys were being screened as guidelines advise. HIV and its medicines both strain kidneys, and catching damage early changes care. Records and questionnaires fed a search for what separates the screened from the missed.

Screening uptake was surprisingly high, about ninety-four percent. Patients with stronger immune counts were more likely screened, while those attending clinic only every six months were far less likely, an obvious contact effect. Oddly, patients who recalled a provider recommending screening had lower odds, a puzzle the authors flag rather than explain. In a system straining to follow its own guidelines, attendance rhythm, not distance or wealth, marked who slipped through.
plos-pone-0352124:
Zelan Wu and seven colleagues hunt for gene patterns linking inflammation, platelets, and heart failure. Their 2026 study merges bulk and single-cell gene data from human heart tissue. A protein pair called NEK7 and the NLRP3 inflammasome sits at the centre of their suspicion. Platelets, famous for clotting, also stoke inflammation. The team used network analysis and machine learning to find genes moving with both processes. A diagnostic scoring chart was drafted from the results.

Four genes formed the signature. All were turned up in failing human hearts. A mouse model of heart failure, driven by a hormone infusion, echoed the pattern for most of them. The signature also tracked with scarring genes, fitting the fibrosis story. The authors are explicit that this generates hypotheses, not proof. Still, a blood-or-tissue signature tying platelet activity to heart failure could eventually guide both diagnosis and anti-inflammatory treatment choices.
plos-pone-0352324:
Hong Nguyen-Thi and four colleagues tackle secure, energy-saving wireless design in a 2026 engineering study. Their setting is a future 6G network. Smart reflecting surfaces bounce signals to where they are needed. Several users share the same channel under a scheme called NOMA. A friendly jammer interferes with a hidden eavesdropper.

The goal is twofold: keep messages secret while wasting little energy, and treat the worst-off user fairly. The team trained a Double Deep Q-Network, a reinforcement learning method, to set power levels and surface angles. Its performance was compared with a standard learning method and with random settings. Simulations covered both shared-channel and separate-channel designs. The results highlight the shared design's edge in balancing secrecy against energy use.
plos-pone-0352424:
Shahab MohammadEbrahimi and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One spatial analysis of heart and circulation hospital admissions in Mashhad, Iran's second-largest city. More than fifty thousand admissions from 2016 to 2020 were mapped and tracked over time to find when and where the burden concentrates.

Admissions followed a repeating yearly rhythm and rose steadily until late 2019, when they dropped sharply. Men accounted for slightly more than half of cases, and the typical patient was in the mid-sixties. Mapping showed clear clustering: the city center formed a high-risk zone where admission risk ran many times higher than elsewhere. The authors say prevention and hospital resources should target that core, and offer the analysis as a template for other cities.
plos-pone-0353524:
Oronel and colleagues, in a 2026 animal study, trace how blocking a hormone system in newborn rats disturbs the growing kidney. Some adult diseases, including high blood pressure and kidney trouble, are now thought to start with early-life stress on development. The hormone endothelin helps kidneys form, and the team blocked its receptors during the first days of life.

Treated male pups showed more oxidative damage in the kidney and a worse balance between a protective gas, nitric oxide, and harmful oxygen radicals. Activity tied to nitric oxide fell in the very structures that become the kidney's filters. Female pups were partly protected, with differences in several protective enzymes and hormone signals. Cell growth and cell death also fell out of balance. The authors argue these early chemical shifts may be the first steps toward the adult kidney problems seen in earlier work.
plos-pone-0354124:
Dongmiao Zhang and colleagues present a protocol, published in 2026, for mapping which surface types of a dangerous newborn bacterium dominate around the world. The bacterium is a strain of E. coli that escapes the gut. It is a severe threat to newborns. Its O antigen, a variable coat component, is the leading candidate target for a protective vaccine. Yet nobody has charted its global variety in this age group.

The planned study will fuse two evidence streams. One is published serotype reports from four databases. The other is serotypes predicted from genome sequences in three public archives. Each strain's disease, site, year, and origin will be extracted. The verdict it seeks is strategic: one multivalent vaccine for the world, or regional recipes.
plos-pone-0354524:
Liu and colleagues, in a 2026 study, examine natural killer cells inside triple-negative breast cancer, an aggressive form that lacks the usual drug targets. These immune killer cells should attack tumors, but in this cancer they often arrive immature and weak. Using public single-cell data, the team sorted the killer cells found in tumor tissue into three subtypes.

One subtype, the strongest killer, was scarcer and weaker in triple-negative tumors than in other breast cancers. Its cells carried more of a brake receptor that switches them off. Signals from neighboring immune cells appeared to set that brake. A second subtype, marked by an alarm gene, was more active in these tumors, and high levels of that gene tracked with worse patient outcomes. The strong subtype's signature, by contrast, tracked with better outcomes. The authors say releasing the brake on killer cells is a concrete target for new treatments.
plos-pone-0354724:
Kelsey Thompson led a team of six authors on this 2026 focus group study of clinicians who treat children with pediatric feeding disorder. In this condition, eating breaks down for medical, nutritional, skill, or emotional reasons. Twenty-five providers in seven groups described their training and daily work across all four areas of the condition.

Training varied wildly between professions, clinics lacked easy access to specialist backup, and everyone wanted fuller yet workable care that honors family views. Thompson calls for earlier teaching, mentorship, and ready evidence-based resources to lift patient care.
plos-pone-0354824:
Gökşen Polat and four colleagues published this 2026 interview study in Türkiye of people whose chronic diseases leave them disabled. Twelve adults holding official disability reports described their daily limits and what they expect from disability services. Recruitment ran through clinics and personal referrals during 2024.

Disability spilled into social, cultural, school, and work life. Although services are a legal entitlement, many participants barely knew what existed or could not reach it. Polat argues the gap is informational and structural, and that fixing awareness and access matters as much as passing laws.
plos-pone-0354924:
Kaiyue Du and colleagues built lifestyle-based risk models for keratoconus, a disease that thins and bulges the cornea. They used records from 711 patients at a Chinese eye center, 275 of them with the disease. Their 2026 study combined standard regression with seven machine learning models. The models were fed demographic and habit data. The team then asked the models to explain which factors mattered most.

Seven risk factors stood out. They included male sex, higher body mass, and less schooling. A more distant childhood home and allergic conjunctivitis counted too. Above all stood rubbing the eyes, harder and more often. The best model sorted patients with fair accuracy. Because eye rubbing is changeable, the authors see a practical opening. Flag high-risk patients early, and coach the habit away before corneas deform.
plos-pone-0355124:
Rogers Kamulegeya and seven colleagues systematically review artificial intelligence models that predict whether tuberculosis treatment will fail, in this 2026 meta-analysis. Failure fuels transmission and drug resistance, so early warning matters. Searching two major databases for a quarter-century of work, they gathered thirty-four studies, most published since 2019, and pooled the accuracy of nineteen of them covering over one hundred thousand patients.

The pooled discrimination looked promising, but the ground beneath it was shaky. Results varied enormously between studies, models performed notably worse in groups including people with HIV, and only a quarter of studies had validated their model on outside data. Just one study earned a low overall risk-of-bias rating, and the analysis detected signs of publication bias. The authors conclude these tools are not ready for routine care and prioritize rigorous external validation in high-burden settings.
plos-pone-0355224:
Rafael Borges and three colleagues examine whether who you have worked alongside predicts reaching ministerial office in Portugal, in this 2026 network study. They scraped the membership of Portuguese governments and parliament over a decade, plus officials' interest registers, and built a network linking people who shared institutional venues. Then they asked whether network position, computed before the fact, screened out future ministers better than chance or a simple career-ladder rule.

It did. Their centrality-based screen caught over half of the in-network ministerial appointments, far above the baselines. Ministers also showed systematically higher institutional reach than colleagues who never made cabinet, with the sharpest gap inside party structures, where ministers scored about double on one key centrality measure. The authors are careful to call the work exploratory, but it suggests appointments flow through relational position, not just résumés.
plos-pone-0355724:
Mirjana Grdinić-Rakonjac and Vladimir Pajković survey more than thirteen hundred licensed drivers in a developing country, in this 2026 case study. They asked about four risky behaviors: speeding, drunk driving, seatbelt use, and phone use. Because crash deaths fall hardest on poorer countries, and because habits differ by road type, they compared men and women separately on high-speed, regional, and urban roads, adjusting for age and experience.

Men were generally more prone to speeding and drinking and driving. Yet women reported significantly more extreme speeding, far over the limit, on high-speed roads, a reversal of the usual pattern, while also buckling up more reliably on regional and urban roads. Both sexes texted and used social media behind the wheel at similar rates, and overall risk awareness was higher than the authors expected. They recommend campaigns aimed at men in cities and at speed among women on fast roads.
plos-pone-0356524:
Pooja Panth and three colleagues studied cancer patients at Bhaktapur Cancer Hospital in Nepal, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. How patients view their illness shapes how they cope, seek care, and keep going through treatment. Panth's cross-sectional study linked those views to resilience, the capacity to bounce back under strain.

The team surveyed patients and compared illness views with measures of resilience. Some beliefs track with stronger coping, while others track with despair. Knowing which views help lets counselors support the beliefs that sustain patients, and gently challenge those that drag them down. In a setting with few support services, that guidance helps staff focus scarce time where it lifts patients most.
plos-pone-0356624:
Alexandra N Sheldon and colleagues reviewed 173 infected artificial joints treated at one center over nearly a decade. All were treated with a joint-saving operation. Surgeons cleaned the implant and kept it rather than replacing it. The team asked which germs doom that approach. Their 2026 retrospective study graded success as lasting eradication without further surgery. It tested fungal, resistant, mixed, and culture-negative infections against the odds.

Two thirds of cases were cured. Fungal infections almost always failed, carrying heavier illness burdens besides. Infections where no germ could be grown were nearly four times likelier to clear. That is a hopeful sign for a frustrating category. Resistant and common skin bacteria also dragged success down. The authors suggest microbe identity should steer the choice between saving and replacing a joint.
plos-pone-0357124:
John Adeleke used Nigeria's 2024 national health survey to ask whether household wealth protects children equally against two kinds of undernutrition. One is stunting, the slow height loss of chronic deprivation. The other is wasting, the rapid weight loss of acute shortage. His 2026 analysis covered more than nine thousand children. It adjusted step by step for other social and geographic factors.

Wealth showed a clear graded link with stunting. Each step up the wealth ladder came with less of it. For wasting, wealth showed no link at all. Adeleke reads the split through one idea. Money buys protection against slow, cumulative harms more readily than against sudden illness or food shocks. Programs fighting wasting, he argues, need tools beyond poverty relief.
plos-pone-0357824: Agrawal and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on sleep apnea using electronic health records. Obstructive sleep apnea makes breathing stop and start during sleep, and it is tied to stroke risk. The team measured how common it is, split by age and sex, along with related conditions. The data set was large and cross-sectional. Clear rates help clinics plan screening for a disorder often missed.
plos-pone-0358224:
Quan Pham Hong leads a team of five designing a neural network that listens for damage in structures, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Bridges and towers betray cracks through subtle changes in how they shake. The warning signs are brief blips in narrow frequency bands. Models that read only the time signal miss the frequency story; models that transform the whole signal lose track of when each frequency occurred. Their network, SpectralTCN, is built to keep both.

Inside each layer of a temporal convolutional network sits a wavelet gating module. It splits the signal into sub bands that correspond to vibration modes. The network then decides how much of each band to keep. Then it rebuilds the signal before moving on. Because wavelets preserve timing and frequency together, a short damage signature keeps its moment and its pitch. The design targets inspection of structures that cannot afford missed hints.
plos-pone-0358424:
Mohamad Kazem Dehghani, Reza Ghasemi-Fasaei, Sajjad Abbasi, and Amin Mojiri wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on plants and pollution. Working with spinach grown in water rather than soil, they study nanoplastics sprayed on leaves. The question is how these tiny plastic particles change the plant's handling of cadmium, a toxic metal.

The responses depend on both time and concentration, so the authors track uptake and the metal's movement from root to shoot under different doses. Cadmium in leafy vegetables is a food safety concern, and plastic particles are now common on farms. Plant scientists and food regulators share an interest in how these two pollutants interact.
plos-pone-0359224:
Sivarama Prasad Tera and five colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It presents an explainable AI framework for detecting cancer from skin lesion images. Explainable means the system shows its reasoning, not just a verdict, which doctors rightly demand before trusting software with diagnosis.

Skin cancer caught early is usually curable, so faster and more reliable screening saves lives. An imaging framework that explains itself can also teach, showing trainees which features drove a decision. Dermatologists and medical imaging researchers are the readers weighing whether this framework is ready to support real clinics.
plos-pone-0359424:
Darío López-Delgado and eight colleagues published this protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026. It plans a review that will gather studies systematically and pool them in a meta-analysis, on infections passed through sex, among women who are pregnant and who are migrants or refugees. Pregnancy plus displacement is a double vulnerability, and infections in pregnancy endanger both mother and child.

The review will gather prevalence figures, how common these infections are in this group, from studies worldwide. Migrant and refugee women often fall outside routine screening systems, so pooled prevalence can expose a hidden burden. Maternal health services designing outreach for displaced women are the audience waiting for this synthesis.
plos-pone-0359524: The PLOS One Staff published a 2026 correction notice in PLOS ONE. It amends an earlier scoping review about coach learning in youth participation sport. A correction keeps the public record straight when a detail in a published paper was wrong. Readers who cited the review can now check what changed. Notices like this are a small but real part of how science fixes its own record.
plos-pone-0359624:
Naim Gheymoumi and four colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies experimental allergic rhinitis, the laboratory version of hay fever's nasal inflammation. The treatment candidate is kynurenic acid, a natural compound made from the amino acid tryptophan, tested for whether it attenuates, or eases, the allergic response.

The authors tie the effect to the AhR receptor, a pathway that keeps immune activity in the nose in balance. A natural compound that calms nasal allergy through this pathway interests drug developers seeking gentler options than steroids. Allergy researchers are the core readers.
pmc-11168924:
Abramson, Adler, Dunger, and co-authors introduce AlphaFold 3, a model that predicts how biological molecules fit together. AlphaFold 2 had already changed the field by predicting protein shapes with high accuracy. Many teams then used it to model proteins and design new ones.

AlphaFold 3 extends that power from single proteins to interactions between molecules. It uses a substantially updated design built around a diffusion approach, the same broad family used in image tools. Predicting how drugs and other molecules bind their targets could speed drug discovery and deepen basic biology at once.
pmc-13191824:
Masaki Shinohara is first author on a 2026 case report of kidney surgery in a child with OHVIRA syndrome. OHVIRA is a rare birth condition. It combines a blocked half-vagina with a kidney anomaly on the same side. Some variant cases have a tiny, poorly formed kidney draining into the vagina, causing constant urine leakage, so removing the kidney is required.

At age five, doctors found the misplaced urine tube opening by vaginal scope and threaded a fluorescent catheter, a glowing tube, backward through it. During keyhole surgery, the glow reliably showed the tube and the small kidney remnant, guiding safe removal. The authors present the technique as feasible and useful for selected children with this condition.
pmc-13195024:
Leticia Gondim Souto is first author on a 2026 veterinary study of platelet counts as a prognostic sign in dogs with cancer. Thrombocytosis means an abnormally high platelet count, and platelets are known to aid cancer progression. In human oncology it marks poor outlook, but its meaning in dogs was little explored.

The authors reviewed one hundred and sixty-six dogs with malignant tumors and high platelet counts. Dogs with moderate-to-severe elevation survived significantly less long than mildly elevated dogs. In mammary carcinoma, higher elevation more than tripled the risk of death, and a similar trend appeared in mast cell tumors. Prospective studies with larger groups are needed, the authors say, to confirm platelet count as a useful marker.
pmc-13195224:
Yunnan Zhang is first author on a 2026 safety analysis of statin use alongside breast cancer treatment. More breast cancer patients now take statins, cholesterol-lowering drugs, during therapy, yet safety data are sparse. The authors mined the United States Food and Drug Administration adverse event reporting system, covering two decades of reports.

Of nearly two hundred and thirty-eight thousand breast cancer related reports, over eight thousand involved statin co-use. Reporting signals ran lower for liver and blood disorders among statin users, but higher for skin, psychiatric, kidney, muscle, and several other categories. Such reporting patterns cannot prove cause, the authors note, but they argue for individualized monitoring and deeper study of the pathways involved.
pmc-13200324:
Chikara Nakagami and colleagues present a 2026 case report on a rare fatty tumor near a past surgery site. A myelolipoma mixes mature fat with blood-forming tissue. It usually grows on the adrenal glands above the kidneys, so one in the belly wall is extremely uncommon.

Their patient was a 62-year-old man who had chest surgery for a thymus tumor at age thirty-nine, using a breastbone-lifting device. Decades later, a scan for another reason found a slowly growing mass by that device site, in front of the belly lining. Scans showed fat inside, raising worry of a cancerous fatty tumor. Full removal proved it benign. The authors add this tumor to the list for fat masses at old surgical sites.
pmc-13200624:
Li-min Wang and colleagues review cardiac mast cells in heart disease in a 2026 article. Mast cells are immune cells that release inflammatory signals. In the heart they help keep tissue balance but also drive swelling, scarring, and remodeling after injury, with roles that can flip by context.

The review traces where heart mast cells come from and where they sit in cardiac tissue. It covers their part in calming inflammation and reshaping tissue after damage. Animal work suggests they act much like other inflammatory cells, directly and indirectly. Their dual roles could cut both ways in disease. The authors map open questions and possible clinical uses for targeting these cells.
pmc-13200924:
Wenjun Liu and colleagues propose a finer fluid metric for children on continuous kidney therapy in a 2026 study. CRRT slowly cleans blood and removes fluid in critically ill children. The usual removal rate ignores each child's starting overload, so the team coined a clearance percentage: balance removed as a share of the initial overload.

They reviewed 432 children treated at one center from 2012 to 2023. Non-survivors got higher removal rates yet cleared no more overload than survivors. Body weight drove the removal rate strongly. The new percentage barely tracked illness severity or starting overload, making it a cleaner progress gauge. Their three-part framework pairs prescription, safety, and clearance for daily care.
pmc-13201324:
How many operations a surgeon needs before robotic hernia repair becomes routine is the question behind a 2026 scoping review by Francesco Brucchi. The review gathers studies that used cumulative sum analysis, a statistical method for spotting when performance stabilizes, during robotic repair of groin hernias.

Brucchi and colleagues searched five databases and found seven studies covering eight learning curves and 1,361 patients. The point where operating time leveled off ranged widely, from 12 to 138 procedures across the included studies. The authors estimate stabilization after roughly 25 to 35 procedures in structured training, while stressing that the evidence is weak and not a credentialing standard.
pmc-13202524:
Turning a biomass byproduct into a valuable chemical without solvents is the goal of a 2026 catalysis study led by Margi Joshi. The research article anchors a tungsten-rich cluster compound onto zeolite HY and uses it to oxidize levulinic acid into succinic acid with hydrogen peroxide.

The catalyst achieved complete selectivity toward succinic acid at a moderate yield, which the authors present as a first for this reaction setup. Careful tuning of reaction conditions and scavenger experiments revealed a controlled radical pathway that cleaves the target bond while suppressing over-oxidation. The material kept working through four reuse cycles, offering a blueprint for sustainable production of dicarboxylic acids from biomass.
pmc-13215524:
Abdulsalam Al-Shami and co-authors report a 2026 cross-sectional study of blood ferritin levels in Yemeni patients with sickle cell anemia. High ferritin can signal iron overload from repeated transfusions, although inflammation can also push the level up.

The study enrolled 80 patients aged fifteen and older at a clinic in Sana'a between June and December 2024. About 85 percent had ferritin above the threshold used for concern, with a median value of 1,645 nanograms per millilitre. Ferritin rose alongside white blood cell counts, which hints at an inflammation link, while background factors such as age and sex showed no association. The authors back routine screening and want follow-up work with transfusion histories.
pmc-13219524:
Lorenz Thurner and colleagues link severe COVID-19 to autoantibodies against two of the body's inflammation brakes in a 2026 study. Some patients' immune systems attack their own proteins, and this work concerns interleukin-1 receptor antagonist and progranulin, blockers of two strong inflammatory signals. When antibodies block those blockers, inflammation can run free.

The autoantibodies appeared with chemically altered, hyperphosphorylated versions of the two proteins, formed complexes with them, lowered their levels in blood, and left the inflammatory signals they usually restrain more active. Using custom antibody fragments, the team tracked the altered proteins and the autoantibodies across a German pandemic cohort. Most positive patients carried both autoantibodies; levels peaked early and faded over twelve months, and the altered proteins disappeared first. Seropositivity tracked with hyperinflammation. Inflammatory signals themselves could force the alteration in blood cells, but at doses up to a thousand times higher than in cells from positive survivors.
pmc-13219924:
Areez Shafqat and colleagues examine how the drug decitabine rewires two different breast cancer cell lines in a 2026 study. Decitabine blocks the enzymes laying down methylation, the marks that silence genes, and cancers carry different marking patterns by subtype. Whether effects follow the subtype, or march to one drum, matters for how it is tested in patients.

Using a dataset, the team compared treated and untreated T-47D, a luminal line, with JIMT-1, a HER2 line resistant to trastuzumab. Decitabine stripped methylation from twelve hundred sites in JIMT-1 and over nineteen hundred in T-47D, switching on hundreds of genes in each. The activated programs diverged, though: immune signaling in one, matrix and collagen pathways in the other. One gene rose while its promoter gained methylation, defying the rulebook. It disturbed the sites used by epigenetic clocks. Survival analyses in cohorts tied 100-plus genes to outcomes in hormone-positive disease.
pmc-13221124:
Chuwen Dou and colleagues map world research on simplifying medication regimens in a 2026 bibliometric analysis. Simpler schedules can cut treatment burden for people juggling many drugs. The team charted 468 publications from 2005 through 2025 in a major citation database, tracking who publishes, where, and on what themes.

Output rose over time, led by the United States, with Monash University the most productive institution. Collaboration clustered in a few networks linking North America and Europe. Topics moved from HIV treatment and adherence toward diabetes, heart failure, and long-term care. The map shows a growing field that still needs wider cooperation and clearer priorities.
pmc-13221424:
Karolina Weiner-Gorzel, Lynda McSorley, and Janice M Walshe review unanswered fertility questions in modern breast cancer care, in a 2026 opinion piece. Survival for younger patients keeps improving, yet worries about fertility and pregnancy safety can lead some to refuse or stop treatment. The authors argue counseling belongs in planning from diagnosis onward.

Chemotherapy remains the main threat to ovarian function, and temporary ovarian suppression deserves routine consideration. Hormone therapy does not permanently damage ovaries, though its long course needs personal pregnancy planning. For newer drug classes, human fertility data are largely absent, so the authors urge caution, preservation before treatment, and honest discussion of uncertainty.
pmc-13223624:
Faith Magut and co-authors test whether community health fairs lowered deaths in rural KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, in a 2026 longitudinal cohort study. The Vukuzazi program screened residents aged fifteen and older for HIV, tuberculosis, hypertension, and diabetes between 2018 and 2020, with referrals into care. Half of eligible residents attended, and deaths were tracked through household surveillance for a median of four years.

Attendance was associated with a twenty-five percent lower hazard of death from any cause, about a one and a half point absolute reduction over five years. Clinic visits rose briefly among attenders after the fairs but not among non-attenders. Linking screening days to ongoing primary care may explain the survival edge.
pmc-13224724:
Xin Yin and colleagues report a 2026 study of virus-based therapy against carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae, a hospital bacterium that shrugs off last-resort antibiotics. Bacteriophages, viruses that kill bacteria, were collected in steps, each round targeting bacteria that survived the previous virus. Three phages from different families formed a cocktail that held bacterial growth down for fifteen hours.

Each virus attacked a different doorway on the cell surface, which explains the teamwork. Bacteria escaping the first phage deleted a large chunk of their sugary coat, and that loss exposed new targets for the others. One phage even killed several unrelated gut bacteria once their coats were gone, a pattern the authors call closing one door while opening another.
pmc-13227224:
Areesha Moiz and co-authors write a 2026 clinical guide to the gains and harms of GLP-1 receptor agonists. These drugs are now widely prescribed for diabetes, obesity, and a growing list of metabolic and kidney-heart conditions. Prescribing increasingly reaches younger and healthier people, where the benefit-risk balance differs from the original trial populations. The guide organises evidence on how the drugs work, who they suit, and what to watch.

Gut side effects receive special attention, with an algorithm for managing early symptoms before patients abandon treatment. Communication strategies aim to support shared decisions, cut stigma around weight treatment, and match therapy to each patient's goals. The authors frame the result as structured, patient-centred guidance for a fast-evolving drug family.
pmc-13229324: The publisher issued a 2026 correction for a study of bird diversity and West Nile virus spread by Culex mosquitoes in Emilia-Romagna, Italy. The notice is a correction only. It states that the author affiliations in the original article were wrong. It then prints the corrected list for the ten authors. Their institutions span London, Brescia, Bologna, Oxford, and Trento. No data, analysis, or conclusions are changed. The publisher apologises for the error.
pmc-13229924:
Majd Abouassi and colleagues trace in 2026 eleven years of repeated spine failure in a sixty-two-year-old woman after lumbar fusion. Her first operation joined three lower back levels for narrowing and instability in 2014. Over time the levels next to the fusion wore out, hardware failed, and bones fractured as deformity grew.

Each setback led to another revision that extended the rods higher, finally reaching the neck area. Surgeons used multi-rod builds, pelvic fixation, and scan-guided screws, yet mechanical failure kept returning. Her last crisis was an unstable chest spine fracture that threatened the spinal cord and needed urgent replacement of a vertebral body. Careful patient choice, bone health, and long follow-up are urged for long fusions.
pmc-13232924:
Jonathan D Mathers and co-authors published a 2026 case report about a breathing emergency during anesthesia in a patient who had earlier weight-loss surgery. The operation, called one anastomosis mini gastric bypass, reshapes the stomach with a single join. A known side effect is bile flowing back into the new stomach pouch.

The patient was being put under anesthesia for planned gallbladder surgery when bile-rich stomach contents entered the lungs, a severe event called pulmonary aspiration. The authors warn that earlier bypass surgery of this type raises aspiration risk in ways standard airway routines may miss. They propose that anesthesia guidelines account for this history when planning how patients are put to sleep.
pmc-13233224:
Jing Yang and colleagues published a 2026 lab study on how the yeast Candida albicans forms biofilms and resists the antifungal drug itraconazole. Biofilms, dense mats of microbes on surfaces, make infections hard to clear. The team compared normal yeast with strains missing the STP1 or MRR2 genes, plus drug-sensitive and drug-resistant strains, measuring growth, gene action, and autophagy, the cell's recycling system.

Resistant strains built stronger biofilms than sensitive ones. Deleting STP1 boosted biofilm growth, while deleting MRR2 weakened it. Autophagy genes switched on in biofilms and resistant strains but fell quiet in both deletion strains. A drug that triggers autophagy raised activity of the SAP2 gene in normal cells only. The findings tie both genes to resistance through the recycling pathway.
pmc-13234324:
Shaoyi Jiang and co-authors reported in 2026 on bacteria that learn to live by recycling the remains of dead cells. The material, called necromass, can feed later generations when food is scarce. Their question was whether better recycling also helps a whole closed microbial system last longer. Escherichia coli bacteria were kept for sixty days in sealed, nutrient-free salt solution.

Adapted bacteria grew better on several carbon sources, moved less, and formed more biofilm, with patterns shaped by spatial layout. The adapted strains were then paired with a green alga in closed biospheres. Under uneven spatial conditions, those systems lasted about a quarter less time than systems with non-adapted bacteria. The result warns that efficient recycling in one species can weaken wider system persistence.
pmc-13234624:
Jason Fanning and colleagues set out in 2026 the design of a trial testing a remote activity program for older adults with joint pain. Participants will have obesity plus chronic knee or hip osteoarthritis, a leading cause of pain in later life. The program works through group support delivered at a distance. It targets eating habits, daily activity, and time spent sitting.

Two hundred low-active adults will be assigned randomly to the program or to enhanced usual care. Everyone receives the same self-monitoring devices so device effects do not confuse the comparison. Daily step count is the main outcome after six months of intervention. Pain interference, weight, and physical function serve as further outcomes. Follow-up extends twelve months beyond the program to test lasting behaviour change and pathways of benefit.
pmc-13234824: Overgaard and colleagues introduce an editorial series on writing scientific articles better. The series targets two linked faults: weak reporting, where key details go missing, and weak method, where the study itself is loosely built. Its stated themes run from transparency and proper presentation to quality improvement and fair peer review. A well-reported study, the editors argue, can be repeated, judged, and used; a poorly reported one cannot, however good its data. The series aims to cut review rounds and raise the share of papers fit to guide practice.
pmc-13235224:
Mohamed Ali Ag Ahmed and co-authors interviewed in 2026 leaders about why drugs fail to reach conflict-hit parts of Mali reliably. Twenty-eight interviews gathered views from health workers, community groups, officials, and aid actors around Mopti and Bamako. Talks were coded by theme with software support. Conflict has disrupted medicine supply across the Sahel for more than a decade.

Four linked problem themes emerged from what people described to the team. Insecurity breaks transport routes and supply chains across the hit areas. Market breakdown drives price swings and repeated gaps of vital products. Weak storage and logistics infrastructure puts medicine quality at risk during distribution. Poor teamwork among public, private, and aid actors deepens every other problem. The authors urge joint teamwork, funding in logistics and information systems, and stronger rules during and after conflict.
pmc-13235324:
Sebastian Lehmann and co-authors checked in 2026 whether skull openings planned in virtual reality match what surgeons actually perform. Eighty-three patients had meningioma surgery planned with interactive headsets from two makers. The planned opening was compared with the real one for position, relative size, and number of drill holes. Meningiomas are common brain tumours where precise opening placement shapes the whole operation.

Average size measures differed only slightly between plan and reality in both directions measured. Drill hole counts changed in under a tenth of the operations performed. Hole position changed in only a small handful of cases in the series. Statistical equivalence tests supported the closeness of planned and real openings. Overall geometric deviation stayed under six percent between the two. The authors say interactive planning transfers faithfully to the operating room.
pmc-13235524:
Tianyi Zhao and co-authors measured in 2026 how efficiently suburban villages near Nanjing use their output, living, and ecological spaces. Rapid urbanization has left many such areas with wasteful, unbalanced land use. An efficiency method compared inputs and outputs across townships over a decade. Geographic mapping, inequality decomposition, and a triangular balance model added views of pattern and teamwork.

Average efficiency across the three space types rose by nearly half between 2011 and 2021. Seventeen townships moved from gap toward teamwork during that decade in the analysis. About half of townships reached at least a basic level of teamwork by the end. Nine townships achieved high-quality teamwork among output, living, and ecological uses. The authors offer their framework to sharpen rural governance and support sustainable countryside development in fast-growing metropolitan regions.
pmc-13236524:
Yohei Tateishi and colleagues built in 2026 a score to spot a specific stroke cause before clot-removal surgery. Some large vessel blockages arise from fatty narrowing inside the skull rather than travelling clots, and they behave differently during the procedure. Records for more than three hundred thrombectomy patients with brain magnetic resonance imaging were analysed retrospectively. Imaging signs and clinical features were ranked, then combined into a point score.

Four features independently pointed to the narrowing-related cause in the final model. Absence of an irregular heartbeat rhythm carried the strongest weight among them. Multiple infarcts in border zones and mixed-age lesions also raised the score in the system. A missing clot sign on a sensitive scan sequence added further points toward the diagnosis. The score separated the two causes with high accuracy in internal validation checks.
pmc-13236924:
Yun Zhang and Tinglei Liu surveyed 1,533 vocational undergraduates at eight universities in China's Hebei Province for a 2026 study of why students stay silent in class. The survey measured how much support students felt from teachers, their confidence about speaking, their speaking anxiety, and their tendency toward silence. A structural model traced paths among the four.

Teacher support showed no direct link to silence. Instead, supported students felt more confident about speaking, and that confidence, partly by easing anxiety, went with less silence. One small path through anxiety alone ran the other way. Because the data were collected once, the authors treat the paths as associations, not proof of cause. Confidence-building teaching is their practical suggestion.
pmc-13237224:
Vamsi and colleagues present HS-RankFormer, a model that rebuilds a full light spectrum from an ordinary colour photo. Hyperspectral images record dozens of narrow colour bands and reveal what eyes cannot see, but the cameras are costly. Rebuilding that data from a normal RGB image is hard: labelled examples are few, and models often fail on new scenes.

Their transformer-based model aims to be both efficient and sturdy across different settings. It tries to keep fine spatial detail while guessing each pixel's spectrum, without the heavy cost of earlier methods. Reliable reconstruction could put spectral imaging into farming, medicine, and inspection using cameras people already own.
pmc-13237424:
Chen and colleagues review how to steer crystal growth in antimony-based solar films. These chalcogenide materials are cheap and promising for thin-film solar cells. Their flaw is structural: their ribbon-like crystals conduct charge well along one direction and badly across it, so the way crystals lie in the film decides performance.

Crystals lying flat create slippery internal walls that block charge flow. Crystals standing upright, the team explains, form clean paths with friendly grain boundaries. The review gathers strategies to favour the upright growth, from seed layers to heat treatments. Mastering crystal direction could lift these films from laboratory promise to real panels.
pmc-13239324:
Shama Patel and a large working group argued in 2026 that artificial intelligence for global health must move from tech optimism to locally led, equity-centered rollout. Their narrative landscape review, joined with talks from a 2025 pre-conference session, surveyed AI across education, epidemiology, and clinical medicine, with data equity at the center. Benefits so far are unevenly shared and thinly tested in real settings.

Five must-dos structure their plan: oversight rules fitted to context, fair capacity building, careful rollout and cost research, open data stores, and community-centered ethical design. Without those shifts, they warn, AI will reinforce the very gaps it claims to solve. The piece asks who designs the tools, for whom, and under whose oversight, and refuses easy answers.
pmc-13239524:
Reem El Sherif and colleagues compare malpractice lawsuits against doctors trained in different countries in a 2026 Canadian cohort study. Using records from the national medical protective body, they asked whether international medical graduates face civil legal actions more often than peers trained in Canada or the United States.

The analysis covered nearly ninety-nine thousand physicians and thousands of cases across several years. Lawsuit rates per year of practice did not differ significantly between the groups. Raw outcomes slightly favoured patients suing internationally trained doctors, yet that gap vanished once other factors were taken into account. The authors conclude that place of training alone does not predict legal risk.
pmc-13240424:
Huishen Yan and Liang He single out a cell membrane pump gene as a survival marker in oesophageal cancer in a 2026 analysis. This cancer kills aggressively and lacks good molecular signposts, so the pair mined public tumour data for genes tied to mitochondrial stress that also track patient outcomes.

One gene, ATP1A1, survived the statistical selection and stood alone in predicting better survival when highly expressed. Tumours rich in the gene showed calmer profiles for invasion and spreading programmes, alongside distinctive immune cell mixes. Single-cell data placed the gene mainly in malignant surface cells but also in support and immune cells. Silencing it in laboratory cells changed behaviour and raised inflammatory gene activity.
pmc-13240924:
Ndengue's team in Douala tested how sample handling distorts breast cancer marker readings in a low-resource lab. One breast tumor from a 34-year-old woman supplied fifty tiny samples. Four cohorts varied the fixing recipe, fixing length, and delay before fixing. Estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and Ki67 were scored by staining.

Non-buffered formaldehyde shifted receptor shares slightly, yet Allred scores never changed. Fixing stayed sound up to 48 hours before values fell away. Cold delays hurt most: markers held for about two hours, then declined. The findings reassure labs that cannot always source buffered formalin.
pmc-13241524:
Tóth and Nagy at the Balaton Limnological Research Institute studied how city life affects common reed along Lake Balaton in Hungary. Reed beds dominate the shallow edges of the lake. Artificial light at night proved much stronger along the shore than over open water. The pair measured vegetative and reproductive traits across sites with different urban pressure.

Most growth traits showed no meaningful link to night lighting. Reproduction told another story: brighter shores held less reproductive biomass and fewer flowering plants. Reed growth also started later in the season at more urbanized sites. The authors argue that city influence acts as a selective filter, hitting reproduction and timing harder than bulk growth.
pmc-13241924:
Rishi Raj Sinha writes a 2026 letter questioning whether time to plasma exchange is the right focus in suspected thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. This rare blood disorder needs urgent plasma exchange, yet outcomes vary widely even with early treatment. Recent population data link timing to results in a curved, weak pattern.

Sinha argues that timing measured from admission misses delays inside the care pathway, such as diagnostic doubt, plasma supply, and coordination between teams. Disease severity at arrival also differs greatly, which muddies simple time targets. He suggests rapid risk scoring when confirmatory testing is unavailable. He also proposes a readiness bundle that readies diagnosis, plasma, and exchange services in parallel, like sepsis care bundles.
pmc-13242424:
Claire Munsie and colleagues evaluated a community exercise program built for teenagers and young adults who had finished cancer treatment. Their study appeared in Supportive Care in Cancer in 2026. Participants aged fifteen to twenty-seven joined twice-weekly group sessions for twelve weeks at a local facility. A trained exercise physiologist tailored aerobic, strength, and flexibility work to each person, and the team measured fitness and well-being before and after.

Of 127 starters, 93 finished the program and final testing. Aerobic fitness, leg and chest strength, and everyday physical function all improved, and lean mass rose while fat mass and fatigue fell. Quality of life improved across physical, role, and social domains, and no one was harmed by the training. Because the program ran in a community setting rather than a hospital, the authors see it as a model that survivorship services could copy widely.
pmc-13242824:
Xiaoshuang Chen and co-authors publish a 2026 multicenter study of an inflammation index as a prognostic marker in advanced liver cancer. Patients whose cancer progressed after first-line therapy received a three-part second-line combination. A simple blood-based immune-inflammation index was tested as a continuous measure rather than a cut-off.

Just under a hundred twenty patients were analyzed. Each step up in the transformed index carried higher risks of progression and death after adjustment for other factors. The pattern held across drug dose and immunotherapy subgroups. The index did not predict tumor shrinkage, yet it did flag higher risk of severe side effects. The authors propose it as a cheap risk-stratification aid alongside liver and tumor measures.
pmc-13245424:
Miyazawa and co-authors investigated a patterned pufferfish's origins in this 2026 PeerJ study. Mushifugu, a poisonous pufferfish found only around Japan, wears a striking labyrinth pattern unlike its plain or spotted relatives. Biologists had speculated it might be a hybrid, since blending two spotted patterns can produce labyrinth designs. The team compared its DNA with its closest spotted relative, komonfugu, across both coasts of Japan.

Mitochondrial DNA split mushifugu into two regional groups, one in the Sea of Japan and one in the Pacific, with the Pacific group linking toward the relative. Genome-wide markers, though, showed little split between the two mushifugu populations and a clean separation from komonfugu. The authors use demographic modeling to weigh the hybrid story, treating the fish as its own lineage whose pattern demands explanation beyond simple mixing.
pmc-13246624:
Shaked Farbstein-Yavin and co-authors follow behavioral addictions in young people across the COVID-19 years in a 2026 study. Gambling, shopping, exercise, and eating can all turn compulsive in youth. The pandemic broke routines and raised strain, which may have fed such patterns.

The team surveyed 1,665 Israeli students aged 9 to about 17 at three points from 2019 to 2022. Exercise, gambling, and shopping symptoms climbed across the waves, while eating symptoms held flat. Dark mood, mental symptoms, and thrill seeking predicted higher symptom levels. Hope, life satisfaction, and secure attachment linked to fewer symptoms, mostly by easing distress. Support from others showed a surprising tie to more symptoms for some habits.
pmc-13247224:
Sun, Zhou, Huang, and co-authors describe a camouflage trick for delivering messenger RNA to the lungs, in this 2026 letter in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy. Inhaled mRNA vaccines could raise immunity right where respiratory viruses enter, but the lung's mucosal barrier blocks the lipid nanoparticles that carry mRNA, and none has finished clinical trials. The team borrowed a component of the lung's own surfactant, the soapy film lining the air sacs.

Swapping the particles' helper lipid for DPPC, surfactant's main lipid, let the particles bind a lung protein that normally recycles surfactant. That binding kept them in the mucosal layer longer and ferried them into and across airway cells. In their tests an inhaled vaccine built this way provoked stronger lung immunity, and the trick also boosted other approved particle designs.
pmc-13248324:
Zhao and co-authors looked for better predictors of cancer drug response in this 2026 Biomarker Research letter. Their patients had advanced esophageal squamous cell carcinoma treated first with immune therapy plus chemotherapy. The usual marker, PD-L1, alone predicts benefit poorly, so the team stained pretreatment biopsies for several immune cell types.

In one hundred forty-seven patients, high PD-L1 pointed to longer time before the cancer grew. Yet dense PD-1 positive killer T cells pointed the other way, toward shorter control. Combining both markers separated patients sharply, from under four months to nearly nine. The authors propose the pair as a practical guide for treatment choices.
pmc-13249124:
Miller and a U.S. team describe a trial protocol aimed at caregivers who sit too much, published in 2026. Caring for a relative with Alzheimer's disease raises a caregiver's own health risks, and long sitting is part of that load. The twelve-week trial sends text messages built on four behavior change techniques, including goal setting, planning, prompts, and self-monitoring.

The goal is a habit: four hourly walks a day, each adding a modest burst of steps, held for a week straight. Wrist trackers record movement passively while surveys probe whether the walking becomes automatic. Forty percent of the planned sample had enrolled by August 2025, with data collection expected to finish in mid 2026.
pmc-13250224:
Beauchamp and co-authors lay out a trial testing whether activity-based coaching can prevent depression after stroke. Their 2026 BMJ Open protocol targets low-income adults aged fifty-five and older, within three months of a stroke. Poststroke depression affects about a third of survivors and worsens recovery, yet no standard prevention approach exists.

Three hundred fifty volunteers with mild symptoms will be assigned to phone-delivered behavioral activation or to usual care. Trained community health workers will run an orientation, five weekly sessions, and two monthly booster calls. Depression scores over nine months form the main outcome, with anxiety, quality of life, and hospital visits also tracked. The team will share deidentified data and code through a national archive.
pmc-13250324:
Mohmmed Margni and co-authors set out a technique paper in 2026 on treating painful knee arthritis from inside the blood vessels. Blocking overgrown small arteries around the knee can ease pain, and the entry point is usually the groin artery.

Drawing on more than ten years of practice, the team instead enters through a foot artery, checking it first with ultrasound. Guided by live X-ray pictures, they steer a fine catheter into the knee branches using a no-wire method, then reduce the excess blood flow while keeping normal flow. They report faster walking after the procedure, plus lower radiation and dye use, making foot entry a practical option.
