pmc-13250724: Feyza Nur Topcu Yenercag, Sule Ozturk, and Gunay Kaya Tarhan published this 2026 correction to their study of premarital spinal muscular atrophy screening in northern Türkiye. The notice is a correction only: it replaces the article's ethics statement with a fuller version. The corrected text names the Samsun University ethics board decision. It adds a second approval from the Samsun Provincial Health Directorate dated July 2024, and confirms that the records review rested on earlier written consent. No findings, data, or conclusions of the study change.
pmc-13251524:
Vlasov and Manley review enhancer RNAs, short-lived transcripts copied from the genome's enhancer switches. Their 2026 RNA Biology paper sorts what these RNAs do and how they blur the line between coding and non-coding RNA. Enhancer RNAs are usually destroyed quickly, yet several roles in switching genes on have been proposed.

The review covers current models of enhancer RNA function and the discoveries behind them. It highlights a surprise: some enhancer RNAs contain readable protein recipes, and a few are actually translated. Proteins from supposedly non-coding transcripts tend to be small and may carry their own jobs. The authors argue these findings reshape thinking about how both enhancer RNAs and ordinary messenger RNAs evolved.
pmc-13253424:
Dongmei Gou, Maomei He, and Jiaquan Zhuo test an acupoint injection for chronic heart failure in a 2026 randomized, double-blind trial. The treatment injects astragalus extract, a traditional herbal preparation, into the Neiguan point on the forearm, which Chinese medicine links to heart function. The trial enrolled patients whose heart failure matched the qi-deficiency and blood-stasis pattern in that diagnostic system.

Two hundred patients received standard therapy plus either the real injection or a placebo, one hundred per group. After treatment, the injection group showed better symptom scores, lower levels of the heart strain marker BNP, and stronger pumping function. They also walked farther in six minutes and reported better quality of life. Readmissions did not differ, and no adverse events occurred in either arm. The authors conclude the add-on is safe and helpful for this patient pattern.
pmc-13253924:
Francesca Alfieri and many colleagues test an AI model that warns of kidney injury in a 2026 study. Acute kidney injury is a sudden loss of kidney function common in intensive care. Their model gives hourly risk scores for moderate and severe injury, and was upgraded to cope with missing data.

Past records covered 70,107 ICU admissions in three countries across 176 units, with strong scores above 0.89 on a key accuracy measure. A live test in three European hospitals with 329 patients scored from 0.82 to 0.96. Warnings came about 14 hours early on average, which the authors say could aid care.
pmc-13254424:
Xiaobin Tang and co-authors run a pilot study of facial microbes in rosacea in a 2026 paper. Rosacea is a chronic facial skin disease with redness and bumps. Skin samples from six patients and two healthy controls, across three skin oil types, were sequenced for bacteria and fungi.

Patients showed higher bacterial diversity than controls, at a Shannon index of 2.26 versus 0.71. Fungal communities were almost fully replaced between individuals, a near-complete restructuring. Skin oil content shaped microbial diversity strongly, while bacteria-fungi links were weak. The authors say care may need to target both kingdoms.
pmc-13256224: A short 2026 retraction notice in Open Forum Infectious Diseases withdraws an IDWeek conference abstract by Monirujjaman Biswas on acute viral hepatitis among dengue patients in northern India. The journal says the abstract overlapped significantly with a previously published paper by Jain and others, without giving credit to it. It also says the authorship of the publication cannot be verified. The notice reports no prevalence figures of its own, so the retracted work is described here only by its subject and the reasons for withdrawal.
pmc-13256324:
Weidong Niu and colleagues report a 2026 process study upgrading cottonseed protein, an abundant cotton-processing by-product held back by a toxin, free gossypol. The team combined microbes and enzymes in one treatment, first testing each ingredient alone, then using a response-surface design to tune dosage, temperature, moisture, and time together.

The optimized recipe used one percent each of microbe and enzyme mixes at thirty-seven degrees with thirty-seven percent moisture for ninety-six hours. Free gossypol fell by over eighty percent, while digestible protein share climbed steeply and acidity dropped. Nearly all resulting peptides were small, and over sixty percent were under a thousand daltons, sizes linked to easy absorption. Antioxidant activity was strong. The authors say the combined treatment turns a risky by-product into a nutritious feed ingredient.
pmc-13256824:
Alejandro Pinta-Castro and co-authors apply network analysis in a 2026 study of Alzheimer's disease. They ask how the co-expression structure of genes in the brain's dorsolateral prefrontal cortex changes as the disease rewires molecular pathways. Instead of single genes, they treat the disease as a breakdown in how gene groups work together.

Building disease-specific networks from bulk RNA sequencing, they found communities enriched for GABA signaling, synapse assembly, and cell adhesion pathways. Key synaptic genes such as NRXN2 and SHANK1 became more central while their modules were broadly turned down. Distances within pathways lengthened across the board, a sign of loosened coordination. The authors read late-onset Alzheimer's as active structural rewiring gathered around synapses.
pmc-13257324:
Marija Ratković-Janković and co-authors test urine and blood markers in children with urine reflux in a 2026 study. In vesicoureteral reflux, urine flows backward toward the kidneys, raising infection and scarring risk. Five matrix-related proteins were measured in children with the condition and in controls.

Blood levels differed only for one chemokine, which ran higher in patients. Urine told a richer story, with two markers raised and one lowered after adjusting for urine concentration. Each urine marker separated patients from controls moderately well. Higher urine levels of three markers tracked severe reflux and scarring on both kidneys. Pediatric kidney specialists gain candidate noninvasive signals of inner kidney inflammation and fibrosis. The authors stress that larger, longer studies must confirm clinical value first.
pmc-13257724:
Marta Joanna Borys and colleagues follow nutrition and growth in children with eosinophilic esophagitis in a 2026 study. Fifty children diagnosed before age eighteen were tracked for at least a year, with height and body mass scores charted over an average of about two years of follow-up.

At diagnosis, one in five children had impaired nutrition, split between moderate malnutrition and obesity. Malnutrition eased by follow-up, while obesity grew more common. Height scores stayed broadly stable throughout. The disease inflames the swallowing tube and often brings restrictive eating, so both under- and over-nutrition can follow. Pediatric gastroenterology teams are urged to monitor the full weight spectrum, not only thinness. Diet management that swaps trigger foods for calorie-dense substitutes may explain part of the obesity drift.
pmc-13257924:
Vlad Constantin and co-authors review bioactive fillers in bulk-fill dental resins in a 2026 article. Fillings shrink as they harden, opening gaps that invite new decay at the edges. Bioactive glasses and calcium phosphate fillers promise to ease shrinkage stress while releasing helpful ions into nearby tooth.

Three filler families are compared on chemistry and behavior: classic bioactive glass, amorphous calcium phosphate, and pre-reacted glass-ionomer particles. Optimized blends cut shrinkage stress by roughly a quarter to two-fifths in the cited work. Bending strength stayed above clinical thresholds and stiffness within accepted ranges. Study methods varied so much that direct ranking stays shaky. Restorative dentists gain a hopeful direction: fillings that seal better and actively remineralize. Standard test protocols would let the next review speak with more certainty.
pmc-13258024:
Michelangelo Fabbrizzi and colleagues present a 2026 study of FEDE, a pipeline for building a digital twin of a human brain. A digital twin is a computer copy that aims to match both the brain's structure and its activity. FEDE combines imaging data, finite-element analysis, a math method for modeling physical structures, and biophysical modeling. The goal is one framework that holds anatomy and whole-brain activity together at fine detail.

The team demonstrated FEDE by building the first brain digital twin of a toddler with autism spectrum disorder. After tuning, the model copied the child's measured neural activity and rebuilt features from whole-brain connections down to synapse timing. It also estimated possible faults in synaptic transmission, the passing of signals between nerve cells, that fit known autism biology. Clinical uses are proposed next.
pmc-13258424:
Xin Guan and co-authors build linked dye molecules to study light-driven electron behavior in a 2026 photophysics paper. Ultrafast and nanosecond spectroscopy, electrochemistry, and quantum calculations tracked what absorbed light does next.

No lasting charge-separated state appeared, which rules out one hoped-for pathway. Energy transfer likely ran between the partners while electron transfer quenched the acceptor glow. Such triplet makers suit sensing and photocatalysis roles that need long-lived excited states without heavy atoms.
pmc-13258524:

Two hundred twelve screws were placed, and almost all sat in the top accuracy grades. Nobody suffered an artery injury, a new nerve deficit, or hardware failure during surgery. One surface wound infection was the only complication recorded. Operations averaged just over two hours, supporting the navigated route as a safe alternative to open surgery.
pmc-13258824:
Dylan Nunnally-Martínez and Amparo Monfort profile grassy scent compounds in Rosaceae berries during a 2026 study. Leaves and fruit at three ripeness stages came from strawberry, raspberry, and blackberry plants. A fiber sampling method with gas analysis identified eleven scent compounds.

Certain compounds rose and fell together across ripening. Outdoor growing differences temper direct species comparisons. pmc-13258924:
Yingzi Zhang and colleagues clean citrus buds of two major pathogens with heat and hormone treatments in a 2026 study. The targets were a bacterium behind greening disease and a widespread citrus virus. Bud germination, pathogen levels, and defense enzyme activity were measured for each treatment.

Warm water at a moderate setting helped buds sprout, while hotter or longer baths hurt them. Melatonin at the best dose cut both pathogen loads by over nine tenths. Heat and melatonin raised a virus resistance gene signal, while a growth hormone did not. Combining heat with melatonin added no extra benefit. Nursery programs gain a simple recipe for cleaner planting stock.
pmc-13259224:
Paulina Salazar-Aguilar and colleagues refine how to photograph nerve-support cells growing on plastic scaffolds. Schwann cells drive peripheral nerve repair, and judging their shape on electrospun mats matters for tissue engineering. Their 2026 pilot compares six preparation recipes under a low-vacuum electron microscope, no metal coating required.

Seeding more cells made far more of them visible on the scaffold surface. Marking the seeded side with graphite helped counts and preserved natural star-like shapes. Marker ink, by contrast, seemed to repel the cells. The team also codified a careful way to trace cell extensions in image software, aiding repeatable measurements.
pmc-13260124:
Yuanjie Sun and colleagues mapped in 2026 the cells of the placenta in early-onset fetal growth restriction, a condition where a baby grows too slowly before birth. Placental failure drives the condition, but the cell-level causes stay unclear. Their team built a single-nucleus gene atlas from patient placentas and matched healthy controls.

The subset releases a signal that stresses surface cells while withholding a growth factor they need. The authors propose this circuit as a possible drug target.
pmc-13260224:
Alim Emre Basaran leads a 2026 retrospective study of swelling around meningioma brain tumors after surgery. This swelling, called peritumoral brain edema, can persist after the tumor is removed and affects prognosis. The single-center study covered seventy-five confirmed meningiomas. Swelling volumes before and after surgery were measured from MRI scans, and tissue staining measured expression of a protein called FOXC1. Statistical analyses searched for independent predictors of how much the swelling shrank.

Higher FOXC1 expression was independently associated with greater swelling resolution, with an odds ratio of 6.36. Larger tumor volume was independently associated with lower resolution, with an odds ratio of 0.25. The authors propose FOXC1 as a possible molecular marker for predicting recovery from swelling after meningioma surgery. They caution that the finding needs validation in larger independent patient groups before clinical use.
pmc-13260724:
Rafael Willems and colleagues present a 2026 prospective pilot MRI study asking whether mRNA COVID-19 vaccination changes brain microstructure in the weeks after vaccination. Twenty-nine healthy adults who had never had the virus were scanned at three points. Scans came before the first dose, one to two weeks after the second dose, and two to three months after it. Both vaccine brands in use were included, giving eighty-five scans in total.

No new or growing white matter hyperintensities, bright spots linked to small vessel changes, were observed. One participant's pre-existing spot shrank by one millimetre. The authors report no evidence of structural brain changes after vaccination in this small healthy group.
pmc-13261124:
Keul and co-authors present a 2026 study proposing a new way to read past ocean temperatures from pteropod shells. Pteropods are small swimming snails whose shells can archive past ocean conditions. The team tested lithium-to-magnesium ratios, a thermometer long used in corals, in the species Heliconoides inflatus for the first time.

Shells were collected along an Atlantic transect from 31° N to 38° S, spanning about 15 °C of surface heat. The lithium-to-magnesium ratios fell steeply as heat rose. That link allows heat reconstruction with an average precision of ± 1–2 °C. Seasonal heat changes were also captured from the early-life to adult parts of the shell. The species is widespread and plentiful in seabed layers. The authors present it as a new tool for rebuilding past surface heat.
pmc-13262724:
Pan Kang leads the study behind a 2026 journal article on how high blood sugar worsens vitiligo, a skin disease where immune cells destroy pigment cells. Patient comparisons linked high blood sugar to the disease, but the mechanism was unclear. The team used patient data and a mouse model, and measured small molecules in blood and tissue to find a mediator.

A fuel-cycle product called succinate emerged as the key link. Succinate switched on killer T cells through its receptor, SUCNR1, the authors found. It also pushed skin cells to release signals that draw those T cells into the skin. Blocking this pathway is therefore a possible treatment route, they argue, and succinate may mark disease activity.
pmc-13262824:
Cosmas Zyambo leads a national survey study of HIV treatment adherence in Zambia in a 2026 journal article. Antiretroviral therapy, the drug regimen that controls HIV, works only when taken as prescribed. The team surveyed people living with HIV at 193 clinics across all ten provinces, using a 2023 national survey, and modeled which factors tracked with missed treatment.

Of 5,204 people surveyed, 7.1 percent were not adhering, with higher rates in men than women. Among those not adhering, 60 percent drank alcohol and 22 percent smoked tobacco. Drinking and smoking each raised the odds of non-adherence roughly two to three times. Older age and more schooling lowered the odds. The authors suggest targeted support around alcohol and tobacco use.
pmc-13263224:
Takeshi Yamashita and co-authors report a relapsing neck spine infection in an 88-year-old man in a 2026 case report. The infection, called spondylodiscitis, attacks a spinal bone and its disc, and neck cases are uncommon. Blood cultures found a strain of Streptococcus gallolyticus, a normal gut germ rarely blamed for spinal infections.

A standard 90-day course of antibiotics first cleared his fever, neck pain, and blood markers. Yet symptoms returned on day 174, even though repeat scans showed no clear active inflammation. Doctors resumed oral antibiotics for nine months, reaching lasting remission without surgery. To their knowledge, no earlier case caused by this strain described a return. They suggest longer, patient-matched treatment and long follow-up for such cases.
pmc-13264024:
Bilguun Mend and colleagues publish a 2026 dataset on cement made with waste-derived ferrous sulfate in place of natural gypsum. Gypsum normally controls how Portland cement sets, so a waste-based substitute needs careful testing. The collection records how the materials were made and how the hardened cement behaved over time and at different curing ages.

Strength results, soluble hexavalent chromium measurements and life-cycle inventory inputs are also provided. Both raw instrument output and processed tables are organized by method and sample. Engineers and researchers can reuse the data to compare sulfate sources, model hydration and judge environmental trade-offs.
pmc-13264824:
Katie de Luca led a 2026 commentary on the role of chiropractic care in rehabilitation, the care that restores daily function after illness or injury. About 2.4 billion people live with conditions that could gain from such care. Chiropractors train in muscle and joint health and person-centered care, and the paper argues they can strengthen health systems.

Gains in low- and middle-income countries and for fair access are weighed. Barriers include uneven laws, low recognition by other professions, and patchy team integration. The paper ends with a call for better training links and advocacy.
pmc-13264924:
Lars Dijk and colleagues published a 2026 interview study on how sudden worsening events shape daily life for people with COPD, a long-term lung disease. Such events were defined by drops in breathing measures, more reliever use, or worse symptoms. The team asked patients in five countries how they spot and handle these turns.

Nineteen patients with moderate to severe disease took part, with interviews right after an event and again six weeks later. Patients described bad days in varied ways, from lost ability to do tasks to needing extra treatment. Events under two days often went unnoticed, while longer ones were usually recognized. Most said they would seek care if needed, but hard-to-get appointments and a wait-and-see habit held some back. The authors link low awareness to under-reporting.
pmc-13265224:
Xiaoxiong Wang and colleagues examine a protein called DKK4 across colorectal growths, in a 2026 study. Colorectal cancer develops stepwise from normal lining through benign adenomas. Markers for early precancerous stages are scarce. Tissue staining and data analysis tracked DKK4 at each stage.

DKK4 was low in normal tissue, rose in adenomas, and peaked in high-grade precancerous lesions. Levels then fell notably in invasive cancer. Expression linked to mutation burden and to a growth pathway called Wnt. A risk model built with DKK4 showed modest predictive accuracy. The pattern may help flag lesions needing closer attention.
pmc-13266024:
Mushrin Malik and colleagues pool evidence on AI-read heart artery scans for predicting major cardiac events, in a 2026 meta-analysis. Automated plaque measurement promises consistency beyond simple narrowing grades. Ten studies covering about twenty thousand patients were included. Searches ran through October 2025.

Plaque burden measured by AI predicted major events with roughly doubled risk. Soft, low-density plaque showed the strongest link. Event rates for death, heart attack, and repeat procedures were pooled across cohorts. Results held when restricted to one AI platform. The authors argue plaque character adds prognostic value beyond stenosis severity alone.
pmc-13266224:
Younghee Park and the team ask whether nodal radiation can be omitted in certain breast cancers after chemotherapy (2026). Patients had small tumours with initial node spread and residual node disease after chemotherapy. Surgery meant full node clearance. The Korean study group evaluated radiation benefit in this niche.

Highlights report no added survival benefit from regional nodal irradiation here. Omission may therefore be considered for selected patients. Decisions after chemotherapy are tricky because response changes risk estimates. Prior registry work supports risk-adapted de-escalation plans. The findings add Korean data to an active international debate on tailoring radiation.
pmc-13266824:
Kun Zhang and colleagues pool in 2026 the results of freezing therapy for early-stage lung cancer, for patients who often cannot face major surgery. Their meta-analysis gathered seven small studies covering 353 patients, most with stage IA disease. They tracked survival, cancer control, local return of tumor, spread, and procedure harms.

Survival stayed high through three years, then fell by year five, a pattern the authors report without a direct surgery comparison. Local recurrence and spread were uncommon in the pooled data. Collapsed lung was the most frequent harm, affecting about a quarter of patients, while no deaths occurred within thirty days. Stage IA patients fared best, supporting freezing as an option for carefully chosen cases.
pmc-13267024:
Xinjing Shen and colleagues report a 2026 study of a drinkable drug carrier aimed at scarred liver tissue. Liver fibrosis builds up when star-shaped liver cells switch on and lay down excess matrix. The team loaded a plant compound called morin into tiny oil droplets marked with vitamin A, which those cells tend to take up.

Treated rats showed less scarring, less of a scar marker, and lower levels of a key scar-driving signal. Liver function also improved. The authors offer the system as a long-term oral option for fibrosis care.
pmc-13267424: Shah and colleagues' letter on lung blood pressure in chronic lung disease is the subject of a 2026 correction notice. The original letter argued that male sex is linked to severe pulmonary hypertension and worse outcomes in COPD patients sent for a heart catheter test. A publisher's error left the published title incomplete. The correction restores the words Letter to the Editor at the start of the title, marking it as a letter. The notice apologizes for the error. No findings or conclusions change.
pmc-13267924:
Min Xu and colleagues report a 2026 survey of fear of movement after pacemaker surgery in China. Kinesiophobia, an excessive fear that movement will cause harm, can keep patients from rehab exercise. About 60 percent of patients showed kinesiophobia. Stronger family functioning went with less fear, less pain, and less worst-case thinking. Pain and worst-case thinking each went with more fear. The chain analysis showed family support linked to lower fear partly through lower pain and calmer thinking about pain, in that order. The authors caution that a one-time survey cannot prove cause and urge follow-up studies.
pmc-13268724:
Jooyun Kim and co-authors review in 2026 how clinicians can judge tissue starvation in shock without leaning only on blood pressure. Large vessels may look restored while the tiny vessels that feed cells stay poorly perfused, a split the authors call hemodynamic incoherence.

Each indicator is explained in terms of what it says about the body and where it helps decisions. pmc-13268924:
Qian Chen and colleagues follow in 2026 the paths of a urine protein marker over time in Chinese patients with type 2 diabetes, asking which paths warn of kidney damage ahead. pmc-13270724:
Manouri Wimalasekera is lead author of a 2026 narrative case study on bringing community engagement and involvement into research in Sri Lanka. Success, they argue, needs tackling structural inequality, matching engagement to local culture, and backing from ethics rules and leaders. pmc-13271424:

pmc-13271924:

Both breaks healed within two months, and later imaging confirmed sound repair.
pmc-13272324:

The authors say fan loyalty repairs pride in other ways than simply backing the winner, which refines how such behavior should be read.
pmc-13272524:

pmc-13273124:

pmc-13273224:

pmc-13273524:

pmc-13273624:

pmc-13274024:

pmc-13276324:

pmc-13276524:

The authors urge including blood profiling in future flu risk assessments.
pmc-13276724:

pmc-13277824:

Inputs leaned on glucose monitors, wearables, lifestyle logs, and health records. pmc-13278424:

Repeated measures in patients were highly reliable. Average tremor frequency was lower in patients than in controls, and the measure separated the groups fairly well. Frequency tracked with age in both groups and with speech, facial expression, and gait features in patients. Medication state made no difference. The measure may support screening, with more work needed.
pmc-13279024:
Phillip A Williford and colleagues published a 2026 conceptual article proposing that measures of epigenetic aging could help counsel patients toward healthier habits. pmc-13279524:

Costs and quality-of-life weights came from published sources.

pmc-13279824:

pmc-13280124:
L Velur Prasuna and colleagues published a 2026 diagnostic accuracy meta-analysis of nerve monitoring during surgery for ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament. The authors call the tool useful but incomplete. They argue level-specific alarm criteria and combined methods must come before the numbers can be trusted in operating rooms.
pmc-13281424:
Wajahat Mirza and colleagues pooled trials on wound suction after stoma reversal surgery in a 2026 review. A stoma is an opening that lets waste leave the body after bowel surgery. Reversal closes it, but the wound gets infected in a large share of cases. A suction dressing pulls fluid from the closed wound and may cut infection. Seven strict trials with four hundred twenty-nine patients met the review's rules. The team split results by how skin was closed, gathered or straight.

The review rated proof quality with a standard grading tool. It tracked infection in the first weeks, hospital stay, healing time, and blood loss. Two reviewers screened and scored each trial on their own to cut bias. The authors frame the work as a check on whether suction helps in all closure styles or just some. Their design aims to guide surgeons who face this common, costly setback.
pmc-13281524:
Ken S Lee and colleagues published a 2026 synthetic chemistry study turning simple alkoxyallenes into versatile three-carbon building blocks carrying a TEMPO group and an aldehyde, which they call linchpins. Their route installs the two handles cleanly, yielding an intermediate reactable at each carbon in turn.

From these linchpins the team built a gallery of nitrogen- and oxygen-containing rings prized in drug discovery, including quinoxalines, imidazoles, oxazoles, and thiazoles. pmc-13281624:
Sunil Thakali and colleagues reviewed eye injections at a community hospital in Nepal in a 2026 paper. The team read charts of patients treated from 2019 to 2022. More than four hundred shots were given to two hundred forty-seven patients. Vision and retina thickness were tracked over follow-up visits.

The swollen center of the retina thinned a great deal after treatment. Overall sight scores, though, held flat across the whole group. The authors say the drug gave real gains even in a low-resource clinic, where repeat visits are hard to secure.
pmc-13281824:
Tobias Sägesser and colleagues built a single-atom probe that scans in three dimensions in a 2026 study. Stray fields from surfaces blur fine measurements and shorten quantum device life. Trapped ions, single charged atoms held in place, are superb field sensors. Past traps could only slide the ion along a line. Their new trap holds the ion with steady fields alone. That frees it to move through a block of space near a metal surface.

The probe mapped still and flickering electric and magnetic fields. It worked from close up to about half a millimeter away. Maps revealed charge patches and the texture of surface noise. By their pattern, the team could tell noise sources apart. The authors say the probe can serve surface science broadly. Any field where surface grit limits tools, from gravity tests to quantum chips, could gain.
pmc-13282324:
Kyriakos Psarakis and co-authors describe a 2026 computer systems paper presenting Styx, a runtime for stateful cloud functions. Cloud functions are small programs that run on demand. Many real tasks also need stored state, strict consistency, and low delay, which current tools handle poorly. Styx organises work as a flowing graph of functions and promises each transaction, a set of linked steps, runs exactly once and in a consistent order.

Three additions cut delay: detecting where a transaction ends, caching function results, and replying before full commit when safe. Styx can also move state between machines to balance load as demand shifts. Standard benchmark tests showed at least ten times the throughput of rival approaches, with near-linear scaling and low delay. Migration tests beat a stop-and-restart method. The authors aim at workflows and microservices that need speed without giving up correctness.
pmc-13282424:
Suey Yee Low and co-authors issued a 2026 correction to their study of zoonotic gut parasites in public spaces in Malaysia. The original study surveyed small animal faeces and soil for parasites that can pass from animals to people. Several figures in the abstract, main text, and a table were wrong. The correction replaces them and leaves the study's topic and setting unchanged.

The corrected count is fifty-six positive samples, about seventy-nine percent, not sixty-three. Cat faeces carried parasites more often than dog faeces, at ninety percent against about sixty-five percent. The risk findings also change direction. Lacking a dustbin, not having one, was linked to higher hookworm infection in dogs. Cat samples from apartment playgrounds carried more hookworm than those from residential parks. Soil from dog-friendly parks showed higher odds of one hookworm type than soil from residential parks.
pmc-13283424:
Noya Doolman and co-authors ran a 2026 proof-of-concept study on freezing human embryos with a shorter soak in protective fluid. Freezing by vitrification, meaning ultra-fast cooling, needs a timed soak in an equilibration fluid first. Shorter soaks worked in eggs and mouse work, but embryos lacked evidence, and no licence covers their use in embryos.

One IVF lab froze 45 blastocysts, 49 early embryos, and 102 abnormally fertilised eggs used as early-stage stand-ins. Groups used either the standard soak or the short soak, in full or tiny fluid volumes. After warming, survival, growth, and re-expansion rates looked much the same across methods. The authors present the short soak as workable in the lab, pending wider checks.
pmc-13283624:
Jeffrey Nepple led a multicentre team in 2026 asking whether loose joints change hip surgery results in teenage girls. The surgery treats femoroacetabular impingement, where hip bones pinch during motion. Generalised joint hypermobility, scored by the Beighton flexibility test, may feed hip instability and pain. The study followed girls aged fourteen to nineteen having first-time keyhole hip surgery across centres.

Ninety-seven patients were grouped by Beighton score: normal in 45 percent, mildly raised in 31 percent, and clearly raised in 24 percent. After about a year, outcome scores for pain, hip function, and sport were gathered, and failure was counted as reoperation or missing set gain marks. Higher Beighton scores did not tie to worse results, and final scores did not differ across the groups.
pmc-13284024:
Over half of men awaiting penile implant surgery report strong pre-surgery anxiety in a 2026 survey by Fayez T Hammad and colleagues. Worry may run high due to the foreign device and partner expectations afterward. No earlier study had measured anxiety in this exact group.

A total of 123 men at one institute answered a standard anxiety scale before surgery. Mean age was about 56 years across the survey group. Just over half scored in the clinically significant anxiety range. Past surgical problems and internet searching predicted high anxiety after adjustment. Top concerns were device failure, trouble activating the device, and size changes. Longer consults also tracked with worry.
pmc-13284324:
Fatma M. Talaat and colleagues present GreenAid, a plant disease detection system described in a 2026 research article. GreenAid combines three image models, VGG16, ResNet50, and InceptionV3, and weights each model by its class-level F1 scores. The system pairs the models with a phone app, a web dashboard, and a chat tool for farmers.

On the PlantVillage set of 87,000 images in 38 classes, the combined system reached high accuracy and beat five other ways of merging model outputs. A small phone version kept most of that accuracy while running offline in 127 ms per image on a mid-range phone. The work matters because plant disease causes large crop losses, and small farms often lack fast expert diagnosis.
pmc-13284424:
T. D. A. Stindt and co-authors report a nationwide Dutch cohort study, published in 2026, on local breast cancer return after mastectomy. Even after full removal of breast tissue, cancer can return at the chest site, yet trials often merge local and regional return. The team used the Netherlands Cancer Registry for women treated from 2012 to 2016.

Among more than 22,000 patients split by whether systemic therapy came first, local return stayed low, near 2 percent in both groups after long follow-up. Lower risk linked to screening detection, radiation, and some drug treatments, while higher stage and missed hormone therapy linked to higher risk. The patterns could help tailor follow-up and added treatment after mastectomy.
pmc-13284524:
Jin-Tao Lí and colleagues tested in 2026 whether soil microbes toughened by one climate stress withstand a different one. Microbes drive soil carbon handling, and their recovery after shocks keeps ecosystems working. The team exposed soil communities to frost or drought, then hit them again with either stress, tracking growth recovery and how efficiently microbes used carbon.

Prior exposure to either stress made microbes more resilient to both stresses afterward, not just the one they had met. Carbon use efficiency also held up better. The authors reason that frost and drought both squeeze microbes through water potential, so the training transfers. Repeated shock cycles added nothing beyond a single event, and the lag phase before growth resumed proved decisive. They call this cross-stressor resilience an overlooked climate factor.
pmc-13285624:
Diabetes more than doubles the odds of severe dengue and nearly quadruples death odds, Jingjing Lin and co-authors pool in a 2026 review. Dengue spreads fast by mosquito bite while diabetes climbs worldwide, and its chronic swelling and weak defenses may deepen dengue harm. Three databases plus hand checks yielded twenty-seven studies with 734,123 patients.

Patients with diabetes faced clearly higher odds of severe dengue than those without, and higher odds still of dying from it in the pooled results reported here. Both gaps held across the varied study set. The authors urge early flagging and tight watch of diabetic patients where dengue thrives, plus care plans that treat both ills together.
pmc-13285824:
A Shreenivas and a large team of colleagues map HER2 changes across solid cancers in a 2026 real-world analysis. HER2, a growth signal protein, can be copied too often, mutated, or simply present at high levels on tumor cells. Using a huge profiling database, the team asked how these forms line up with each other and with survival.

The set held more than 200,000 tumors with gene data and a smaller group with protein stain results. Gene copies often, but not always, matched high protein levels, and some mutated tumors showed raised protein without extra copies. Patients whose tumors stained strongest lived longest on median, though the edge came mostly from breast and stomach cancers with known HER2 drugs. The mixed picture argues for testing each tumor on its own terms.
pmc-13285924:
Kien Trung Nguyen and colleagues describe late-pregnancy preeclampsia care at a large hospital in Vietnam in a 2026 retrospective study. The blood pressure disorder can turn severe fast and endangers both mother and baby. The team reviewed one year of cases to map how the disease looked, how staff handled it, and which signs warned of poor outcomes for newborns.

The review covered 154 women who gave birth at the hospital between August 2022 and July 2023, and severe disease made up well over half the cases. Older mothers, first pregnancies, past stillbirth, and assisted conception each came with higher odds of severe illness. Every woman with severe disease gave birth by cesarean, and early birth struck more than a third of the group. Birth before 34 weeks stood as the strongest warning sign for harm to the baby.
pmc-13286324:
Tri Budiati leads a 2026 quasi-experimental study of breastfeeding support after caesarean birth in Indonesia. Mothers who deliver by surgery often start nursing late and doubt their milk supply, and local myths feed that doubt. A culture-aware support model was tested against usual care in 116 mothers, with belief in milk adequacy and newborn weight tracked before and after.

Mothers receiving the model gained more confidence in their milk supply than the control group did. Their babies also put on more weight across the study window. After myths and family support entered the math, the model more than doubled the odds of a mother rating her milk as very sufficient. Nurses gain a ready option for coaching surgical-birth mothers through the shaky first days of nursing.
pmc-13286524:
Christina Ping and colleagues run a randomized trial on paid invitations to research through patient portals in a 2026 study. Portal messages recruit cheaply, but the same groups missing from trials also use portals least, so the tool might widen the gap it promises to close. Twelve hundred cancer patients, half from historically underrepresented groups, got a message about a fictitious survey study, with a third randomly offered twenty dollars to respond.

Only about four in ten patients even opened the message, and 13.3% answered with interest. White patients responded at 18%, against 7% for Black patients, and patients over 65 engaged far less than younger ones. The twenty-dollar offer moved nothing: response rates with and without it sat within noise of each other. Portal recruiting, the authors conclude, mirrors the very disparities it was meant to heal.
pmc-13286924:
Yunzhang Zhao and colleagues ask whether taking aspirin and a statin together improves survival when sepsis injures the heart muscle. Their 2026 study mines a large intensive care database covering 1,884 patients with this complication, which carries high death rates and few proven drug treatments. Only 119 patients received both medicines.

Those patients died far less often at twenty-eight days, ninety days, and one year than patients on neither drug. The gap was large, with risk cut by well over half at each point. A separate intensive care cohort of about four thousand patients confirmed lower early mortality, though the advantage shrank. Subgroups behaved consistently. The authors call the pairing promising for a condition short on options.
pmc-13287224:
Martin Pingel and colleagues mapped farming systems across Germany in 2026 so that payments for wildlife-friendly practice can be fitted to local conditions instead of applied uniformly. They grouped districts using land cover, field patterns, farming intensity, climate, and terrain, then refined the grouping with specialists from farming, conservation, and public agencies.

Eight system types emerged, ranging from cash-crop dominated areas to livestock dominated areas and mixed mosaics. Each type carries its own pressures on farmland wildlife, from heavy inputs to loss of varied habitat. The authors outline where tailored schemes could relieve each pressure and note that the grouping method could be repeated in other countries.
pmc-13288724:
Ismail Cifci, Bilal Durmaz, and Esra Meltem Koc test a muscle screen in Turkey in 2026. The screen is the five-question SARC-F. Records covered 396 adults. All were aged sixty-five or more. Two family health centers in Izmir took part. Blood tests joined the screen data.

Risk hit 16.9 percent of the group. Women showed risk more often than men. Older age raised the odds. Female sex and higher body weight also raised them. Lower ferritin tracked with more risk. Lower albumin did the same. When time blocks the screen itself, blood values may help. They can flag patients worth a full check.
pmc-13289224:
Elsa Martins and a large team report a 2026 phase Ib trial of mosunetuzumab given under the skin in systemic lupus erythematosus. Mosunetuzumab is a lab-made antibody that links T cells to B cells so T cells can remove B cells. The open-label study tested safety, drug levels in blood, and effects on immune cells across several centers.

Fifteen adults with active, antibody-positive lupus joined between January 2022 and December 2023. Some got one fixed dose, while others got a small first dose then a larger dose on day 8, up to 60 mg in the highest group. Two people stopped care because of side effects during treatment. No severe cytokine release events or nerve toxicity linked to immune cells were reported, which supports further careful study.
pmc-13289324:
Flávio Fidêncio de Lima headed a 2026 systematic review on whether poor diet links to painful temporomandibular disorders. These disorders cause jaw joint and muscle pain, and interest in lifestyle drivers of chronic pain is growing. The team searched five major databases for clinical and observational work through November 2025, then rated bias with a standard tool.

From 7,760 records, only seven studies passed with low risk of bias for synthesis. Birth and teen diet quality did not predict later jaw pain in cohort work. Cross-sectional work hinted that some eating patterns track with symptoms, and women with muscle-based jaw pain ate fewer key nutrients than controls. One lab test found a flavor enhancer raised pain, while the sole trial found no clear vitamin D benefit.
pmc-13290124:
Plant compounds packed into tiny carriers are reviewed as weapons against drug-resistant Staphylococcus aureus by Neha Gupta and a large team in 2026. The bacterium is a leading cause of hospital-acquired infection, and standard antibiotics increasingly fail against it.

Plant chemicals alone disappoint, the authors note, because they dissolve poorly, break down fast, and miss their targets. Loading them into nanoscale carriers fixes much of that. The loaded particles attack on several fronts: they jam efflux pumps, break membranes, make reactive oxygen species, and stop biofilms from forming. Curcumin particles broke MRSA membranes in the studies reviewed, and quercetin in liposomes entered biofilms better than the free compound. Gains also appeared when such particles were paired with standard antibiotics.
pmc-13290624:
Priyanka and colleagues report in 2026 that the gel inside the eye clings to the retina more often in diabetes, though how much sticks does not clearly differ. Their prospective study comes from central India. Vitreomacular adhesion is a normal stage of vitreous separation that may steer how diabetic retinopathy advances.

The team used optical coherence tomography scans at four angles. They measured the share of retinal surface still attached in 68 eyes of 40 diabetic patients without proliferative disease and 50 eyes of 25 matched controls. Adhesion was present in 96% of diabetic eyes against 84% of controls, a significant gap. The attached percentage, though, averaged 65% versus 58% without reaching significance, and early retinopathy stages did not separate either. The authors call for studies in advanced disease with newer scanners.
pmc-13290724:
Each drug in one leukemia family carries its own danger signature, Yong Wang and colleagues find in a study from 2026 of the FDA's adverse event database. Anthracyclines anchor acute myeloid leukemia treatment, but their harms differ by drug and by patient.

Mining reports from 2004 to 2024, the team analyzed 1,079 cases and 3,622 adverse events. Epirubicin showed the strongest heart-toxicity signal, doxorubicin the most pregnancy-related events, daunorubicin blood-vessel disorders, and idarubicin marrow suppression and infections. Most events arrived within 180 days of treatment. Idarubicin's onset ran late in older patients, and timing differed by sex for two drugs. Wang and colleagues argue the distinct profiles should steer drug choice and monitoring in leukemia care.
pmc-13290824:
Speed, prior revision, and mixed germs decide whether an infected hip implant can be saved, Ernesto Muñoz-Mahamud and colleagues report in a long-term study from 2026. Debridement with implant retention is a main option for acute prosthetic joint infection, but reported success swings wildly, from 16 to 92%.

The retrospective series covered 115 patients treated between 1999 and 2018 and followed a mean 7.1 years; by five years, 30.4% had failed. Failure roughly doubled when surgery waited past the first week after diagnosis, when the infected joint was a revision rather than a primary implant, and when infections were polymicrobial rather than single-organism. No other traits mattered significantly. The authors urge fast action while flagging the timing result as needing confirmation.
pmc-13291024:
Abel Trujillo-Ocampo heads a 2026 laboratory study of a calming immune cell type called NKT10, grown from cord blood invariant natural killer T cells. Such cells can steer immune responses toward control rather than attack, yet their medical use in stem cell transplantation had barely been tested before this work.

Cord-derived cells held many cells with a regulatory profile and produced calming signals when triggered, and gene checks set them apart from adult donor cells, which leaned toward attack-ready programs. Single-cell analysis confirmed a distinct NKT10-like group rich in control pathways. In dishes the cord cells slowed other immune cells from multiplying, and in mice they eased graft-versus-host disease, supporting their promise as a cell therapy.
pmc-13291224:
Growing onions in very dry soil takes smart feeding. Abeer Abd EL Moiez Ahmed Bakr leads a 2026 field study in Upper Egypt. Poor soil, scant water, and storage losses cut profits. The team paired organic waste with tiny mineral sprays.

Sugarcane filter mud was spread as organic feed. Sprays held copper or calcium particles at varied doses. Trials ran over two growing seasons. Best yields beat plain controls by a wide margin. Low copper with high calcium worked best. Too much copper with too little calcium harmed plants. Storage quality also improved under good mixes. Balanced pairing is the core lesson for dry farms.
pmc-13291324:
A learning agent can design light gear faster than old searches. Nada Yazeed M. Dawood leads a 2026 study of fiber modulator design. The part switches light using a phase-change film layer. Low signal loss was the design goal.

The agent learned by trial inside a physics simulator. No pre-made training set was needed. Repeated runs with varied seeds found the same best design. It took just twelve steps and about three minutes. Rival methods needed far more steps each. Loss fell well below the target value. Stable, fast search is the main win here. Photonics design may gain from such self-driving tools.
pmc-13291424:
Masab Mansoor writes a 2026 editorial on large language models in children's diagnostic reasoning. His starting point is a study that pitted four models against seventy-eight clinicians on fifty real cases from a Barcelona children's hospital. Half the cases were common conditions and half were rare diseases. Two models, o1-preview and Claude 3.5 Sonnet, beat the clinician group by a wide margin. The edge grew largest on the rare diseases, where diagnosis often takes years.

For rare cases, one model's top-five odds reached six times the clinicians' level. Clinician experience, strikingly, did not predict accuracy across seniority levels. Mansoor argues that such results demand a place for these tools in the diagnostic workflow. He also weighs where the evidence falls short, including the limits of testing on already gathered case data. The piece calls for responsible integration rather than adoption on accuracy scores alone.
pmc-13291924:
Brenig and Pach reported in 2026 a rare case of haemophilia A in a female German Shepherd dog. The bleeding disorder stems from a fault in the F8 gene on the X chromosome, so females are usually only carriers. Mating a mildly affected male with a carrier can produce daughters carrying the fault on both copies. Their patient bled heavily from minor injuries from puppyhood, starting with swelling after microchip placement at three months.

Clotting tests showed a greatly prolonged clotting time with factor VIII activity at only about six percent of normal, while related factors were normal. Whole-genome sequencing found the same fault on both gene copies, changing one building block in a region vital to the factor's stability. The variant had been seen once before in an unrelated German Shepherd over a decade earlier. The authors stress full genetic workups in rare disease with odd inheritance.
pmc-13292024:
Mohammad Hosein Taziki Balajelini and co-authors pool a 2026 systematic review and cumulative meta-analysis on how often fluid returns in children's ears after ventilation tube surgery. Otitis media with effusion is common in childhood, and recurrence after tubes fall out worries clinicians. Their August 2024 search covered eight databases under PRISMA guidance.

From 1,117 articles, 21 studies qualified, and the pooled recurrence rate came to 30 percent of children worldwide. Tubes alone gave 31 percent recurrence, against 20 percent when antibiotics were added, though the authors urge caution about that comparison. Children who also had cleft palate surgery fared worst, at 45 percent recurrence in the analysis. Year-by-year pooling showed recurrence easing from 39 percent in 2005 to 24 percent by 2019.
pmc-13292424:
Heikki Opoku Ofori and Emre Debreli dig into a 2026 classroom question in Ghana: what actually decides whether English teachers use AI tools well? Working in senior high schools, they combined teacher interviews, classroom observations, and stimulated recall sessions. The study leans on the Technology Acceptance Model and self-efficacy theory to explain reading and writing instruction.

Teachers generally saw AI tools as useful and fairly easy, yet those views alone did not predict classroom practice. Confidence was the hinge: self-assured teachers built structured, meaningful AI activities, while less confident colleagues stuck to shallow uses. Positive attitudes also collided with thin infrastructure and scarce time. The authors argue teacher psychology is the missing middle layer between what AI could do and what lessons actually deliver.
pmc-13292924:
Graeme C. Hays leads a 2026 study tracking how green turtles steer across open ocean between nesting beaches and feeding grounds. How sea animals find distant targets far from land has puzzled scientists for over a century.

New tags sent compass headings by satellite during trips over 1000 kilometers that lasted about 27.5 days on average, a span the authors report. Turtles often held one steady heading for long stretches, even when that path drifted off course, then turned to correct it. Steady legs with rare fixes fit the idea that turtles use magnetic signposts or rough maps, rather than constant fine tuning.
pmc-13293124:
Abhineet Sheoran and colleagues test a lab-made antibody treatment for a dangerous gut infection in mice, in research published in 2026. The target is Shiga toxin made by certain E. coli bacteria, which can damage the kidneys and cause hemolytic-uremic syndrome, a leading cause of kidney failure in young children. No specific treatment exists, and antibiotics can make matters worse.

The team built a mouse version of the infection using a related bacterium engineered to produce the toxin, which caused gut lesions and kidney damage much like human disease. A single injection of the toxin-blocking nanobody product, given as late as four days after infection, protected the mice completely. The result supports developing the treatment for people during the short window between diarrhea and kidney illness.
pmc-13293824:
Ning-chen Wang and colleagues report a 2026 retrospective cohort study on early breast cancer care. Their focus is why some people who choose breast-conserving surgery later need full mastectomy because tumor remains at the cut edge. Records cover operations from January 2015 through December 2024.

Among 290 patients, 31 needed the larger operation while 259 kept the smaller one. Four traits stood out as independent predictors: low body mass index, disease in more than one spot, larger tumor size, and a ductal carcinoma in situ part. Spotting these traits before surgery could help teams plan better and counsel patients more honestly.
pmc-13294124:
Abdullah, Zulaikha Fatima, and José Luis Oropeza Rodríguez present ApneaSense in 2026, a home-friendly system for spotting sleep apnea without a costly lab study. Standard overnight testing can cost over $6,000 per unit and reaches few people. Their setup fuses heart, oxygen, breathing effort, and motion signals on a low-power Raspberry Pi unit with a phone app for live viewing and telehealth sync.

Validation mixed a public database of 25 people with a clinic set of 61 people. On a held-out group of 17, the EvoApneaFormer model scored near 99.9% on accuracy, precision, and recall across six event classes. Home accuracy reached 96.9%, even with movement and signal dropouts.
pmc-13294224:
Manqi Cai, Xinxin Song, and Jun Tong pool therapy trials for teen borderline personality disorder in a 2026 meta-analysis. Four databases were searched through January 2026 for randomized trials of manual-based therapies in ages 12 to 18. Twelve trials held 844 teens, mean age 15.8 years and 81% female, covering dialectical, mentalization-based, and other structured programs.

Therapy gave small but clear gains for core symptoms, emotion control, and general mental health scores. No clear effect appeared for depressive symptoms or quality of life, though quality data came from just two trials. Variation between studies stayed low and no publication bias showed. Gains are real but modest, so expectations should stay measured.
pmc-13294324:
Yu Huang and colleagues grade two MRI methods for facial pain surgery planning in a 2026 retrospective study. In primary trigeminal neuralgia, a vessel pressing the nerve is the usual target for decompression surgery. Records covered 412 patients whose surgical findings served as truth, comparing vessel angiography imaging, a steady-state sequence called FIESTA-c, and both together.

Surgeons found a culprit vessel in 407 of 412 patients, most often the superior cerebellar artery at 60.68% in the reported share. Simple presence checks scored near 91% for each scan alone and 96.36% combined. Exact vessel matching also favored pairing both scans. Preoperative confidence rises when the two views agree.
pmc-13294424:
Feng Xu and colleagues hunt scan signs of tumor spread through air spaces in early lung cancer for a 2026 study. Such spread worsens outlook even in stage IA disease, yet it is usually confirmed only after surgery. Records for 765 resected patients fed group comparisons and a prediction model, checked in an outside cohort, with tissue and mutation profiles compared as well.

Four scan signs independently flagged spread: high solid share, cut-off airways, pleural pulling, and satellite dots. Model accuracy areas reached 0.823 in training and 0.829 outside in the reported figures. High-risk patients relapsed sooner. Spread-positive tumors favored solid growth patterns and KRAS or ALK changes.
pmc-13295224:
Jordana Chaves and co-authors pool the evidence on artificial intelligence for timing orthodontic treatment, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Growth-modifying braces work best around the pubertal growth spurt, and judging that moment from head or hand X-rays takes expertise. Following a registered protocol, the team searched four databases through December 2025 for studies where AI read cephalometric or hand-wrist films in patients up to twenty-one years old.

Twenty-one studies entered the pooled analysis. Overall accuracy sat in the low eighties in percentage terms, with hand-wrist models more sensitive and head-film models more specific. Deep learning and combined-input approaches generally outperformed older machine learning, while large language model attempts looked shaky. Wide variation between studies and thin external testing temper the promise, and the authors call for multicenter work before clinics rely on these tools.
pmc-13295324:
Andrzej Falniowski, Aleksandra Jaszczyńska, and Sebastian Hofman describe a new snail genus and species from the Dominican Republic in a 2026 article. Minute freshwater snails were found in 2001 in the Dudu cenote, a pond formed where a cave roof partly fell in. Island snail life remains poorly studied despite its rich history.

Body features and DNA evidence placed the snails in the family Cochliopidae but apart from every known genus. The new genus honours Robert Hershler, a leading specialist on that family. The snails still live in the same pond today, underlining how much hidden diversity small island waters may hold.
pmc-13295424:
Andrea Briceño and colleagues study a brain toxin linked to Parkinson's disease in a 2026 laboratory article. Aminochrome forms inside dopamine neurons and is suspected in their loss. Its effects on the cell's waste clearing system, beyond known stress and skeleton damage, were poorly mapped.

In neuron-like cells, the toxin delayed the meeting of waste sacs with the digestive sacs that should clear them. Protein clumps marked by vimentin and ubiquitin piled up near and even inside the nucleus. Boosting the clearing process partly saved cells from death. The authors point to skeleton steadying and waste system support as joint treatment directions.
pmc-13295524:
Nan Wang and colleagues link how long pregnant women sleep with how they feel, in a 2026 survey of 1,035 women across ten counties in rural northwest China. Professional mental health care is scarce in such areas, so finding household-level levers matters. Women reported their nightly sleep, sorted into short, medium, and long bands, and completed a standard scale for depression, anxiety, and stress.

About a fifth slept short and another fifth slept long, while roughly a third scored in the moderate-to-severe range on each symptom measure. Both tails of sleep carried extra stress risk, with short and long sleepers each showing clearly higher odds than the middle band. The links grew stronger when husbands skipped prenatal visits, when relations with mothers-in-law were poor, or when women distrusted counseling. Helping families guard a healthy sleep window, the authors suggest, is cheap, practical mental health care.
pmc-13296024:
Antonio Farina and colleagues follow, in 2026, long-term nerve damage after cancer immunotherapy at a French national centre. Such side effects can be severe, yet how often they leave lasting problems was unclear, so records for 164 patients treated between 2015 and 2024 were reviewed.

Half the patients had recovered well by three months, but among those alive at one year, two in five still had notable nerve problems. Little improvement came after the first year. Relapses affected about one in seven patients, while restarting immunotherapy rarely triggered one. Cancer-linked nerve syndromes and early relapse predicted lasting harm.
pmc-13296224:
Thomas J. Nicholl and Maree J. Abbott interview professional classical musicians who perform without crushing anxiety, in a 2026 qualitative study. Performance anxiety is often treated as part of the job, and most work studies those who suffer it. Six ensemble players, three women and three men, told how they think and feel before and during concerts, and the team sorted the talks into themes.

All six knew anxiety early in their careers, then built calm through repeated playing and the good pull of others. They lean on firm technical, performance, and mental skills, plus a strong sense of why they play. On stage they describe feeling bound up with the music itself, close to fellow players, and turned outward toward the hall. The authors urge training that grows such values-led preparation in anxious players.
pmc-13296324:
Sergio Navas-León and Jon Andoni Duñabeitia test, in 2026, whether Easy-to-Read formatting, designed for readers with cognitive needs, also helps university students. Twenty-four young adults without disabilities read passages in hard, standard and easy formats while eye movements were tracked.

Comprehension scored highest in the easy format and clearly beat the hard format. Easy text also brought shorter fixations and longer jumps between them, hinting at lighter mental load. Hard text drew the most fixations overall. The authors suggest plain formatting may ease reading for everyone, not just its target group.
pmc-13297324:
Fabián Leonardo Barreto and colleagues test a cannabis extract that does not intoxicate against relapse-like behaviour in cocaine-trained mice, in a 2026 study. No approved drug treatment exists for cocaine use disorder, so memory-based routes draw interest. Mice learned to link one chamber with cocaine, then received the extract, rich in cannabidiol with little THC, around memory tests.

The extract weakened the return of cocaine seeking triggered both by a small cocaine dose and by stress. Given after memory recall sessions, it also seemed to disrupt the re-saving of the drug memory, with effects lasting at least two weeks. The extract alone caused neither liking nor dislike of a place. The work supports more study, in both sexes and other test setups.
pmc-13297424:
Kidney function might one day be read from a light scan of blood serum rather than a chemistry lab, propose Diogo Serrano and colleagues in a 2026 methods paper. They tested whether vibrational spectroscopy can estimate the markers clinicians use to stage chronic kidney disease.

The team prepared 54 serum-like solutions mimicking five disease stages and measured creatinine, urea, and albumin with mid- and near-infrared light. Mid-infrared scans, taken after a simple drying step, predicted urea best, while chosen near-infrared regions excelled for creatinine and albumin, with top models above R2 of 0.9. Classification separated healthy from diseased profiles with AUC above 0.93, supporting point-of-care potential.
pmc-13297624:
A simple ratio from two routine blood tests may warn which heart attack patients risk poor blood flow after stenting. Xhevdet Krasniqi and co-authors report in 2026 on 201 patients with STEMI treated by percutaneous coronary intervention, testing the C-reactive protein-to-albumin ratio against the no-reflow problem.

Patients split at a ratio of 48.4 into low and high groups that differed in smoking, cholesterol, and final vessel flow. The ratio predicted reduced flow with an area under the curve of 0.9, close to a related combined index at 0.94 and ahead of either component alone. The authors propose the cut-off as an accessible way to flag patients needing extra vigilance.
pmc-13297724:
Waste fiber from coconut oil production yielded peptides that eased diabetes in mice, report Dingyan Sun and co-authors in a 2026 study. Breaking down coconut kernel fiber protein gave a small fraction, sized 1 to 3 kDa, that blocked the starch-digesting enzyme α-glucosidase by 74.49% in tests.

In diabetic mice the fraction improved insulin resistance and sensitivity to about three-quarters of metformin's effect, repaired liver damage, and calmed inflammation. Docking analysis named three peptides, including FDLPAR, as likely active agents. The material survived digestion well and cut glucose release from bread by over 50%, pointing toward low-glycemic functional foods built from an industry by-product.
pmc-13297824:
A deliberately simple two-dimensional stand-in for water can still reproduce its famous oddities, argue Peter Ogrin and Tomaz Urbic in a 2026 review of the Rose model. Water's strange behaviors, from expanding as it cools to its large heat capacity, stem from directional hydrogen bonding that full molecular models handle at heavy cost.

The authors compare results for the model across Monte Carlo and molecular dynamics simulations, perturbation theory, integral equation methods, and an analytical treatment. They cover pure Rose water and mixtures with nonpolar solutes, mapping where anomalous behavior and phase changes appear. The model captures the essential physics while staying cheap to compute and open to pen-and-paper analysis.
pmc-13298024:
Computer modeling can rank which gene variants deserve laboratory attention for heart disease in Serbia, argue Tamara Drljača and colleagues in a 2026 in silico study. They focused on a variant in the PSPH gene that is common in the Serbian population and asked how it disturbs the protein's interaction network.

Using a sequence-based spectrum method, they singled out the ten partners most affected, including SHMT1 and SHMT2, which cluster in serine, glycine, and sphingolipid pathways tied to lipid metabolism. Frequent variant combinations also surfaced in four other genes, LRCH1, CEP126, PIK3CG, and PIKFYVE. The authors offer these candidates as hypotheses for follow-up work on cardiovascular risk.
pmc-13298124:
Talia Costa Rodrigues and co-authors simulate opinion dynamics on directed random networks, in a 2026 statistical physics study. Their majority-vote model adds inertia, meaning agents partly stick with their own current opinion. Extensive Monte Carlo runs varied network size, local field, and inertia while tracking relaxation time, a Binder cumulant, and susceptibility.

Behaviour changed sharply with inertia strength. Weak inertia allowed a continuous phase transition, a middle band showed no transition, and stronger inertia produced a first-order jump. Beyond the highest band, inertia dominated fully and ordering vanished again. The authors note this richer pattern differs from results on regular networks studied earlier.
pmc-13298224:
Tooth enamel dissolves in acid, but the full chemistry is subtler than low pH alone, explain Joachim Enax and co-authors in a 2026 review. They examine enamel demineralization from a chemist's viewpoint, covering both cavity formation and erosive wear from acidic food and drink.

Enamel mineral is hydroxyapatite, and its dissolution depends on how saturated the surrounding fluid is. Protein films and bacterial plaque on the tooth slow or redirect the attack, while calcium-binding molecules in saliva drag calcium ions away and keep dissolution going. Because saliva and mouth bacteria differ between people, so does risk. The review closes by weighing prevention strategies and treatments that aim to rebuild mineral.
pmc-13298524:
Oleg Gorshkov and Hernando Ombao analyse brain network synchronisation during epileptic seizures, in a 2026 study using a public scalp EEG database. Connectivity indices chosen resist distortion from volume conduction, and a neural classifier was tested by leaving one patient out at a time, which keeps scoring patient-independent.

That matching departed from baseline in a time-dependent pattern that repeated across patients. Connections between hemispheres peaked earlier and higher than connections within one hemisphere, which changed more slowly and lasted longer. Theta-band signals contributed most consistently, and longer seizures showed higher peak values. The authors propose a summary measure capturing how abnormal the matching pattern becomes.
pmc-13298924:
Yingyue Xing, Siyuan Zou, and Guohua Liu build a machine learning framework for predicting carbon allowance prices across China's regional markets, in a 2026 study. Markets differ in trading activity, price formation, and response to outside signals, which weakens single-model forecasts. Their system pools price history, trading volume, cross-market signals, and macroeconomic variables.

Three ensemble algorithms feed a weighted combination that proved more stable across seven pilot markets than any single model. Removing feature groups showed predictor importance varies by market, with no universal best set. Forecast outputs then support allowance sale timing and dynamic cost assessment for offshore wind projects.
pmc-13299224:
Timothy Pittaway, Leanne Townsend, and Claire Hardy analyse European urban treescape projects by working backward from benefits to the weak spots beneath, in a 2026 study. Metadata from 131 nature-based case studies across eight biogeographical regions were grouped by public benefit and mapped on maps. Tree planting eases heat and green space shortages, which fall hardest on poorer groups.

Eleven benefit categories emerged with clear regional patterns. Mediterranean projects targeted heat and drought, Alpine projects targeted slope stability, and Continental plus Atlantic projects emphasised social cohesion, recreation, and heritage. The authors recommend place-sensitive, equity-driven designs that join ecological and social aims.
pmc-13300024:
Shinnosuke FUKAMI and co-authors report delayed lung flooding after a burst brain aneurysm, in a 2026 case report. Neurogenic pulmonary edema usually strikes immediately after brain injury, so this timing was unusual. A man in his late sixties developed fast breathing and low oxygen with fluid across both lungs four days after bleeding from a ruptured aneurysm.

Heart ultrasound was normal, which ruled out a heart cause and confirmed the neurogenic diagnosis. Fluid restriction and diuretics brought rapid improvement, and the aneurysm was then sealed successfully with coils. The authors warn clinicians to consider this delayed complication when breathing worsens days after such bleeding.
pmc-13300824:
Shortened telomeres mark aging cells, but do they warn of trouble ahead in lupus? Leyre Riancho-Zarrabeitia and colleagues followed ninety-seven women with systemic lupus erythematosus for a 2026 prospective cohort study. Telomere length in white blood cells was measured by qPCR at entry, and fifty healthy women served as a comparison group.

Over a mean follow-up of 9.7 years, telomeres shortened with age and ran shorter in women with blood-related disease features. Lengths barely differed from controls, though. Early links to damage, heart events, and kidney function mostly faded once age was accounted for. The authors conclude telomere length mirrors general aging more than lupus activity, limiting its value as a forecast tool.
pmc-13301224:
K De Silva and co-authors test a mapping catheter design meant to care less about which way an electrical wave is traveling, in a 2026 experimental study. Ordinary paired electrodes read a signal that swells or shrinks depending on wave direction, which can mislead maps near scar. Their array adds a perpendicular pairing, one contact electrode on the tissue and one floating just off it, tested against two conventional spacings in five beating pig hearts prepared for external mapping.

Pacing from four compass directions made the conventional signals swing with direction, while the unipolar reference stayed steady. After normalizing each setup to its own maximum, the perpendicular pairing showed the least shortfall across directions, beating the ultra close and the two millimeter spacings. The authors present the geometry as a step toward direction fair mapping inside a clinical catheter, with consequences for how scar and block lines get read.
pmc-13301324:
Alessia Pennacchi and co-authors review three decades of attempts to reshape a bent nasal septum with energy instead of the scalpel, in a 2026 systematic review. Two methods dominate: laser heating, which softens cartilage so it holds a shape, and electromechanical reshaping, which uses needle electrodes and low voltage. Searching three databases to June 2025, the authors found eighteen studies, evenly split between the two techniques.

Laser reshaping worked within a narrow temperature band around fifty-five to seventy-five degrees, but higher doses injured cartilage cells and broke down the matrix. Only three human studies exist, all in mild deformities. The electromechanical method reshaped reproducibly near body temperature with dose dependent control, yet has no human studies. Neither touches bony bends, and none measured airflow benefit computationally. The authors keep both methods in the adjunct category for cartilage only cases, pending dosimetry standards and long term human data.
pmc-13301824:
Algorithms beat the standard nursing checklist at spotting pressure-injury risk, Fredy Barriga-Gallegos and colleagues report in a 2026 comparison from a Chilean tertiary hospital. Using records from 446 inpatients, they trained five classic machine-learning models on routine clinical variables, deliberately excluding Braden Scale inputs. Fairness came from matching decision thresholds to the scale's own operating points.

The XGBoost model discriminated best, with an area under the curve of 0.835 in the test. Matched at the Braden Scale's recall, it cut false alarms by roughly seventeen percent in specificity terms. Matched the other way, recall rose by thirteen to twenty-five percent. The authors propose machine learning as a sharpening partner for, not a replacement of, bedside judgment.
pmc-13302324:
K Tokutake and co-authors ask, in a 2026 study, whether pulsed field ablation can be used safely in lung veins already narrowed by an earlier heat-based ablation. Narrowing, called stenosis, is a feared side effect of thermal treatment, and redo procedures might worsen it. The new energy source mainly harms heart muscle while sparing nearby tissue.

Six patients with recurrent atrial fibrillation had repeat ablation after earlier radiofrequency or freezing-balloon treatment. CT scans measured vein openings before treatment and three months afterwards, slice by slice. Average narrowing stayed essentially unchanged after the new procedure, and no vein with severe pre-existing narrowing got worse. Nobody developed symptoms or major complications, supporting the redo approach in this small group.
pmc-13302824:
Lei Wang, Peng Tan, and Rantao Zuo introduce, in a 2026 editorial, a journal special issue gathering six studies on fish nutrition, gut microbes, and metabolic balance. Aquaculture feeds the world, yet judging new feeds by growth alone misses how diets reshape gut communities and body chemistry. The collected papers span farmed fish and shrimp.

Two studies test feed additives that mobilise fat and enrich helpful gut bacteria in bass and yellow drum. Another shows a crayfish by-product supplement easing the strain of low-fishmeal diets in shrimp. Two more compare rice-paddy rearing with ponds, finding better antioxidant defences and flesh quality in carp. A final study profiles bone ageing with untargeted metabolite screening.
pmc-13303124:
A dietitian in a box beat general chatbots at writing medical diets, Yanan Wang and colleagues test in a 2026 evaluation of their Med-Diet system. Built on DeepSeek-R1 with clinical dietary guidelines injected, the system drafted meal plans for seventy-nine real cases spanning common, rare, and complex chronic diseases. Fourteen blinded clinical experts scored its plans against four general-purpose language models.

Med-Diet topped the expert scores, ahead of its own base model and of GPT-4o and the others, winning on accuracy, safety, balance, and ease of use. Dietitians using it cut planning time from a median of seventeen and a half minutes to thirteen minutes, with better-rated output. Prospective safety trials remain ahead, the authors caution.
pmc-13304424:
Ibrahim Mahariq heads a 2026 math study of a hybrid nanofluid flowing over a stretching sheet. The fluid mixes copper and alumina particles in water, thickens and thins in a thixotropic way, and carries swimming microbes.

The model folds in magnetic pull, heat radiation, internal heating, friction heat, melting, and chemical change. Equations were reshaped into a simpler set and solved with a standard numeric solver. Magnetic pull slowed the flow while melting sped it. Heat rose with the heat source but fell with radiation and melting. Microbe levels dropped with one transport ratio and rose with another.
pmc-13304924: Indriya Laras Pramesthi and co-authors issue a 2026 correction to a study of Indonesia's national school feeding program. The study looked at effects on child nutrition and school settings. One Ghana finding in the discussion was credited to the wrong source; the reference now points to Abizari and colleagues from 2014, with the full reference restored in the list. The notice states that results and conclusions stand, no discussion wording needed change, and the article has been updated with editor approval.
pmc-13305424:
Claudio Ucciferri and co-authors test adding an immune booster drug to HPV vaccination for men with stubborn infections in a 2026 pilot study. Vaccines prevent new infections well, but whether they help clear existing ones faster is unsettled.

Twenty-three men without HIV and with anal or genital infections received the nine-type vaccine alone or with pidotimod tablets around each dose. After twelve months the combined group carried far fewer lingering virus types per man than the vaccine-only group. Full clearance rates favored the combo too, though the tiny sample kept that gap from firm proof. Pre-exposure HIV prevention drugs tied to slower clearance.
pmc-13305524:
Catarina Simões, Margarida Vieira, and Ana Paula Sapeta explore how family caregivers grieve before a loved one's death in a 2026 grounded theory study. Care before death shapes grief after it, yet nurses rarely map that early phase closely.

Semi-structured interviews with 20 bereaved caregivers who lost an adult family member to chronic illness grounded the analysis. Fitting into the caregiver role and bracing for loss formed the twin adaptation work, with awareness of the illness gravity opening grief itself.
