Information access, satisfaction with care, recognition of effort, and feelings of abandonment all colored the process.
pmc-13305924:
Haisong Xu compared liver surgery with and without augmented reality guidance in a 2026 hospital study. Ninety-six patients with liver cancer had laparoscopic removal between January 2019 and December 2021, split into three care groups.

One group had navigation help with non-anatomical removal, while two groups had standard anatomical or non-anatomical surgery. Starting traits were similar across groups in the reported checks. Navigation cases finished faster and lost less blood, with median loss of 125ml in that group. Follow-up ran to 36 months, and the authors present navigation as a useful aid for orientation and precision.
pmc-13306224:
Urszula Leszczyńska and co-authors study in 2026 whether the immune protein lactoferrin can help a newly isolated virus that attacks Staphylococcus aureus. Phages, viruses that infect bacteria, offer an alternative when antibiotics fail against resistant skin infections. The phage, named vB_Sau-E, was characterised for growth and killing range.

The phage infected twelve of twenty-two resistant clinical isolates, with a life cycle near thirty minutes. Lactoferrin raised plating efficiency and kept the phage stable at mild acidity and in frozen storage. Combined use also added antibacterial effect, although strength varied by strain. Skin cell tests supported compatibility with human tissue models. The authors propose lactoferrin as a stabilising partner for phage treatment of staphylococcal skin infections, especially where biofilms block antibiotics.
pmc-13306824:
Antonio Ivanov reviewed why reusing old drugs for new diseases stalls before reaching patients in a 2026 scoping review. A total of 73 articles from two databases were sorted into scientific, clinical, legal, money and delivery barriers.

Moving candidates into care was the central block, since fresh mid and late trials must still prove benefit, safety and dose in each new use. Cancer subgroup quirks, infection drug access problems and scarce rare-disease data added field-specific drag. Off-patent drugs also lack profit protection to draw private funding, trapping academic teams at an institutional bottleneck.
pmc-13307124:
Jorge Crespo-Sánchez chose best 3D printing settings for two unlike polymers by weighing heat behaviour in a 2026 study. Flexible TPU 95A and high-performance Z-PEEK were printed under planned parameter sets, then pulled and flexed across temperatures.

Analysis of variance showed which settings mattered for each material, covering peak pull force, stretch and stiffness at chosen heats. Entropy weights and a compromise ranking method then picked balanced winners for service above room temperature. The framework answers a common gap where room-temperature tests alone mislead functional part design.
pmc-13307924:
Milad Golsharifi, Nita Rajan, and Solomon Pudi describe seven patients in 2026 with benign bone death in the ear canal, a rare condition easily mistaken for malignant or aggressive ear disease. Records came from one British ear clinic between 2023 and 2025. Diagnosis required examination, biopsy, cultures, and high-resolution scans.

All seven patients healed with conservative care: repeated gentle cleaning and topical antimicrobial treatment over three to eight months. None needed surgery or oxygen therapy. Three patients had taken bone-protecting drugs for years, and three used hearing aids, both known risk factors. Biopsies showed chronic inflammation and dead bone fragments without cancer in every case. The authors insist biopsy and scanning remain mandatory to exclude look-alike diseases. Awareness matters most, they argue, for patients on antiresorptive drugs or wearing hearing aids.
pmc-13308324:
Bethany M Potter and co-authors review in 2026 linked pairs of microbe signals, called chimeric PAMPs, as vaccine boosters that wake the innate immune arm. Each signal in a pair hits a unlike sensor on immune cells, and linking them with a chemical bond forces both signals into the same cell.

Linked pairs often sparked stronger joint action than the same signals merely mixed, across infection, allergy, and cancer settings in the work reviewed. Linking can also cut the harm that single signals cause at high doses in some cases. Not every pair works, and how link shape and pair choice steer the response stays poorly known. Those gaps set the next tests for the field.
pmc-13308624:
Yue Li and co-authors present in 2026 a skin patch of liquid metal, named HELP, that tracks breathing and heart signals at home for chronic lung disease. Home care lacks tools that stay true, straight, and steady over long wear, so the team rebuilt both the stuff and the shape.

Silver wires alloyed with indium anchor the metal and stop drift, while graded bumps act as strain gates that open in steps. Readings stayed straight with tiny lag, felt strain as low as 0.01 percent, and lasted past half a million bends in lab tests. Trial runs caught sleep apnea, asthma drug response, and night oxygen dips that day checks missed.
pmc-13308724:
Eglė Vasylė and co-authors study in 2026 tiny RNA switches in two eosinophil subtypes in allergic asthma, white cells that drive airway swelling. Their group held 13 patients and 16 healthy people, and patients faced a mite allergen challenge with blood drawn again after 24 hours.

Two switches ran high in both cell types before the challenge, and one sat higher in the roving type than in the lung settled type. After the challenge, one switch fell in roving cells yet rose in settled cells in the same patients. Two switches stayed high in blood plasma after the challenge, which hints they mark long term swelling more than the fresh flare.
pmc-13310624:
Lauren C Cutmore and colleagues engineer immune cells in 2026 to hunt cancers arising from gamma-delta T cells, a rare T cell class with no approved targeted treatment. The team built chimeric antigen receptors aimed at the gamma-delta receptor itself, varying the targeting fragment, hinge, and costimulatory parts. Candidate receptors were screened by cytokine release against receptor-bearing target cells.

Two targeting fragments showed clean specificity, and one design, labelled MGDL, transferred into T cells most efficiently. Among three MGDL versions, the one using CD28 parts released the most cytokine on target contact. In two mouse models of gamma-delta leukaemia, that version gave the strongest anti-leukaemia activity and the longest survival. Cancers of this type, including hepatosplenic lymphoma, carry grim outlooks with median survival sometimes under a year. The authors support moving the winning design into a clinical trial.
pmc-13310824:
Mackenzie Bourke led a 2026 interview study on whether standard life quality forms fit people with rare genetic conditions and their carers. Forms built for general health may miss key parts of rare disease life. The team asked adults, carers, and proxies for children to speak aloud while filling in three forms.

Sixty interviews took place in Australia and England. Most people grasped the forms and backed their use for patients. Carers wanted a wider lens than health alone. Missed themes included drug access, work and money strain, doubt, passing a condition to children, and care system strain. Broader forms may serve carers better.
pmc-13310924:
Johannes Fischer and colleagues track metal markers in welders across blood, serum, and urine in a 2026 pilot study. Welding fumes mix many metals, and manganese draws concern for nerve harm. Blood manganese is widely used yet may miss true exposure, so the team tested several fluids at once.

Twelve welders and matched controls gave samples before and after shifts, with 17 metals measured. Urine levels of several metals ran higher in welders, while blood manganese barely split the groups. Serum and urine manganese split groups more clearly. Welders also showed high ferritin with low related markers, which hints at shifted iron stores. Respirator use shaped levels.
pmc-13311124:
Rongyu Liang and co-authors study sense of coherence in stable schizophrenia inpatients in a 2026 survey. Sense of coherence, the feeling that life is clear, manageable, and meaningful, aids stress coping and recovery. Its drivers in settled inpatients were little known, so traits, support, and health facts were mapped together.

A poll covered 438 inpatients at a Guangzhou hospital from late 2024 to early 2025. Scores were compared across age, illness, and social groups, and links with Big Five traits and support were modeled. Results should guide personal resilience plans that lift recovery and daily function. Full driver ranks await wider samples for proof.
pmc-13311324:
Xingyu Wang, Hao Lv, Long Liang, and Ting Jiang test in 2026 whether osteoporosis and arthritis travel together, and whether one might cause the other. Survey data from a national American health examination programme fed the observational half. Genetic instruments from large genome studies fed a Mendelian randomisation half, which uses inherited variants to probe causality.

In the survey, people with osteoporosis had about seventy-six percent higher odds of arthritis after adjustment, and the link survived missing-data checks. Genetic analysis tied osteoporosis to several inflammatory arthritides, including rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, lupus, and gout. No causal link appeared for osteoarthritis or its knee and hip forms. Sensitivity checks found no sign of the biases that usually undermine such genetic tests. Both diseases burden older adults heavily, so shared pathways matter for clinic planning. The authors read the pattern as partly causal, not mere co-occurrence.
pmc-13311624:
Yifan Yang and colleagues, in 2026, present a brain scan study on how sex and lupus status together shape the cortex. Lupus can affect the brain, and its course differs sharply by sex.

The study scanned 196 people: 30 men and 66 women with lupus, plus 33 male and 67 female healthy controls. Measures covered cortical thickness, folding, and groove depth in set regions. Two spots showed a clear sex-by-disease interplay, one in a left orbital groove and one in a left frontal groove. Thickness ran lower in lupus across much of both hemispheres. No firm link to disease activity scores appeared.
pmc-13311924:
Nima Alaeiilkhchi and co-authors give a 2026 systematic review on stopping versus continuing beta-blockers during hospital stays for acute heart failure. The right call during a flare has long been unsettled.

Searches through September 2025 found thirteen studies: one trial with 147 patients and twelve cohorts with 14,654. Pooled cohort data left the effect on in-hospital death unclear, with widely spread results. Short-term stopping may raise death risk up to three months, with a pooled hazard ratio of 2.30 across two studies in this review. The single trial was too small to settle anything. More trial data are needed.
pmc-13312024:
Molly A. Chakraborty and co-authors report, in a 2026 study, how patients fared with a second course of radiation given as protons after breast cancer returned in the same region. Pencil beam scanning proton therapy can shape dose tightly, which matters when nearby tissue has already been irradiated once.

The team reviewed 70 patients treated between 2019 and 2025 whose new radiation fields overlapped the old ones. Recurrence rates were 14 percent at two years and 17 percent at three years, while rib fractures developed in 21.1 percent of patients and tracked with chest wall dose measures. Severe side effects stayed limited, and the authors offer dose figures that can anchor safety limits for future repeat treatments.
pmc-13312824:
Ahmad Yusroni and co-authors write a 2026 letter to the editor about a study of dental decay microbes in elderly prisoners. The letter urges readers to treat the prison itself as part of the exposure. The original study compared saliva microbes in prisoners with and without cavities, a rare look at a little-studied population, and the letter writers welcome it while doubting its framing.

A restricted setting trims lifestyle variation, they argue. But it also patterns the microbial environment through fixed diet, scarce dental care, rationed hygiene supplies, fluoride access, antibiotics, and extraction habits, all set by the institution. Without recording those factors, microbe patterns risk being read as the person's own biology. The letter urges pairing future carceral microbiome work with a minimum institutional dataset covering attendance, supplies, diet rules, and treatment history. That would make results more interpretable and prevention planning sharper.
pmc-13312924:
Miyuki Suzuki and colleagues built, in a 2026 study, a glowing reporter frog that lets researchers watch peripheral nerves grow and regrow inside living limbs. Peripherin, a filament protein of peripheral nerves, rises during axon growth and repair, making its gene a natural beacon. First the team had to find the DNA switches that turn it on in neurons.

Promoter and intron tests pinned down the regulatory regions, and stable transgenic African clawed frog lines lit up brightly in developing nerve tissue and in tadpole limbs. Filming through development showed nerves threading the growing limb. During regeneration, young tadpole stumps drew modest early nerve entry much like first development, while post-metamorphic limbs were invaded extensively from the start, and adult forelimb nerves brightened as they regrew. The authors offer the line as a long-term window on neural remodeling.
pmc-13313024:
Hiam O Mulla maps, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, the Kell blood group antigens carried by Saudi blood donors at King Abdulaziz Medical City in Jeddah. The Kell system's K antigen is strongly immunogenic and can trigger transfusion reactions and hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn, so knowing its frequency guides safe blood banking for the region.

Standard immunohematology screening of 19,769 donors found the K antigen in 13.93 percent and its partner k antigen in 98.92 percent of the reported figures, with the K-negative, k-positive phenotype dominating at 86.07 percent. One vanishingly rare phenotype, negative for both antigens, appeared at 0.005 percent. K frequency differed significantly from donor pools in Saudi Arabia's central and southwestern regions but matched the west. As one of the country's largest such cohorts, the study gives transfusion services a baseline for matching blood to patients.
pmc-13313224:
Jihye Choi leads a 2026 study of school nurse training and how nurses talk with parents about the HPV vaccine. The vaccine can prevent six cancer types, yet US teens still get it at rates below targets, and school nurses are a trusted source of advice for families.

As part of the All for Them program, 72 school nurses and nurse managers in Texas took a continuing education course. The team used surveys before and after to gauge blocks to advising parents, faith in their own skill, and knowledge of HPV and its vaccine. Data ran from November 2021 to May 2023, and paired tests compared each nurse with herself. The study shows whether training can lift the talks that help parents say yes to vaccination.
pmc-13313524:
Owen Wong, Claire Mountford, and Stéfanie von Hlatky analyze, in a 2026 article, how Russia wields gender-based disinformation as a geopolitical weapon. Research on such campaigns usually stops at domestic social harm, leaving their foreign policy function underexplored. The authors ran a qualitative content analysis over 367 pro-Kremlin disinformation articles, looking for the stories they tell about gender and what strategic work those stories perform.

Eight recurring narratives emerged, all aimed at Western governments and bodies such as NATO and the European Union. Two mechanisms organize them: sabotaging the adversary's moral legitimacy and burnishing Russia's own. The content is tuned to resonate with conservative audiences abroad, turning culture-war material into leverage in great power competition. The authors frame this as hybrid warfare through identity, and argue analysts should read gendered disinformation as deliberate statecraft rather than background noise.
pmc-13314324:
Susumu Iwaide and co-authors train, in a 2026 study, a learning model to sort cattle liver lesions from slide images. Pathologists face lymphoma, necrosis, and fibrosis in bovine livers, and an automatic classifier could speed their work. The team assembled ten cases for each of the four classes, normal liver included. They scanned the slides and cut them into fifty patches per slide, then trained a DenseNet-based convolutional network with cross-validation and judged it on a test set.

The model classified test patches with 84.5 percent accuracy and an F1 score of 83.5 percent across labels. It handled necrosis and fibrosis confidently, with recall above ninety percent for both. It caught half the lymphoma patches, despite precision when it did commit. Normal liver showed the opposite problem, catching everything while over-calling. The authors call the performance promising for a support tool, with lymphoma detection the target for improvement.
pmc-13316224:
Faezeh Ghasemi and a very large team dissected in 2026 the expanded Ato transporter family in Candida albicans. That yeast lives in humans and must feed on alternative carbon when glucose runs low. Baker's yeast uses one Ato protein for acetate uptake, while Candida carries ten family members, most of unknown job.

Computer analysis of motifs, pore size, and binding sites suggested varied roles, and lab tests confirmed differing carboxylate transport. CaAto1 proved the main acetate carrier, driven by the proton gradient. Several members switched on with carboxylates and sat in the cell membrane, and gene fusion events shaped the family history.
pmc-13316624:
Sungje Park and a Korean team report a 2026 gene screen that found a fix for a factory headache. The human kidney cells used to make gene therapy viruses clump together in liquid culture. Clumping blocks the large-scale growth needed for adeno-associated virus production.

Using a virus-free CRISPR library, the team knocked out genes one by one and kept only cells that stayed floating. One gene, TM9SF2, stood out: removing it cut clumping by 53 percent and 28 percent in the two cell lines tested. Virus output, full particle share, and infectivity held steady for three virus types. The edit gives manufacturers a cleaner path to bigger batches.
pmc-13316824:
Xuejie Shao and co-authors test, in a 2026 study, a refined herbal blend called ECC-BYF against the broken air sac barrier in COPD, the chronic lung disease where that barrier drives decline. The blend comes from the Bufei Yishen formula, a traditional prescription.

Rats made ill with smoke and repeated infection breathed and healed better on the blend, with tidier air sac cells and stronger barrier proteins. Lung wash fluid showed more of a calming signal and less of three inflammatory ones. In dish-grown lung cells, the blend likewise restored barrier proteins and blocked a key inflammatory switch, p38 MAPK; a compound that reopens that switch erased the benefit. The pathway anchors the formula's claim.
pmc-13318624:
Junnan Chen and colleagues review, in 2026, how pancreatic cancer spreads across the lining of the abdomen, a pattern that sharply worsens survival and quality of life. Their account follows the step-by-step route cancer cells take from the main tumour to new growths.

Key steps covered include cells breaking away, changing character, resisting death signals, escaping immune attack, sticking to the abdominal lining, and growing new blood vessels. Four linked drivers get special attention: altered energy use, tiny vesicles that carry messages between cells, stem-like cancer cells, and a reshaped immune setting. The review closes with treatments delivered inside the abdomen, in normal, heated, or pressurised forms, and their possible pairing with immunotherapy.
pmc-13318824:
Anteneh M. Feyissa writes a 2026 commentary on sleep, thinking, and dementia risk in focal epilepsy. He discusses a Neurology study by Tai and co-workers using the UK Biobank cohort. Sleep disruption and cognitive problems are common partners of this epilepsy type. Whether sleep changes long-term dementia risk was unclear.

The discussed study followed 482,207 participants without dementia at baseline. Sleep of six to eight hours counted as optimal. That pattern linked to better executive function in epilepsy, stroke, and control groups alike. The benefit was significantly stronger in focal epilepsy than in controls. People with epilepsy and poor sleep faced a fivefold dementia risk against well-sleeping controls. Their hazard ratio was 5.15 in the reported model. Feyissa presents better sleep as a promising protective target.
pmc-13320424:
Brandy T. Cervantes and co-authors describe twenty six years of ocean buoy data from a marine sanctuary off Washington State in a 2026 data article. The sanctuary, named in 1994, sits in a rich cold current system rocked by heat waves, warm phase years, low oxygen, and acid seas. Four coastal treaty tribes hold protected rights to sea goods there, so sound local sea records carry legal as well as science weight.

Buoys at fifteen sites on five cross shelf lines have logged water heat, salt, oxygen, pressure, and flow since 2000, chiefly in the summer upwelling season. Two sites also log winter heat all year in recent runs. Cleaned joined series now sit in a public store for free reuse in climate and care of the sanctuary.
pmc-13321024:
Yu-Yang Sha and a large team map the state of medical large language models in a 2026 review. Such models now help with decision support, note writing, patient messages, image plus text analysis, and remote care. Fast growth has raised hard questions about reliability and safe use in real clinics.

Clinical value, the authors argue, cannot rest on test scores alone. Models must rest on sound evidence, stay in line with current medical knowledge, and fit daily workflows. Gaps remain in how models are judged, kept up to date, and kept safe once deployed. Stronger clinical trials and careful rollout across settings are presented as the way forward.
pmc-13321224:
Jyoti Lama and a large team search, in 2026, for genetic variants that predict eye pressure rises after steroid treatment. Some patients develop ocular hypertension from glucocorticoid medicines, including eye injections used for diabetic macular swelling. Knowing who is vulnerable could guide monitoring.

Discovery data came from 530 participants in fluocinolone implant trials, with pressure measured repeatedly during six months after exposure. Genotyping and exome sequencing were combined with a replication cohort of 588 clinic patients. One variant near a gene involved in protein tagging reached genome-wide significance, and a second variant in the same region held up in the combined analysis. Tissue data linked the region to regulation of that gene in several organs including the aorta. A rare-variant analysis flagged one further gene after correction.
pmc-13323224:
Mahmoud Albashier leads a review comparing two enoxaparin doses after bariatric surgery, published in 2026, for preventing venous blood clots. Obesity changes how this blood thinner behaves in the body, so the standard 40 mg dose may under-protect surgical patients.

Following PRISMA guidance, the team searched five databases to September 2025 for trials and cohort studies of 40 mg against 60 mg dosing. Ten studies with 1,276 patients qualified. The main outcome was reaching target anti-factor Xa levels, with clots, bleeding, deaths and other complications also tracked. Random-effects pooling compared drug levels and clinical events, aiming to judge whether higher dosing protects without added bleeding harm.
pmc-13324524:
Wei Mao and colleagues compare how astringency unfolds in green, black, and oolong teas in a 2026 sensory study. The drying, puckering feel shapes whether buyers like a tea, yet most past checks scored it at one moment only.

Six teas were tracked with time-intensity scoring, dominance tracking, an electronic tongue, and LC-MS chemistry. Green tea hit a higher peak, lasted longer, and started faster than the others. Tasters called green tea harsh and grainy, black tea smooth and dry, and oolong tea rough and dry in turns. Chemistry tied strong astringency to anthocyanins, quercetin forms, and catechin products. The type and structure of polyphenols seem to set both strength and character.
pmc-13325124:
Hongyi Cheng and co-authors show that a skin channel boosts the nerve signal from electroacupuncture in a 2026 mouse study. The channel TRPV4 senses pressure and stretch, but it sits in skin cells rather than in nerves themselves.

Calcium imaging in living mice watched sensory neurons at the fourth lumbar ganglion during hindpaw stimulation. Stronger current at 2 mA recruited more neurons than 0.5 mA stimulation did. Staining found TRPV4 in skin macrophages, not in the sensory neurons. A drug that opens TRPV4 raised neuron activity, while a blocker cut the acupuncture response. The results cast skin immune cells as early partners in how acupuncture signals begin.
pmc-13325324:
Xin-Xiang Lim and co-authors survey interdisciplinary learning in a forensic science program in a 2026 education study. Forensic work joins science with law, so graduates must blend fields and judge evidence across them.

Across six semesters from 2022 to 2024, 260 undergraduate and postgraduate students rated their skills on an 18-item survey. Interdisciplinary skills scored highest, at a mean of 4.33 on the five-point scale. Reflective behavior lagged at 3.89, and grasp of other fields views trailed at 3.83 on the same scale. Students felt strong at merging knowledge but weaker at weighing the limits of each field. The authors advise more direct coaching in reflection.
pmc-13325724:
Rahul S. Nanduri and colleagues recount an eye tumor that hid behind a wrong diagnosis for three years in a 2026 case report. Medulloepithelioma is a rare tumor of the ciliary body that can invade nearby eye tissues.

A 54-year-old woman came in with falling vision in her left eye and signs read as a vasoproliferative retinal tumor. She received freezing treatment, a scleral buckle, and several vitrectomies without success. When the blind eye turned painful, it was removed, and pathology revealed a malignant teratoid medulloepithelioma invading iris, choroid, retina, and beyond. Radiation followed, with no spread found. The authors urge ultrasound checks of the ciliary body in such cases.
pmc-13326124:
Saba Alyas and co-authors interview asthma patients in Malaysia about managing their own care in a 2026 qualitative study. Daily self-management keeps asthma in check, but habits and beliefs shape how well it works.

Nineteen adults spoke in semi-structured interviews held from February to May 2025, online and in person. Patients understood their disease and most care tasks well, yet self-monitoring habits lagged. Confidence, faith in traditional remedies, and views on inhalers all steered practice. Work hazards and passive smoke stood out as barriers. The authors suggest counseling seminars and personal action plans as supports, plus policy action on smoke exposure at work.
pmc-13327524:
Yajing Zhou and co-authors propose a new statistics method in a 2026 article on causal mediation with continuous treatments. Standard tools handle yes-or-no treatments well, but dose-like treatments plus thousands of possible background factors strain them. Their framework joins variable selection with propensity modeling in a weighted semiparametric design.

Tests in simulation showed better variable picking and more efficient estimates than rival regularization methods, because outcome-linked factors were kept and noise factors dropped. The team then applied the method to UK Biobank data, measuring how much of the link between diabetes risk and cancer runs through apolipoprotein B levels. The approach offers a steadier balance of accuracy, clarity, and strength for large biomedical datasets.
pmc-13328024:
Ashit Kumar Dutta and co-authors review AI and eye-tracking methods for screening dyslexia in a 2026 article. Formal reading assessments take much time and staff, limiting how many children can be checked early. The team searched four databases for studies from January 2015 to March 2026 that used eye movement data, with or without predictive models.

Twenty-three papers qualified, including fourteen on machine learning prediction models, and samples ranged from under twenty people to over three hundred. Dyslexic readers consistently showed longer fixations, more backward eye jumps, and weaker forward jump efficiency while reading. Models built on those signals could sort readers well, pointing to low-cost screening that flags risk before failure sets in.
pmc-13328524:
Shuo Li and co-authors study in 2026 how lighting changes contact-free heart rate checks that use face video. Such methods read tiny colour shifts in skin as blood flows. The team split the face into 15 regions based on anatomy. They tested each region on two public video sets with four different signal methods.

Three areas held up best under hard lighting: the space between the brows, the bridge of the nose, and the cheeks. Using several regions together beat using one region alone or the whole face. The findings offer practical guidance for building camera-based heart rate tools that stay accurate when light is uneven or weak.
pmc-13332124:
Mengru Yang and co-authors argue in a 2026 review that cancer treatment should stop trying to simply dissolve the stiff tissue around tumors. In cancers such as pancreatic and breast tumors, the extracellular matrix can grow five to ten times stiffer than normal tissue, shutting immune cells out and teaching them to tolerate the tumor.

Breaking that matrix down wholesale has failed in trials and may even help cancer spread, so the authors propose rebuilding a healthy stiffness instead. They define a mechano-therapeutic window, a stiffness range where immune entry and drug response peak without raising spread risk. Smart nanoparticles could soften tissue in a controlled priming step before immunotherapy, chemotherapy, or radiation, and future carriers might sense stiffness and adjust in real time. The framework targets scar-like solid tumors where physical barriers block treatment.
pmc-13333624:
Lucinda Grummitt and co-authors describe a 2026 mixed-methods study of the KidsXpress School Partnership Program in Australian primary schools. The program places creative expressive therapists and trauma consultants inside schools to support children affected by trauma.

Five primary schools took part, and the team gathered surveys and interviews from teachers, therapists, and consultants. They also tracked wellbeing scores for students referred to therapy, using the Child Outcome Rating Scale from first to last session. The evaluation used the RE-AIM framework to judge reach, uptake, and delivery in real school settings. Early evidence on how such whole-school, trauma-informed support works in practice can guide schools planning similar partnerships.
pmc-13334124:
So Young Lim wrote a 2026 narrative review of syndromic craniosynostosis, where several skull sutures fuse early alongside facial and neurological problems. The review centers on raised pressure inside the skull, skull base pathology, and surgical management.

Older thinking blamed high pressure mainly on a too-small cranial vault. Newer evidence spreads the blame: faulty spinal fluid circulation, venous hypertension, blocked upper airways, and early fusion of skull base joints all contribute. In Crouzon syndrome especially, premature skull base fusion lines up with returning pressure problems and repeat vault surgery. Many patients keep near-normal skull volume through compensating growth, so pressure symptoms can be vague and easy to miss. The review gathers clinical, imaging, and institutional experience to guide monitoring and operations.
pmc-13335324:
Kaustubh Kishor Jadhav and colleagues study 2026 metabolite patterns in adolescent depression using a focused approach. Depression ranks among the top causes of death around the world and keeps growing as a public health worry. Most past work has centered on adults, even though evidence shows the teen years often mark the start of mental health problems. Metabolite profiling reflects ongoing bodily chemical processes, offering a promising avenue to find possible signs of disease state.

The study aims to find early occurring blood patterns linked to teen depression. The study compared 204 teens with clinical depression against 78 healthy peers, using focused nuclear magnetic resonance scans on serum samples. In total, 250 blood measures were counted, including absolute levels and percent measures.
pmc-13336024:
Takuya Kuwahara and colleagues study 2026 shear-induced appearance of ring-shaped ultra-low-friction contact layers in glassy carbon, foreign atoms and atomic-scale workings. Mismatched graphite contact layers represent a classic friction system to achieve ultra-low friction. Another route uses shear-induced ring-forming of glassy carbon.

This process occurs right at surface rough contacts, relying on foreign atoms like hydrogen and oxygen. To address these gaps, the authors undertake a careful computer study with 1,000 1-ns-long quantum molecule motion runs of sheared glassy carbon with and without foreign atoms. No ring-shaped contact layers emerge for four-valent systems like pure or silicon-doped glassy carbon, while shear-induced ring-forming is always observed for foreign atoms with valency lower than four.
pmc-13336224:
Marina Melo Martin and co-authors profiled young adults treated in intensive care for COVID-19 in São Paulo in a 2026 retrospective study. Most pandemic ICU research centered on older patients, leaving the young adult picture thinner.

The longitudinal study covered 105 patients aged 20 to 40 admitted between April 2021 and December 2022 at a university hospital. Mortality reached 27.6 percent. Sex, ethnicity, arriving from the emergency room, hemodynamic instability, and use of vasoactive drugs, ventilation, heparin, and corticosteroids all associated with death, as did C-reactive protein, lactate, and lymphocyte levels. Raised lactate and longer time on vasoactive drugs emerged as risk factors. The profile helps intensivists spot which younger patients are sliding toward danger.
pmc-13336424:
Luxiang Zhao and co-authors built a fully flexible cold plasma patch for skin cancer treatment in a 2026 device study. Plasma devices promise noninvasive therapy with reactive species, but rigid hardware touches skin poorly and flexes not at all.

The All-Flex Plasma Patch stretches, runs on ambient air, and presses reactive oxygen and nitrogen species through skin better than rigid sources. In a mouse melanoma model, one week of treatment shrank tumors to one nineteenth of the control volume in their comparison. Proteomic work showed the treatment rewires tumor metabolism and disturbs calcium balance through several newly reported protein targets. The team also mapped an exposure window, since excessive dosing provoked adverse responses, and reported minimal systemic burden at tuned settings.
pmc-13337124:
Liping Yang and colleagues traced a gene that drives escalating cocaine use to a brain reward hub, in a 2026 rat study. The gene ANKS1B had already surfaced as a shared risk factor for heroin, methamphetamine, and alcohol dependence in human genetics. Here the team asked what it does in the nucleus accumbens as cocaine intake grows out of control.

Long-access cocaine lowered ANKS1B in that hub, and tuning its level changed escalation and later drug seeking without touching baseline intake. ANKS1B binds the acetyltransferase CBP, steering histone acetylation that represses the factor FoxO3. The chain marks ANKS1B and its epigenetic partners as candidate targets for curbing compulsive drug use.
pmc-13337424:
Zsuzsanna Szőke and colleagues describe a first-of-its-kind deer case in a 2026 report from Hungary. A middle-aged fallow deer hind, aged 6–7 years and in good condition, was legally culled and examined after death. The team found retained fetal skull bones in the front vagina and a smooth-muscle tumor, a leiomyoma, in the left uterine horn.

Tissue study and a desmin stain backed the tumor diagnosis, claimed as the first published uterine leiomyoma in this species. Gene sequencing compared microbes from the healthy horn, the tumor tissue, and feces; the tumor sample resembled feces, with more Bacteroides and Escherichia–Shigella. As a single case with no treatment, it can only hint that blockage and retained material may reshape local microbes.
pmc-13337624:
Aleigha Lawless and colleagues gave real world results in 2026 for immune drugs given around surgery for melanoma that can be cut out. Trials favour giving immune drugs before surgery over after surgery alone, yet the best plan around surgery and sound blood markers remain unsettled. The team looked back at care, outcomes, and safety in patients treated in routine clinics.

Whether small surgery after pre surgery drugs is safe and whether tumour DNA in blood can flag relapse were key questions. Real world data of this kind help doctors judge whether trial gains hold in day to day care and which patients need close watch. The findings back refining surgery plans while stronger blood marker proof is awaited.
pmc-13338424:
Thystere Matondo Bantidi and colleagues tested a traffic light warning idea in 2026 for volcanic eruptions at eight well watched volcanoes. Eruptions often follow rock failure around magma paths, and a falling b value in quake data tends to precede failure, signalling rising stress. The team asked whether that signal can sharpen near real time forecasts.

They flagged red light when b values fell more than 10 percent below background and checked whether eruptions followed within 10 days. Sites spanned Iceland, Hawaii, and Japan, giving varied tectonic settings. The system offers a simple, testable rule for eruption priming, though local calibration will decide its worth at each volcano.
pmc-13339024:
Gonzalo Gomez-Munoz and a large team write periodic patterns on conductive glass with ultrafast lasers in a 2026 study. Fluorine-doped tin oxide films gain rippled structures that split electrical behavior by direction. Such surfaces could serve as clear heaters, sensors, or switchable wetting bases.

Films were scanned with high-rate femtosecond pulses at 1030 nm under varied power, pulse length, and overlap. Good pattern spread depended on how fluorine content evolved during writing as reported. Uneven fluorine in starting films caused problems the authors discuss frankly. Still, strongly directional surfaces formed at scan speeds above 1.0 m per second in the reported runs.
pmc-13341324:
Ping Jin and colleagues tested a new drug, BGM0504, in 2026 in Chinese adults with type 2 diabetes, comparing it with semaglutide. The multicentre, randomised, placebo controlled trial assigned 64 adults to BGM0504 at 5, 10, or 15 milligrams, placebo, or semaglutide 1 milligram, each once weekly for twelve weeks. Safety, drug levels, drug effects, and efficacy were all tracked.

The main endpoint was change in HbA1c from baseline, with fasting glucose, two hour glucose, and body weight as secondary endpoints. Early phase trials of this kind test whether a new drug merits larger trials. The comparison with semaglutide gives a first read on relative potency and tolerability.
pmc-13341424:
An eyebrow cyst that lingered 29 years is reported by Yanpeng Zhu and coauthors in their 2026 case report. Pilonidal sinus usually appears near the tailbone; facial cases number only about 10 worldwide, all on the cheek, and none had formed a bridging scar before.

The 56-year-old man's trouble began with a school injury, leaving swelling and drainage beside his right eyebrow plus a scar band toward the nose that tugged at his vision. Staged surgery, tissue expansion, and scar revision, followed by three injection sessions, cleared the lesion. Tissue study confirmed chronic pilonidal sinus. At one year, appearance and visual field had improved without recurrence.
pmc-13341524:
Screening dialysis patients for depression with machine learning is developed by Yugang Cao's team in a 2026 multicenter study. The project enrolled 601 peritoneal dialysis patients from two hospitals, counting a Self-Rating Depression Scale score of 53 or more as high symptoms.

Six factors survived selection: age, peritonitis, catheter problems, anxiety score, social support score, and time on dialysis. Among nine models, XGBoost did best with an outside testing AUC of 0.869. The team built an online visualization tool for bedside use and confirmed subgroup differences. Early flagging could connect kidney patients with mental health help sooner.
pmc-13341624:
Healthcare workers' willingness to screen for dormant tuberculosis is surveyed by Yalan Liu's team in a 2026 Chongqing study. Staff at 46 named institutions across 31 districts answered a structured form on knowledge, attitudes, and acceptance of screening and preventive care.

Of 1,022 respondents, 39.7% had limited knowledge and 67.4% had never been screened, yet most would accept screening (78.7% of them) and preventive treatment (93.3% of them). Fear of drug side effects dominated refusal of treatment at 79.4% of those who refused. Prior screening experience raised screening acceptance odds fivefold, with an odds ratio of 5.145 in the model. Department, job type, and years on the job each shaped willingness, pointing to focused staff training.
pmc-13341724:
Expert consensus on safe teen technology use is built by Andrés Arana-Rodríguez's team, in their 2026 Delphi study. A mixed expert panel worked through three rounds between November 2024 and June 2025, proposing, voting on, and rating measures for schools and families.

Of 100 invited experts, 38 joined, with round replies falling from 28 to 17. Consensus was set at 80% agreement and very high agreement at 95%, and a composite score ranked measures into three relevance levels. Risks covered span problem use, health misinformation, cyberbullying, and unsuitable content. The resulting framework aims to give policy and practice shared, evidence-based priorities.
pmc-13341824:
The tumor neighborhood decides whether engineered T cells succeed, in a 2026 review by Helen P. Cashman and Cameron J. Turtle on large B-cell lymphoma. CD19 CAR-T therapy transformed care for relapsed disease, yet over half of patients never reach durable remission.

The authors synthesize how tissue structure, cell mix, molecular signals, and spatial layout inside tumors shape response, including suppressive elements that blunt the infused cells. New CAR designs aim to reprogram that environment rather than merely punch through it. Reading these ecosystems will need tools that fuse many data types at once, a methodological frontier the review maps in detail.
pmc-13341924:
A celebrated gut microbe cuts both ways in heart disease, in a 2026 review by Shihao Li and colleagues on Akkermansia muciniphila. The mucus-living bacterium supports gut barrier repair, steadier glucose and lipids, and calmer immunity, protecting against hypertension, atherosclerosis, heart failure, and aortic aneurysm in studies.

Yet when the barrier is damaged or fiber is scarce, it can overgrow, chew through mucus, and worsen inflammation. Diet, drugs, and each person's starting microbiome shift its abundance, so blanket supplementation is risky. The authors call for strain-level clarity, safe dosing, and smarter delivery before clinical use.
pmc-13342124:
When childhood harm happens may decide how it echoes into adult relationships, in a 2026 study by Siyao Yan's team. Forms from 856 Chinese adults fed a new integrative model tested with structural equations, cross-checks, and sensitivity checks against relationship addiction.

Infancy risk worked by a side path, damaging attachment security (β 0.21), while late school-age risk hit head-on and harder (β 0.34). The maternal attachment pathway ran twice the paternal one, and ego-resiliency plus family routines each cushioned damage at key nodes. One-size trauma theory, the authors conclude, flattens pathways that prevention could actually target.
pmc-13342324:
André Pontes-Silva and colleagues probed missing data methods in 2026 for fibromyalgia drug trials, with hands on guidance for linear mixed models. Many fibromyalgia trials still use weak methods, such as dropping volunteers with gaps in data, which skews results and wastes data. The methods paper weighs repeated measures ANOVA against linear mixed model routes within an intention to treat frame.

A step by step guide for linear mixed models in SPSS is given, next to a review of recent trials that flags common long term analysis flaws. Better gap handling lifts fibromyalgia proof, where dropouts and shifting symptoms are common. The guidance helps trial teams analyse all randomised volunteers soundly.
pmc-13343224:
Kathryn Fletcher and co-authors explore how people experience ketamine-assisted psychotherapy for methamphetamine use disorder in a 2026 qualitative study. Treatment options for this addiction stay limited, and little was known about how patients themselves read the therapy, so the team interviewed 14 people after they finished an open-label pilot program.

Four themes emerged. Patients entered after past treatments failed and felt held by a structured, caring setting. They entered altered states with quieter emotional and mental reactivity. Then they turned those shifts into changed drug use, with uneven success. Patients described ketamine as opening psychological space for therapy work. Lasting change seemed to hinge on continued therapy, motivation, and life context.
pmc-13343524:
Antônio Vinícius Pimentel Lima and co-authors update treatment of carotid artery narrowing in a 2026 narrative review. Fatty narrowing of these neck arteries causes roughly a tenth of ischemic strokes. Care has widened from surgery alone to strong drug therapy, endarterectomy, and stenting. Fresh 2025 trial data are shaking old assumptions.

In CREST-2, adding stenting to top medical therapy beat drugs alone on the four-year combined endpoint, while adding surgery did not reach significance. ECST-2 found no gain from intervention in lower-risk patients at two years. Modern drug control now anchors all care, the authors argue, with procedures reserved for selected patients guided by plaque and personal risk.
pmc-13343924:
Amy L. Forehand and co-authors uncover a surprising zinc-starvation trick in the gonorrhea germ in 2026. Neisseria gonorrhoeae steals zinc from human guard proteins. How its inner machinery copes when zinc runs low was unknown. The team tracked two spare ribosomal proteins switched on under zinc shortage.

Unlike in other bacteria, where spare parts keep growth brisk, the gonococcus mixes old and new ribosome parts side by side. The slowdown may be the point: easing off protein making could stretch survival against the host's metal-withholding defenses.
pmc-13346024:
Christopher R. VanDreumel and co-authors review three rare chest-center conditions in 2026: acute mediastinitis, mediastinal granuloma, and fibrosing mediastinitis. Each attacks the same crowded space by a different route, so the team searched a decade of literature to set their causes, care, and outlook side by side.

Acute infection, usually after surgery, a torn food pipe, or a deep neck abscess, kills often and demands fast, aggressive care. Granulomas left by old infection mostly sit quietly and can even vanish, harming only when bulk presses on neighbors. Fibrosing disease slowly strangles vessels and airways with scar, resists treatment, and carries the grimmest outlook of the three.
pmc-13347324:
Sunisa Suwatthi and colleagues turn pineapple leaf fibre into sound-absorbing material that also resists flame, in a materials study from 2026. Leaves left from farming are rich in cellulose and full of pores, which suits nonwoven panels. Yet that same makeup burns easily and fails building fire rules, so fibres were cleaned by enzyme routes and padded with phosphorus flame retardants.

Oil applied before the flame treatment spread the coating better, and those fibres and panels passed the vertical burn checks best in the reported tests. Noise reduction values stayed in the 0.55 to 0.60 range after finishing, which means fire treatment did not spoil sound uptake. Farm waste could thus serve in safer building panels.
pmc-13349824:
Lang Wang and co-authors reviewed small-sided games as basketball training in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. They searched five databases through early January 2026 for randomised trials comparing these scaled-down games with traditional training.

Nine trials covering 180 players qualified. Players in small-sided games improved more in agility, shooting, passing, and dribbling than those in traditional training. Clear advantages were not shown for every physical measure, such as aerobic fitness, sprinting, and jumping. Because the format keeps players involved with the ball in game-like settings, it may build skill and quickness together. More and larger trials would firm up the picture.
pmc-13349924:
Yi Wu and co-authors hunted for breast cancer genes tied to the drug vinorelbine in a 2026 combined data and lab study. They screened public cancer databases for genes that both changed in breast cancer and related to the drug, then tested which predicted survival.

Eight genes passed, including BRCA1 and TGFB1, and a survival forest model plus a nomogram built on them predicted patient outcomes well. Pathway and immune analyses linked the genes to cancer growth routes and the tumour's immune setting, and single-cell data added detail. Lab testing confirmed gene expression patterns. Such genes could help match patients to vinorelbine-based treatment.
pmc-13350024:
Marcos Vidal-Manrique and a large team engineered natural killer cells in 2026 to resist suppression inside tumours. Their cells are grown from stem cells under clean production rules. A tumour signal, prostaglandin E2, blunts them through its EP2 and EP4 receivers. The cells also fade without support.

Deleting both receivers with gene editing fully restored growth and killing power. This held even in prostaglandin-rich settings. Adding a built-in IL-15 support tether helped the cells survive without outside growth factors. They also kept attacking several tumour targets. Combining both changes yields NK cells that persist and keep working in hostile tumour surroundings.
pmc-13350524:
Ruijin Lu and co-authors introduced a statistical method in 2026 for picking predictive signals from repeated body chemistry profiles over time. Data such as microbe or fat profiles are proportions that shift irregularly, and most tools handle either the proportion problem or the timing problem, not both.

Their method hunts a few time-changing ratios between components that predict an outcome, smoothing each person's trajectory mathematically so sparse and dense sampling both work. Simulations beat snapshot methods on accuracy and precision. Applied to pregnancy lipid data, it found one interpretable fat ratio that predicted large babies more stably than rival approaches.
pmc-13350624:
Dominik Jarczak and a large international team reported real-world use of intravenous fosfomycin for brain and spinal cord infections in a 2026 interim analysis of the FORTRESS study. The wider study had enrolled 1,019 patients with severe infections by June 2025.

Central nervous system infections kill and disable often, and many antibiotics barely reach the spinal fluid. Fosfomycin crosses well and covers a broad range of germs, making it a partner drug in combinations. The subgroup analysis records how it was actually used, whether treatment succeeded by its end, and what side effects appeared, evidence doctors need when resistance narrows their choices.
pmc-13353224:
Ron Aldwin S Navales and co-authors feed S-abscisic acid to nursery pigs and track growth and antioxidant status in 2026. A total of 320 pigs, weaned at about 18 days and starting at 5.4 kg, ate a shared first diet for 7 days. Pens were then assigned a standard diet or the same diet with S-abscisic acid at 0.5, 1.0, or 5.0 mg per kilogram.

Treatments ran through two phases ending at day 35, with weekly growth checks. Blood at set days measured glutathione forms and serum antioxidant capacity, plus enzyme and damage markers. At the end, gut lining from three bowel sections was sampled for glutathione. The design tests whether a plant hormone supplement can support young pig health after weaning.
pmc-13353924:
Carmen López-Carriches and co-authors surveyed body-wide ills among people attending a dental clinic, ran the snapshot study in 2026. Knowing a patient's chronic problems helps dentists avoid harm and medical emergencies, mainly during oral surgery. Yet the pattern of disease in an ordinary dental people is rarely told of in detail.

The team studied medical questionnaires from 862 people seen over six months, using descriptive statistics to summarise age, sex, and told of problems. The results sketch which body-wide ills dentists most often encounter. The study supports better pre-care screening and safer planning for people with complex medical histories.
pmc-13354824:
Eda Nur İnkaya and co-authors expose mice to two persistent pollutants, PFOS and PFOA, and ask how the mixture changes lung immune responses during a virus-like challenge. Their 2026 study uses sixty-six male mice in eleven groups, combining three dose levels of the chemical mixture with an airway dose of poly(I:C), a synthetic mimic of viral infection.

The viral mimic raised several T cell types associated with antiviral and inflammatory responses, as expected. Adding the pollutants blunted those rises in a dose-dependent fashion, while a different T cell type linked to allergy increased. Gene activity measurements in tissue suggested the IL-17 signalling pathway, a driver of this inflammation style, was also modulated. The authors conclude such mixtures can reshape the lung immune environment under inflammatory conditions, and argue immune endpoints belong in safety evaluation of these chemicals.
pmc-13356724:
Peter Gloviczki and others summed evidence on microsurgery for lower limb lymphedema, ran the umbrella review in 2026. Lymphovenous link and vascularised lymph node transfer are set microsurgical options for chronic lymphedema, but guidance on who should receive them needed a higher-level making. The review supports forthcoming rules from the American Venous Forum and the American Vein and Lymphatic Society.

Full reviews and meta-studies issued between 2010 and recent years were searched across multiple databases, and their results on indications and results were joined. The umbrella approach summarises the best on hand evidence rather than single trials. Rule writers and surgeons gain a consolidated basis for recommending lymphatic microsurgery.
pmc-13358624:
Shangqing Xu and co-authors study the worry that comes with lung nodules in a 2026 paper. Scans now find small lung spots in many people, and most prove harmless. Yet living with doubt can push some patients to seek reassurance again and again, almost like an addiction. The team built a scale to measure this behavior.

They surveyed 1,800 adults with nodules at a large chest surgery center from 2021 to 2024. Patients sat at different stages: some awaited a firm answer, others already knew their spot was harmless or cancer. Sorting patients into worry profiles could help clinics give calm, clear support to those who need it most.
pmc-13359524:
Haotian Yuan and co-authors study sheep muscle cells under insulin in a 2026 paper. Muscle holds satellite cells that can become either muscle fibers or fat cells. Insulin pushed the cells toward muscle: they formed fibers, burned fatty acids, and held back from becoming fat. Gene activity scans traced the shift, and two small regulatory molecules stood out as possible coordinators. Understanding this switch could help breeders raise marbling without simply fattening the whole animal.
pmc-13359624:
Murat Günaltılı and co-authors test a simple blood score in kidney cancer in a 2026 study. The HALP score joins hemoglobin, albumin, and two blood cell counts to reflect anemia, nutrition, immunity, and inflammation at once. A Turkish multicenter group asked whether the score, taken before treatment, forecasts survival in patients with spread kidney cancer starting targeted pills.

pmc-13360824:

pmc-13362824:

pmc-13364124:

pmc-13371424:

pmc-13372524:

pmc-13377824:

pmc-13379524:

pmc-13380024:

pmc-13381024:

pmc-13381724:

pmc-13382524:

pmc-13382724:

pmc-13383724:

pmc-13385324:

pmc-13390024:

Meng Zhang and co-authors uncover a two-factor module that arms millet and wheat against drought and salt while lifting yield. Their 2026 study works in foxtail millet, where the transcription factors TAF10 and ERF109 team up to switch on flavonoid-making genes. Flavonoids, plant pigments with protective chemistry, sit at the heart of the stress shield the pair builds.

Spraying the flavonoids themselves (apigenin, naringenin or hesperetin) rescued plants whose module was silenced. Field protocols for apigenin then raised wheat yields by 12.3 to 19.6 percent and millet yields by 15.8 to 23.9 percent under dry and salty field conditions in the trials reported. A spray-on shield beats breeding timelines where climates are already turning.
pmc-13399124:
Yuya Ueno, Shota Yamazaki, Hiromichi Hoshina, and Masahiko Harata report in 2026 that terahertz radiation can speed up repair of broken DNA in living cells. Double-strand breaks are the most dangerous kind of DNA damage. Slow or faulty repair can lead to cancer and other diseases. Terahertz waves sit between microwaves and infrared light and cannot ionize molecules, which makes them attractive as a gentle tool.

In their experiments, exposing cells to terahertz waves lowered the amount of chemically induced double-strand breaks. The effect size depended on the wave frequency used. Heating the samples instead raised the number of breaks, which told the team the benefit was not a simple warming effect. Earlier work showed terahertz exposure promotes actin polymerization, a process also involved in break repair inside the nucleus. The authors suggest such exposure might one day support treatments for diseases tied to genomic instability.
pmc-13399424:
Rafael Mathias Pitta and colleagues followed Brazilian men over time to see whether changing their own physical activity habits changed their risk of erectile dysfunction, in a 2026 longitudinal study. Earlier studies linked leisure exercise to lower risk, but they mostly froze people at one moment and came from wealthy countries. The effect of real-world habit change stayed untested.

The cohort drew on employer-sponsored health checkups at a São Paulo hospital between 2008 and 2022. The analysis included 925 men over 39 who had no erectile dysfunction at their first visit and who returned for a second assessment 300 to 800 days later. Each man was classed by how his activity pattern moved between visits: persistently inactive, becoming inactive, becoming active, or persistently active. Erectile function was scored with the standard international index questionnaire at both visits. The authors expected men who became or stayed active to fare better than those who stayed inactive.
pmc-13400224:
Nelson-Georges Dengo and colleagues report two years of a French national emergency committee that advises, within twenty-four hours, on pregnant and postpartum women with thrombotic microangiopathy, in a 2026 article. The committee, under the national TMA reference center since October 2023, convenes experts from eight specialties per case.

The first 76 reviewed women were most often in a preeclampsia context, 47 percent, or peripartum hemorrhage, 40 percent. Thirty-eight percent were first-time mothers. Acute kidney injury appeared in 62 percent, including nine women with renal cortical necrosis, the extreme phenotype the authors highlight. True TTP accounted for only thirteen cases, 17 percent, and none was judged atypical HUS. The committee changed management in 26 percent of cases, most often by de-escalating therapy, sparing women plasma exchange or costly drugs they did not need. The authors advocate real-time multidisciplinary conferences as standard support.
pmc-13400624:
Behnam Taherizadeh and colleagues apply, in 2026, an eagle-inspired search algorithm to place solar panels and batteries in local power networks. Adding solar generation and storage can cut losses and steady voltage, but only if units are sized and sited well. The team framed it as an optimization problem.

Their enhanced Bald Eagle Search was tested on two standard networks with 33 and 69 connection points, under solar-only and solar-plus-battery plans. It beat a genetic algorithm and a whale-inspired method on every run. On the larger network, daily energy losses fell by up to roughly half depending on setup, the weakest voltage improved, and operating costs were lowest. The authors claim the method scales across network layouts.
pmc-13400724:
Zakiur Rehman Ansari and colleagues present, in 2026, a man whose heart stent, placed years earlier, fractured and seeded a slowly draining chest fistula. Delayed inflammatory complications of stents are exceptionally rare, and a skin-draining tract years later can masquerade as a simple chest wall infection. Untangling it required several imaging methods.

The 53-year-old, who had diabetes and heart disease, had a right coronary stent placed in 2018 and later developed months of intermittent fever and a draining pit near the breastbone. Scans revealed the broken, blocked stent wrapped in inflamed tissue reaching through the diaphragm. Surgeons removed the stent, the inflamed tissue and the tract after antibiotic cover. The case shows how cross-sectional imaging guides such operations.
pmc-13401324:
Inês Martins Esteves wrote a 2026 cohort study of a programme-level revamp in specialist eye nursing training in the United Kingdom, asking whether structural reform of a whole curriculum lifts student grades. Post-registration programmes often stay fragmented across results, assessments, and workload even when theory favours joined-up design.

Nine cohorts of registered nurses, 106 students in all, were compared. Six cohorts, 73 students, finished the traditional structure between 2018 and 2021, while three cohorts of 33 students took the redesigned programme in 2022 and 2023. The revamp drew on constructive alignment, programmatic assessment, competency-based education, and cognitive load theory. Esteves also introduces the Integrated Programme Reform Model as a framework for programme-level reform. Tests whether the new structure was linked to measurable gains in achievement.
pmc-13401524:
Lidiane Araujo Cezário and co-authors wrote a 2026 study of long-term cancer survivors in Brazil moving from oncology follow-up back to primary health care. After five years at a major cancer centre, survivors are referred onward, and the study asks how that transition actually works.

At the National Cancer Institute, 91 survivors answered a structured phone questionnaire about demographics, lifestyle, nutrition, prevention, and surveillance. Their average age was about 69 years. The most reported late effects were cognitive difficulties, hormonal symptoms, sleep problems, and chronic pain. Fewer than half said they had been referred to a primary care unit after treatment ended. Only 11 members, about 12 percent, recalled receiving a discharge summary to hand to their primary care provider, exposing a weak handover.
pmc-13402424:
Amouzadeh and co-authors study, in 2026, what makes mobile banking hard for older adults. They test six widely used Iranian banking apps through expert review and hands-on trials with 1,200 users aged 60 and above. Five human-computer interaction experts applied smartphone usability rules, while the older users completed tasks, rating scales, and interviews in a mixed-methods design.

The experts logged 135 usability problems, with error blocking the most severe category at a mean severity of 2.27, followed closely by visibility of system status at 2.22 on their scale. Usability scores diverged widely between apps, from 27.50 for the worst to 59.02 for the best on the hundred-point System Usability Scale. Age mattered within the older group too: users aged 60 to 63 averaged 54.2, while those aged 72 to 75 averaged 45.3 in the comparisons. Talks blamed cultural mismatches and cognitive overload as key barriers to handling money alone.
pmc-13402824:
Chenglin Wang and colleagues searched for blood-cell gene markers that separate sepsis from systemic inflammatory response syndrome, or SIRS. Their 2026 study addresses a hard bedside distinction: both conditions inflame the body, but sepsis stems from infection and needs urgent antimicrobial care. Lysosome genes, tied to cell cleanup and immune signaling, offered a promising discriminator.

Sequencing blood from 12 SIRS and 20 sepsis patients yielded 21 overlapping lysosome-linked genes enriched in autophagy and vacuolar transport. Meta-analysis narrowed them to four core genes in total: CD1C, RNASE6, and SNCA fell in sepsis, while DRAM1 rose. All four showed good discrimination, with DRAM1 strongest at an AUC of 0.888. Single-cell data pinpointed the immune cells expressing them. The markers need larger clinical validation before diagnostic use.
pmc-13402924:
Qing Li and Mario Plebani argue that machine learning in laboratory medicine needs two kinds of traceability kept distinct. One is the metrological kind that anchors a measurement to reference standards. The other is an algorithmic kind that lets auditors rebuild how a model turned data into output. Labs now use learning models to interpret tests, predict outcomes, and run operations, and each use carries different proof burdens.

A model can eat perfectly traceable lab values yet transform them in ways that leak information, hide uncertainty, or drift after deployment as methods and populations shift. The authors propose a functional framework aligning calibration thinking with model documentation, plus traceability dossiers and tiered rules backed by international teamwork. Their aim is reproducibility and comparability strong enough for clinical trust, without pretending a training set is a reference material.
pmc-13403024:
Tierra L Mosher leads a team reporting a 26-month-old girl whose acute liver failure traced to HHH syndrome. It is a rare urea cycle disorder named for its three blood and urine markers: high ornithine, high ammonia, and homocitrullinuria. The condition can bring lethargy, unsteadiness, seizures, coma, and liver failure, and newborn screening does not catch it. She was diagnosed one week into her admission.

Liver tissue showed an acute hepatitis-like injury with many acidophil cells and glycogen-filled nuclei, a pairing the authors say is rarely discussed. Acute care used intravenous dextrose and intralipids; long-term care restricts protein, adds glycerol phenylbutyrate to mop up nitrogen, and supplements citrulline to support the cycle. A telling clue was the child own avoidance of protein. The authors urge early metabolic labs and biopsy in pediatric liver failure.
pmc-13404624:
Cia Sin Lee and co-authors examine, in 2026, how health workers in Singapore viewed the OPTIMUM remote monitoring system for diabetes. The system was rolled out in primary care across the country after a trial showed good health outcomes. Knowing what helped or hindered its use matters for keeping it running.

Staff involved in the trial gave individual semi-structured interviews, which were transcribed, coded and analysed for themes. Analysis followed the CFIR framework, which sorts influences into the tool itself, outside pressures, clinic setting, individual staff and process. Workers said remote monitoring helped patients change habits and that its treatment algorithm allowed steady monitoring with tailored advice. Other setting and workload factors also shaped how the system landed.
pmc-13405024:
Shahana Singh and colleagues describe a 2026 quality project to strengthen child health checks at a Delhi primary care centre. Young children often arrive with one complaint while other problems stay hidden. The IMCI approach, a standard method for assessing sick children, covers danger signs and common illness together.

Age-specific checklists were introduced for children from 2 months to 5 years, backed by a dedicated children's clinic room and better measuring equipment. Two six-week improvement cycles followed. Complete assessment rose from low levels to 50 percent by the second cycle in the reported figures. Checking for danger signs reached 97.2 percent, and screening for cough, fever and diarrhoea all climbed.
pmc-13406324:
Yunjiao Shen and co-authors test the plant Centella asiatica against diabetic liver and fat problems in mice, in 2026 work. Diabetic mice were created with a fatty diet plus streptozotocin, then treated with plant extract or its component asiatic acid. A standard diabetes drug served as comparison.

Fasting glucose fell by about half in both treatment groups, 51.01 and 53.01 percent in the reported figures, with better glucose tolerance and blood fats. Liver fat and insulin resistance eased as well. The mechanism traced to pyrimidine metabolism: liver uridine and related compounds rose, supporting glycogen storage. A protein called UPP1 sits at the centre of the proposed pathway.
pmc-13407324:
Barbora Mechúrová and co-authors review what builds trust when a patient meets a doctor for the first time. While trust in long-term relationships is well studied, the very first encounter is not. Their 2026 scoping review searches PubMed for studies where trust was measured around that first visit.

From 2,825 initial records, ten studies passed full screening for thematic analysis. Trust was shaped in three phases. Before the visit, reputation, care coordination, and past good experiences helped. During the consultation, warmth, visible technical skill, information sharing, participation, listening, and empathy built trust. Afterward, symptom relief reinforced it, and apologising for errors proved crucial. Barriers included little chance to ask questions, time pressure, unmet expectations, and stigmatising language. The authors conclude trust formation starts before the door opens.
pmc-13407724:
Keng Siang Lee and co-authors set out, in a 2026 protocol, to build expert consensus on using artificial intelligence to measure vestibular schwannomas, benign tumours of the hearing nerve. Growth decides treatment for these tumours. Volume measurement beats simple diameters for sensitivity. Yet hand segmentation is slow and variable. AI tools can now outline tumours on MRI automatically.

The plan runs in three phases. First comes a systematic review of how tumours get measured. That drafts candidate indicators. A steering committee then refines them into questionnaire items. Last comes a two-round Delphi survey plus a consensus meeting. Experts come from British and European skull-base societies. The resulting core reporting set will be spread through journals, funders, and conferences, aiming to standardise how AI-assisted measurement enters routine care.
pmc-13408624:
Homayouni-Rad and co-authors review, in 2026, the psychobiotic potential of postbiotics, the metabolic leftovers of probiotic bacteria, for depression, psychosis, and mania, a little-studied corner of gut-brain research. Their search covered PubMed, Medline, EMBASE, and the Cochrane Library for English-language studies from January 2015 to January 2025, covering mood control, brain inflammation, and neurotransmitter tuning.

The surveyed evidence shows postbiotics raising serotonin and GABA signals, damping neuroinflammation, and tuning the body's stress axis. One cited mix, a Lactobacillus brevis strain from Thai fermented sausage, carried a GABA content of 2.85 milligrams per milliliter in the reported assay, showing how potent these metabolites can be. The clinical need is large: depression was about 50 percent more common among women than men in 2023, one of the gaps the review cites. The authors conclude postbiotics are promising drug candidates but insist on proper trials to pin down how they work and dosing.
pmc-13408724:
Saud Alsaleh, Mariam Shikshok, Ahmed Abdel-Aal, and Ammar Almehmi review in 2026 how to perform a kidney biopsy through the skin safely and well. The procedure diagnoses kidney disease, tracks treatment response, and informs prognosis, and it has evolved from a blind stick into an image-guided technique. Major bleeding still occurs in roughly one to six percent of cases in modern series, so preparation matters.

The narrative review gathers current guidance on when to biopsy, when not to, how to plan and perform the sampling, and how to manage the hours around it. Difficult groups get their own discussion, including patients with severe obesity, pregnancy, advanced age, a single kidney, or abnormal anatomy. Alternatives for cases where the standard route is impossible close the survey, giving nephrology teams a single bedside reference.
pmc-13408924:
Michał Papaj, Lingyuan Kong, Stevan Nadj-Perge, and Patrick Lee propose in 2026 an explanation for a strange pattern seen in flakes of iron-based superconductors. In them, the superconducting gap itself rises and falls with the rhythm of the crystal lattice. Their model starts from materials whose unit cells already break internal symmetry, and lets the superconductivity break fourfold rotation symmetry as well, a nematic state.

That combination textures the electronic surface. The gap peaks on one iron sublattice and dips on the other. The pairs themselves carry no net momentum. The authors spell out how local probes could read the signs of the pairing components from the pattern and even watch a transition into a mixed two-component state. Their framework turns a microscopy curiosity into a diagnostic for the nature of unconventional pairing.
pmc-13409624:
Yu Zhang, Rui Zhu, and Yin Li propose in 2026 a way to search encrypted cloud documents by meaning without the server ever reading them. Searchable encryption usually forces a trade: coarse indexes make queries slow, while expanding a query with related terms drags in noise. Their scheme, SES-HI, attacks both ends of the problem at once.

A two-stage clustering pipeline builds a balanced, many-branched index whose groups are semantically tight, sharpening the bounds that prune dead branches early. Query expansion is guided by topic modelling and then filtered by word-embedding similarity to keep the noise out. A dual pruning rule, global threshold plus top-k competition, trims the ranking work further. Security is proven against adaptive keyword attacks under a stated leakage profile, and experiments on a standard text collection improved the accuracy-latency balance over leading rivals.
pmc-13411524:
Bin-bin Gu and colleagues reviewed 36 adults with severe tetanus treated in intensive care at a specialist infectious disease hospital from 2014 to 2024. Tetanus is preventable by vaccine, yet severe cases still strike older rural men hardest, often with little prior preventive care after injury.

Swallowing trouble and whole-body stiffness showed up earlier than the classic locked jaw. Most patients needed breathing machines and deep sedation, and lung infections hit about four in five. With a median stay near 28 days and deaths at about one in six, the paper gives intensive care teams a current picture of a rare but grueling illness.
pmc-13412324:
Lanlan Ji and co-authors present CellCover in 2026, a method that picks small gene panels defining a cell type when genes are judged together rather than one by one. Single-cell RNA atlases keep growing, and naming cell classes inside them depends on marker genes. Standard differential expression tests miss redundancy between genes, so panels picked that way carry wasted overlap.

CellCover treats panel selection as a set-covering puzzle over on-off expression data, which scales to the huge cell counts in modern atlases. Trials on blood and brain data showed leaner panels with signals distinct from standard picks. Applied across mouse, primate, and human data, the method tracked brain development stages and dated parts of a key stem cell program to rodent ancestors.
pmc-13413524:
Tenzin Choden Gyeltshen, Dimple Sajin, and Hang Thu Ta sift in 2026 through published liver-on-a-chip systems to find the settings that recur most often. These microfluidic devices aim to replace flat cell cultures and animal tests for drug screening, yet every lab builds them differently, which hampers comparison. The analysis catalogued cell sources, seeding densities, scaffold materials, and the assays used to prove the mini-livers work.

Immortalized HepG2 cells dominate current platforms by a wide margin in the literature surveyed. Typical seeding runs near three million cells per millilitre for flat systems, with lower ranges in three-dimensional builds. Collagen I, alone or blended with Matrigel, is the commonest scaffold, and albumin plus urea serve as the trusted function checks. Benchmarks for builders close the paper.
pmc-13413624:
Edwin Chrabieh and colleagues review in 2026 whether low-level light therapy can speed burn wound healing. Photobiomodulation uses red or near-infrared light at gentle intensities to nudge tissue repair and calm inflammation, a trick borrowed from cosmetic and rehabilitation practice. Their systematic search across three databases through 2024 gathered every study of the therapy in human burn patients that reported a clinical outcome.

Seven studies covering 190 patients qualified for the synthesis. Healing time and pain scores were the outcomes most often reported, with scar quality and wound area close behind. Results leaned promising, suggesting faster closure and less pain, yet dosing varied wildly and reporting was inconsistent, blocking any pooled analysis. The authors demand standardized, high-quality trials before burn units adopt the light.
pmc-13415824:
Amira A. E. Satti and co-authors reuse old vancomycin, a drug waste set for burning, to guard steel pipe from acid rust, in 2026. Tests used X60 carbon steel in strong hydrochloric acid. Weight loss, cell based power tests, surface scans, and math models all weighed the drug's guard film.

Protection rose with dose, reaching about 94 to 95 percent efficiency at room temperature by the best measures. Rust flow fell from 244 to 54 in the units used as dose rose. Scans showed a drug coat on the steel face. The coat forms one layer thick and sits by weak force, not strong bonds, the fits say.
pmc-13416124:
Reham A. Mohamed, Ali S. Shanour, and Taha A. El-Sayed bend test concrete floor slabs reinforced with carbon fiber polymer bars instead of steel, in 2026.
