Alejandro Lopez-Bezanilla and colleagues use frustrated magnets shaped like fullerene cages to stress-test quantum annealers. Their 2026 study builds Ising models on these closed carbon-like shapes, where magnetic moments cannot all please their neighbors at once, leaving a huge set of equally good layouts. Quantum fluctuations must do the choosing.

The team saw quantum swings lift that tie, favoring certain coherent setups through tunneling between states. Since the models have no edges and high symmetry, they make clean test cases for quantum hardware. Scores rose sharply across successive generations of superconducting annealers on these problems. The authors argue that hitting the shared ground state exactly is where quantum rigs prove themselves. Frustrated cages, they conclude, offer a sharp benchmark for the young field.
pmc-13562524:
Sudenur Ozkan and two colleagues show that the spacing of footstep sounds can change how fast a walking figure seems to move. Earlier work used simple flashes and clicks, leaving open whether sound timing also bends the perceived speed of real human motion. The 2026 experiments used point-light walkers, figures made of dots on the joints, shown one after another with identical visuals. Only the gap between footstep sounds differed. Viewers judged the walker with shorter sound gaps as walking faster, every time.

Shifting the first or last sound did not remove the effect, so the whole interval mattered rather than any single alignment moment. Mismatched sounds worked too, which points to timing itself as the driver. The authors argue that hearing supplies a strong timing cue that vision borrows, helping the brain keep a moving, sounding world in step.
pmc-13562724:
Jingjin Li and five colleagues study what moves Chinese herders to turn grassland ecology into income, selling the value of pasture rather than only livestock. Policy wants those green hills to pay, and herders must act. Working from an ecological-ethics lens, the 2026 study names five factors. They span how herders see their bond with nature, what they know of grassland functions and laws, their pro-environment attitudes, and their husbandry knowledge. Survey data was modelled two ways, with structural equations and with fuzzy-set comparison.

All five factors shaped both intention and behaviour, and intention carried part of the effect. Government policy support strengthened the step from intention to action. Six combinations of conditions sufficed to produce the behaviour, showing there is no single recipe. The authors advise policy that works on beliefs, knowledge, and legal awareness, rather than paying for outcomes alone.
pmc-13562924:
Vladimir Krivtsov, Peter M. Hollingsworth, and a Darwin Tree of Life consortium publish the genome sequence of common heather, Calluna vulgaris. Heather dominates heathlands and moorlands across the British Isles and much of Europe, yet lacked a reference genome. The 2026 assembly covers both copies of the plant's genome, its two haplotypes, at about 522 and 520 million bases. Nearly all of each copy is organised into eight chromosome-scale scaffolds. The team also assembled the mitochondrial genome at about 441 thousand bases and the plastid genome at about 208 thousand bases.

The work sits inside the Darwin Tree of Life project, which is sequencing every eukaryotic species in Britain and Ireland. Background notes trace heather's history: mainly outcrossing, pollinated by bees and flies, with little population structure in Scotland and a likely French refuge after the ice age. A chromosome-level reference now lets researchers probe how this landscape-defining shrub adapts and spreads.
pmc-13563724:
Meo Nguyen and seven colleagues test, in dishes, whether adding a collagen membrane changes how a blood-derived material treats gum ligament stem cells. Advanced platelet-rich fibrin, spun from a patient's blood, is a staple of gum regeneration, and collagen membranes partner it in surgery. Whether the pairing helps or hinders the cells was unclear. The 2026 study soaked the materials into extracts at full strength and at 20 percent, using fibrin from four donors, then fed them to periodontal ligament stem cells.

Only the full-strength combined extract met the toxicity bar, while full-strength fibrin alone wobbled near it, unevenly across donors. Growth activity peaked around day five for all groups. In a scratch test, diluted extracts closed the gap better than full-strength ones, and fibrin beat the pairing at 20 percent. The authors call the pairing's profile mixed and in need of tuning, not an upgrade.
pmc-13563824:
Maiko Kobayashi and two colleagues benchmark GPT-4o's emotional reading of photographs against human raters, and test two tricks meant to make the machine more culturally Polish. Models inherit cultural biases, and vendors suggest persona prompts or native-language prompts as fixes. Their 2026 study had the model rate 1,276 standardised pictures on pleasantness, arousal, and approach-avoidance, fifty-five times per image, under three setups: plain, a Polish-student persona, and Polish language. The human yardstick came from 204 raters, sixty percent Polish.

Every setup tracked human ratings, with correlations from 0.525, up to 0.809 at best. Neither trick helped consistently. Polish prompting matched humans better on arousal yet drifted further on approach-avoidance. Pleasantness agreed best overall; landscapes were the easiest category, reaching 0.933, and faces the hardest, dropping to 0.253. Distribution shapes differed in all nine comparisons. The authors advise validating each fix dimension by dimension before trusting machine judges across cultures.
pmc-13569824:
Feifei Huang, Zhongyi Tong, and Yi Jiang review, in a 2026 retrospective study, 265 patients with invasive breast cancer tested for inherited BRCA1 or BRCA2 gene variants. These variants raise cancer risk and open the door to targeted PARP inhibitor drugs. Tumor features, immune markers, and outcomes were compared by variant status.

Inherited faulty variants clustered with distinct tumor traits, enrichment for triple-negative breast cancer, and worse outlook. Adding standard tissue markers, including an immune marker used in triple-negative disease, may sharpen risk grouping. The authors argue that pairing genetic testing with routine marker panels can guide more personal treatment choices for patients carrying these inherited variants.
pmc-13570824:
Danzeng Awang and colleagues tested whether salidroside, a Rhodiola compound, protects the heart from low-oxygen injury, publishing the study in 2026. High-altitude hypoxia strains the oxygen-hungry heart, driving oxidative stress, mitochondrial failure, and cell death, while current drugs carry notable side effects. The team combined network pharmacology and docking with experiments in cobalt-chloride hypoxia models in cells and rats.

Salidroside improved cell survival, cut reactive oxygen species, restored mitochondrial energy output, and curbed cell death, while in rats it eased ECG abnormalities, heart-muscle injury, hypertrophy, and lung and liver damage. Mechanistic tests showed it steered a protective GSK-3β switch largely without Akt. The work supports salidroside as a candidate shield against hypoxia-related heart injury.
pmc-13570924:
Yiyao Fu and colleagues compared gut microbes and blood chemistry in young and aged mice whose ovaries had failed. Ovary failure goes with ageing of the reproductive system and body-wide metabolic upset, but the microbial causes are poorly mapped. Their 2026 study read gut-microbe genes from faeces and scanned blood serum from 7-week-old and 12-month-old female mice.

Old mice had a changed gut community, with fewer Firmicutes and more Bacteroidetes, plus more Alistipes and Akkermansia. Their blood held 246 differing metabolites, mostly tied to amino-acid and energy pathways. Tryptophan metabolism stood out as the link between gut imbalance and metabolic change. The authors point to those microbes and blood markers as targets for future care in ovary failure.
pmc-13572524:
Constance Denoyelle, with 16 colleagues, reports a 2026 survey of a gut protozoan in French broiler chickens. Blastocystis is the most common such organism found in people, and birds may pass it to humans. No French farm survey had been done, so the team sampled birds at one slaughterhouse from 66 farms.

A total of 967 gut samples covered three farm systems, from free-range label birds to standard indoor flocks. The organism turned up in 49.7 percent of samples and on 83.3 percent of farms. Farm type and season shaped how often it appeared. Subtype 7 led by far, with subtype 6 next, and near a fifth of positive birds carried two or more subtypes. Gene reads showed wide variety within subtype 7. The authors flag flocks as a real source of human exposure.
pmc-13575124:
Narek Abelyan introduces PocketMaster, a 2026 software tool for comparing the pockets in protein structures where molecules bind. Small shape changes in these pockets can alter how a protein works and how a drug fits. Comparing many structures by hand is slow, so the tool automates lining up, grouping, and charting pockets.

Two case studies show its range. For the TYK2 protein, the tool separated kinase and pseudokinase pocket shapes and found subtypes within each. For the estrogen receptor, it caught a known shift in one helix between active and inactive states. Results come with automatic reports and visuals. Abelyan positions the tool for early drug design, with code shared openly online.
pmc-13576124:
Wu Weiwei and five colleagues test a spiral form of arc radiotherapy for bulky tumours in a 2026 planning study. GRID therapy aims high dose at peaks inside a tumour while keeping valleys between them low. Standard linear accelerator methods struggle to keep that contrast sharp.

Twenty patients' plans were rebuilt three ways: the spiral method, standard arc therapy, and helical tomotherapy. The spiral approach pairs couch movement with gantry rotation to trace a helical path. It produced the steepest dose fall-off and the highest peak-to-valley ratios under both measures used. Healthy organ limits were met by all three methods with no meaningful gaps. Beam time for the spiral method sat between the other two. The authors judge the spiral method dosimetrically strongest for single-session GRID work.
pmc-13576224:
Szymon Kuliś and three colleagues test whether brief targeted cooling calms the tremor that follows hard exercise in young swimmers, in a 2026 crossover trial. Tremor rises after intense effort as muscles tire. Cold therapy is common in sports medicine, yet its effect on exercise tremor had not been directly tested.

Thirty-four competitive teenage swimmers each completed both conditions: 60 seconds of localised cooling on tender muscle trigger points, and a no-treatment control. Tremor in both legs was recorded before and after a 30-second maximal tethered swim, with a set recovery gap. Exercise raised tremor power as expected. Cooling blunted that rise in the 9 to 14 hertz band, the frequency range tied to nerve-driven tremor. Frequency shifts were less tidy. The authors note the value for actual performance is still unknown.
pmc-13576324:
Andrea Stašek leads a 2026 study mapping how problem gaming and problem social media use connect to teenage wellbeing across ten European countries. Most past work scored each habit as a single total. This team used symptom networks on survey data from 33,586 adolescents aged 11 to 15, gathered in 2021 and 2022.

One symptom sat at the centre of both habits: escapism, using games or feeds to dodge feelings. It was the most common symptom and the main bridge to loneliness in both sexes, and to overall wellbeing and nervousness in girls. Symptoms reflecting fallout, such as conflict, deception, and trouble with others, linked tightly across the two habits, hinting at a shared condition rather than separate ones. The authors argue prevention should target single symptoms, starting with escapism.
pmc-13577924:
Ximing Ran leads a 2026 study hunting blood proteins that foretell when a healthy carrier of an ALS gene fault will develop the disease. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a fatal nerve disease, and prevention trials are blocked by not knowing who will convert, or when. The team used a high-throughput protein platform on stored blood samples.

The collection held 516 samples from 33 people who later developed ALS, 35 patients, 10 symptom-free carriers, and 59 controls. Ninety-two proteins shifted in level before symptoms began. A core panel of 19 predicted conversion with ranking scores between 0.80 and 0.89 across half-year to five-year windows, and estimated the timing to within a mean of 1.6 years. Checks in UK Biobank data backed several of the signals. The authors say the panel beats the single best-known marker used alone.
pmc-13578324:
Xiaoyu Zhang and colleagues test whether hemoglobin, the oxygen carrying protein in blood, can calm inflamed vessel lining cells, in a 2026 lab study. Vessel diseases grow from long term injury and oxidative stress, a state where reactive oxygen overwhelms cell defenses. The team stressed human vein cells with peroxide, then added hemoglobin and watched stress and inflammation markers.

Hemoglobin lowered three key inflammatory signals and cut cell death, along with the waste markers of oxidative damage. The gain ran through a defense pathway that switches on protective genes. Blocking that pathway largely erased the benefit, which ties the effect to the pathway itself. Since the anti-inflammatory effect followed the drop in stress, the authors frame stress control as the root of the gain.
pmc-13578424:
Temesgen Debas Awoke, Semu Mitiku Kassa, and Gizaw Mengistu Tsidu model short, sharp control bursts against visceral leishmaniasis, a deadly parasite disease spread by sandflies, in a 2026 study. Heat and rain drive sandfly numbers, so spread swings with the seasons. Steady year round control is too costly for many poor regions, which pushed the team toward brief, well timed pushes.

Their model folds weather into the spread math and tests spray rounds, breeding site clearing, and culling of infected host animals. Sandfly linked factors drove cases far more than host factors, so fly control won priority. Two one week pushes a year cut human cases by about ninety five percent in the model. Starting six weeks after the infection peak worked best, and pairing fly control with culling beat either alone.
pmc-13578724:
Haelim Yoon and colleagues test an old drug, emetine, against liver cancer cells that learn to spread, in a 2026 lab study. Spread starts when cancer cells loosen their neat sheet form and gain a wandering form, a shift driven by a protein called Twist1. The drug, long used for other ills, had never been checked for this anti-spread role.

At doses that spared cell life, the drug slowed migration and invasion across five liver cancer cell lines. Twist1 levels fell, sheet markers rose, and wandering markers dropped. Rescue tests showed the drug shortens the life of the Twist1 protein itself. A mutant form that cannot take a key chemical tag resisted the drop. Two stress pathways that place that tag went quiet under the drug, tying the pieces together.
pmc-13579824:
Xue Huang, Xingya Liu, Huibo Dai, and Mei Xu report a benign cyst that made an early ovarian cancer look far advanced, in a 2026 case report. A 58 year old woman past menopause carried a large belly and pelvis tumor of a clear cell type. Scans showed odd patches in the gut lining membrane, and a blood marker ran high, both hinting that cancer had seeded widely.

Surgery told another story. The membrane patches were one blood filled cyst, not spread at all. Lab work confirmed the ovarian tumor was still early stage, and the cyst was harmless. Twelve months after surgery she remained free of disease. The authors warn that scans and markers alone can overstage such cases, and that eyes in the operating room plus lab proof should settle the stage.
pmc-13584424:
Xiaoling Wang and a large team trace a brain circuit that links lasting pain with memory loss in mice in this 2026 study. Long-term pain often brings both sharp sensitivity and foggy memory, yet the shared wiring was unclear. The team used a nerve injury model and tested the animals on mazes and object tasks while recording activity in a front brain region called the prelimbic cortex.

One set of calming nerve cells in that region stayed overactive after injury, which threw off the balance between go and stop signals and dulled memory. Quieting those cells eased both pain sensitivity and memory faults. Switching them on in healthy mice created the same faults. A protein named ATF4 sat upstream of the shift, which gives drug hunters a concrete target to test.
pmc-13586324:
Chuan Gao and colleagues report a genetic puzzle in a 94-year-old man that mimicked Li-Fraumeni syndrome, a hereditary cancer syndrome. The same TP53 hotspot variant, Arg175His, appeared in both his blood and his tumour, initially raising concern for an inherited syndrome. Given his atypical presentation, the team tested multiple tissues to pin down the variant's origin. This 2026 case report shows why that extra step matters.

Bladder and skin samples carried just a faint trace of the variant, while fingernail DNA showed none. Those results support two independent somatic acquisitions of the same hotspot mutation, one in blood-forming cells and one in the tumour, rather than an inherited variant. The authors stress multi-tissue testing to avoid mislabelling older cancer patients with hereditary syndromes.
pmc-13587324:
Benjamin Wee Y and colleagues map gene networks that help hemp cope when phosphorus runs short. Phosphorus is a core plant nutrient, and hemp, shaped by centuries of human selection for fiber and seed, handles poor soils better than many crops. Their 2026 study grew hemp under rich and poor phosphate supply and read gene activity across roots, leaves, and other organs, then grouped genes that rose and fell together.

Twelve gene groups appeared, tied to jobs such as root growth, fiber making, and flowering. Two groups, one in leaves and one in roots, tracked the plant's phosphorus state closely, and both overlapped with genes marked by domestication. A gene called SPX3 sat at the hub of the leaf response, while root shape changes ran through known regulator families. Hormones called strigolactones also steered the root response.
pmc-13587824:
Julianna Bernardi and colleagues build a new early-warning index for hospitals in financial trouble. Closures and distressed hospitals stretch care thin across the United States, yet the standing public scores were designed for narrow hospital types or demand complete data, which shaky hospitals often lack. Their 2026 measure, the integrated vulnerability measure, extends a rural model to every general acute-care hospital filing Medicare cost reports between 2017 and 2022.

The index sorted checked hospitals into four risk bands, with about half called low risk and under one in ten high risk. Higher bands were far more likely to land in real financial distress within two years. Because the model stays readable and forgiving of missing data, the authors pitch it for targeting help and oversight before a closure is on the table.
pmc-13589924:
Yilun Qu heads a large team in a 2026 study of a kidney disease marked by fast growth of cells in the filters of the kidney. That growth, driven by swelling and irritation, can end in kidney failure. The team tested chlorogenic acid, a natural plant compound, and asked how it protects the kidney. Their work used a rat model of the disease plus lab tests on the compound.

Qu and the team found that the acid binds a protein called RAC1 and blocks its action. That step lowered signals that spur cell growth and calmed immune cells called macrophages. Levels of key irritant signals fell as well. The authors propose the acid as a lead for a new drug, though human tests lie ahead.
pmc-13592324:
Xiao Wang leads a 2026 team building a flow battery with no membrane at all, pairing lithium metal with an organic liquid cathode. Membranes usually keep the two fluids apart yet add cost and resistance. Their cell stacks two liquids that refuse to mix. A deep eutectic lithium fluid sits below, while a chlorine solvent floats above it. The upper fluid holds a sulfur nitrogen dye that stores charge and stays in its own layer.

The stack reached about 3.6 volts, high for this class. After 100 cycles it kept most of its charge with near perfect charge recovery, and a flowing version ran ten days with little self drain. Cost estimates undercut vanadium systems, and both fluids resist flame. Wang and the team credit the eutectic lithium mix for the wide, stable window.
pmc-13594224:
Mo Yan leads a fourteen-author team that mined thirty years of published experiments on making methanol from carbon dioxide to find operating lessons hidden across two hundred papers. Their 2026 study assembled the results into one dataset on copper and zinc oxide catalysts, then trained six machine learning models and used an explanation tool to rank what actually drives performance.

The models pointed to combinations of catalyst makeup, preparation, and reaction settings that deliver high methanol output at milder pressures than plants usually assume. A smaller dataset on activation energy, a measure of how strongly temperature drives the reaction, revealed patterns tied to the operating regime. A follow-up experiment on commercial catalysts confirmed one predicted link between flow speed and activation energy. The authors pitch the approach as a way to squeeze guidance out of legacy data for mature technologies.
pmc-13594324:
Gizem Vural, Sarina Drexler, Daniel Keeser, and Alexander Soutschek tested whether stimulating the striatum changes how hard people are willing to think. The striatum is a deep brain hub for weighing rewards against costs. They used a new technique that sends interfering electrical fields through the head to reach deep tissue, while volunteers performed an effort-based decision task inside a brain scanner.

Under stimulation, participants grew more sensitive to both sides of the bargain: bigger rewards pulled them more, and higher effort demands pushed them off more sharply. Brain recordings matched, with effort demands represented more strongly in the striatum and tighter coupling to the anterior cingulate, a region where motivation meets cognition. The authors suggest such targeted stimulation could one day inform treatments for the loss of motivation seen in several mental disorders.
pmc-13595624:
Catriona Connell, David Griffiths, Jessica Greenhalgh, and Morgan Torrance mapped the social networks of fifty people. All were in contact with the criminal justice system. The team wanted to understand why they do or do not seek help for mental health and substance use problems. Their 2026 mixed-methods study combined network mapping with interviews about stigma and the perceived value of support.

Five distinct network types emerged, differing in structure, membership, and culture. What the people around someone knew and believed about mental health, substance use, and asking for help proved to shape the individual's own choices, as did attitudes in the wider community. The authors advise services to design outreach around network type rather than the isolated person. Adding diverse contacts with different perspectives can shift a network's culture. Messages also need tailoring. People should know when, where, and how to get help.
pmc-13596824:
Koray Samet Altınçekiç and co-authors ran a randomized trial in 102 male youth basketball players. They tested whether how long each body region is rolled changes the benefit of foam rolling for reaction speed. Players rolled thirty seconds per region, sixty seconds per region, or rested quietly, with reaction time for the dominant hand measured before and after.

The shorter rolling dose beat the longer one on every scoring method, by roughly twenty-two milliseconds on the best-trial measure. Against rest, the short dose looked better on the best-trial analysis but not on average-based ones, and the long dose actually scored worse than rest in the extended model. Because the comparisons shifted with baseline speed and scoring choice, the authors decline to crown a best duration: brief rolling never hurt, and longer rolling may dull the quickness players want.
pmc-13597124:
Jorge and colleagues introduced hicream, a software framework for finding regions where genome folding differs between conditions, in a 2026 bioinformatics paper. Genome folding, measured by the Hi-C technique that counts contacts between DNA segments, shapes gene control, and its disruption contributes to cancer and birth defects. Existing comparison tools mostly hunt one preset structure type, such as loops or domains, or return local hits that are hard to interpret.

Jorge built hicream to detect changed regions of any shape. It first tests contact differences pixel by pixel across the interaction matrix, then clusters neighboring signals into candidate regions using the data. It attaches a strength measure to each region through after-the-fact inference. Results can be explored in an interactive visualization interface. The authors argue this frees researchers from preset structure definitions and can surface complex folding changes, and the package is available through the R archive.
pmc-13597624:
Ori Meir Komemi and Yaniv Efrati sorted porn use in 608 young adults aged eighteen to twenty-seven by two styles: use to fill a gap, and use to tune out of life. The model grew from game-use work, where a short shift from stress differs from a deep cut from real life. Folks scored use style, past harm, mood signs, rash acts, lone feel, mood control, and basic needs.

Group sorts gave low, mid, and high gap-and-tune-out groups. The high group fared worst in mind and mood, the low group best. Past sex harm went with more out-of-hand use and more use in all, yet the mid group, oddly, used most of all. Help should thus fit each use style and past harm, not just count hours of use.
pmc-13609424:
Anca Cristina Ferician and three colleagues profile diabetic nerve damage patients by whether records list a modern GLP-1-based medicine. These drugs, including semaglutide and the dual agent tirzepatide, are prescribed more often to sicker patients, so simple comparisons mislead. Working from a Romanian county hospital's exports covering February 2024 to February 2026, the team aggregated records for 4,120 patients.

GLP-1-based medicines appeared in 20.7 percent of records. That subgroup had diabetes about three years longer and carried more recorded conditions. Heart failure showed in 35.7 percent of them against 22.2 percent of the rest, and lower-limb amputation in 3.3 against 1.2 percent. Adjustment softened but did not erase the heart failure gap. The files held no dates for treatment or outcomes, so the authors insist the study cannot show these drugs help or harm nerves. What it shows is that a GLP-1 record flags a complex subgroup planners should not average away.
pmc-13612224:
Lehrnbecher and colleagues report a 2026 analysis of mold infections in children treated for acute lymphoblastic leukemia, the most common childhood cancer, within a large European trial. The trial enrolled 6,136 children, and the team reviewed proven and probable invasive mold infections in detail.

The team found 162 invasive mold infections, most of them aspergillosis of the lung. Risk ran much higher in children classed as high-risk leukemia, about five in a hundred, than in lower-risk groups at about two in a hundred. Older children and those with T-cell disease were hit more often. Most struck during the first, strongest treatment phases, and over a third within six weeks of diagnosis. One-year death after infection stood near one in seven. The timing map helps teams aim preventive antifungal drugs at the riskiest weeks.
pmc-13614924:
Guanlong Li and colleagues report a 2026 study of a small rice bran protein piece, named PV9. It shields stomach lining cells from damage by Helicobacter pylori. That bacterium infects the stomach and drives ulcers. In lab dishes, PV9 cut how many bacteria stuck to stomach cells called GES-1. Computer models showed the peptide and its fragments can latch onto the bacterium's grip proteins, held mainly by hydrogen bonds, and bench tests confirmed binding to two of them, SabA and BabA.

With fewer bacteria attached, the stomach cells cleared harmful oxygen waste faster and kept their energy and growth cycles in better shape. Cell death fell, protective enzymes rose, and inflammation signals dropped while calming signals climbed. A food-derived peptide that both blocks attachment and calms damage could one day support gentler stomach protection.
pmc-13617224:
Sonya Stacey and five colleagues report a 2026 Australian project to govern innovative medicines for children, meaning promising new drugs used before the usual evidence and approval pathways are complete. Such treatments can help rare or untreatable conditions, yet they raise safety, cost, and fairness questions. The team combined an expert consensus process, a hospital records review, and an adapted ethical framework from the United Kingdom.

Eighteen Australian paediatric experts agreed a working definition after four feedback rounds. Reviewing nearly three thousand medication approval applications at a tertiary children's hospital found one hundred twenty requests for drugs not on the national register. Just six counted as innovative under the new definition. The authors say the framework gives hospitals a practical tool to judge these requests consistently while protecting young patients.
pmc-13617624:
Awol Yemane Legesse and five colleagues report corrective surgery for a twenty-four-year-old woman born with an imperforate anus and a rectoperineal fistula, an anorectal malformation where no normal anal opening formed. Rich countries usually repair such defects in early infancy, yet limited antenatal and newborn care in low-resource settings means some patients reach adulthood untreated, carrying physical, social, and psychological burdens. The authors believe she is the oldest such patient ever reported.

Surgeons used a modified posterior sagittal anorectoplasty that preserves the perineum while transposing the anal canal into the correct position. Six months later the reconstruction looked smooth, and she could control gas and stool, tell the two apart, and reported neither constipation nor soiling. The team concludes this perineum-sparing modification is an appropriate option when adults present late with anorectal malformations in resource-limited settings.
pmc-13617724:
Max M. Lang and eight colleagues report a 2026 study of malaria across the age range in rural Uganda, where research concentrates on children under five. Data came from the SchistoTrack cohort: four thousand three hundred eight participants aged five to ninety from fifty-two villages in three lakeside districts, enrolled January 2022 to February 2024. Infection was checked by rapid test and microscope. Satellite data mapped vegetation exposure.

About forty-one percent tested positive, mostly with the falciparum parasite at low densities. Prevalence peaked at ages ten to eleven, fell through adolescence and leveled off in adults. Fever among infected people dropped from thirty-one percent in young children to eleven percent in adults. Dense vegetation more than tripled the odds of infection, distance from government clinics raised them, and living near vegetated ponds, marshes, or rivers beat beaches. The authors support age-specific control covering older children and adults.
pmc-13619324:
Khadija El Aalaoui and five colleagues report a case of spleen-preserving total removal of the pancreas and duodenum for an aggressive pancreatic cancer. Their patient, a sixty-five-year-old man with insulin-treated diabetes, first received chemotherapy. Surgeons then removed the organs through a laparoscopic approach while keeping the spleen, a choice meant to lower later infection and blood problems.

On the ninth day after surgery he reported pain in the upper left belly, and a scan showed a small area of dead spleen tissue. Doctors treated it with pain relief and a short course of antibiotics rather than more surgery. He went home on day sixteen. Final pathology confirmed moderately differentiated cancer with clear margins, though several lymph nodes held tumor. The authors say careful vessel work and close follow-up can make this demanding operation workable for selected central tumors.
pmc-13621624:
Yasmeen Mohamed Mohamed Shehata and five colleagues tested a structured study routine, the modified KWHLAQ strategy, on critical care nursing students at Alexandria University. The routine walks learners through what they know, want, and learned, then how to apply it and what questions remain. One hundred third-semester students split into two groups: fifty learned through the framework for twelve weeks, fifty through standard lectures.

Both groups took thinking and self-direction tests before and after. The framework group finished with clearly higher critical thinking scores, a moderate-to-large advantage, while the lecture group's scores actually slipped. The sharpest gains landed in the evaluating subskill. Self-directed learning jumped dramatically in the framework group, improving across all four measured dimensions. The authors recommend weaving the low-cost, copyable routine into nursing curricula, arguing it builds the reflective reasoning and decision-making that high-acuity wards demand from new nurses.
pmc-13624024:
Linus Alexander Völker and colleagues test a get-fit-before-surgery programme for patients aged sixty-five and older facing oesophagus removal for cancer. This operation carries heavy complication rates, and older patients start with less reserve. The programme mixed home exercise, breathing training, balance work, and a geriatric review with medication tidying, run over four weeks.

Twenty-six patients enrolled and twenty-two finished, then were matched against forty-two historical controls. Early check-ins showed most patients following the programme fully or mostly, though paperwork thinned by the second check. Complications, leaks at the surgical join, deaths, and hospital stay matched the control group. Readmission to intensive care looked lower after the programme, but that gap vanished once the surgical approach was taken into account. Controls were fitter at baseline. The authors call the approach feasible and safe, and ask for a proper randomised trial.
pmc-13625024:
Miki Scaravaglio and a large multi-center team build a bedside model to tell two look-alike bile duct diseases apart. Primary sclerosing cholangitis scars the ducts slowly, while secondary forms follow other causes, and no single test separates them cleanly. Reviewing records of 234 adults, the team found six facts that leaned toward the primary form, from younger age and bowel disease to no past duct surgery and no pancreas changes.

Those six facts became the PSC-DM score, and on a fresh group of 142 patients the score sorted the diseases with an AUROC of 0.95, a value near the top of the scale. The score also lifted non-expert doctors' accuracy in a trial run. A simple checklist could shorten the long road to a firm diagnosis.
pmc-13625224:
Yue Hu and co-authors map the chemistry of a parasitic worm, Angiostrongylus cantonensis, across its whole life cycle. The worm, spread through snails and rats, can invade the human brain lining and cause a rare meningitis. Using liquid chromatography with mass spectrometry, the team profiled five life stages, from early larvae to adult males and females, in both mouse and rat hosts.

Thousands of chemical signals shifted across stages, with the jump from the infective larva to the next stage the largest, and 127 compounds could be named, spanning fats, steroids, and purine pieces. Certain compounds peaked at single stages, such as xanthosine in adult females. Such stage fingerprints may expose weak points for drugs or tests that catch infection earlier.
pmc-13632924:
Levi Kadiri, Anthony Maher, and Andy Bridgen reviewed how well two lab tests on bone samples agree in diabetic foot bone infection. The infection, called diabetic foot osteomyelitis, can lead to amputation when missed. A bone biopsy is the surest test, and labs can study the sample two ways: growing microbes from it, or examining its tissue structure under a microscope. The team searched five databases for studies that ran both tests on the same patients.

Five studies covering three hundred eight patients qualified. The two methods agreed only modestly, both positive in well under half of cases on average. Tissue examination was more specific, while microbe growing caught more true infections but picked up more contamination. A positive tissue result also predicted later revision surgery or longer antibiotics more strongly. The authors advise reading both results together with the clinical picture.
pmc-13635224:
Ingvild E Bjerke and nine colleagues published this 2026 image collection tracking two calcium-handling proteins across the developing mouse brain. The proteins, calbindin and parvalbumin, sit inside neurons that help control excitability, navigation, and memory. Nobody had mapped when and where these neurons appear across the whole brain. The team stained brain sections from five age groups, from nine-day-old pups to adults, and aligned every image to age-matched brain atlases.

The collection can be browsed interactively online or downloaded for analysis. It gives researchers a brain-wide view of how these neuron populations emerge region by region, instead of the single-area snapshots that dominated earlier work. Because calcium control goes wrong in several developmental and psychiatric disorders, knowing the normal timetable matters. The authors tailored the images for counting workflows, so others can measure change across ages without redoing the staining work themselves.
pmc-13638724:
Flávia Alessandra Maciel and eleven colleagues report a 2026 rat study on how low protein intake during pregnancy and nursing affects lungs. The work covers both the mothers and their female pups, a pairing the authors note has rarely been studied for lung outcomes.

Rats fed a diet with six percent protein were compared with a control diet of seventeen percent. In mothers, low protein raised collagen and mast cells in lung tissue. In female pups it shrank air sacs and changed proteins tied to muscle and energy use. The study links poor early nutrition to lasting lung changes.
pmc-13639024:
Yassine Guennoun and seven colleagues describe a 2026 deep learning system that outlines brain tumors on MRI scans while also reporting how unsure it is. Clinicians hesitate to trust automated tumor outlines that give no sense of their own uncertainty.

Trained on 1,655 scans from 788 patients, the system segmented meningiomas with a median Dice score of 0.93 on held-out scans, and its doubt maps matched areas that radiologists found ambiguous. A separate group of 353 patients confirmed the accuracy. The authors argue that honest uncertainty estimates can make medical imaging software safer to use in daily practice.
pmc-13642924:
Runlai Xu and eight colleagues present a 2026 field study on how wheat roots recruit microbes that fight Fusarium crown rot, a soil fungus that can halve yields. Plants under attack are thought to cry for help chemically, yet how wheat varieties differ in that call was unclear.

In diseased fields, plant variety and health together shaped root-zone microbe communities and chemistry. Healthy roots favored Bacillus, while a susceptible variety also leaned on Pseudomonas, and both microbes fought the fungus in lab and pot tests. The tolerant variety kept more complex microbe networks. The work ties root chemistry to disease suppression.
pmc-13646124:
Jinbiao Han and three colleagues pool randomized trials of omalizumab, an antibody drug, for allergic asthma in children and teenagers. Six trials with 1,835 participants aged six to twenty met their rules, most of them under eighteen. The team compared the drug with placebo or standard therapy. Outcomes covered asthma attacks, lung function, symptom control scores, and harms, under a registered review plan.

The drug cut asthma attacks by about a third and hospital admissions by roughly two thirds. Serious side effects were also less frequent in the drug groups, while overall side effects matched the control groups. Evidence on lung function and day-to-day control was too thin to pool. The authors support omalizumab as an add-on for young patients whose moderate to severe allergic asthma stays uncontrolled on standard treatment, while flagging the gaps that remain.
pmc-13647424:
Gabriela Carrasco-Torres and six colleagues pair the dietary compound quercetin with a thiol-reactive agent to overwhelm cervical cancer cells' antioxidant defenses. Cancer cells lean on glutathione, a protective molecule, to survive treatment stress. The strategy primes cells with quercetin first, then strikes with the partner agent, called DMAB. Effects were mapped across a grid of combined doses in dishes, then tested in mice carrying a lymphoma model.

The pairing acted synergistically, draining glutathione and wrecking the cells' redox balance. Treated cervical cancer cells mostly died by apoptosis, with survival down to under a quarter and movement blocked. Healthy epithelial cells were hurt far less. In mice, the combination cut tumor burden by about two thirds and lengthened survival without obvious toxicity. The authors offer redox sensitization as a template for combinations that attack cancer's chemical safety net.
pmc-13647624:
Xiaoli Xu led a 2026 cohort study of whether lifetime estrogen exposure and heart health together shape kidney disease risk in postmenopausal women in China. Life after menopause itself raises kidney risk, possibly as sex hormones fall, but how lifetime estrogen from reproductive history interacts with heart health was unexplored. The team followed 33,700 women past menopause from the China Cardiometabolic Disease and Cancer Cohort, enrolled in 2011 to 2012 and followed for a median of 3.1 years.

Shorter lifetime estrogen exposure, measured three ways, raised kidney disease risk by roughly 28 to 42 percent. Risk fell steadily as the number of optimal heart health measures rose, and women with short estrogen exposure but five or more optimal measures no longer carried excess risk. The authors urge women past menopause to protect heart health as kidney prevention. Readers should note the short follow-up and study design, which limit causal claims.
pmc-13648224:
Sebastian Hilscher and twelve colleagues ask if a new-found histone mark can be wiped off by the enzymes that clear such marks. Histones are spools that wind DNA, and their marks help switch genes on and off. The new mark carries two tags at once on the same spot, an acetyl tag and a methyl tag, long thought to bar each other.

The team built short protein chains with the dual mark and fed them to two enzyme families. The plain chains lost their tags as expected. The dual-mark chains did not lose theirs at all. The methyl tag also blocked most side acts of the enzymes. Crystal views showed the tag twists the chain so the cut point sits wrong. The mark may last a long time on DNA spools.
pmc-13649124:
Jie Ren and five colleagues show how gut fat handling steers defence in the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans. A gene switch called NHR-68, set in the gut, keeps a fat called linoleic acid in balance. Worms must split scarce fuel between growth and two kinds of defence: fleeing germs and fighting them inside.

Without the switch, worms lost the fat balance and stopped shunning germ food. Feeding the fat back brought the shunning back. Gut signals reached a smell circuit through gut-to-nerve talk, which steered the flight. The switch also held two inside fight paths in check. The team frames this as one gut-brain loop that tunes both arms of defence at once.
pmc-13649424:
Yueyao Zhao and seven colleagues checked if a low heart stress marker can rule out early heart strain in people with type 2 diabetes. The marker can run low in people with more body fat, which may hide real problems. The team studied 191 adults in hospital who had both the blood test and a heart scan within two days.

Among those with a low marker score, one in nine still had a stiff heart pattern, and one in four had some heart change. Extra weight strongly raised the odds of these hidden changes. Blood fat and sugar scores also tracked with how well the heart's upper and lower chambers worked as a pair. The authors warn that a low marker alone is not a clean bill of health.
pmc-13649724:
Manuela Iglesias and six colleagues asked if the chance a neighbourhood offers shapes how toddlers grow and learn. They studied children born in Northern Virginia from 2020 to 2023 and tested them at age two to three with a standard development scale. Home zip codes gave each child a neighbourhood chance score.

Higher chance scores tied to stronger thinking and language scores, in a steady step pattern. The social and money part of the score drove the link most. Motor scores showed no such tie. A mother's schooling explained a bit more than the score did, though not by a firm margin. Gaps ran widest for Hispanic and Latino children in areas weak on health and surroundings. The authors urge focused help for such areas.
pmc-13651624:
Petr Rozhin and seventeen colleagues stack two atom-thin semiconductors to make one of them glow six times brighter. Layered materials called transition metal dichalcogenides emit light from excitons, bound electron-hole pairs, but most of that energy usually leaks away as heat instead of photons.

Placing a palladium selenide layer against a molybdenum selenide monolayer created a type-I alignment that funnels excitons into the brighter channel. The main emission line strengthened roughly sixfold at room temperature, reaching a quantum yield several times the bare monolayer's. The competing higher-energy exciton dimmed, evidence that populations were being redirected rather than merely added. Power and temperature sweeps showed fewer exciton collisions and a reshaped energy landscape, and excitation scans found the boost spanning a broad wavelength range. No chemistry or heavy strain was needed. The authors present interlayer coupling as a clean dial for emission efficiency.
pmc-1794324:
Achard and Bullmore examine how well human brain networks work compared with what they cost. Brain wiring is sparse yet complex, with economical small-world traits that keep signals fast without endless links. The authors used brain scans that track activity over time.

They compared functional networks in two groups of healthy older adults, weighing efficiency against connection cost. A brain that achieves high efficiency at low cost can share information widely without wasting resources. Their results help explain how ageing brains stay organised, and give a baseline for spotting costly breakdowns in disease.
pmc-3214824:
Lee, Macfarlane, Lam, and co-authors review studies testing the International Physical Activity Questionnaire Short Form. The short questionnaire had been recommended as a cost-effective way to assess physical activity in surveys. Several validation studies had been run, with differing results, and no systematic review had gathered them.

The team weighs how well the questionnaire matches objective measures across those studies. Their verdict helps survey designers judge when the cheap tool is good enough and when it misleads. National health monitoring depends on such checks, since policy rests on the numbers.
pmc-4290824:
Li, Xu, Xiao, and their team presented MAGeCK in 2014 for CRISPR screening data. Genome-scale knockout screens switch off genes one by one across a whole library of cells. Finding which genes are truly essential in that flood of data takes a strong statistical method.

MAGeCK models the data to rank guide RNAs, genes, and pathways by importance. In tests it performed better than existing methods and found both positive and negative selection signals. Essential genes point to a cell's weak spots, which matters for cancer drug research. A robust ranking method helps labs trust the short list a huge screen produces.
pmc-4668324:
Sørensen, Pelikan, Röthlin, and their colleagues reported health literacy results for Europe in 2015. Health literacy means how well people can find, grasp, and act on health information in daily life. European policy makers wanted firmer facts on its status across countries.

The European health literacy survey measured these skills in a comparative way across nations. Results showed wide gaps, with many people struggling to find, understand, and use health information. Such findings guide programs that make health systems easier to navigate. The survey gave Europe a shared baseline for tracking progress on a skill that shapes care and outcomes.
pmc-5039924:
Ewels, Magnusson, Lundin, and their colleagues built MultiQC in 2016. Studies built on next-generation sequencing stand or fall on fast, accurate quality control. Numerous tools exist to quantify quality metrics, but there was no common way to combine their outputs flexibly.

MultiQC summarizes analysis results for multiple tools and samples in a single report. Instead of opening dozens of files, a researcher gets one clear view of a whole run. That makes it easy to spot a failing sample hiding among hundreds of good ones. MultiQC became a standard final step in sequencing pipelines across genomics labs.
pmc-5051824:
Shen, Le, Li, and their team presented SeqKit in 2016, a toolkit for sequence files. Nearly every lab stores sequences in FASTA or FASTQ, the two basic formats for nucleotide and protein data. Daily chores on such files range from format conversion and search to filtering, removing duplicates, splitting, shuffling, and sampling.

Existing tools each implemented only some of those manipulations, forcing users to chain many programs. SeqKit is cross-platform and ultrafast, covering the common tasks in one toolkit. It is built for the huge file sizes of modern sequencing. A single reliable tool for file chores removes friction from nearly every genomics workflow.
pmc-6324024:
Sara El-Gebali, Jaina Mistry, Alex Bateman, and coauthors reported the Pfam database in 2019. Pfam groups protein regions into families that share ancestry and often share a job. Recent years brought big growth and change to the resource.

The release described here holds close to eighteen thousand families. Work focused on refining older families and sharpening domain boundaries, not only on adding new ones. Users scan a new protein against Pfam to learn its likely parts at a glance. The database remains a first stop for interpreting unknown protein sequences.
pmc-7145624:
Brian Alcock, Amogelang Raphenya, Tammy Lau, and coauthors described CARD, a shared database on drug resistance in germs, in its 2020 form. CARD gathers the genes and changes that let germs survive drugs meant to kill them. It pairs those records with search models and free software tools.

The update reports growth in curated entries and in the tools that scan whole genomes for them. Health programs use CARD to read resistance straight from the DNA of a germ sample. Shared names let labs in many lands compare what they find with ease. As resistance spreads, such shared records support the work of tracking it across the globe.
pmc-7402624:
Divij Mathew and many co-authors profiled the immune systems of patients with COVID-19 in unusual depth in 2020. At the time it was still unclear how a person's immune response shapes whether the illness stays mild or turns severe. The team used high dimensional methods that can measure many immune cell types and states in a single blood sample.

Their work grouped patients into distinct immunotypes, patterns of immune activity that lined up with different disease courses. Some patterns hinted at which treatments might help which patients, rather than giving everyone the same drug. The atlas they built helped other researchers compare results across hospitals, and it showed how much the immune response differs from one patient to the next.
pmc-8005924:
Matthew Page and a team of methods experts issued the PRISMA 2020 statement in 2021, an updated guideline for reporting systematic reviews. The original statement, published in 2009, taught reviewers to say plainly why the review was written, how the work was carried out, and what came out of it. Over the following decade, both review methods and the expectations around them moved forward.

The update refreshes the checklist of items every review report should include, from search details to how results were combined. It also reflects new topics such as judging certainty in the evidence. Journals and funders around the world point authors to this guideline, so its wording shapes how thousands of evidence summaries are written each year.
pmc-8728224:
Mihaly Varadi and co-authors introduced the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database in 2021, a free archive of predicted protein shapes. The database is powered by DeepMind's AlphaFold system, which computes a protein's folded structure from its sequence. Before it appeared, known structures covered only a modest fraction of the proteins scientists study.

The archive opened with models for a vast range of organisms, including the full human set, and kept expanding from there. The authors explain how the models are made, how confidence scores guide their use, and how to search and download them. By putting a plausible shape for nearly any protein a click away, the database changed the starting point of countless studies.
podcast-dannyjones-ZC3Rr_UKJ24:
Aaron Smith-Levin, a former member of Scientology, joins Danny Jones to argue the church is near collapse. The episode title says the group is on the verge of ruin. Smith-Levin now spends his time reporting on the church he left.

Smith-Levin points to shrinking numbers, lost staff, and bad press as signs of deep trouble. He tells stories from inside the group and from his years of reporting since he left. Jones asks what would prove the church can still bounce back. Listeners get an insider's view of a secretive faith under strain. The library keeps the talk as an archive record.
podcast-tuckercarlson-rpQop5vPm24:
Preparing for nuclear war is the grim subject of this Tucker Carlson episode, explained by a chemical engineer. The guest lays out the practical steps a family can take if the sirens ever sound. The talk treats the unthinkable in plain, calm terms.

The engineer covers fallout, shelter, water, and how long to stay inside. He explains which supplies matter most and which myths could get people killed. Carlson asks how likely such an attack now is, given world tensions. Preppers and the merely worried get a clear guide to the worst day imaginable.
procopius-wars-gothic-2-dewing-1924:
Books six and seven of the Wars of Procopius, in H. B. Dewing's Loeb volume of 1924, carry the Gothic War into its brutal second act. Ravenna falls by guile, Belisarius is recalled in disgrace, and Italy slips back into fire. Procopius wrote from reports and from his own years in the country.

Under their new king Totila, the Goths rise again and take Rome itself, twice. Plague, famine, and the wreck of the Italian cities fill these books. Procopius counts the cost of Justinian's dream of a restored empire with open doubt. The war that began in triumph becomes a warning. Dewing's notes guide readers through the tangled campaigns.
proust-budding-grove-moncrieff-1924:
Within a Budding Grove is the second volume of Marcel Proust's In Search of Lost Time. Proust published it in French in 1919, and C. K. Scott Moncrieff translated it into English in 1924. The young narrator leaves Paris for the seaside resort of Balbec with his grandmother.

At Balbec he watches a band of lively girls on the beach and falls in love more than once. Albertine, the most vivid of them, enters his life for good here. First love, snobbery, and the sea air fill long, drifting scenes. The volume won Proust the Prix Goncourt in France. It deepened his great theme: how time and desire change all we see.
res-gestae-divi-augusti-shipley-1924:
Before his death in 14 CE, Augustus wrote a short account of his own deeds and had it cut in stone at his tomb. Copies were set up across the empire, and the best one survives on a temple wall in Ankara. Frederick W. Shipley's Loeb version of 1924 gives the text with a full study of that monument.

The emperor lists the offices he held, the wars he won, the games he gave, and the gold he spent on Rome. It is cool, plain, and masterful self-praise. No single paper tells us more about how Augustus wished to be seen. Historians call it the queen of inscriptions.
robertson-works-vol-1-1824:
Volume one opens the 1824 Works of William Robertson, the nine-volume gathering of Scotland's great Enlightenment historian. Robertson published his histories from 1759 and rose to lead the historical writing of his age. The Works collect his History of Scotland, his reign of Charles V, his History of America, and his Historical Disquisition on India.

Robertson wrote history as philosophy teaching by examples, in prose of unusual grace. His Scotland made him famous; his Charles V made him Europe's historian. The collected edition of 1824 fixed his full achievement between covers for the Victorian reader. Volume one begins that monument, the life's work of Edinburgh's royal historiographer in full.
robertson-works-vol-2-1824:
The Works of William Robertson continue into volume two of the nine-volume edition of 1824. Robertson, who issued his histories from 1759 onward, wrote the past of nations as a single, connected advance. His History of Scotland, his Charles V, his America, and his Disquisition on India make up the gathered set.

In each field Robertson joined archives to argument, telling not only what happened but how society itself had changed. His calm, elevated style won readers far beyond Britain. The Works were the standard shelf form of his achievement for a century. Volume two holds its share of that achievement, from northern kingdoms to southern empires, in one historian's steady hand.
robertson-works-vol-3-1824:
Volume three of Robertson's Works, in the collected edition of 1824, carries on the nine-volume set. William Robertson published his first history in 1759 and soon stood in the front rank of European letters. The Works bind his Scotland, his Charles V, his America, and his study of ancient India into one uniform whole.

Robertson's histories trace how manners, laws, and commerce grow together across the centuries. He was the Scottish Enlightenment's great popularizer of that broad view of the past. Students of America and India still cite his volumes as starting points in their fields. Volume three keeps the set's wide world in view, told with its usual poise.
robertson-works-vol-4-1824:
Robertson's Works reach volume four in the nine-volume edition of 1824. William Robertson, whose writing career in history began in 1759, became the model of the philosophical historian in Britain. The set gathers the fruits of that career: Scotland, the Emperor Charles V, America, and the Historical Disquisition on India.

His pages move from Highland clans to Mexican temples with the same inquiring calm. Robertson asks in each place how peoples lived, traded, believed, and were governed. That method, history as the study of society, shaped generations of writers after him. Volume four stands mid-set, holding its portion of one of the Enlightenment's widest historical minds.
robertson-works-vol-5-1824:
Volume five stands at the center of the 1824 Works of William Robertson, nine volumes in all. Robertson issued his histories from 1759 and won a European name beside Hume and Voltaire. The Works collect the History of Scotland, the History of Charles V, the History of America, and the Historical Disquisition on India in one edition.

Across those fields Robertson practiced a single art: clear narrative steered by reflection on manners and causes. His America taught Britain about the Spanish conquests; his India opened ancient eastern trade to his readers. The middle volume of the set holds that range in balance. Robertson's calm authority fills every part of it.
robertson-works-vol-6-1824:
William Robertson, the Scottish historian, stands with Hume and Gibbon among the masters of Enlightenment history. Volume six here forms part of the nine-volume Works of 1824. The Works gather his History of Scotland and his History of Charles V. His History of America and his Historical Disquisition on India stand with them. Robertson wrote with a broad, philosophical sweep across nations and ages.

His histories joined deep research to a clear, elevated style that readers across Europe admired. The Charles V made his name; the America and the India carried his reach worldwide. A single volume of the Works holds a cross-section of that range. Volume six keeps the set's portrait of its author whole: Scotland's great practitioner of philosophical history.
robertson-works-vol-7-1824:
The Works of William Robertson reach volume seven in the nine-volume edition of 1824. Robertson, principal of Edinburgh University and royal historiographer, published his famous histories from 1759 onward. His books on Scotland, on the Emperor Charles V, on America, and on India form the core of this collected set.

Robertson's gift was scope joined to calm judgment: he wrote the history of continents as one connected story. His account of Charles V opened a new era in English history writing. The Disquisition on India showed his range reaching to Asia's ancient trade. Volume seven carries its share of that wide, ordered vision. The set preserves Enlightenment historiography in full dress.
robertson-works-vol-8-1824:
Volume eight of the 1824 Works of William Robertson stands one volume from the end of the nine-volume set. Robertson's histories, issued from 1759, made him a leader of the Scottish Enlightenment's historical school. Scotland, the reign of Charles V, America, and India all came under his pen, and the Works bind them together.

His method joined narrative grace to a philosopher's search for causes in society and manners. Readers in his day placed him beside Hume, and the comparison still instructs. This volume holds part of that achievement in the standard collected form. To read through the Works is to watch history become a science of human progress, in one master's hands.
robertson-works-vol-9-1824:
Volume nine completes the Works of William Robertson in the edition of 1824. Robertson, publishing from 1759, had gathered his histories of Scotland, Charles V, America, and India into a single fame. The nine uniform volumes of 1824 gave that fame its lasting shelf form for the century that followed.

The closing volume ends the set as Robertson's work deserves, in the company of all his great subjects. His school of history, calm, connected, and alive to society's growth, ruled British taste for decades. Readers finishing the Works hold the Enlightenment's historical project nearly entire. Robertson taught his age to see the past whole, and volume nine sets the last stone.
russell-icarus-1924:
Icarus, published in 1924 in the To-day and To-morrow pamphlet series, is Russell's dark little prophecy about the future of science. Written against J. B. S. Haldane's sunny Daedalus, it warns that knowledge multiplies power faster than wisdom.

Russell foresees science used to sharpen war, tighten propaganda, and extend the reach of governments and great firms. He doubts that ordinary human nature will improve to match its new tools. The pamphlet is brief, bleak, and often quoted, a founding text of the debate about technology's dangers. Its title is the whole argument: wings, wax, and the sun.
scott-hermetica-vol-1-1924:
Walter Scott spent years building his monumental edition of the Hermetica, published from 1924. The Hermetica are Greek and Latin writings ascribed to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage. Volume one gives the texts with facing English translation.

Readers find the Corpus Hermeticum, the Latin Asclepius, and excerpts preserved by Stobaeus. A long introduction untangles the writings' tangled history and authorship. These dialogues treat God, the soul, and the cosmos in mystical terms. They shaped Renaissance magic and later spiritual movements deeply. Scott's first volume became the standard English Hermetica of its age.
spr-proceedings-vol34-1924:
Volume thirty four binds parts eighty nine through ninety two, dated 1924. The SPR Proceedings are in their fifth decade, and the format holds. Experiments in thought reading appear with their chance scores computed. Long trance reports, checked line by line, fill the center.

Spontaneous experiences, from hauntings to death bed visions, arrive in steady flow. The society's committees sift them by rules set in the census years. Physical phenomena stay rare and closely watched in these parts. Volume thirty four is a late brick in the central archive. It documents a debate that shaped how Britain argued about survival. The record stays, as ever, open.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5024:
Abraham Lincoln gives four yearly addresses, from December 3, 1861, to December 6, 1864, in a set parted by three stars. The first opens in the midst of political troubles past all past measure. Still, Lincoln says, there is cause for great thanks: the folk have known rare good health and the most plenteous harvests. Dealings with foreign nations have been held in deep care, chiefly as they turn on home affairs.

A disloyal part of the American people, he reports, has spent the whole year in a bid to split and wreck the Union. A nation torn by factious strife at home lies open to slight abroad, and one side, if not both, is sure in time to call in foreign help. The rebels, though, have won less backing and cheer from abroad than they likely hoped for, Lincoln notes, a point he takes up with grave care.
suess-face-of-earth-vol5-sollas-1924:
Volume 5 of Sollas's translation of Suess's Face of the Earth appeared in 1924, completing the English set. Eduard Suess had died in 1914, and his great synthesis closed with this volume. Sollas's translation project had run for twenty years by its end.

The final volume draws the threads together into a completed global geology: continents, oceans, and mountain systems in one account. Suess's Earth, cooling and contracting, ordered the facts his age possessed. Within decades, continental drift and then plate tectonics replaced that frame, yet his terms and maps endured. The volume completes the most ambitious work of geology written by a single author in the nineteenth century.
t-mann-buddenbrooks-vol-1-of-2-1924:
The Buddenbrook family of Luebeck rises through trade in the first half of Thomas Mann's great saga. The text is Helen Lowe-Porter's 1924 English translation, Volume One of two. Wealthy merchants across the early 1800s fill its drawing rooms: consuls, senators, and their carefully married children. Mann was twenty-five when the novel made him famous.

Mann traces the firm's prosperity and the family's vitality together, with ironic tenderness for both. Christenings, weddings, and business deals mark the generations as the century turns. Seeds of decline already hide inside the success, for readers who watch closely. The novel that eventually won Mann the Nobel Prize begins with this confident ascent. Few family sagas open at such full stretch.
t-mann-buddenbrooks-vol-2-of-2-1924:
Decline governs the second half of Buddenbrooks, in Lowe-Porter's 1924 English translation, Volume Two of two. As the nineteenth century wears on, the Buddenbrook energy drains away into art, illness, and introspection. The firm's grip loosens as each generation finds commerce less natural than the last.

Thomas Buddenbrook holds the house together by will until the effort consumes him. His son Hanno, frail and musical, closes the line with his early death. Mann renders a bourgeois dynasty's fall with love rather than scorn, which gives the book its ache. The portrait stands among the most moving in European literature. Readers finish the two volumes feeling they have lived a whole family's century.
tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontaine-vol:
The Indiscreet Confession, The Contract, and The Quid Pro Quo, or The Mistakes, fill the twenty-fourth volume of La Fontaine's Tales and Novels. Parisian love and its written bonds govern the three tales.

The first opens on Aminta, whose lot of magic charms famed Paris never matched within its walls: youth, beauty, temper, and fortune, all that should render a husband blessed. Her mother still kept her beneath her wing, while her father's riches drew lovers, and whatever his daughter wished he would provide, amusements, jewels, and dress. Blithe Damon won her heart and became her lord and master by Hymen's right. What an indiscreet confession then undoes, and how contracts and mistaken identities finish the volume, is La Fontaine's usual dance of candor and cost.
taylor-mystical-hymns-orpheus-1824:
Thomas Taylor published his translation of the Orphic Hymns in a second edition in 1824. The hymns are ritual songs of the Orphic mysteries of ancient Greece. Taylor first issued his rendering in 1792 and later revised it.

Each short hymn calls upon a god with offerings and storied titles. Night, the Stars, Sleep, and Death all receive their invocations. Worshippers chanted these hymns at secret rites two thousand years ago. Taylor's verse keeps a strange, solemn music in English. He believed in the hymns' spiritual power, not merely their antiquity. His version became the classic English Orpheus for later occult and literary readers.
temple-word-of-lalla-1924:
Richard Carnac Temple gave English readers his own rendering of the sayings of Lalla in The Word of Lalla the Prophetess, printed at Cambridge in 1924. Lalla, or Lal Ded, was the fourteenth-century mystic of Kashmir whose vakhs passed by mouth for five centuries. Temple's edition stands independent of the Grierson and Barnett version of 1920.

Short, fierce verses tell of her leaving home, her guru, her dance of joy in the self, and her scorn for rite without love. Temple adds an introduction, notes, and an index to guide the reader. He reads her as a prophetess of the inner life for all faiths. The two English Lallas of the 1920s still frame her for the West.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: No. 24 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It, dated April 22, 1897, is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and one advertisement, for The Sportsman's Magazine of New York. That magazine is an 80-page monthly, written and published by sportsmen, for sportsmen. A copy costs twenty cents, and a year two dollars. Its premium list offers guns, pistols, bicycles, and fishing-rods for new subscriptions. Readers may send five two-cent stamps for a sample copy.

The issue of June 16, 1898 is number 24 of volume 2 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It. Its whole-run number is 84. The paper is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and a publisher's notice of rates. A year's subscription costs $1.50, and six months seventy-five cents. Foreign subscriptions cost two dollars and a quarter. The publisher is at 3 and 5 West 18th Street, New York. Remittances go to the Great Round World Publishing Company.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2-part:
The Ormsby Don Quixote, Cervantes' tale in English, opens Volume 2, Part 24 here. Chapter twenty-one continues Camacho's wedding, with other delightful incidents. Don Quixote and Sancho are deep in the discussion set out in the last chapter when loud shouts and a great noise break in.

Men on mares ride at full gallop, shouting, to receive the bride and bridegroom. Music, pageantry, the priest, kin of both sides, and the chief people of the place surround the pair. Cervantes fills the road with noise and show, as a rich wedding draws the knight and his squire into village rivalry and display.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
Bolsover Castle in Derbyshire is described in No. 566 of The Mirror, dated September 15, 1832. Bolsover is a populous village on the county's eastern edge near Chesterfield. The castle stands on the flat top of a rocky hill rising sharply from meadows, a landmark for the country around.

A castle has stood there since the Norman Conquest, though nothing of the first building survives. At the Domesday survey the place belonged to William Peveril. King John ordered its governor, Bryan de L'Isle, to fortify Bolsover against the rebellious barons or demolish it if it could not be held. Later owners included the Howard dukes of Norfolk and a fifty-year grant to Sir John Byron. Gilbert Talbot sold it in 1613 to Sir Charles Cavendish.

No. 584 of The Mirror, marked as a supplement to volume 20, is present here only as a title page followed by the single heading Preface. No preface text and no article text appear. The title page gives the magazine's full name, The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction, with London and the year 1832 below.

What the title page promises is the magazine's usual range. Original essays stand first, followed by historical narratives, biographical memoirs, and sketches of society. Topographical descriptions, novels and tales, anecdotes, and poetry follow. Extracts from new and expensive works, the spirit of the public journals, discoveries in the arts and sciences, and useful domestic hints complete the printed list.
theodori-kerckringii-doctoris-medici-anm: Theodor Kerckring, a doctor of medicine, is named on a badly garbled title page dated by the record to 1724. His notes concern Basilius Valentinus and other spagyric writings, the old chemical medicine tradition. Much of the German title survives only in broken lettering. What can be read gives the author, his profession, and his subject, plus a note that some material was translated into German. The page shown here is the title alone, in damaged form, so Kerckring's annotations themselves are not present.
tob-0144-54824:
Blavatsky called The Secret Doctrine, published in 1888, her masterwork, and volume one bears the subtitle Cosmogenesis. She claimed its core came from the secret Stanzas of Dzyan, an ancient text few others have seen. The volume explains how the universe unfolds in great cycles.

Worlds appear, evolve through rounds, and dissolve, again and again, over spans too vast to picture. Matter and spirit are two faces of one reality. The style is dense and demands patience, with long quotes from science and scripture. For Theosophists, Cosmogenesis stands as the movement's deepest account of where everything came from.
tob-10024:
Thomas à Kempis, a fifteenth-century monk, wrote the devotional guide known in English as The Imitation of Christ, here in an alternative translation as The Following of Christ. Only the Bible has been read more widely among Christian devotional books. Its chapters are short and direct, meant for daily use.

Kempis urges humility, warns against vanity and idle learning, and teaches readers to imitate Christ in ordinary life. Much of it reads like quiet counsel from a wise friend rather than formal theology. Saints and skeptics alike have carried the book for six hundred years, returning to its plain call to turn inward.
tob-10824:
William Q. Judge's American Theosophical magazine The Path, in its first volume for 1886-87, shows the movement's work in the United States. Contributions by various Theosophists mix practical spiritual advice with defenses of Blavatsky and reports from the lodges. Compared with Blavatsky's Lucifer, the tone is less flamboyant and more workmanlike.

Theosophy appears here as a lived discipline: study, meditation, ethics, and organized local work. News from branches shows a young occult movement building itself month by month. Readers interested in how ideas travel will value the volume as a record of American Theosophy finding its own voice beside the louder London center.
tob-13324:
A different edition of Brother Lawrence's classic presents the lay brother's method of turning kitchen work into prayer. Letters from Lawrence and the recollections of those who knew him carry the teaching. He was a Carmelite lay brother in seventeenth-century Paris, assigned to the kitchen and later to sandal repair.

Lawrence's method needs no retreat: return the mind to God, again and again, in the middle of ordinary tasks. Short enough to finish in one sitting, the account is deep enough to practice for a lifetime, as generations of readers testify. Comparing editions shows how stable the core of his conversations and letters has remained.
tob-4024:
René Descartes put out his Discourse on the Method in 1637. In it he sets rules for the search for sure truth. Doubt all that can be doubted. Split hard tasks into small parts. Move from the plain to the hard. Take as true only what is clear and plain.

In the course of the tale comes the most famed line in all thought: I think, therefore I am. From that one firm point Descartes builds back out to God, the world, and the sciences. The short book stands as the birth deed of modern rational thought. A reader can finish it in an afternoon and argue with it for life.
tob-4224:
Francis Barrett published The Magus, or Celestial Intelligencer, in London in 1801, and English occultism revived around it. Barrett compiled natural magic, magnetism, Kabbalah, alchemy, and the evocation of spirits into one grand summa, much of it drawn from Agrippa and older masters. His school of magic taught from the book.

Plates of talismans, circles, and spirit forms give the volume its famous look. Bulwer-Lytton studied it for his novels; the founders of the Golden Dawn studied it for their rites. Verified from the 1919 edition, Barrett's Magus remains the great English grimoire-compilation of the Romantic age.
un-ga-res-24:
When the League of Nations died, its work had to go somewhere. Resolution 24, passed by the General Assembly on 12 February 1946, maps the handoff. Under a web of treaties and deals, the League and its arms had long held tasks that some states wished the new UN to keep alive. League members told the Assembly they would move, at the League's last meeting, to bless the steps set out here.

The Assembly keeps a free hand. It may refuse any one task after fair study. For each task it takes, it will name the UN arm or linked agency fit to hold it. Out of this dry text grew the UN's quiet grip on old League work, from drug pacts to refugee files.
un-ga-res-a-69-24:
Jerusalem's status stands at the core of Resolution A/69/24, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text recalls the 1947 partition vote and its terms for the city. It recalls a long chain of later votes as well. In them, the Assembly held that all steps by Israel, the occupying power, to change the face or status of the Holy City are void and must be undone.
